Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Vinayapiṭake

The Basket of the Discipline

Mahāvagga-aṭṭhakathā

The Commentary on the Great Chapter

1. Mahākhandhakaṃ

1. The Great Section

Bodhikathā

Discourse on Awakening

Ubhinnaṃ [P 5.0951][M 0.0233] pātimokkhānaṃ, saṅgītisamanantaraṃ;

Saṅgāyiṃsu mahātherā, khandhakaṃ khandhakovidā.

Immediately after the communal recitation of the two Pātimokkhas, the great elders, skilled in the Khandhakas, communally recited the Khandhaka.

Yaṃ tassa dāni sampatto, yasmā saṃvaṇṇanākkamo;

Tasmā hoti ayaṃ tassa, anuttānatthavaṇṇanā.

Since the turn for its exposition has now arrived, therefore this is the exposition of its unmanifest meaning.

Padabhājaniye atthā, yehi yesaṃ pakāsitā;

Te ce puna vadeyyāma, pariyosānaṃ kadā bhave.

The meanings which were made clear in the Padabhājanīya—if we were to speak of them again, when would there be an end?

Uttānā [V 0.0225] ceva ye atthā, tesaṃ saṃvaṇṇanāya kiṃ;

Adhippāyānusandhīhi, byañjanena ca ye pana.

And as for those meanings that are manifest, what is the use of an exposition of them? But those that, through intention, connection, and wording, are unmanifest...

Anuttānā na te yasmā, sakkā ñātuṃ avaṇṇitā;

Tesaṃyeva ayaṃ tasmā, hoti saṃvaṇṇanānayoti.

Since those unmanifest meanings, being unexplained, cannot be known, therefore this is the method of exposition for those very meanings.

1. Tena samayena buddho bhagavā uruvelāyaṃ viharati najjā nerañjarāya tīre bodhirukkhamūle paṭhamābhisambuddhoti ettha kiñcāpi “tena samayena buddho bhagavā verañjāya”ntiādīsu viya karaṇavacane visesakāraṇaṃ natthi, vinayaṃ patvā pana karaṇavacaneneva ayamabhilāpo āropitoti ādito paṭṭhāya āruḷhābhilāpavasenevetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Esa nayo aññesupi ito paresu evarūpesu.

1. Herein, regarding the passage 'At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained supreme enlightenment': although, as in passages like 'At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was at Verañjā,' there is no special reason for the use of the instrumental case, nevertheless, having come to the Vinaya, this expression was established with the instrumental case only. Thus, it should be understood that from the very beginning this was spoken by the force of the established expression. This is the principle also in other similar passages that follow.

Kiṃ panetassa [P 5.0952] vacane payojananti? Pabbajjādīnaṃ vinayakammānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya nidānadassanaṃ. Yā hi bhagavatā “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, imehi tīhi [M 0.0234] saraṇagamanehi pabbajjaṃ upasampada”nti (mahāva. 34) evaṃ pabbajjā ceva upasampadā ca anuññātā, yāni ca rājagahādīsu upajjhāyaupajjhāyavattaācariyaācariyavattādīni anuññātāni, tāni abhisambodhiṃ patvā sattasattāhaṃ bodhimaṇḍe vītināmetvā bārāṇasiyaṃ dhammacakkaṃ pavattetvā iminā anukkamena idañcidañca ṭhānaṃ patvā imasmiñca imasmiñca vatthusmiṃ paññattānīti evametesaṃ pabbajjādīnaṃ vinayakammānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya nidānadassanaṃ etassa vacane payojananti veditabbaṃ.

What then is the purpose of this statement? It is to show the origin, from the beginning, of the Vinaya acts such as the going forth. For the going forth and the higher ordination were permitted by the Blessed One with the words, 'I allow, monks, the going forth and higher ordination by means of these three refuges.' And the rules concerning the preceptor, the preceptor's duties, the teacher, the teacher's duties, and so on, were permitted in places like Rājagaha. These were laid down after he had attained supreme enlightenment, spent seven weeks at the seat of awakening, set in motion the Wheel of the Dhamma at Bārāṇasī, and, proceeding in this sequence, arrived at this and that place and on this and that occasion. Thus, it should be understood that the purpose of this statement is to show the origin, from the beginning, of these Vinaya acts such as the going forth.

Tattha uruvelāyanti mahāvelāyaṃ; mahante vālikarāsimhīti attho. Atha vā “urū”ti vālikā vuccati; “velā”ti mariyādā; velātikkamanahetu āhaṭā uru uruvelāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Atīte kira anuppanne buddhe dasasahassakulaputtā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tasmiṃ padese viharantā ekadivasaṃ sannipatitvā katikavattaṃ akaṃsu – “kāyakammavacīkammāni nāma paresampi pākaṭāni honti, manokammaṃ pana apākaṭaṃ; tasmā yo kāmavitakkaṃ vā byāpādavitakkaṃ vā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā vitakketi, tassa añño codako nāma natthi, so attanāva attānaṃ codetvā pattapuṭena vālikaṃ āharitvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne ākiratu, idamassa daṇḍakamma”nti. Tato paṭṭhāya yo tādisaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakketi, so tattha pattapuṭena vālikaṃ ākirati. Evaṃ tattha anukkamena mahāvālikarāsi jāto, tato naṃ [V 0.0226] pacchimā janatā parikkhipitvā cetiyaṭṭhānamakāsi. Taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “uruvelāyanti mahāvelāyaṃ; mahante vālikarāsimhīti attho”ti. Tameva sandhāya vuttaṃ – “atha vā urūti vālikā vuccati; velāti mariyādā; velātikkamanahetu āhaṭā uru uruvelāti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo”ti.

Therein, 'at Uruvelā' means on the great shore; the meaning is 'on a great heap of sand.' Alternatively, 'uru' is said to be sand, and 'velā' is said to be a boundary; sand brought on account of transgressing the boundary is 'Uruvelā.' In this way, too, the meaning should be understood here. It is said that in the past, when a Buddha had not yet arisen, ten thousand sons of good families went forth into the ascetic life and, while dwelling in that region, they assembled one day and made an agreement: 'Bodily and verbal actions are manifest even to others, but mental action is not manifest. Therefore, whoever thinks a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of harmfulness has no other accuser. He himself should accuse himself and, bringing sand in a leaf-container, should scatter it in this place. This will be his penance.' From then on, whoever thought such a thought would scatter sand there with a leaf-container. In this way, a great heap of sand gradually formed there. Later generations of people enclosed it and made it a place for a shrine. With reference to this it was said: ''at Uruvelā' means on the great shore; the meaning is 'on a great heap of sand.'' With reference to this very thing it was said: 'Alternatively, 'uru' is said to be sand, and 'velā' is said to be a boundary; sand brought on account of transgressing the boundary is 'Uruvelā.' In this way, too, the meaning should be understood here.'

Bodhirukkhamūleti bodhi vuccati catūsu maggesu ñāṇaṃ; taṃ bodhiṃ bhagavā ettha pattoti rukkhopi “bodhirukkho”tveva nāmaṃ labhi, tassa bodhirukkhassa mūle bodhirukkhamūle. Paṭhamābhisambuddhoti [P 5.0953] paṭhamaṃ abhisambuddho; abhisambuddho hutvā sabbapaṭhamaṃyevāti attho. Ekapallaṅkenāti sakimpi anuṭṭhahitvā yathāābhujitena ekeneva pallaṅkena. Vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti vimuttisukhaṃ phalasamāpattisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedayamāno.

'At the foot of the Bodhi tree': 'Bodhi' is said to be the knowledge in the four paths. Because the Blessed One attained that Bodhi here, the tree also received the name 'Bodhi tree.' The compound means 'at the foot of that Bodhi tree.' 'Having just attained supreme enlightenment' is parsed as 'first, supremely enlightened'; the meaning is 'having become supremely enlightened, at the very first.' 'With one sitting' means with a single cross-legged posture, without having risen even once, just as it was assumed. 'Experiencing the bliss of liberation' means experiencing the bliss of liberation, which is the bliss of the attainment of fruition.

Paṭiccasamuppādanti [M 0.0235] paccayākāraṃ. Paccayākāro hi aññamaññaṃ paṭicca sahite dhamme uppādetīti “paṭiccasamuppādo”ti vuccati. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana sabbākārasampannaṃ vinicchayaṃ icchantena visuddhimaggato gahetabbo. Anulomapaṭilomanti anulomañca paṭilomañca. Tattha “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādinā nayena vutto avijjādiko paccayākāro attanā kattabbakiccakaraṇato “anulomo”ti vuccati. “Avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”tiādinā nayena vutto sveva anuppādanirodhena nirujjhamāno taṃ kiccaṃ na karotīti tassa akaraṇato “paṭilomo”ti vuccati. Purimanayena vā vutto pavattiyā anulomo, itaro tassā paṭilomoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ādito pana paṭṭhāya yāva antaṃ, antato ca paṭṭhāya yāva ādiṃ pāpetvā avuttattā ito aññenatthena anulomapaṭilomatā na yujjati.

'Dependent Origination' means the mode of conditionality. For the mode of conditionality is called 'dependent origination' because, by depending on one another, it originates conascent states. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation, however, should be taken from the Visuddhimagga by one who desires a determination that is complete in all aspects. 'In forward and reverse order' means both forward and reverse. Therein, the mode of conditionality beginning with 'from ignorance as condition, formations come to be,' spoken in this way, is called 'forward' because it performs the function that is to be done. The very same, when spoken of in the way beginning with 'from the complete fading away and cessation of ignorance itself, comes the cessation of formations,' is called 'reverse' because, ceasing with the cessation of non-arising, it does not perform that function, and thus because of its non-performance. Alternatively, that which is spoken of in the former way is 'forward' in relation to the process of becoming; the other is the 'reverse' of that process. In this way, too, the meaning should be understood here. However, because it is not stated by tracing from the beginning up to the end, and from the end back to the beginning, the state of being 'forward and reverse' is not appropriate with a meaning other than this.

Manasākāsīti manasi akāsi. Tattha yathā anulomaṃ manasi akāsi, idaṃ tāva dassetuṃ “avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avijjā ca sā paccayo cāti avijjāpaccayo. Tasmā avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā sambhavantīti iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Ayamettha saṅkhepo. Vitthāro pana sabbākārasampannaṃ vinicchayaṃ icchantena visuddhimaggatova gahetabbo.

'He applied his mind' means: he attended in the mind. Therein, to show, first of all, in what manner he applied his mind in forward order, the passage beginning, 'With ignorance as a condition, formations...' was spoken. Therein, 'ignorance as a condition' (avijjāpaccayo) means: it is both ignorance (avijjā) and it is a condition (paccayo). Therefore, from ignorance as a condition, formations arise. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all phrases. This is the summary here. But the detailed explanation, for one who desires a determination complete in all aspects, should be taken from the Visuddhimagga itself.

Yathā pana paṭilomaṃ manasi akāsi, idaṃ dassetuṃ avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodhotiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha avijjāya tvevāti avijjāya tu eva. Asesavirāganirodhāti [V 0.0227] virāgasaṅkhātena maggena asesanirodhā[P 5.0954]. Saṅkhāranirodhoti saṅkhārānaṃ anuppādanirodho hoti. Evaṃ niruddhānaṃ pana saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhā viññāṇaṃ niruddhaṃ, viññāṇādīnañca nirodhā nāmarūpādīni niruddhāniyeva hontīti dassetuṃ saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodhotiādīni vatvā evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hotīti vuttaṃ. Tattha kevalassāti sakalassa; suddhassa vā sattavirahitassāti attho. Dukkhakkhandhassāti dukkharāsissa. Nirodho hotīti anuppādo hoti.

But as to the manner in which he applied his mind in reverse order, to show this, the passage beginning, 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, there is the cessation of formations...' was spoken. Therein, 'avijjāya tveva' means: 'tu' (as for the reverse order), 'eva' (of ignorance itself). 'Asesavirāganirodhā' means: due to the remainderless cessation through the path called dispassion. 'Saṅkhāranirodho' means: it is the non-arising-again cessation of formations. Furthermore, to show that with the cessation of formations that have thus ceased, consciousness has ceased, and with the cessation of consciousness and so on, name-and-form and the rest have also ceased, having stated the passages beginning, 'With the cessation of formations, there is the cessation of consciousness...', it was said, 'Thus there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.' Therein, 'kevalassa' means: of the whole; or, of the mere, devoid of a being—this is the meaning. 'Dukkhakkhandhassa' means: of the heap of suffering. 'Nirodho hoti' means: it is non-arising-again.

Etamatthaṃ [M 0.0236] viditvāti yvāyaṃ “avijjādivasena saṅkhārādikassa dukkhakkhandhassa samudayo ca avijjānirodhādivasena ca nirodho hotī”ti vutto, sabbākārena etamatthaṃ viditvā. Tāyaṃ velāyanti tāyaṃ tassa atthassa viditavelāyaṃ. Imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti imaṃ tasmiṃ vidite atthe hetuno ca hetusamuppannadhammassa ca pajānanāya ānubhāvadīpakaṃ “yadā have pātubhavantī”tiādikaṃ somanassayuttañāṇasamuṭṭhānaṃ udānaṃ udānesi, attamanavācaṃ nicchāresīti vuttaṃ hoti.

'Having known this meaning' means: having known in all its aspects this meaning which was spoken thus, 'Through the power of ignorance and so on, there is the arising of the mass of suffering beginning with formations; and through the power of the cessation of ignorance and so on, there is its cessation.' 'At that time' means: at that time of knowing that meaning. 'He uttered this inspired utterance' means: regarding that known meaning, he uttered this inspired utterance—beginning with 'When indeed phenomena become manifest...'—which is arisen from knowledge associated with joy and which illuminates the power of distinctly knowing the cause and the phenomena well-arisen from the cause; he caused to issue forth the speech of one with a pleased mind. This is what is said.

Tassattho – yadā haveti yasmiṃ bhave kāle. Pātubhavantīti uppajjanti. Dhammāti anulomapaccayākārapaṭivedhasādhakā bodhipakkhiyadhammā. Atha vā pātubhavantīti pakāsanti; abhisamayavasena byattā pākaṭā honti. Dhammāti catuariyasaccadhammā. Ātāpo vuccati kilesasantāpanaṭṭhena vīriyaṃ; ātāpinoti sammappadhānavīriyavato. Jhāyatoti ārammaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇena ca lakkhaṇūpanijjhānalakkhaṇena ca jhānena jhāyantassa. Brāhmaṇassāti bāhitapāpassa khīṇāsavassa. Athassa kaṅkhā vapayantīti athassa evaṃ pātubhūtadhammassa kaṅkhā vapayanti. Sabbāti yā etā “ko nu kho bhante phusatīti; no kallo pañhoti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā, tathā “katamaṃ nu kho bhante jarāmaraṇaṃ; kassa ca panidaṃ jarāmaraṇanti[P 5.0955]; no kallo pañhoti bhagavā avocā”tiādinā ca nayena paccayākāre kaṅkhā vuttā, yā ca paccayākārasseva appaṭividdhattā “ahosiṃ nu kho ahaṃ atītamaddhāna”ntiādikā soḷasa kaṅkhā āgatā, tā sabbā vapayanti apagacchanti nirujjhanti. Kasmā? Yato pajānāti sahetudhammanti yasmā avijjādikena hetunā sahetukaṃ imaṃ saṅkhārādiṃ kevalaṃ dukkhakkhandhadhammaṃ pajānāti aññāti paṭivijjhatīti.

Its meaning is: 'Yadā have' means: indeed (`have`), at which time (`yasmiṃ kāle`). 'Pātubhavanti' (become manifest) means: they arise. 'Dhammā' means: the factors of awakening which accomplish the penetration of the conditional process in forward order. Or alternatively, 'pātubhavanti' means: they become clear; by the power of breakthrough, they become evident and manifest. 'Dhammā' means: the dhammas of the Four Noble Truths. 'Ātāpa' (ardor) is called energy (vīriya) in the sense of burning up the defilements. 'Ātāpino' (of the ardent one) means: of one possessing the energy of the right exertions. 'Jhāyato' (of one contemplating) means: of one who contemplates with the two kinds of jhāna, that which is characterized by close examination of the object and that which is characterized by close examination of the characteristics. 'Brāhmaṇassa' (of the brahmin) means: of one who has banished evil, of one whose cankers are destroyed. 'Athassa kaṅkhā vapayanti' (Then his doubts are dispelled) means: then, the doubts of this one, for whom the dhammas have become manifest in this way, are dispelled. 'Sabbā' (all) means: all those doubts which were spoken of by the Blessed One concerning the conditional process, by way of passages such as, 'Venerable sir, who indeed touches?' and 'The question is not suitable, the Blessed One said'; and likewise, by way of passages such as, 'Venerable sir, what indeed is aging-and-death? And whose is this aging-and-death?' and 'The question is not suitable'; and also the sixteen doubts that have come about due to not having penetrated the conditional process itself, beginning with, 'Did I indeed exist in a past time?'—all those doubts are dispelled, they depart, they cease. Why? 'Yato pajānāti sahetudhammaṃ' (Because he understands the dhamma with its cause) means: because, by means of the cause beginning with ignorance, he distinctly knows, knows, and penetrates this mere dhamma which is a mass of suffering, beginning with formations, as being together with its cause.

2. Dutiyavāre – imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti imaṃ tasmiṃ vidite atthe “avijjāya tveva asesavirāganirodhā saṅkhāranirodho”ti evaṃ pakāsitassa nibbānasaṅkhātassa paccayakkhayassa avabodhānubhāvadīpakaṃ [V 0.0228] vuttappakāraṃ udānaṃ udānesīti attho. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yasmā paccayānaṃ khayasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ avedi aññāsi paṭivijjhi, tasmā yadāssa ātāpino jhāyato [M 0.0237] brāhmaṇassa vuttappakārā dhammā pātubhavanti, athassa yā nibbānassa aviditattā uppajjeyyuṃ, tā sabbāpi kaṅkhā vapayantīti.

2. In the second instance, 'he uttered this inspired utterance' means: regarding that known meaning, he uttered an inspired utterance of the kind described, which illuminates the power of penetrating knowledge of the exhaustion of conditions, called Nibbāna, which was declared thus: 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, there is the cessation of formations.' This is the meaning. Therein, this is the summary meaning: because he knew, understood, and penetrated Nibbāna, called the exhaustion of conditions, therefore, when for that ardent, contemplating brahmin the dhammas of the kind described become manifest, then whatever doubts of his that might arise due to not having known Nibbāna, all those doubts are dispelled.

3. Tatiyavāre – imaṃ udānaṃ udānesīti imaṃ yena maggena so dukkhakkhandhassa samudayanirodhasaṅkhāto attho kiccavasena ca ārammaṇakiriyāya ca vidito, tassa ariyamaggassa ānubhāvadīpakaṃ vuttappakāraṃ udānaṃ udānesīti attho. Tatrāpāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā ātāpino jhāyato brāhmaṇassa, tadā so brāhmaṇo tehi vā uppannehi bodhipakkhiyadhammehi, yassa vā ariyamaggassa catusaccadhammā pātubhūtā, tena ariyamaggena vidhūpayaṃ tiṭṭhati mārasenaṃ “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādinā nayena vuttappakāraṃ mārasenaṃ vidhūpayanto vidhamento viddhaṃsento tiṭṭhati. Kathaṃ? Sūriyova obhāsayamantalikkhaṃ, yathā sūriyo abbhuggato attano pabhāya antalikkhaṃ obhāsentova andhakāraṃ vidhamento tiṭṭhati, evaṃ sopi brāhmaṇo tehi dhammehi tena vā maggena saccāni paṭivijjhantova mārasenaṃ vidhūpayanto tiṭṭhatīti.

3. In the third instance, 'he uttered this inspired utterance' means: he uttered an inspired utterance of the kind described, which illuminates the power of that Noble Path by which that meaning called the arising and cessation of the mass of suffering was known, both by way of its function and by way of the act of taking it as an object. This is the meaning. Therein also, this is the summary meaning: when indeed the dhammas become manifest to the ardent, contemplating brahmin, then that brahmin stands dispelling Māra's army, either by those arisen factors of awakening, or by that Noble Path for which the dhammas of the Four Truths have become manifest. He stands dispelling, scattering, and destroying Māra's army of the kind described by way of the passage beginning, 'Desires are your first army.' How? Like the sun illuminating the sky. Just as the sun, having risen, stands dispelling the darkness while illuminating the sky with its own radiance, so too does that brahmin stand dispelling Māra's army while penetrating the truths by means of those dhammas or by that path.

Evamettha paṭhamaṃ udānaṃ paccayākārapaccavekkhaṇavasena, dutiyaṃ nibbānapaccavekkhaṇavasena[P 5.0956], tatiyaṃ maggapaccavekkhaṇavasena uppannanti veditabbaṃ. Udāne pana “rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomaṃ, dutiyaṃ yāmaṃ paṭilomaṃ, tatiyaṃ yāmaṃ anulomapaṭiloma”nti vuttaṃ; taṃ sattāhassa accayena “sve āsanā vuṭṭhahissāmī”ti rattiṃ uppāditamanasikāraṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tadā hi bhagavā yassa paccayākārapajānanassa ca paccayakkhayādhigamassa ca ānubhāvadīpikā purimā dve udānagāthā, tassa vasena ekekameva koṭṭhāsaṃ paṭhamayāmañca majjhimayāmañca manasākāsi, idha pana pāṭipadarattiyā evaṃ manasākāsi. Bhagavā hi visākhapuṇṇamāya rattiyā paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsaṃ anussari, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhesi, pacchimayāme paṭiccasamuppādaṃ anulomapaṭilomaṃ manasi katvā “idāni aruṇo uggamissatī”ti sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇi. Sabbaññutappattisamanantarameva ca aruṇo uggacchi. Tato taṃ divasaṃ teneva pallaṅkena vītināmetvā sampattāya pāṭipadarattiyā tīsu yāmesu evaṃ manasi katvā imāni udānāni udānesi. Iti [M 0.0238] pāṭipadarattiyā evaṃ manasi katvā taṃ “bodhirukkhamūle sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisīdī”ti evaṃ vuttasattāhaṃ tattheva vītināmesi.

Thus, herein, it should be known that the first inspired utterance arose by means of reflecting on Dependent Origination, the second by means of reflecting on Nibbāna, and the third by means of reflecting on the path. However, in the Udāna it is said: “During the first watch of the night, [he contemplated] Dependent Origination in forward order; during the second watch, in reverse order; during the third watch, in forward and reverse order.” That was said referring to the attention that arose on the night after the passing of seven days, [when he thought,] “Tomorrow I shall rise from my seat.” Indeed, at that time, the Blessed One—for whom the first two inspired verses are indicators of the power of his distinct knowledge of Dependent Origination and his attainment of the destruction of causes—by means of that, attended to each single part during the first and the middle watches. But here, on the night of the first day of the waning moon, he attended thus. Indeed, on the night of the full moon of Visākha, in the first watch, the Blessed One recollected his former existences; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; in the last watch, having attended to Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order, he attained omniscience at the time when it was said, “Now the dawn will break.” And immediately after attaining omniscience, the dawn broke. Thereafter, having spent that day on that very same cross-legged seat, on the following night that had arrived—the night of the first day of the waning moon—having attended thus in the three watches, he uttered these inspired utterances. Thus, having attended in this way on the night of the first day of the waning moon, he spent that seven-day period, which was spoken of thus: “He sat for seven days at the foot of the Bodhi tree in a single cross-legged posture,” right there.

Bodhikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Bodhi Tree is concluded.

Ajapālakathā

The Exposition on the Ajapāla Banyan Tree

4. Atha [V 0.0229] kho bhagavā sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā bodhirukkhamūlā yena ajapālanigrodho tenupasaṅkamīti ettha na bhagavā tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā anantarameva bodhirukkhamūlā yena ajapālanigrodho tenupasaṅkami. Yathā pana “bhutvā sayatī”ti vutte na “hatthe adhovitvā mukhaṃ avikkhāletvā sayanasamīpaṃ agantvā aññaṃ kiñci ālāpasallāpaṃ akatvā sayati”cceva vuttaṃ hoti, bhojanato pana pacchā sayati, na nasayatīti idamevattha dīpitaṃ hoti. Evamidhāpi “na tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā anantarameva pakkāmī”ti vuttaṃ hoti, vuṭṭhānato ca pana pacchā pakkāmi, na napakkāmīti [P 5.0957] idamevettha dīpitaṃ hoti.

4. Regarding the passage: 'Then, after the passing of seven days, the Blessed One, having arisen from that concentration, approached the Ajapāla banyan tree from the foot of the Bodhi tree.' Herein, it was not that the Blessed One, having arisen from that concentration, immediately approached the Ajapāla banyan tree from the foot of the Bodhi tree. Just as when it is said, “Having eaten, he sleeps,” it is not meant that “Without washing his hands, without rinsing his mouth, without going near the bed, and without making any other conversation, he sleeps.” Rather, it is shown herein that after eating, he sleeps; it is not that he does not sleep. Similarly, here too, it is not meant that “Having arisen from that concentration, he departed immediately.” Rather, it is shown herein that after arising, he departed; it is not that he did not depart.

Anantaraṃ pana apakkamitvā bhagavā kiṃ akāsīti? Aparānipi tīṇi sattāhāni bodhisamīpeyeva vītināmesi. Tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā – bhagavati kira buddhattaṃ patvā sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinne “na bhagavā vuṭṭhāti; kiṃ nu kho aññepi buddhattakarā dhammā atthī”ti ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ kaṅkhā udapādi. Atha bhagavā aṭṭhame divase samāpattito vuṭṭhāya devatānaṃ kaṅkhaṃ ñatvā kaṅkhāvidhamanatthaṃ ākāse uppatitvā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā tāsaṃ kaṅkhaṃ vidhamitvā pallaṅkato īsakaṃ pācīnanissite uttaradisābhāge ṭhatvā cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca upacitānaṃ pāramīnaṃ balādhigamanaṭṭhānaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bodhirukkhañca animisehi akkhīhi olokayamāno sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ animisacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Atha pallaṅkassa ca ṭhitaṭṭhānassa ca antarā puratthimato ca pacchimato ca āyate ratanacaṅkame caṅkamanto sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanacaṅkamacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Tato pacchimadisābhāge devatā ratanagharaṃ māpayiṃsu. Tattha pallaṅkena nisīditvā abhidhammapiṭakaṃ visesato cettha anantanayaṃ samantapaṭṭhānaṃ [M 0.0239] vicinanto sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanagharacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

Not having departed immediately, what did the Blessed One do? He spent another three seven-day periods right near the Bodhi tree. Herein, this is the sequential account: It is said that while the Blessed One, having attained Buddhahood, was sitting for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, a doubt arose in some deities: “The Blessed One does not rise. Could it be that there are other qualities that bring about Buddhahood?” Then, on the eighth day, the Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment, knowing the deities’ doubt, and in order to dispel their doubt, rose into the sky, displayed the twin miracle, and having dispelled their doubt, stood in the northeastern quarter, slightly to the east of the throne. Gazing with unblinking eyes for seven days at the throne and the Bodhi tree—the place where mastery was gained through the power of the perfections accumulated over four incalculables and one hundred thousand aeons—he spent seven days. That place came to be named the Animisa Cetiya. Then, for seven days, he spent the time walking on a jeweled cloister-walk that was long, extending from east to west, between the throne and the place where he had stood. That place came to be named the Ratanacaṅkama Cetiya. From there, in the western quarter, deities created a jeweled house. There, sitting in a cross-legged posture, he spent seven days contemplating the Abhidhammapiṭaka, and especially herein the Samantapaṭṭhāna with its endless methods. That place came to be named the Ratanaghara Cetiya.

Evaṃ bodhisamīpeyeva cattāri sattāhāni vītināmetvā pañcame sattāhe bodhirukkhamūlā yena ajapālanigrodho tenupasaṅkami. Tassa kira nigrodhassa chāyāya ajapālakā gantvā nisīdanti; tenassa ajapālanigrodhotveva nāmaṃ udapādi. Sattāhaṃ vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedīti tatrāpi dhammaṃ vicinantoyeva vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento nisīdi. Bodhito puratthimadisābhāge esa rukkho hoti. Evaṃ nisinne ca panettha bhagavati eko brāhmaṇo gantvā pañhaṃ pucchi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho aññataro”tiādi. Tattha huṃhuṅkajātikoti so kira diṭṭhamaṅgaliko nāma[V 0.0230], mānavasena kodhavasena ca “huṃhu”nti karonto vicarati, tasmā “huṃhuṅkajātiko”ti vuccati. “Huhukkajātiko”tipi [P 5.0958] paṭhanti.

Thus, having spent four seven-day periods right near the Bodhi tree, in the fifth seven-day period, he approached the Ajapāla banyan tree from the foot of the Bodhi tree. It is said that goatherds would go and sit in the shade of that banyan tree; for that reason, its name 'Ajapāla banyan tree' arose. As for the phrase 'for seven days experiencing the bliss of liberation,' there too, while contemplating the Dhamma, he sat experiencing the bliss of liberation. This tree is in the eastern quarter from the Bodhi tree. And while the Blessed One was sitting there thus, a certain brahmin approached and asked a question. For that reason, it was said, 'Then a certain...' and so on. Therein, as for 'of the Huṃhuṅka class': it is said that because he, being one who believes in auspicious sights, wanders about making the sound 'huṃ huṃ' by the power of conceit and anger, he is called 'Huṃhuṅkajātika.' Some also recite it as 'Huhukkajātika.'

Etamatthaṃ viditvāti etaṃ tena vuttassa vacanassa sikhāpattamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi. Tassattho – yo bāhitapāpadhammatāya brāhmaṇo na diṭṭhamaṅgalikatāya, huṃhuṅkārakabhāvādipāpadhammayutto hutvā kevalaṃ jātimattakena brahmaññaṃ paṭijānāti, so brāhmaṇo bāhitapāpadhammattā huṃhuṅkārappahānena nihuṃhuṅko, rāgādikasāvābhāvena nikkasāvo, bhāvanānuyogayuttacittatāya yatatto, sīlasaṃvarena vā saññatacittatāya yatatto, catumaggañāṇasaṅkhātehi vedehi antaṃ, vedānaṃ vā antaṃ gatattā vedantagū, maggabrahmacariyassa vusitattā vusitabrahmacariyo. Dhammena brahmavādaṃ vadeyya, “brāhmaṇo, aha”nti etaṃ vādaṃ dhammena vadeyya, yassa sakale lokasannivāse kuhiñci ekārammaṇepi rāgussado dosussado mohussado mānussado diṭṭhussadoti ime ussadā natthīti.

Having understood this meaning—that is, the supreme meaning which is the pinnacle of the statement spoken by him—he uttered this inspired utterance at that time. Its meaning is this: A brahmin is not one who, due to believing in auspicious signs in what is seen, claims brahminhood merely by birth while being endowed with evil qualities beginning with the state of making the 'hum-hum' sound [of pride and anger]. Rather, a brahmin is one who, by having banished evil qualities, is free from the 'hum-hum' sound, without astringents such as passion, self-controlled through being yoked to the practice of meditation, or self-controlled through a mind restrained by moral restraint, has gone to the end by means of the Vedas—that is, the four path-knowledges—and has lived the holy life of the path. He may rightly declare, 'I am a brahmin,' for whom, in the entire inhabited world, in any single object, there are no protuberances of lust, protuberances of hatred, protuberances of delusion, protuberances of pride, or protuberances of wrong view.

Ajapālakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Ajapāla Banyan Tree is concluded.

Mucalindakathā

The Story of Mucalinda

5. Akālameghoti asampatte vassakāle uppannamegho. Ayaṃ pana gimhānaṃ pacchime māse udapādi. Sattāhavaddalikāti tasmiṃ uppanne sattāhaṃ avicchinnavuṭṭhikā ahosi. Sītavātaduddinīti sā ca pana sattāhavaddalikā [M 0.0240] udakaphusitasammissena sītavātena samantā paribbhamantena dūsitadivasattā sītavātaduddinī nāma ahosi. Atha kho mucalindo nāgarājāti tasseva mucalindarukkhassa samīpe pokkharaṇiyā nibbatto mahānubhāvo nāgarājā. Sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvāti evaṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā uparimuddhani mahantaṃ phaṇaṃ karitvāva ṭhite; tasmiṃ tassa parikkhepabbhantaraṃ lohapāsāde bhaṇḍāgāragabbhappamāṇaṃ ahosi, tasmā bhagavā nivāte pihitadvāravātapāne kūṭāgāre nisinno viya jāto. Mā bhagavantaṃ sītantiādi tassa tathā karitvā ṭhānakāraṇaparidīpanaṃ. So hi “mā bhagavantaṃ sītaṃ bādhayittha, mā uṇhaṃ, mā ḍaṃsādisamphasso bādhayitthā”ti tathā karitvā aṭṭhāsi. Tattha kiñcāpi sattāhavaddalikāya uṇhameva natthi, sace pana antarantarā megho vigaccheyya uṇhaṃ bhaveyya[P 5.0959], tampi naṃ mā bādhayitthāti evaṃ tassa cintetuṃ yuttaṃ. Viddhanti ubbiddhaṃ; meghavigamena [V 0.0231] dūrībhūtanti attho. Vigatavalāhakanti apagatameghaṃ. Devanti ākāsaṃ. Sakavaṇṇanti attano rūpaṃ.

5. “Akālamegha” is a cloud that appears out of season, before the rainy season has arrived. This one, however, arose in the last month of summer. “Sattāhavaddalikā” means that when it appeared, there was continuous rain for seven days. “Sītavātaduddinī” means that the seven-day continuous rain was a day spoiled by a cold wind mixed with water droplets blowing all around; hence it was called sītavātaduddinī. Then, the Nāga king Mucalinda: this refers to a Nāga king of great power who was born in a lotus pond near that very Mucalinda tree. “Sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhipitvā” means that having thus encircled him seven times with his coils, he remained with a large hood spread above his head. The space within his coils was the size of a treasury chamber in a bronze palace; thus the Blessed One was as if seated in a windless, peaked-roof chamber with its doors and windows sealed. “Mā bhagavantaṃ sītaṃ” and so forth is an explanation of the reason for his standing thus. For he stood thus, thinking: “May the Blessed One not be troubled by cold, nor by heat, nor by the touch of gadflies and the like.” Here, although there was no heat during the seven days of continuous rain, if the clouds were to disperse even intermittently, heat might arise; it was fitting for him to think, “May that not trouble him.” “Viddha” means driven away; the meaning is, gone far away due to the dispersal of the clouds. “Vigatavalāhaka” means the clouds have departed. “Deva” refers to the sky. “Sakavaṇṇa” means his own form.

Sukho vivekoti nibbānasaṅkhāto upadhiviveko sukho. Tuṭṭhassāti catumaggañāṇasantosena santuṭṭhassa. Sutadhammassāti pakāsitadhammassa. Passatoti taṃ vivekaṃ yaṃ vā kiñci passitabbaṃ nāma, taṃ sabbaṃ attano vīriyabalādhigatena ñāṇacakkhunā passantassa. Abyāpajjanti akuppanabhāvo; etena mettāpubbabhāgo dassito. Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamoti sattesu ca saṃyamo; avihiṃsanabhāvo sukhoti attho. Etena karuṇāpubbabhāgo dassito. Sukhā virāgatā loketi vītarāgatāpi sukhāti dīpeti. Kāmānaṃ samatikkamoti yā “kāmānaṃ samatikkamo”ti vuccati; sā virāgatāpi sukhāti attho. Etena anāgāmimaggo kathito. Asmimānassa yo vinayoti iminā pana arahattaṃ kathitaṃ; arahattañhi asmimānassa “passaddhivinayo”ti vuccati. Ito parañca sukhaṃ nāma natthi, tenāha “etaṃ ve paramaṃ sukha”nti.

“Sukho viveko”: seclusion from the substrates, which is called Nibbāna, is happiness. “Tuṭṭhassa”: for one who is content with the contentment of the four path-knowledges. “Sutadhammassa”: for one who has understood the Dhamma. “Passato”: for one who sees that seclusion, or whatever is to be seen, all of it, with the eye of wisdom attained by the power of his own effort. “Abyāpajjaṃ”: the state of non-ill-will is happiness; by this, the preliminary part of loving-kindness is shown. “Pāṇabhūtesu saṃyamo”: restraint toward living beings; the meaning is that the state of non-harming is happiness. By this, the preliminary part of compassion is shown. “Sukhā virāgatā loke”: this shows that being without passion in the world is also happiness. “Kāmānaṃ samatikkamo”: that which is called “the transcending of sensual pleasures”; the meaning is that this passionlessness is also happiness. By this, the path of the non-returner is taught. “Asmimānassa yo vinayo”: by this, however, Arahantship is taught; for Arahantship is called the “tranquil removal” of the conceit ‘I am.’ Beyond this, there is no such thing as happiness; therefore, He said, “This indeed is the supreme happiness.”

Mucalindakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Story of Mucalinda is concluded.

Rājāyatanakathā

The Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree

6. Mucalindamūlāti mahābodhito pācīnakoṇe ṭhitamucalindarukkhamūlā. Rājāyatananti dakkhiṇadisābhāge ṭhitaṃ rājāyatanarukkhaṃ upasaṅkami[M 0.0241]. Tena kho pana samayenāti katarena samayena. Bhagavato kira rājāyatanamūle sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisinnassa samādhito vuṭṭhānadivase aruṇuggamanavelāyameva “bhojanakiccena bhavitabba”nti ñatvā sakko devarājā osadhaharītakaṃ upanesi. Bhagavā taṃ paribhuñji, paribhuttamattasseva sarīrakiccaṃ ahosi. Sakko mukhodakaṃ adāsi. Bhagavā mukhaṃ dhovitvā tasmiṃyeva rukkhamūle nisīdi. Evaṃ uggate aruṇamhi nisinne bhagavati.

6. From the foot of the Mucalinda tree: from the base of the Mucalinda tree standing in the eastern direction from the Great Bodhi tree. As for the Rājāyatana tree: he approached the Rājāyatana tree situated in the southern direction. 'At that very time': At what time? It is said that on the day the Blessed One, after sitting for seven days in a single cross-legged posture at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, arose from his concentration, Sakka, the king of the devas, knowing at the very time of dawn's appearance, “There must be the business of a meal,” offered a medicinal myrobalan. The Blessed One partook of it, and just as he had finished partaking, the need of the body arose. Sakka provided water for the mouth. The Blessed One, having washed his face, sat down at the foot of that very tree. Thus, as the dawn was rising, while the Blessed One was seated.

Tena kho pana samayena tapussabhallikā vāṇijāti tapusso ca bhalliko cāti dve bhātaro vāṇijā. Ukkalāti ukkalajanapadato. Taṃ desanti yasmiṃ dese bhagavā viharati. Katarasmiñca dese bhagavā viharati? Majjhimadese. Tasmā majjhimadesaṃ gantuṃ addhānamaggappaṭipannā [P 5.0960] hontīti ayamettha attho. Ñātisālohitā devatāti tesaṃ ñātibhūtapubbā devatā. Etadavocāti sā kira nesaṃ sabbasakaṭāni appavattīni akāsi. Tato [V 0.0232] te kiṃ idanti maggadevatānaṃ baliṃ akaṃsu. Tesaṃ balikammakāle sā devatā dissamāneneva kāyena etaṃ avoca. Manthena ca madhupiṇḍikāya cāti abaddhasattunā ca sappimadhuphāṇitādīhi yojetvā baddhasattunā ca. Patimānethāti upaṭṭhahatha. Taṃ voti taṃ patimānanaṃ tumhākaṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya. Yaṃ amhākanti yaṃ paṭiggahaṇaṃ amhākaṃ assa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya. Bhagavato etadahosīti yo kirassa padhānānuyogakāle patto ahosi, so sujātāya pāyāsaṃ dātuṃ āgacchantiyā eva antaradhāyi. Tenassa etadahosi – “patto me natthi, purimakāpi ca na kho tathāgatā hatthesu paṭiggaṇhanti, kimhi nu kho ahaṃ paṭiggaṇheyyaṃ manthañca madhupiṇḍakañcā”ti.

'The merchants Tapussa and Bhallika' means: Tapussa and Bhallika, two brothers who were merchants. 'From Ukkala' means: from the country of Ukkala. 'To that region' means: to the region where the Blessed One was dwelling. And in which region was the Blessed One dwelling? In the Middle Country. Therefore, 'they were proceeding on a long road'; this is the meaning here: they had set out on the road to go to the Middle Country. 'A deity who was a blood relative' means: a deity who had formerly been their kin. 'She said this' means: It is said that she made all their carts immobile. Then they, thinking, 'What is this?', made an offering to the deities of the road. At the time of their offering, that deity, with a visible body, said this. 'With roasted grain meal and a honey-ball' means: with unbound roasted grain flour, and with roasted grain flour mixed and bound with things such as ghee, honey, and molasses. 'Revere him' means: attend upon him. 'That for you' means: that reverence of yours will be for your long-term welfare and happiness. 'Which for us' means: the acceptance of which would be for our long-term welfare and happiness. 'The Blessed One had this thought' means: It is said that the bowl he had during the time of his striving disappeared just as Sujātā was approaching to offer the milk-rice. Because of that, he had this thought: “I have no bowl, and indeed, previous Tathāgatas do not accept offerings in their hands. In what, then, should I accept the roasted grain meal and the honey-ball?”

Parivitakkamaññāyāti ito pubbeva bhagavato sujātāya dinnabhojanaṃyeva ojānuppabandhanavasena aṭṭhāsi, ettakaṃ kālaṃ neva jighacchā na pipāsā na kāyadubbalyaṃ ahosi. Idāni panassa āhāraṃ paṭiggahetukāmatāya “na kho tathāgatā”tiādinā nayena parivitakko udapādi[M 0.0242]. Taṃ evaṃ uppannaṃ attano cetasā bhagavato cetoparivitakkamaññāya. Catuddisāti catūhi disāhi. Selamaye patteti muggavaṇṇaselamaye patte. Idaṃyeva bhagavā paṭiggahesi, teyeva sandhāya vuttaṃ. Cattāro pana mahārājāno paṭhamaṃ indanīlamaṇimaye patte upanāmesuṃ, na te bhagavā aggahesi. Tato ime cattāropi muggavaṇṇasilāmaye patte upanāmesuṃ, bhagavā cattāropi patte aggahesi tesaṃ pasādānurakkhaṇatthāya, no mahicchatāya. Gahetvā ca pana cattāropi yathā ekova patto hoti tathā adhiṭṭhahi, catunnampi ekasadiso puññavipāko ahosi. Evaṃ ekaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhite paṭiggahesi bhagavā paccagghe selamaye patte manthañca madhupiṇḍikañca. Paccaggheti paccagghasmiṃ; pāṭekkaṃ mahagghasminti attho. Atha vā paccaggheti abhinave abbhuṇhe; taṅkhaṇe nibbattasminti attho. Dve vācā etesaṃ ahesunti dvevācikā. Atha vā dvīhi vācāhi upāsakabhāvaṃ pattāti attho[P 5.0961]. Te evaṃ upāsakabhāvaṃ paṭivedetvā bhagavantaṃ āhaṃsu – “kassa dāni bhante amhehi ajja paṭṭhāya abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaṃ kātabba”nti? Atha bhagavā sīsaṃ parāmasi, kesā hatthe laggiṃsu. Te tesaṃ adāsi “ime tumhe pariharathā”ti. Te kesadhātuyo labhitvā amateneva abhisittā haṭṭhatuṭṭhā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā pakkamiṃsu.

'Having known his thought': Before this, the food given by Sujātā had sustained the Blessed One by means of the uninterrupted connection of its nutritive essence; for such a long time there was neither hunger, nor thirst, nor bodily weakness. But now, because of his desire to accept food, the thought arose in the manner of 'Indeed, Tathāgatas do not…' and so on. It was this thought of the Blessed One, which had thus arisen, that they knew with their own minds. 'From the four directions' means: from the four directions. 'Stone bowls' means: bowls made of stone the color of mung beans. The Blessed One accepted these very ones, and it was said in reference to them. However, the Four Great Kings first offered bowls made of sapphire, but the Blessed One did not accept them. Then these four offered the bowls made of mung-bean-colored stone. The Blessed One accepted all four bowls in order to protect their faith, not out of great desire. And having taken them, he resolved that the four would become as one bowl, and the fruit of merit for all four was identical. Thus, in the precious stone bowl that had been made one by his resolution, the Blessed One accepted the roasted grain meal and the honey-ball. 'Precious' (paccagghe) means: in a precious one; the meaning is that each one was of great value. Or alternatively, 'paccagghe' means 'new,' 'fresh'; the meaning is 'produced at that moment.' They are 'dvevācikā' (of two declarations) because they had two declarations. Or alternatively, the meaning is that they attained the state of lay followers by means of two declarations. They, having thus declared their state as lay followers, said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, to whom should homage and rising in respect be done by us from this day forward?” Then the Blessed One touched his head, and hairs adhered to his hand. He gave them to them, saying, “You should take care of these.” They, having received the hair relics, joyful and elated as if sprinkled with ambrosia, paid homage to the Blessed One and departed.

Rājāyatanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Rājāyatana Tree is concluded.

Brahmayācanakathā

The Account of Brahmā's Request

7. Atha [V 0.0233] kho bhagavā sattāhassa accayena tamhā samādhimhā vuṭṭhahitvā vuttappakārametaṃ sabbaṃ kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā rājāyatanamūlā punapi yena ajapālanigrodho tenupasaṅkami. Parivitakko udapādīti tasmiṃ nisinnamattasseva sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇo ayaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi. Kasmā panāyaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ uppajjatīti? Dhammassa mahantabhāvaṃ garubhāvaṃ bhāriyabhāvaṃ paccavekkhaṇāya brahmunā yācite desetukāmatāya ca. Jānanti hi buddhā “evaṃ parivitakkite brahmā āgantvā dhammadesanaṃ yācissati, tato sattā dhamme gāravaṃ uppādessanti, brahmagaruko hi lokasannivāso”ti. Iti imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi ayaṃ vitakko uppajjatīti.

7. Then, after seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration. Having completed all those duties as mentioned, he went from the foot of the Rājāyatana tree to the Ajapāla banyan tree once more. 'A thought arose' means: just as he was seated there, this thought, customary and well-practiced for all Buddhas, arose in his mind. But why does this thought arise for all Buddhas? It is due to reflecting on the greatness, gravity, and weightiness of the Dhamma, and due to the desire to teach only when requested by a Brahmā. For the Buddhas know: 'When it is thus reflected upon, Brahmā will come and request the teaching of the Dhamma; then beings will generate respect for the Dhamma, for indeed the world of beings holds Brahmā in high regard.' Thus, for these two reasons, this thought arises.

Tattha [M 0.0243] adhigato kho myāyanti adhigato kho me ayaṃ. Ālayarāmāti sattā pañca kāmaguṇe allīyanti, tasmā te “ālayā”ti vuccanti. Tehi ālayehi ramantīti ālayarāmā. Ālayesu ratāti ālayaratā. Ālayesu suṭṭhumuditāti ālayasammuditā. Yadidanti nipāto. Tassa ṭhānaṃ sandhāya “yaṃ ida”nti paṭiccasamuppādaṃ sandhāya “yo aya”nti evamattho daṭṭhabbo. Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādoti imesaṃ paccayā idappaccayā, idappaccayāva idappaccayatā, idappaccayatā ca sā paṭiccasamuppādo cāti idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo. So mamassa kilamathoti yā ajānantānaṃ desanā nāma, so mama kilamatho assa; sā mama vihesā assāti attho. Bhagavantanti bhagavato. Anacchariyāti anu acchariyā. Paṭibhaṃsūti paṭibhānasaṅkhātassa ñāṇassa gocarā ahesuṃ, parivitakkayitabbabhāvaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

Herein, 'adhigato kho myāyaṃ' means: 'This Dhamma has been attained by me.' 'Ālayarāmā' means: beings cling to the five strands of sensual pleasure; therefore, these are called 'ālaya' (attachments). Because that generation of beings delights in those attachments, they are called 'ālayarāmā'. Because that generation of beings is attached to attachments, they are called 'ālayaratā'. Because that generation of beings greatly rejoices in attachments, they are called 'ālayasammuditā'. 'Yadidaṃ' is a particle. In reference to its position, it should be understood as 'yaṃ idaṃ'; in reference to dependent origination, as 'yo ayaṃ'. Thus the meaning should be seen. 'Idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo' means: the conditions for these results are 'idappaccayā'; the very state of having these conditions is 'idappaccayatā'; and that 'idappaccayatā' is also 'paṭiccasamuppādo'; thus, it is 'idappaccayatāpaṭiccasamuppādo'. 'So mamassa kilamatho' means: whatever teaching there is for those who do not know, that would be a cause of weariness for me; that would be a cause of vexation for me. This is the meaning. 'Bhagavantaṃ' means 'bhagavato'. 'Anacchariyā' means 'anu' (repeatedly) + 'acchariyā' (wonderful). 'Paṭibhaṃsu' means: they became the objects of the knowledge called 'paṭibhāna' (ready wit); they reached a state of being fit for repeated consideration.

Halanti ettha hakāro nipātamatto; alanti attho. Pakāsitunti desituṃ. Alaṃ dāni [P 5.0962] me imaṃ kicchena adhigataṃ dhammaṃ desetunti vuttaṃ hoti. Paṭisotagāminti paṭisotaṃ vuccati nibbānaṃ; nibbānagāminti attho. Rāgarattāti kāmarāgabhavarāgadiṭṭhirāgena rattā. Na dakkhantīti na passissanti. Tamokhandhena āvuṭāti avijjārāsinā ajjhotthaṭā. Appossukkatāyāti nirussukkabhāvena; adesetukāmatāyāti attho.

Herein, in the word `halaṃ`, the letter `ha` is merely a particle; the meaning is `alaṃ` (enough; no benefit). `Pakāsituṃ` means `desituṃ` (to teach). Thus it is said: 'Enough now of my teaching this Dhamma attained with difficulty.' In `paṭisotagāmiṃ`, Nibbāna is called `paṭisotaṃ` (against the stream); the meaning is 'going to Nibbāna.' `Rāgarattā`: Infatuated by the lust for sensual pleasures, lust for existence, and lust for views. `Na dakkhanti` means 'they will not see.' `Tamokhandhena āvuṭā`: Overwhelmed by the mass of ignorance. `Appossukkatāya`: Due to the state of having no exertion; the meaning is 'due to the desire not to teach.'

8. Yatra hi nāmāti yasmiṃ nāma loke. Bhagavato purato pāturahosīti dhammadesanāyācanatthaṃ dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu mahābrahmāno gahetvā āgamma bhagavato purato pāturahosi[V 0.0234]. Apparajakkhajātikāti paññāmaye akkhimhi appaṃ rāgadosamoharajaṃ etesaṃ evaṃsabhāvāti apparajakkhajātikā. Bhavissanti dhammassa aññātāroti paṭivijjhitāro.

8. `Yatra hi nāma`: In whatever world he inclines. `Bhagavato purato pāturahosi`: For the purpose of requesting the teaching of the Dhamma, having gathered the Mahābrahmās from the ten thousand world-systems and come, he appeared before the Blessed One. `Apparajakkhajātikā`: In the wisdom-eye of these beings, there is little dust of lust, hatred, and delusion. Because they have such a nature, they are called `apparajakkhajātikā`. `Bhavissanti dhammassa aññātāro`: They will be those who penetrate the Dhamma.

Pāturahosīti pātubhavi. Samalehi cintitoti rāgādīhi malehi samalehi chahi satthārehi cintito. Apāpuretanti vivara etaṃ. Amatassa dvāranti amatassa nibbānassa dvārabhūtaṃ ariyamaggaṃ. Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhanti [M 0.0244] ime sattā rāgādimalānaṃ abhāvato vimalena sammāsambuddhena anubuddhaṃ catusaccadhammaṃ suṇantu.

`Pāturahosi` means 'he became manifest.' `Samalehi cintito`: Contemplated with wrong knowledge by the six teachers who are stained with defilements such as lust. `Apāpuretaṃ`: Open this. `Amatassa dvāraṃ`: The Noble Path, which has become the door to the Deathless, Nibbāna. `Suṇantu dhammaṃ vimalenānubuddhaṃ`: May these beings listen to the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, sequentially realized by the Perfectly Enlightened One, who is stainless due to the absence of defilements such as lust.

Sele yathā pabbatamuddhaniṭṭhitoti selamaye ekagghane pabbatamuddhani yathāṭhitova yathā cakkhumā puriso samantato janataṃ passeyya, tvampi sumedha sundarapañña sabbaññutaññāṇena samantacakkhu bhagavā dhammamayaṃ paññāmayaṃ pāsādamāruyha sayaṃ apetasoko sokāvatiṇṇaṃ jātijarābhibhūtañca janataṃ avekkhassu upadhāraya.

Just as a man with sight, standing on a mountain peak of solid rock, might see the multitude of beings all around, likewise, O you of good wisdom, O Blessed One with the all-seeing eye of omniscience, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma and wisdom, yourself being free from sorrow, please look upon and carefully consider the multitude of beings sunk in sorrow and overcome by birth and aging.

Uṭṭhehīti bhagavato dhammadesanatthaṃ cārikacaraṇaṃ yācanto bhaṇati. Vīrātiādīsu bhagavā vīriyavantatāya vīro. Devaputtamaccukilesābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ vijitattā vijitasaṅgāmo. Jātikantārādinittharaṇasamatthatāya satthavāho. Kāmacchandaiṇassa [P 5.0963] abhāvato aṇaṇo.

Regarding `Uṭṭhehi`: He speaks, requesting the Blessed One to wander on tour for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma. In `Vīra`, etc.: The Blessed One is a `vīra` (hero) because of his possession of energy. He is `vijitasaṅgāmo` (victorious in battle) because of having conquered the Māras of the devaputta, death, defilements, and formations. He is `satthavāho` (caravan leader) because of his ability to lead out from the wilderness of birth and so on. He is `aṇaṇo` (debtless) because of the absence of the debt of sensual desire.

9. Ajjhesananti yācanaṃ. Buddhacakkhunāti indriyaparopariyattañāṇena ca āsayānusayañāṇena ca. Imesañhi dvinnaṃ ñāṇānaṃ buddhacakkhūti nāmaṃ. Apparajakkhāti paññācakkhumhi rāgādirajaṃ appaṃ yesaṃ, te apparajakkhā. Yesaṃ taṃ mahantaṃ te mahārajakkhā. Yesaṃ saddhādīni indriyāni tikkhāni te tikkhindriyā. Yesaṃ tāni mudūni te mudindriyā. Yesaṃ teyeva saddhādayo ākārā sundarā te svākārā. Yesaṃ teyeva saddhādayo ākārā asundarā te dvākārā. Ye kathitakāraṇaṃ sallakkhenti, sukhena sakkā honti viññāpetuṃ te suviññāpayā. Ye paralokañca vajjañca bhayato passanti te paralokavajjabhayadassāvino. Uppaliniyanti uppalavane. Itaresupi eseva nayo. Antonimuggaposīnīti yāni udakassa anto nimuggāneva posayanti. Samodakaṃ ṭhitānīti udakena samaṃ ṭhitāni. Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitānīti udakaṃ atikkamitvā ṭhitāni.

9. `Ajjhesana` means a request. `Buddhacakkhunā`: By the knowledge of the maturity of others' faculties and by the knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies. Indeed, the name 'Buddha-eye' is given to these two knowledges. `Apparajakkhā`: Those in whose wisdom-eye the dust of lust and so on is little, they are `apparajakkhā`. Those in whom it is great, they are `mahārajakkhā`. Those whose faculties of faith and so on are keen, they are `tikkindriyā`. Those whose faculties are soft, they are `mudindriyā`. Those whose very qualities of faith and so on are good, they are `svākārā`. Those whose very qualities of faith and so on are not good, they are `dvākārā`. Those who can mark well the reason spoken and can be made to understand easily, they are `suviññāpayā`. Those who see the next world and faults as a danger, they are `paralokavajjabhayadassāvino`. `Uppaliniyaṃ`: In a water-lily grove. In the other terms as well, this is the method. `Antonimuggaposīni`: Those lotuses that grow while remaining submerged within the water. `Samodakaṃ ṭhitāni`: Standing level with the water. `Udakaṃ accuggamma ṭhitāni`: Standing having surpassed the water.

Apārutāti vivaṭā. Amatassa dvārāti ariyamaggo. So hi amatasaṅkhātassa nibbānassa dvāraṃ. Pamuñcantu saddhanti sabbe attano saddhaṃ pamuñcantu. Pacchimapadadvaye ayamattho[V 0.0235], ahañhi attano paguṇaṃ suppavattimpi imaṃ [M 0.0245] paṇītaṃ uttamaṃ dhammaṃ kāyavācākilamathasaññī hutvā manujesu devamanussesu na bhāsinti.

`Apārutā`: Opened. `Amatassa dvārā`: The Noble Path. For that Noble Path is the door to Nibbāna, which is called the Deathless. `Pamuñcantu saddhaṃ`: Let all beings release their faith. In the last two phrases, this is the meaning: For I, perceiving it as mere weariness of body and speech, did not speak this excellent, supreme Dhamma—which is well-practiced and well-established for me—among humans, that is, among devas and humans.

Brahmayācanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of Brahmā's Request is concluded.

Pañcavaggiyakathā

The Account of the Group of Five

10. Paṇḍitoti paṇḍiccena samannāgato. Byattoti veyyattiyena samannāgato. Medhāvīti ṭhānuppattiyā paññāya samannāgato. Apparajakkhajātikoti samāpattiyā vikkhambhitattā nikkilesajātiko visuddhasatto. Ājānissatīti sallakkhessati paṭivijjhissati. Bhagavatopi kho ñāṇaṃ udapādīti sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ uppajji “ito sattamadivasamatthake kālaṃkatvā ākiñcaññāyatane nibbatto”ti. Mahājāniyoti sattadivasabbhantare [P 5.0964] pattabbamaggaphalato parihīnattā mahatī jāni assāti mahājāniyo akkhaṇe nibbattattā. Abhidosakālaṃkatoti hiyyo kālaṃkato, sopi nevasaññānāsaññāyatane nibbattoti addasa. Bahūkārāti bahūpakārā. Padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsūti padhānatthāya pesitattabhāvaṃ mukhodakadānādinā upaṭṭhahiṃsu.

10. `Paṇḍita` means endowed with sagacity. `Byatta` means endowed with proficiency. `Medhāvī` means endowed with wisdom that arises according to the circumstances. `Apparajakkhajātika` means one whose nature is without defilements because they have been suppressed by meditative attainment; a purified being. `Ājānissati` means he will discern and penetrate. “Knowledge also arose in the Blessed One” means the knowledge of omniscience arose thus: ‘On the seventh day from today, having passed away, he is reborn in the base of nothingness.’ `Mahājāniyo` means one with a great loss, because he was deprived of the path and fruit that should have been attained within seven days, having been reborn at an inopportune time. `Abhidosakālaṅkato` means he passed away yesterday; He saw that he, too, was reborn in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. `Bahūkārā` means they were of great help. `Padhānapahitattaṃ upaṭṭhahiṃsu` means they attended to me, who was resolved on the striving, with duties such as giving water for washing the face.

11. Antarā ca gayaṃ antarā ca bodhinti upako bodhimaṇḍassa ca gayāya ca antare bhagavantaṃ addasa. Addhānamaggappaṭipannanti addhānamaggaṃ paṭipannaṃ.

11. “Between Gayā and the Bodhi”—Upaka saw the Blessed One between the Bodhi-maṇḍa and Gayā. `Addhānamaggappaṭipannaṃ` means proceeding on a long road.

Sabbābhibhūti sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ abhibhavitvā ṭhito. Sabbavidūti sabbaṃ catubhūmakadhammaṃ avediṃ aññāsiṃ. Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalittoti sabbesu tebhūmakadhammesu kilesalepena alitto. Sabbañjahoti sabbaṃ tebhūmakadhammaṃ jahitvā ṭhito. Taṇhakkhaye vimuttoti taṇhakkhaye nibbāne ārammaṇato vimutto. Sayaṃ abhiññāyāti sabbaṃ catubhūmakadhammaṃ attanāva jānitvā. Kamuddiseyyanti kaṃ aññaṃ “ayaṃ me ācariyo”ti uddiseyyaṃ.

`Sabbābhibhū` means I stand having overcome all phenomena of the three planes. `Sabbavidū` means I have understood and known all phenomena of the four planes. `Sabbesu dhammesu anūpalitta` means I am untainted by the stain of defilements in all phenomena of the three planes. `Sabbañjaha` means I stand having relinquished all phenomena of the three planes. `Taṇhakkhaye vimutta` means I am liberated through the destruction of craving, with Nibbāna as the object. `Sayaṃ abhiññāya` means having known all phenomena of the four planes by myself. `Kamuddiseyyaṃ` means whom else should I designate, saying, ‘This is my teacher’?

Na me ācariyo atthīti lokuttaradhamme mayhaṃ ācariyo nāma natthi. Natthi me paṭipuggaloti mayhaṃ paṭibhāgapuggalo nāma natthi. Sītibhūtoti sabbakilesagginibbāpanena sītibhūto. Kilesānaṃyeva nibbutattā nibbuto.

“Na me ācariyo atthi” means: in the supramundane Dhamma, I have no one called a teacher. “Natthi me paṭipuggala” means: there is no individual equal to me. “Sītibhūto” means: I have become cool by the extinguishing of the fire of all defilements. “Nibbuto” means: I am extinguished because the defilements themselves are extinguished.

Kāsīnaṃ [M 0.0246][V 0.0236] puranti kāsiraṭṭhe nagaraṃ. Āhañchaṃ amatadundubhinti dhammacakkappaṭilābhāya amatabheriṃ paharissāmīti gacchāmi.

“Kāsīnaṃ puraṃ” means: to the city of Bārāṇasī in the Kāsi country. “Āhañchaṃ amatadundubhiṃ” means: I go to beat the drum of the Deathless in order to obtain the Wheel of Dhamma.

Arahasi anantajinoti anantajino bhavituṃ yutto. Hupeyyapāvusoti āvuso evampi nāma bhaveyya. Sīsaṃ okampetvāti sīsaṃ cāletvā.

“Arahasi anantajino” means: you are fit to be the Infinite Conqueror. “Hupeyyā, āvuso” means: ‘Friend, it might be so.’ “Sīsaṃ okampetvā” means: having shaken his head.

12. Saṇṭhapesunti katikaṃ akaṃsu. Bāhullikoti cīvarabāhullādīnaṃ atthāya paṭipanno. Padhānavibbhantoti [P 5.0965] padhānato vibbhanto bhaṭṭho parihīno. Āvatto bāhullāyāti cīvarādibahulabhāvatthāya āvatto. Odahatha bhikkhave sotanti upanetha bhikkhave sotaṃ; sotindriyaṃ dhammasavanatthaṃ abhimukhaṃ karothāti attho. Amatamadhigatanti amataṃ nibbānaṃ mayā adhigatanti dasseti. Iriyāyāti dukkarairiyāya. Paṭipadāyāti dukkarapaṭipadāya. Abhijānātha me noti abhijānātha nu me samanupassatha. Evarūpaṃ bhāsitametanti etaṃ evarūpaṃ vākyaṃ bhāsitanti attho. Asakkhi kho bhagavā pañcavaggiye bhikkhū saññāpetunti “ahaṃ buddho”ti jānāpetuṃ asakkhi.

12. “Saṇṭhapesuṃ” means: they made an agreement. “Bāhullika” means: he practiced for the sake of abundance in robes and so on. “Padhānavibbhanta” means: strayed from the striving, fallen away, and declined. “Āvatto bāhullāya” means: he returned for the sake of an abundance of robes and so on. “Odahatha, bhikkhave, sotaṃ” means: ‘Monks, apply your ears; direct your faculty of hearing towards listening to the Dhamma’—this is the meaning. “Amataṃ adhigataṃ” means: he shows, ‘The Deathless, Nibbāna, has been realized by me.’ “Iriyāya” means: by the deportment of practicing austerities. “Paṭipadāya” means: by the practice of austerities. “Abhijānātha me no” means: ‘Do you recognize me? Do you see?’ “Evarūpaṃ bhāsitametaṃ” means: ‘Do you recognize that such a statement as this was spoken before?’—this is the meaning. “Asakkhi kho bhagavā pañcavaggiye bhikkhū saññāpetuṃ” means: he was able to make them know, ‘I am the Buddha.’

13. Cakkhukaraṇīti paññācakkhuṃ sandhāyāha. Ito paraṃ sabbaṃ padatthato uttānameva. Adhippāyānusandhiyojanādibhedato pana papañcasūdaniyā majjhimaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Ito paṭṭhāya hi ativitthārabhīrukassa mahājanassa cittaṃ anurakkhantā suttantakathaṃ avaṇṇayitvā vinayakathaṃyeva vaṇṇayissāma.

13. “Cakkhukaraṇī”: this was said referring to the eye of wisdom. From here onward, all terms are clear in their literal meaning. But regarding the distinctions of intention, connection, application, and so on, it should be understood according to the method explained in the Papañcasūdanī, the commentary to the Majjhima Nikāya. For, from this point onward, wishing to protect the minds of the great assembly who are fearful of excessive detail, we will comment only on the Vinaya discourse, without commenting on the Suttanta discourse.

18. Sāva tassa āyasmato upasampadā ahosīti āsāḷhīpuṇṇamāya aṭṭhārasahi devatākoṭīhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhitassa “ehi bhikkhū”ti bhagavato vacanena abhinipphannā sāva tassa āyasmato ehibhikkhūpasampadā ahosi.

18. “Sāva tassa āyasmato upasampadā ahosi” means: that very ordination of the venerable Koṇḍañña, which was accomplished by the Blessed One’s words “Come, monk,” on the full-moon day of Āsāḷha, when he was established in the fruit of stream-entry along with eighteen crores of devas and brahmās, was indeed the ‘Come, monk’ ordination.

19. Atha kho āyasmato ca vappassāti ādimhi vappattherassa pāṭipadadivase dhammacakkhuṃ udapādi, bhaddiyattherassa dutiyadivase, mahānāmattherassa tatiyadivase, assajittherassa catutthiyanti. Imesañca pana [M 0.0247] bhikkhūnaṃ kammaṭṭhānesu uppannamalavisodhanatthaṃ bhagavā antovihāreyeva ahosi. Uppanne uppanne kammaṭṭhānamale ākāsena gantvā malaṃ vinodesi. Pakkhassa pana pañcamiyaṃ sabbe te ekato sannipātetvā anattasuttena ovadi. Tena vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā pañcavaggiye”tiādi.

19. Regarding “Atha kho āyasmato ca Vappassā” and so on, the determination should be understood thus: for the venerable Vappa, the Dhamma-eye arose on the first day of the waning moon; for the venerable Bhaddiya, on the second day; for the venerable Mahānāma, on the third day; and for the venerable Assaji, on the fourth. And the Blessed One remained within the monastery to cleanse the impurities that arose in the meditation subjects of these monks. Whenever an impurity in the meditation subject arose, he went through the air and removed the impurity. Then, on the fifth day of the waning fortnight, having gathered all of them together, he instructed them with the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta. Therefore it was said by the compilers of the canon, “Then the Blessed One addressed the group of five,” and so on.

24. Tena [V 0.0237] kho pana samayena cha loke arahanto hontīti pañcamiyā pakkhassa lokasmiṃ cha manussā arahanto hontīti attho.

24. “Tena kho pana samayena cha loke arahanto honti” means: on the fifth day of the waning fortnight, there were six human arahants in the world—this is the meaning.

Pañcavaggiyakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Group of Five is concluded.

Pabbajjākathā

The Discourse on the Going Forth

31. Pubbānupubbakānanti [P 5.0966] paveṇivasena porāṇānuporāṇānanti attho. Tena kho pana samayena ekasaṭṭhi loke arahanto hontīti purimā cha ime ca pañcapaññāsāti antovassamhiyeva ekasaṭṭhi manussā arahanto hontīti attho.

“Of a continuous lineage” means: by way of succession, of families that follow in succession to ancient families. “At that time there were sixty-one arahants in the world” means: the former six and these fifty-five, thus within the rains-retreat itself, sixty-one men became arahants.

Tatra yasaādīnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ ayaṃ pubbayogo – atīte kira pañcapaññāsajanā sahāyakā vaggabandhena puññāni karontā anāthasarīrāni paṭijaggantā vicaranti, te ekadivasaṃ gabbhiniṃ itthiṃ kālaṃkataṃ disvā “jhāpessāmā”ti susānaṃ nīhariṃsu. Tesu pañca jane “tumhe jhāpethā”ti susāne ṭhapetvā sesā gāmaṃ paviṭṭhā. Yaso dārako taṃ sarīraṃ vijjhitvā parivattetvā ca jhāpayamāno asubhasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. So itaresampi catunnaṃ janānaṃ “passatha bho imaṃ asuciṃ paṭikūla”nti dassesi. Tepi tattha asubhasaññaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Te pañcapi janā gāmaṃ gantvā sesasahāyakānaṃ kathayiṃsu. Yaso pana dārako gehampi gantvā mātāpitūnnañca bhariyāya ca kathesi. Te sabbepi asubhaṃ bhāvayiṃsu. Ayametesaṃ pubbayogo. Tenāyasmato yasassa nāṭakajanesu susānasaññāyeva uppajji, tāyeva ca upanissayasampattiyā sabbesaṃ visesādhigamo nibbattīti.

31. Herein, this was the past meritorious deed of the clansmen beginning with Yasa: It is said that in the past, fifty-five people who were companions went about performing meritorious deeds by forming a group and taking care of helpless bodies. One day, seeing a pregnant woman who had died, they carried her to the charnel ground, thinking, “We will cremate her.” Leaving five men at the charnel ground, saying, “You cremate her,” the rest entered the village. The boy Yasa, while cremating that body, piercing it and turning it over, obtained the perception of foulness. He showed it to the other four men, saying, “Behold, sirs, this impure, repulsive thing.” They too obtained the perception of foulness there. All five men went to the village and told their other companions. The boy Yasa, for his part, also went home and told his parents and his wife. All of them developed the meditation on foulness. This was their past meritorious deed. Because of that, for the Venerable Yasa, the perception of a charnel ground itself arose in regard to the female entertainers; and through that very perfection of supporting conditions, the attainment of distinction was accomplished for all of them.

Atha kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesīti bhagavā yāva pacchimakattikapuṇṇamā, tāva bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanto ekadivasaṃ te khīṇāsave saṭṭhi bhikkhū āmantesi.

“Then the Blessed One addressed the monks” means: the Blessed One, while dwelling in Bārāṇasī until the last full moon day of the Kattika month, one day addressed those sixty monks whose taints were destroyed.

32. Dibbā [M 0.0248] nāma dibbesu visayesu lobhapāsā. Mānusā nāma mānusakesu visayesu lobhapāsā. Mā ekena dveti ekena maggena dve mā agamittha. Assavanatāti assavanatāya. Parihāyantīti anadhigataṃ nādhigacchantā visesādhigamato parihāyanti.

“Divine” means: the snares of greed concerning divine sense-objects. “Human” means: the snares of greed concerning human sense-objects. “Let not two go by one” means: ‘Let not two of you go by one path.’ “Due to not hearing” means: because of not hearing. “They decline” means: not attaining what has not yet been attained, they decline from the attainment of distinction.

33. Antakāti [V 0.0238] lāmaka hīnasatta. Antalikkhacaroti rāgapāsaṃ sandhāyāha. Tañhi so “antalikkhacaro”ti mantvā āha.

32. “Antaka” means: a base, inferior being. Regarding “one who moves in the sky,” he said this referring to the snare of passion. Indeed, he said this, thinking of it as ‘one who moves in the sky.’

34. Nānādisā nānājanapadāti nānādisato ca nānājanapadato ca. Anujānāmi bhikkhave tumheva dāni tāsu tāsu disāsu tesu tesu janapadesu [P 5.0967] pabbājethātiādimhi pabbajjāpekkhaṃ kulaputtaṃ pabbājentena ye parato “na bhikkhave pañcahi ābādhehi phuṭṭho pabbājetabbo”tiādiṃ katvā yāva “na andhamūgabadhiro pabbājetabbo”ti evaṃ paṭikkhittā puggalā, te vajjetvā pabbajjādosavirahito puggalo pabbājetabbo. Sopi ca mātāpitūhi anuññātoyeva. Tassa anujānanalakkhaṇaṃ “na bhikkhave ananuññāto mātāpitūhi putto pabbājetabbo, yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassā”ti etasmiṃ sutte vaṇṇayissāma.

34. ‘From various directions and various districts’ means from various directions and from various districts. In the passage beginning, ‘I allow you, monks, to now give the going forth in those various directions and those various districts,’ when a preceptor is ordaining a clansman who is a postulant, he should ordain a person who is free from the faults of ordination, having avoided those persons who are rejected later in the text, from the passage beginning, ‘Monks, one afflicted with five diseases should not be ordained,’ up to ‘A blind, mute, or deaf person should not be ordained.’ And that person, too, should be ordained only if permitted by his parents. We will explain the characteristic of their permission in the discourse that says, ‘Monks, a son who is not permitted by his parents should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrong-doing.’

Evaṃ pabbajjādosavirahitaṃ mātāpitūhi anuññātaṃ pabbājentenāpi ca sace acchinnakeso hoti, ekasīmāya ca aññepi bhikkhū atthi, kesacchedanatthāya bhaṇḍukammaṃ āpucchitabbaṃ. Tassa āpucchanākāraṃ “anujānāmi, bhikkhave, saṅghaṃ apaloketuṃ bhaṇḍukammāyā”ti ettha vaṇṇayissāma. Sace okāso hoti, sayaṃ pabbājetabbo. Sace uddesaparipucchādīhi byāvaṭo hoti, okāsaṃ na labhati, eko daharabhikkhu vattabbo “etaṃ pabbājehī”ti. Avuttopi ce daharabhikkhu upajjhāyaṃ uddissa pabbājeti, vaṭṭati. Sace daharabhikkhu natthi, sāmaṇeropi vattabbo “etaṃ khaṇḍasīmaṃ netvā pabbājetvā kāsāyāni acchādetvā ehī”ti. Saraṇāni pana sayaṃ dātabbāni. Evaṃ bhikkhunāva pabbajito hoti. Purisañhi bhikkhuto añño pabbājetuṃ na labhati, mātugāmaṃ bhikkhunito añño. Sāmaṇero pana sāmaṇerī vā āṇattiyā kāsāyāni dātuṃ labhati. Kesoropanaṃ yena kenaci kataṃ sukataṃ.

Furthermore, when ordaining one who is thus free from the faults of ordination and has been permitted by his parents, if he has uncut hair and there are other monks within the same boundary, permission should be asked for the act of making him bald. We will explain the manner of asking for this in the passage, ‘I allow, monks, to ask the Saṅgha for the act of making one bald.’ If there is an opportunity, he should be ordained by the preceptor himself. If the preceptor is occupied with recitation, questioning, and so on, and does not get an opportunity, a junior monk should be told, ‘Ordain this one.’ Even if the junior monk is not told, if he ordains him for the sake of the preceptor, it is permissible. If there is no junior monk, a novice may also be told, ‘Take this one to a temporary boundary, ordain him, clothe him in the ochre robes, and come back.’ The refuges, however, should be given by the preceptor himself. In this way, he is ordained by a monk. For another than a monk does not get to ordain a man, and another than a nun does not get to ordain a woman. A male novice or a female novice, however, may give the ochre robes by command. The shaving of the hair, done by anyone whatsoever, is well done.

Sace [M 0.0249] pana bhabbarūpo hoti sahetuko ñāto yasassī kulaputto, okāsaṃ katvāpi sayameva pabbājetabbo. “Mattikāmuṭṭhiṃ gahetvā nhāyitvā kese temetvā āgacchāhī”ti ca pana na vissajjetabbo. Pabbajitukāmānañhi paṭhamaṃ balavaussāho hoti, pacchā pana kāsāyāni ca kesaharaṇasatthakañca disvā utrasanti, ettoyeva palāyanti, tasmā sayameva nahānatitthaṃ netvā sace nātidaharo hoti, “nahāhī”ti vattabbo. Kesā panassa sayameva mattikaṃ gahetvā dhovitabbā. Daharakumārako pana sayaṃ udakaṃ otaritvā gomayamattikāhi ghaṃsitvā nahāpetabbo. Sacepissa kacchu vā piḷakā vā honti, yathā mātā puttaṃ [P 5.0968] na jigucchati[V 0.0239], evameva ajigucchantena sādhukaṃ hatthapādasīsāni ghaṃsitvā nahāpetabbo. Kasmā? Ettakena hi upakārena kulaputtā ācariyupajjhāyesu ca sāsane ca balavasinehā tibbagāravā anivattidhammā honti, uppannaṃ anabhiratiṃ vinodetvā therabhāvaṃ pāpuṇanti, kataññū katavedino honti.

If, however, the clansman is of a nature fit for liberation, has the supporting conditions, is well-known and of high repute, then even by making an opportunity, he should be ordained by the preceptor himself. And he should not be sent away with instructions like, ‘Take a lump of clay, bathe, wet your hair, and come back.’ For those who wish to go forth, the initial enthusiasm is strong, but afterwards, upon seeing the ochre robes and the razor for removing the hair, they become frightened and run away from that very spot. Therefore, the preceptor himself should take him to the bathing place, and if he is not too young, he should be told, ‘Bathe.’ His hair, however, should be washed by the preceptor himself after taking some clay. A young boy, on the other hand, should be bathed by the preceptor himself, who should enter the water and scrub him with cow-dung and clay. Even if he has scabies or boils, he should be bathed without disgust, thoroughly scrubbing his hands, feet, and head, just as a mother is not disgusted with her son. Why? Because with this much assistance, clansmen become possessed of strong affection and keen respect for their teachers and preceptors and for the Teaching, and they become of an un-reverting nature. Dispelling any discontent that arises, they reach the state of an elder, and they become grateful and appreciative.

Evaṃ nahāpanakāle pana kesamassuṃ oropanakāle vā “tvaṃ ñāto yasassī, idāni mayaṃ taṃ nissāya paccayehi na kilamissāmā”ti na vattabbo, aññāpi aniyyānikakathā na kathetabbā. Atha khvassa “āvuso, suṭṭhu upadhārehi satiṃ upaṭṭhāpehī”ti vatvā tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ, ācikkhantena ca vaṇṇasaṇṭhānagandhāsayokāsavasena asucijegucchapaṭikūlabhāvaṃ nijjīvanissattabhāvaṃ vā pākaṭaṃ karontena ācikkhitabbaṃ. Sace hi so pubbe madditasaṅkhāro hoti bhāvitabhāvano, kaṇṭakavedhāpekkho viya paripakkagaṇḍo, sūriyuggamanāpekkhaṃ viya ca pariṇatapadumaṃ, athassa āraddhamatte kammaṭṭhānamanasikāre indāsani viya pabbate kilesapabbate cuṇṇayamānaṃyeva ñāṇaṃ pavattati, khuraggeyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Ye hi keci khuragge arahattaṃ pattā, sabbe te evarūpaṃ savanaṃ labhitvā kalyāṇamittena ācariyena dinnanayaṃ nissāya no anissāya. Tasmāssa āditova evarūpī kathā kathetabbāti.

Furthermore, at the time of bathing or at the time of shaving the hair and beard, one should not say, ‘You are well-known and have a large following; now, relying on you, we will not be troubled for requisites.’ Nor should any other speech not conducive to release be spoken. Rather, having said to him, ‘Friend, consider this well and establish mindfulness,’ the meditation subject of the five parts of the body should be explained. And the one explaining should explain it by making clear its state of being impure, disgusting, and repulsive by way of its color, shape, smell, origin, and location, or its state of being lifeless and without a soul. For if he has previously trained his dispositions and developed his mind, like a ripe boil awaiting the piercing of a thorn, or like a mature lotus awaiting the rising of the sun, then as soon as he begins to apply his mind to the meditation subject, knowledge arises, crushing the mountains of defilements just like Indra's thunderbolt on a mountain, and he attains Arahantship right at the razor's edge. Indeed, all those who have attained Arahantship at the razor's edge have done so by receiving such a hearing and by relying on the method given by a teacher who is a good friend; they did not attain it without relying on one. Therefore, from the very beginning, such a discourse should be given to him.

Kesesu pana oropitesu haliddicuṇṇena vā gandhacuṇṇena vā sīsañca sarīrañca ubbaṭṭetvā gihigandhaṃ apanetvā kāsāyāni tikkhattuṃ vā dvikkhattuṃ [M 0.0250] vā sakiṃ vā paṭiggāhetabbo. Athāpissa hatthe adatvā ācariyo vā upajjhāyo vā sayameva acchādeti, vaṭṭati. Sacepi aññaṃ daharaṃ vā sāmaṇeraṃ vā upāsakaṃ vā āṇāpeti “āvuso, etāni kāsāyāni gahetvā etaṃ acchādehī”ti taṃyeva vā āṇāpeti “etāni gahetvā acchādehī”ti sabbaṃ vaṭṭati. Sabbaṃ tena bhikkhunāva dinnaṃ hoti.

Furthermore, when the hair has been shaved off, after rubbing the head and body with turmeric powder or scented powder to remove the householder’s odor, he should be made to receive the ochre robes three times, or twice, or once. Then, without placing them in his hands, if the teacher or preceptor himself clothes him, it is allowable. And if he instructs another—a junior monk, a novice, or a layman—saying, ‘Friend, take these ochre robes and clothe him,’ or if he instructs that very candidate, ‘Take these and clothe yourself,’ all this is allowable. Everything is considered to have been given by that monk.

Yaṃ pana nivāsanaṃ vā pārupanaṃ vā anāṇattiyā [P 5.0969] nivāseti vā pārupati vā, taṃ apanetvā puna dātabbaṃ. Bhikkhunā hi sahatthena vā āṇattiyā vā dinnameva kāsāvaṃ vaṭṭati, adinnaṃ na vaṭṭati, sacepi tasseva santakaṃ hoti, ko pana vādo upajjhāyamūlake! Ayaṃ “paṭhamaṃ kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādāpetvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ kārāpetvā”ti ettha vinicchayo.

Furthermore, whatever lower robe or upper robe he puts on or wears without instruction, that must be removed and given again. For an ochre robe is allowable only if it is given by a monk, either with his own hand or by his instruction; what is not given is not allowable. Even if it is the candidate's own property, it is not allowable if not given—what then needs to be said in the case of a robe that originates from the preceptor! This is the ruling here on the phrase, ‘having first had the hair and beard shaved off, having had him clothed in ochre robes, having had the upper robe arranged over one shoulder...’

Bhikkhūnaṃ [V 0.0240] pāde vandāpetvāti ye tattha sannipatitā bhikkhū, tesaṃ pāde vandāpetvā; atha saraṇaggahaṇatthaṃ ukkuṭikaṃ nisīdāpetvā añjaliṃ paggaṇhāpetvā evaṃ vadehīti vattabbo. “Yamahaṃ vadāmi, taṃ vadehī”ti vattabbo. Athassa upajjhāyena vā ācariyena vā “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”tiādinā nayena saraṇāni dātabbāni yathāvuttapaṭipāṭiyāva na uppaṭipāṭiyā. Sace hi ekapadampi ekakkharampi uppaṭipāṭiyā deti, buddhaṃ saraṇaṃyeva vā tikkhattuṃ datvā puna itaresu ekekaṃ tikkhattuṃ deti, adinnāni honti saraṇāni.

Regarding ‘having made him pay homage at the feet of the monks’: having made him pay homage at the feet of whatever monks have assembled there. Then, for the purpose of taking the refuges, having made him sit in a squatting position and raise his joined palms, he should be told, ‘Speak thus.’ Or he should be told, ‘Say what I say.’ Then the preceptor or the teacher should give him the refuges by the method beginning with ‘I go to the Buddha for refuge,’ in the exact sequence as it has been stated, not out of sequence. For if he gives even one word or one syllable out of sequence, or if, having given ‘I go to the Buddha for refuge’ three times, he then gives each of the others three times, the refuges are considered not given.

Imañca pana saraṇagamanūpasampadaṃ paṭikkhipitvā anuññātaupasampadā ekato suddhiyā vaṭṭati. Sāmaṇerapabbajjā pana ubhatosuddhiyāva vaṭṭati, no ekato suddhiyā. Tasmā upasampadāya sace ācariyo ñattidosañceva kammavācādosañca vajjetvā kammaṃ karoti, sukataṃ hoti. Pabbajjāya pana imāni tīṇi saraṇāni bukāradhakārādīnaṃ byañjanānaṃ ṭhānakaraṇasampadaṃ ahāpenteneva ācariyenapi antevāsikenapi vattabbāni. Sace ācariyo vattuṃ sakkoti, antevāsiko na sakkoti; antevāsiko vā sakkoti, ācariyo na sakkoti; ubhopi vā na sakkonti, na vaṭṭati. Sace pana ubhopi sakkonti, vaṭṭati.

Furthermore, this higher ordination by going for refuge having been rejected, the authorized higher ordination is valid with purity on one side. The novice ordination, however, is valid only with purity on both sides, not with purity on one side. Therefore, in the higher ordination, if the teacher performs the formal act while avoiding faults in the motion and in the proclamation, it is well-done. In the novice ordination, however, these three refuges must be spoken by both the teacher and the pupil without failing in the perfection of the place of articulation and the articulator for consonants such as ‘bu’, ‘dha’, and so on. If the teacher is able to speak them but the pupil is not; or the pupil is able but the teacher is not; or both are not able, it is not allowable. But if both are able, it is allowable.

Imāni [M 0.0251] ca pana dadamānena “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti evaṃ ekasambandhāni anunāsikantāni vā katvā dātabbāni, “buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti evaṃ vicchinditvā makārantāni vā katvā dātabbāni. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ nāmaṃ sāvetvā “ahaṃ bhante buddharakkhito yāvajīvaṃ buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ ekaaṭṭhakathāyampi natthi, pāḷiyampi na vuttaṃ, tesaṃ rucimattameva, tasmā na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi tathā avadantassa saraṇaṃ kuppatīti.
