Idāni imaṃ adiṭṭhapubbaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvāpi tumhākaṃ pāde vandāmi, ayaṃ me tatiyavandanā”ti.

While they were seated thus, the Blessed One, discerning their inclination, thought, 'My relatives do not pay homage to me. Very well, I will make them pay homage.' Then, entering the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for supernormal powers, he emerged and rose into the sky by his supernormal power. As if scattering the dust of his feet on their heads, he performed a miracle similar to the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree. Seeing this marvel, the king said, 'Blessed One, on your auspicious day, when you were brought for the purpose of paying homage to the brahmin, even having seen your feet turn around and become established on the brahmin's head, I paid homage to you—this was my first homage. On the day of the Ploughing Ceremony, while you were lying on the glorious couch in the shade of the Jambu tree, even having seen the shade of the Jambu tree not move, I paid homage to your feet—this was my second homage. Now, even having seen this miracle, never seen before, I pay homage to your feet—this is my third homage.'

Suddhodanamahārājena pana vandite bhagavati avanditvā ṭhito nāma ekasākiyopi nāhosi, sabbeyeva vandiṃsu. Iti bhagavā ñātayo vandāpetvā ākāsato oruyha paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisinne bhagavati sikhāppatto ñātisamāgamo ahosi, sabbe ekaggā sannipatiṃsu. Tato mahāmegho pokkharavassaṃ vassi, tambavaṇṇamudakaṃ heṭṭhā viravantaṃ gacchati. Kassaci sarīre ekabindumattampi na patati, taṃ disvā sabbe acchariyabbhutajātā ahesuṃ. Bhagavā “na idāneva mayhaṃ ñātisamāgame pokkharavassaṃ vassati, atītepi vassī”ti imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā vessantarajātakaṃ kathesi. Dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sabbe uṭṭhāya vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Ekopi rājā vā rājamahāmatto vā “sve amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā gato nāma natthi.

Now, when the Blessed One was paid homage to by King Suddhodana, there was not even a single Sākyan who stood without paying homage; all indeed paid homage. Thus, the Blessed One, having made his relatives pay homage, descended from the sky and sat on the prepared seat. When the Blessed One was seated, the gathering of relatives reached its peak, and all gathered with a single focus. Then a great cloud rained a lotus-rain. Reddish-colored water flowed below, making a sound. Not even a single drop fell on anyone's body. Seeing that, all became filled with wonder and amazement. The Blessed One said, 'It is not only now that this lotus-rain falls at my gathering of relatives; it has rained in the past as well.' And on this occasion, he related the Vessantara Jātaka. Having heard the Dhamma discourse, all rose, paid homage, circumambulated respectfully, and departed. There was not a single king or royal minister who departed after saying, 'Tomorrow, accept our alms.'

Bhagavā dutiyadivase vīsatibhikkhusahassaparivāro kapilavatthuṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi, na koci paccuggantvā nimantesi vā pattaṃ vā aggahesi. Bhagavā indakhīle ṭhito āvajjesi – “kathaṃ nu kho pubbe buddhā kulanagare [P 5.1007] piṇḍāya cariṃsu, kiṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā issarajanānaṃ [V 0.0274] gharāni agamaṃsu, udāhu sapadānacārikaṃ cariṃsū”ti. Tato ekabuddhassapi uppaṭipāṭiyā gamanaṃ adisvā “mayāpi idāni ayameva vaṃso ayaṃ paveṇī paggahetabbā, āyatiñca me sāvakāpi mameva anusikkhantā piṇḍacāriyavattaṃ pūressantī”ti koṭiyaṃ niviṭṭhagehato paṭṭhāya sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya carati. “Ayyo kira siddhatthakumāro piṇḍāya caratī”ti catubhūmakādīsu pāsādesu sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā mahājano dassanabyāvaṭo ahosi. Rāhulamātāpi devī “ayyaputto kira imasmiṃyeva nagare mahatā rājānubhāvena [M 0.0289] suvaṇṇasivikādīhi vicaritvā idāni kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyavatthavasano kapālahattho piṇḍāya carati, “sobhati nu kho no vā”ti sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokayamānā bhagavantaṃ nānāvirāgasamujjalāya sarīrappabhāya nagaravīthiyo obhāsetvā buddhasiriyā virocamānaṃ disvā uṇhīsato paṭṭhāya yāva pādatalā narasīhagāthāhi nāma aṭṭhahi gāthāhi abhitthavitvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “tumhākaṃ putto piṇḍāya caratī”ti rañño ārocesi. Rājā saṃviggahadayo hatthena sāṭakaṃ saṇṭhāpayamāno turitaturitaṃ nikkhamitvā vegena gantvā bhagavato purato ṭhatvā āha – “kiṃ bhante amhe lajjāpetha, kimatthaṃ piṇḍāya caratha, kiṃ ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ na sakkā bhattaṃ laddhunti evaṃsaññino ahuvatthā”ti. Vaṃsacārittametaṃ mahārāja amhākanti. Nanu bhante amhākaṃ mahāsammatakhattiyavaṃso nāma vaṃso, tattha ca ekakhattiyopi bhikkhācāro nāma natthīti. Ayaṃ mahārāja vaṃso nāma tava vaṃso, amhākaṃ pana buddhavaṃso vaṃso nāma, sabbabuddhā ca piṇḍacārikā ahesunti antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitova –

On the second day, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand monks, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. No one came forward to invite him or take his bowl. Standing near the city-gate post, the Blessed One reflected: "How indeed did the Buddhas of the past go for alms in the city of their kinsmen? Did they go out of sequence to the houses of the powerful, or did they go on an alms-round in uninterrupted sequence?" Then, not seeing any instance of a single Buddha going out of sequence, he thought, "Now, I too must uphold this very lineage, this very tradition. And in the future, my disciples, following my example, will fulfill the practice of the alms-round." Thus, starting from the house situated at the end of the street, he went for alms in uninterrupted sequence. The great populace exclaimed, "It is said the noble Prince Siddhattha is going for alms!" and from palaces of four stories and so on, they opened the lion-windows and were busy watching. The queen, Rāhula's mother, also thought, "My noble lord, who once wandered in this very city with great royal majesty in golden palanquins and the like, has now shaved his hair and beard, is wearing saffron robes, and with a bowl in hand, wanders for alms. Does he look beautiful or not?" Opening the lion-window and looking, she saw the Blessed One shining with the splendor of a Buddha, illuminating the city streets with the radiance of his body, brilliant with various colors. She then praised him from the topknot of his head down to the soles of his feet with the eight verses known as the 'Narasīha Gāthā'. Having praised him, she went to the king and informed him, "Your son is wandering for alms!" The king, with an agitated heart, adjusting his lower garment with his hand, went out in great haste. Going quickly, he stood before the Blessed One and said: "Venerable sir, why do you shame us? Why do you go for alms? Is it because you thought it was not possible to obtain food for so many monks?" "This, great king, is the practice of our lineage." "But venerable sir, is not our lineage the great Mahāsammata Khattiya lineage? And in it, there is not a single khattiya who was one to go for alms!" "Great king, that lineage is your lineage. But our lineage is the lineage of the Buddhas, and all Buddhas were alms-wanderers." And standing in the middle of the street—

“Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya, dhammaṃ sucaritaṃ care;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti.

One should arise, and not be heedless! One should practice the good conduct of the alms-round. One who practices this conduct dwells happily, in this world and in the next.

Imaṃ [P 5.1008] gāthamāha. Gāthāpariyosāne rājā sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchākāsi.

He spoke this verse. At the end of the verse, the king realized the fruit of stream-entry.

“Dhammaṃ care sucaritaṃ, na naṃ duccaritaṃ care;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti.

One should practice the good conduct of the alms-round; one should not practice it badly. One who practices this conduct dwells happily, in this world and in the next.

Imaṃ pana gāthaṃ sutvā sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi, dhammapālajātakaṃ sutvā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi, maraṇasamaye setacchattassa heṭṭhā sirisayane nipannoyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Araññavāsena padhānānuyogakiccaṃ rañño nāhosi.

Now, having heard this verse, he was established in the fruit of once-returning. Upon hearing the Dhammapāla Jātaka, he was established in the fruit of non-returning. At the time of death, while lying on the glorious couch beneath the white parasol, he attained Arahantship. For the king, there was no need for the task of striving by dwelling in the forest.

Sotāpattiphalañca [V 0.0275] sacchikatvā eva pana bhagavato pattaṃ gahetvā saparisaṃ bhagavantaṃ mahāpāsādaṃ āropetvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisi. Bhattakiccāvasāne sabbaṃ itthāgāraṃ āgantvā bhagavantaṃ vandi ṭhapetvā rāhulamātaraṃ. Sā pana “gaccha ayyaputtaṃ vandāhī”ti parijanena vuccamānāpi “sace mayhaṃ guṇo atthi, sayameva ayyaputto āgamissati[M 0.0290], āgataṃ naṃ vandissāmī”ti vatvā na agamāsi. Atha bhagavā rājānaṃ pattaṃ gāhāpetvā dvīhi aggasāvakehi saddhiṃ rājadhītāya sirigabbhaṃ gantvā “rājadhītā yathāruciyā vandamānā na kiñci vattabbā”ti vatvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Sā vegena āgantvā gopphakesu gahetvā pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ sīsaṃ parivattetvā parivattetvā yathājjhāsayaṃ vandi.

And having realized the fruit of stream-entry, he took the Blessed One’s bowl, had the Blessed One together with his retinue ascend to the great palace, and served him with excellent hard and soft food. At the conclusion of the meal, the entire women's quarters, except for Rāhula’s mother, came and paid homage to the Blessed One. Although she was told by her attendants, “Go and pay homage to the noble lord,” she said, “If there is any virtue in me, the noble lord himself will come. When he has come, I will pay homage to him,” and she did not go. Then the Blessed One, having had the king take his bowl, went with the two chief disciples to the princess’s glorious chamber, and saying, “While the princess pays homage according to her wish, nothing should be said,” he sat down on the prepared seat. She came quickly, grasped his ankles, and rolling her head again and again on the top of his feet, paid homage according to her heart's desire.

Rājā rājadhītāya bhagavati sinehabahumānādiguṇasampattiṃ kathesi. Bhagavā “anacchariyaṃ mahārāja yaṃ idāni paripakke ñāṇe tayā rakkhiyamānā rājadhītā attānaṃ rakkhi, sā pubbe anārakkhā pabbatapāde vicaramānā aparipakke ñāṇe attānaṃ rakkhī”ti vatvā candakinnarījātakaṃ kathesi.

The king spoke of the princess's endowment with virtues such as affection and great reverence for the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, “It is not wonderful, great king, that now, with her wisdom mature, the princess, being protected by you, has protected herself. In the past, while unprotected and wandering at the foot of a mountain when her wisdom was immature, she protected herself,” and he related the Candakinnarī Jātaka.

Taṃdivasameva ca nandarājakumārassa kesavissajjanaṃ paṭṭabandho gharamaṅgalaṃ āvāhamaṅgalaṃ chattamaṅgalanti pañca mahāmaṅgalāni honti. Bhagavā nandaṃ pattaṃ gāhāpetvā maṅgalaṃ vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Janapadakalyāṇī kumāraṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “tuvaṭaṃ kho ayyaputta āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā gīvaṃ pasāretvā olokesi. Sopi bhagavantaṃ “pattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti [P 5.1009] vattuṃ avisahamāno vihāraṃyeva agamāsi. Taṃ anicchamānaṃyeva bhagavā pabbājesi. Iti bhagavā kapilapuraṃ āgantvā dutiyadivase nandaṃ pabbājesi.

And on that very day, five great ceremonies for Prince Nanda occurred: the unbinding of the top-knot, the tying of the royal headband, the house-entering ceremony, the wedding ceremony, and the raising of the parasol. The Blessed One, having had Nanda take his bowl, spoke a blessing, rose from his seat, and departed. Seeing the prince departing, Janapadakalyāṇī said, “May you return quickly, noble lord,” and stretching her neck, she looked on. He also, not daring to say to the Blessed One, “Take the bowl,” went right to the monastery. The Blessed One gave the going-forth to him even while he was unwilling. Thus, having come to Kapilapura, the Blessed One gave the going-forth to Nanda on the second day.

Sattame divase rāhulamātā kumāraṃ alaṅkaritvā bhagavato santikaṃ pesesi – “passa tāta etaṃ vīsatisahassasamaṇaparivutaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ brahmarūpavaṇṇaṃ samaṇaṃ, ayaṃ te pitā, etassa mahantā nidhayo ahesuṃ, tyassa nikkhamanato paṭṭhāya na passāma, gaccha naṃ dāyajjaṃ yāca, ahaṃ tāta kumāro chattaṃ ussāpetvā cakkavattī bhavissāmi, dhanena me attho, dhanaṃ me dehi, sāmiko hi putto pitusantakassā”ti. Rāhulakumāro bhagavato santikaṃ gantvāva pitusinehaṃ paṭilabhitvā haṭṭhacitto “sukhā te samaṇa chāyā”ti vatvā aññampi bahuṃ attano anurūpaṃ vadanto aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā katabhattakicco anumodanaṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Kumāropi “dāyajjaṃ me samaṇa dehi, dāyajjaṃ me samaṇa dehī”ti bhagavantaṃ anubandhi. Tena vuttaṃ [V 0.0276] – “anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno yena kapilavatthu…pe… dāyajjaṃ me samaṇa dehī”ti.

On the seventh day, Rāhula’s mother adorned the prince and sent him to the Blessed One, saying: “Look, dear son, at this ascetic surrounded by twenty thousand ascetics, with a golden complexion and the appearance of Brahmā. He is your father. He had great treasures, but from the day of his renunciation, we have not seen them. Go and ask him for the inheritance, saying: ‘Father, I am the prince. Having raised the parasol, I will become a wheel-turning monarch. I have need of wealth; give me my wealth. For a son is the master of his father’s property.’ ” Prince Rāhula, upon going to the Blessed One, received a father’s affection and, with a joyful mind, said, “Pleasant is your shadow, ascetic,” and stood there speaking many other things appropriate for himself. The Blessed One, having completed his meal and given the anumodanā, rose from his seat and departed. The prince also followed the Blessed One, saying, “Give me my inheritance, ascetic! Give me my inheritance, ascetic!” For that reason it was said: “Wandering on tour by stages, to Kapilavatthu… and so on… ‘Give me my inheritance, ascetic!’”

Atha [M 0.0291] kho bhagavā āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesīti bhagavā kumāraṃ na nivattāpesi, parijanopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ gacchantaṃ nivattetuṃ na visahati. Atha ārāmaṃ gantvā “yaṃ ayaṃ pitusantakaṃ dhanaṃ icchati, taṃ vaṭṭānugataṃ savighātakaṃ, handassa bodhimaṇḍe paṭiladdhaṃ sattavidhaṃ ariyadhanaṃ demi, lokuttaradāyajjassa naṃ sāmikaṃ karomī”ti āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi. Āmantetvā ca panāha – “tena hi tvaṃ sāriputta rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājehī”ti. Yasmā ayaṃ dāyajjaṃ yācati, tasmā naṃ lokuttaradāyajjapaṭilābhāya pabbājehīti attho.

As to the text, Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Sāriputta: The Blessed One did not make the prince turn back, and his retinue also did not dare to make him turn back as he was going with the Blessed One. Then, having gone to the monastery, the Blessed One thought: “The wealth belonging to his father that he desires follows the round of existence and is fraught with affliction. Come now, I shall give him the sevenfold noble wealth that I obtained at the seat of enlightenment. I shall make him the owner of the supramundane inheritance.” Thus thinking, he addressed the Venerable Sāriputta. And having addressed him, he said: “Well then, Sāriputta, you give the going-forth to Prince Rāhula.” The meaning is: “Because he asks for an inheritance, therefore, give him the going-forth for the sake of obtaining the supramundane inheritance.”

Idāni yā sā bhagavatā bārāṇasiyaṃ tīhi saraṇagamanehi pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca anuññātā, tato yasmā upasampadaṃ paṭikkhipitvā garubhāve ṭhapetvā ñatticatutthena kammena upasampadā anuññātā, pabbajjā pana neva paṭikkhittā, na puna anuññātā, tasmā anāgate bhikkhūnaṃ vimati uppajjissati – “ayaṃ pabbajjā nāma pubbe upasampadāsadisā, kiṃ nu kho idānipi upasampadā viya kammavācāya [P 5.1010] eva kattabbā, udāhu saraṇagamanehī”ti. Imañca panatthaṃ viditvā bhagavā puna tīhi saraṇagamanehi sāmaṇerapabbajjaṃ anujānitukāmo, tasmā dhammasenāpati taṃ bhagavato ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā bhagavantaṃ puna pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetukāmo āha – “kathāhaṃ bhante rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājemī”ti.

Now, the Blessed One had permitted in Bārāṇasī a going-forth and a higher ordination by means of the three refuges. Since, from that time, the higher ordination was rejected and, having been established as a weighty matter, was permitted by means of a formal act with a motion as the fourth part, while the going-forth, on the other hand, was neither rejected nor permitted again, therefore, in the future, a doubt will arise for the monks: “This going-forth was formerly like the higher ordination. Should it now be performed by a formal act, like the higher ordination, or by means of the refuges?” And the Blessed One, knowing this matter, wished to permit the novice going-forth by means of the three refuges again. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma, knowing that intention of the Blessed One and wishing to have the Blessed One permit the going-forth again, said: “How, venerable sir, shall I give the going-forth to Prince Rāhula?”

Atha kho āyasmā sāriputto rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājesīti kumārassa mahāmoggallānatthero kese chinditvā kāsāyāni datvā saraṇāni adāsi. Mahākassapatthero ovādācariyo ahosi. Yasmā pana upajjhāyamūlakā pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca, upajjhāyova tattha issaro, na ācariyo, tasmā vuttaṃ – “atha kho āyasmā sāriputto rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājesī”ti.

As to the text, Then the Venerable Sāriputta gave the going-forth to Prince Rāhula: The Elder Mahāmoggallāna cut the prince’s hair, gave him the ochre robes, and administered the refuges. The Elder Mahākassapa was the instructing teacher. However, because both the going-forth and the higher ordination are rooted in the preceptor, and it is the preceptor who is the authority in this matter, not the other teachers, it was therefore said: Then the Venerable Sāriputta gave the going-forth to Prince Rāhula.

Evaṃ “kumāro pabbajito”ti sutvā uppannasaṃvegena hadayena atha kho suddhodano sakkoti sabbaṃ vattabbaṃ. Tattha yasmā uñchācariyāya jīvato pabbajitassa avisesena “varaṃ yācāmī”ti vutte “yācassū”ti vacanaṃ appatirūpaṃ, na ca buddhānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ, tasmā “atikkantavarā kho gotama tathāgatā”ti vuttaṃ. Yañca bhante kappati yañca anavajjanti yaṃ tumhākañceva dātuṃ kappati, anavajjañca hoti, mama ca sampaṭicchanapaccayā viññūhi na garahitabbaṃ[V 0.0277], taṃ yācāmīti attho. Tathā nande adhimattaṃ rāhuleti [M 0.0292] yatheva kira bodhisattaṃ evaṃ nandampi rāhulampi maṅgaladivase nemittakā “cakkavattī bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Atha rājā “puttassa cakkavattisiriṃ passissāmī”ti ussāhajāto bhagavato pabbajjāya mahantaṃ icchāvighātaṃ pāpuṇi. Tato “nandassa cakkavattisiriṃ passissāmī”ti ussāhaṃ janesi, tampi bhagavā pabbājesi. Iti tampi dukkhaṃ adhivāsetvā “idāni rāhulassa cakkavattisiriṃ passissāmī”ti ussāhaṃ janesi, tampi bhagavā pabbājesi. Tenassa “idāni kulavaṃsopi pacchinno, kuto cakkavattisirī”ti adhikataraṃ dukkhaṃ uppajji. Tena vuttaṃ – “tathā nande adhimattaṃ rāhule”ti. Rañño pana ito pacchā anāgāmiphalappatti veditabbā.

Thus, upon hearing, 'The prince has gone forth,' with a heart in which spiritual urgency had arisen, all that is to be said, beginning with 'Then King Suddhodana the Sakyan...' should be stated. Therein, because for one who has gone forth, who lives by gleaning and wandering for alms, when it is said without distinction, 'I ask for a boon,' the response, 'Ask for it,' is unfitting, and it is not the custom of the Buddhas, therefore it was said, 'Tathāgatas, Gotama, have passed beyond boons.' The meaning of 'And, venerable sir, what is suitable and what is blameless' is: I ask for that boon which is both suitable for you to give and is blameless, and for which, on account of my accepting it, I would not be censured by the wise. Regarding 'Likewise with Nanda, and exceedingly with Rāhula': just as, it is said, the fortune-tellers had predicted of the Bodhisatta, so too on an auspicious day they predicted of both Nanda and Rāhula, 'He will become a wheel-turning monarch.' Then the king, having become enthusiastic with the thought, 'I will see my son's glory as a wheel-turning monarch,' experienced a great frustration of his desire at the Blessed One's going forth. After that, he generated enthusiasm with the thought, 'I will see Nanda's glory as a wheel-turning monarch,' but the Blessed One ordained him too. Thus, having endured that sorrow as well, he then generated enthusiasm with the thought, 'Now I will see Rāhula's glory as a wheel-turning monarch,' but the Blessed One ordained him too. Because of that, an even greater sorrow arose in him, thinking, 'Now even the family lineage is cut off; whence the glory of a wheel-turning monarch?' Therefore it was said: 'Likewise with Nanda, and exceedingly with Rāhula.' Furthermore, it should be known that after this, the king attained the fruit of non-returning.

Sādhu bhante ayyāti idaṃ kasmā āha? So kira cintesi – “yatra hi nāma ahampi buddhamāmako dhammamāmako saṅghamāmako samāno attano piyataraputte pabbājiyamāne ñātiviyogadukkhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ na [P 5.1011] sakkomi, aññe janā puttanattakesu pabbājitesu kathaṃ adhivāsessanti, tasmā aññesampi tāva evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ mā ahosī”ti āha. Bhagavā “sāsane niyyānikakāraṇaṃ rājā vadatī”ti dhammakathaṃ katvā “na bhikkhave ananuññāto mātāpitūhi putto pabbājetabbo”ti sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi.

Why did he say this: 'It is good, venerable sir, noble one'? It is said that he thought: 'Indeed, even though I am one who reveres the Buddha, reveres the Dhamma, and reveres the Sangha, when my own most beloved son was being ordained, I was not able to endure the suffering of separation from relatives. How then will other people be able to endure when their sons and grandsons are ordained? Therefore, may such suffering not befall others either.' Thinking thus, he spoke. The Blessed One, thinking, 'The king speaks of a cause for release in the Dispensation,' gave a Dhamma talk and then laid down the training rule: 'Monks, a son is not to be ordained without the permission of his parents.'

Tattha mātāpitūhīti jananijanake sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace dve atthi, dvepi āpucchitabbā. Sace pitā mato mātā vā, yo jīvati so āpucchitabbo. Pabbajitāpi āpucchitabbāva. Āpucchantena sayaṃ vā gantvā āpucchitabbaṃ, añño vā pesetabbo, so eva vā pesetabbo “gaccha mātāpitaro āpucchitvā ehī”ti. Sace “anuññātomhī”ti vadati, saddahantena pabbājetabbo. Pitā sayaṃ pabbajito puttampi pabbājetukāmo hoti, mātaraṃ āpucchitvāva pabbājetu. Mātā vā dhītaraṃ pabbājetukāmā, pitaraṃ āpucchitvāva pabbājetu. Pitā puttadārena anatthiko palāyi, mātā “imaṃ pabbājethā”ti puttaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ deti, “pitāssa kuhi”nti vutte “cittakeḷiyaṃ kīḷituṃ palāto”ti vadati, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mātā kenaci purisena saddhiṃ palātā hoti, pitā pana “pabbājethā”ti deti, etthāpi eseva nayo. Pitā vippavuttho hoti, mātā puttaṃ “pabbājethā”ti anujānāti, “pitā [M 0.0293] tassa kuhi”nti vutte “kiṃ tumhākaṃ pitarā, ahaṃ jānissāmī”ti vadati, pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Therein, 'by mother and father' is said in reference to the birth-mother and birth-father. If there are two, both should be asked. If the father is dead or the mother is dead, the one who is alive should be asked. Even parents who have gone forth should be asked. The one asking should either go and ask himself, or send another, or send the candidate himself, saying, 'Go, ask your mother and father, and then come back.' If he says, 'I have been permitted,' he should be ordained by one who trusts him. If a father, having himself gone forth, wishes to ordain his son, he should ordain him only after asking the mother. Or if a mother wishes to ordain her daughter, she should ordain her only after asking the father. If a father, having no interest in his son and wife, has run away, and the mother gives the son to the monks, saying, 'Ordain this one,' and when asked, 'Where is his father?' she says, 'He has run off to amuse himself as he pleases,' it is permissible to ordain him. If a mother has run away with some man, but the father gives the son, saying, 'Ordain him,' here too the same principle applies. If the father is living abroad, and the mother gives permission for the son, saying, 'Ordain him,' and when asked, 'Where is his father?' she says, 'What is his father to you? I will take responsibility,' it is permissible to ordain him. So it is said in the Kurundī.

Mātāpitaro matā, dārako cūḷamātādīnaṃ santike saṃvaddho, tasmiṃ pabbājiyamāne ñātakā [V 0.0278] kalahaṃ vā karonti, khiyyanti vā, tasmā vivādupacchedanatthaṃ āpucchitvāva pabbājetabbo. Anāpucchā pabbājentassa pana āpatti natthi. Daharakāle gahetvā posanakā mātāpitaro nāma honti, tesupi eseva nayo. Putto attānaṃ nissāya jīvati, na mātāpitaro. Sacepi rājā hoti, āpucchitvāva pabbājetabbo. Mātāpitūhi anuññāto pabbajitvā puna vibbhamati, sacepi satakkhattuṃ pabbajitvā vibbhamati, āgatāgatakāle punappunaṃ āpucchitvāva pabbājetabbo. Sace evaṃ vadanti – “ayaṃ vibbhamitvā gehaṃ āgato amhākaṃ kammaṃ na karoti, pabbajitvā tumhākaṃ vattaṃ na pūreti, natthi imassāpucchanakiccaṃ, āgatāgataṃ [P 5.1012] pabbājeyyāthā”ti evaṃ nissaṭṭhaṃ puna anāpucchāpi pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

If the parents are dead and the child has been raised in the presence of a maternal aunt and so on, when he is being ordained, the relatives might quarrel or they might complain. Therefore, in order to cut off disputes, he should be ordained only after asking them. However, for one who ordains him without asking, there is no offense. There are those called adoptive parents who take a child in his youth and raise him; for them too, this is the same principle. The son lives depending on himself, not on his parents. Even if he is a king, he should be ordained only after asking. If one who was ordained with his parents' permission later disrobes, even if he disrobes after being ordained seven times, each time he returns he should be ordained again and again only after asking. But if they say: 'This one, having disrobed and come home, does not do our work; having been ordained, he does not fulfill his duties to you. Therefore, there is no need to ask concerning him. Ordain him whenever he returns,' then, having been thus given up, it is permissible to ordain him again even without asking.

Yopi daharakāleyeva “ayaṃ tumhākaṃ dinno, yadā icchatha, tadā pabbājeyyāthā”ti evaṃ dinno hoti, sopi āgatāgato puna anāpucchāva pabbājetabbo. Yaṃ pana daharakāleyeva “imaṃ bhante pabbājeyyāthā”ti anujānitvā pacchā vuḍḍhippattakāle nānujānanti, ayaṃ na anāpucchā pabbājetabbo. Eko mātāpitūhi saddhiṃ bhaṇḍitvā “pabbājetha ma”nti āgacchati, “āpucchitvā ehī”ti ca vutto “nāhaṃ gacchāmi, sace maṃ na pabbājetha, vihāraṃ vā jhāpemi, satthena vā tumhe paharāmi, tumhākaṃ ñātakaupaṭṭhākānaṃ vā ārāmacchedanādīhi anatthaṃ uppādemi, rukkhā vā patitvā marāmi, coramajjhaṃ vā pavisāmi, desantaraṃ vā gacchāmī”ti vadati, taṃ jīvasseva rakkhaṇatthāya pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace panassa mātāpitaro āgantvā “kasmā amhākaṃ puttaṃ pabbājayitthā”ti vadanti, tesaṃ tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “rakkhaṇatthāya naṃ pabbājayimha, paññāyatha tumhe puttenā”ti vattabbā. “Rukkhā patissāmī”ti āruhitvā pana hatthapāde muñcantaṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva.

Even if a child was given at a very young age with the words, ‘This one is given to you; you may ordain him whenever you wish,’ he must be ordained without asking permission again whenever he comes. However, if permission was granted for a child with the words, ‘Venerable sir, please ordain him,’ but later, when he comes of age, they do not grant permission, he should not be ordained without asking permission. If a person quarrels with his parents and comes saying, ‘Ordain me,’ and when told, ‘Go and ask for permission,’ he says, ‘I will not go. If you do not ordain me, I will burn down the monastery, or I will strike you with a weapon, or I will cause harm to your relatives and supporters by such acts as cutting down the monastery garden, or I will fall from a tree and die, or I will enter into the midst of thieves, or I will go to another country’—it is permissible to ordain him for the sake of protecting his life. But if his parents come and say, ‘Why did you ordain our son?’ they should be told the reason, saying, ‘We ordained him to protect his life. Be reconciled with your son.’ It is indeed permissible to ordain one who, saying, ‘I will fall from a tree,’ has climbed it and is releasing his hands and feet.

Ekopi [M 0.0294] videsaṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācati, āpucchitvā ce gato, pabbājetabbo. No ce daharabhikkhuṃ pesetvā āpucchāpetvā pabbājetabbo, atidūrañce hoti; pabbājetvāpi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ pesetvā dassetuṃ vaṭṭati. Kurundiyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “sace dūraṃ hoti maggo ca mahākantāro, ‘gantvā āpucchissāmā’ti pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sace pana mātāpitūnaṃ bahū puttā honti, evañca vadanti – “bhante etesaṃ dārakānaṃ yaṃ icchatha, taṃ pabbājeyyāthā”ti. Dārake vīmaṃsitvā yaṃ icchati, so pabbājetabbo. Sacepi sakalena kulena vā gāmena vā anuññātaṃ hoti “bhante imasmiṃ kule vā gāme vā yaṃ icchatha, taṃ pabbājeyyāthā”ti. Yaṃ icchati, so pabbājetabboti.

A person may go to another country and request ordination. If he has gone after asking permission, he should be ordained. If he has not, he should be ordained only after a young monk has been sent to ask for permission. If it is very far, it is also proper to ordain him and then send him with monks to be shown to his parents. However, in the Kurundī it is said: 'If it is far and the path is a great wilderness, it is permissible to ordain with the intention, “We will go and ask permission afterward.”' Furthermore, if parents have many sons and they say, 'Venerable sir, you may ordain whichever of these boys you wish,' the boys should be examined, and the one the bhikkhu desires should be ordained. Even if permission is granted by the entire family or village, saying, 'Venerable sir, you may ordain whomever you wish from this family,' or 'from this village,' the one the bhikkhu desires should be ordained.

Yāvatake [V 0.0279] vā pana ussahatīti yattake sakkoti.

The phrase 'however many one is able for' means 'as many as one is able'.

Rāhulavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The story concerning Rāhula is finished.

Sikkhāpadadaṇḍakammavatthukathā

Discourse on the Grounds for Penal Acts Regarding the Training Rules

106. Dasasu sikkhāpadesu purimānaṃ pañcannaṃ atikkamo nāsanavatthu[P 5.1013], pacchimānaṃ atikkamo daṇḍakammavatthu.

106. Among the ten training rules, the transgression of the first five is a ground for expulsion; the transgression of the latter five is a ground for a penal act.

107. Appatissāti bhikkhū jeṭṭhakaṭṭhāne issariyaṭṭhāne na ṭhapenti. Asabhāgavuttikāti samānajīvikā na bhavanti, visabhāgajīvikāti attho. Alābhāya parisakkatīti yathā lābhaṃ na labhanti; evaṃ parakkamati. Anatthāyāti upaddavāya. Avāsāyāti “kinti imasmiṃ āvāse na vaseyyu”nti parakkamati. Akkosati paribhāsatīti akkosati ceva bhayadassanena ca tajjeti. Bhedetīti pesuññaṃ upasaṃharitvā bhedeti. Āvaraṇaṃ kātunti “mā idha pavisā”ti nivāraṇaṃ kātuṃ. Yattha vā vasati yattha vā paṭikkamatīti yattha vasati vā pavisati vā; ubhayenāpi attano pariveṇañca vassaggena pattasenāsanañca vuttaṃ.

107. Regarding `Appatissā` (irreverence): The bhikkhus do not place him in the position of a senior or in a position of authority. Regarding `Asabhāgavuttikā` (having an incompatible livelihood): They are not of the same livelihood; the meaning is that they have an incompatible livelihood. Regarding `Alābhāya parisakkati` (striving for non-gain): He strives in such a way that they do not obtain gain. Regarding `Anatthāya` (for harm): For danger. Regarding `Avāsāya` (for non-residence): He strives, thinking, 'How might they not dwell in this monastery?' Regarding `Akkosati paribhāsati` (he reviles and threatens): He both reviles and threatens by showing danger. Regarding `Bhedeti` (he causes division): He causes division by bringing slander. Regarding `Āvaraṇaṃ kātuṃ` (to make an obstruction): To make a prohibition, saying, 'Do not enter here.' Regarding `Yattha vā vasati yattha vā paṭikkamati` (wherever he dwells or wherever he returns): Wherever he either dwells or enters; by both phrases are meant both his own teacher's compound and the lodging obtained by seniority of rains-residences.

Mukhadvārikaṃ āhāraṃ āvaraṇaṃ karontīti “ajja mā khāda, mā bhuñjā”ti evaṃ nivārenti. Na bhikkhave mukhadvāriko āhāro āvaraṇaṃ kātabboti [M 0.0295] ettha “mā khāda, mā bhuñjā”ti vadatopi “āhāraṃ nivāressāmī”ti pattacīvaraṃ anto nikkhipatopi sabbapayogesu dukkaṭaṃ. Anācārassa pana dubbacasāmaṇerassa daṇḍakammaṃ katvā yāguṃ vā bhattaṃ vā pattacīvaraṃ vā dassetvā “ettake nāma daṇḍakamme āhaṭe idaṃ lacchasī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhagavatā hi āvaraṇameva daṇḍakammaṃ vuttaṃ. Dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi pana aparādhānurūpaṃ udakadāruvālikādīnaṃ āharāpanampi kātabbanti vuttaṃ, tasmā tampi kātabbaṃ. Tañca kho “oramissati viramissatī”ti anukampāya, na “nassissati vibbhamissatī”tiādinayappavattena pāpajjhāsayena “daṇḍakammaṃ karomī”ti ca uṇhapāsāṇe vā nipajjāpetuṃ pāsāṇiṭṭhakādīni vā sīse nikkhipāpetuṃ udakaṃ vā pavesetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

‘They make an obstruction to food at the door of the mouth’ means they prohibit thus: ‘Today, do not chew, do not eat.’ In the text, ‘Bhikkhus, an obstruction to food at the door of the mouth is not to be made,’ for a bhikkhu who says, ‘Do not chew, do not eat,’ and for one who, thinking, ‘I will prevent the food,’ places the bowl and robe inside, there is an offense of wrong-doing in all such efforts. However, for a novice of improper conduct who is difficult to admonish, having imposed a penal act, it is proper to show him gruel, or cooked rice, or the bowl and robe and say, ‘When a penal act of such a measure has been carried out, you will receive this.’ Indeed, by the Blessed One, only obstruction has been stated as a penal act. However, by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, it has been said that, in accordance with the offense, causing him to bring water, firewood, sand, and so on, should also be done. Therefore, that too should be done. And that should be done with compassion, thinking, ‘He will avoid, he will desist,’ not with a wicked intention proceeding in the manner of, ‘He will be ruined, he will disrobe.’ And, thinking, ‘I will perform a penal act,’ it is not proper to make him lie down on a hot stone slab, or to have stones, bricks, and so on, placed on his head, or to make him enter water.

Sikkhāpadadaṇḍakammavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Grounds for Penal Acts Regarding the Training Rules is concluded.

Anāpucchāvaraṇavatthuādikathā

The Discussion on the Grounds for Obstruction Without Asking Permission, and So Forth.

108. Na [V 0.0280] bhikkhave upajjhāyaṃ anāpucchāti ettha “tumhākaṃ sāmaṇerassa ayaṃ nāma aparādho, daṇḍakammamassa karothā”ti tikkhattuṃ vutte, sace upajjhāyo daṇḍakammaṃ na karoti, sayaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sacepi āditova upajjhāyo vadati “mayhaṃ sāmaṇerānaṃ dose sati tumhe daṇḍakammaṃ karothā”ti kātuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Yathā ca sāmaṇerānaṃ evaṃ saddhivihārikantevāsikānampi daṇḍakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

Here, regarding 'Monks, without asking the preceptor,' if, after it has been said three times, 'This novice of yours has committed such-and-such an offense; impose a penal act on him,' the preceptor does not impose the penal act, it is proper to do so oneself. Even if the preceptor says from the outset, 'When my novices are at fault, you may impose penal acts,' it is indeed proper to do so. And just as for novices, so too is it proper to impose a penal act on co-residents and pupils.

Apalāḷentīti “tumhākaṃ [P 5.1014] pattaṃ dassāma, cīvaraṃ dassāmā”ti attano upaṭṭhānakaraṇatthaṃ saṅgaṇhanti. Na bhikkhave aññassa parisā apalāḷetabbāti ettha sāmaṇerā vā hontu upasampannā vā, antamaso dussīlabhikkhussāpi parassa parisabhūte bhinditvā gaṇhituṃ na vaṭṭati, ādīnavaṃ pana vattuṃ vaṭṭati “tayā nhāyituṃ āgatena gūthamakkhanaṃ viya kataṃ dussīlaṃ nissāya viharantenā”ti. Sace so sayameva jānitvā upajjhaṃ vā nissayaṃ vā yācati, dātuṃ vaṭṭati.

108. `Apalāḷenti` means they entice, saying, 'We will give you a bowl, we will give you robes,' intending to make them their own attendants. Here, regarding 'Monks, another's following should not be enticed away,' whether they are novices or fully ordained monks, it is not proper to take another's followers, even those of an immoral monk, by causing a split. However, it is proper to speak of the disadvantage: 'For you, living in dependence on an immoral person is like smearing yourself with excrement after having come to bathe.' If that person, knowing this for himself, requests a preceptor or dependence, it is proper to grant it.

Anujānāmi bhikkhave dasahaṅgehi samannāgataṃ sāmaṇeraṃ nāsetunti ettha kaṇṭakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttāsu tīsu nāsanāsu liṅganāsanāva adhippetā, tasmā yo pāṇātipātādīsu ekampi kammaṃ karoti, so liṅganāsanāya nāsetabbo. Yathā ca bhikkhūnaṃ pāṇātipātādīsu nānāāpattiyo honti, na tathā sāmaṇerānaṃ. Sāmaṇero hi kunthakipillikampi māretvā maṅguraṇḍakampi bhinditvā nāsetabbataṃyeva [M 0.0296] pāpuṇāti, tāvadevassa saraṇagamanāni ca upajjhāyaggahaṇañca senāsanaggāho ca paṭippassambhati, saṅghalābhaṃ na labhati, liṅgamattameva ekaṃ avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti. So sace ākiṇṇadosova hoti, āyatiṃ saṃvare na tiṭṭhati, nikkaḍḍhitabbo. Atha sahasā virajjhitvā “duṭṭhu mayā kata”nti puna saṃvare ṭhātukāmo hoti, liṅganāsanakiccaṃ natthi. Yathānivatthapārutasseva saraṇāni dātabbāni, upajjhāyo dātabbo, sikkhāpadāni pana saraṇagamaneneva ijjhanti. Sāmaṇerānañhi saraṇagamanaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ upasampadakammavācāsadisaṃ, tasmā bhikkhūnaṃ viya catupārisuddhisīlaṃ, imināpi dasasīlāni samādinnāneva honti, evaṃ santepi daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ āyatiṃ saṃvare patiṭṭhāpanatthaṃ puna dātabbāni. Sace purimikāya puna saraṇāni gahitāni, pacchimikāya vassāvāsikaṃ lacchati. Sace pacchimikāya gahitāni, saṅghena apaloketvā lābho dātabbo.

Here, regarding 'Monks, I allow the expulsion of a novice endowed with ten factors,' among the three types of expulsion mentioned in the explanation of the Kaṇṭaka training-rule, only expulsion by removal of the outward signs is intended. Therefore, a novice who commits even a single act among killing living beings, and so forth, should be expelled by removal of the outward signs. And just as monks have various offenses for killing living beings, and so forth, it is not so for novices. For a novice, by killing even an ant or by breaking a fish egg, reaches the very state of deserving expulsion. At that very moment, his going for refuge, his acceptance of a preceptor, and his taking of a lodging cease. He does not obtain the Sangha's gains; only the mere outward signs remain. If he is indeed overwhelmed by faults and does not maintain restraint in the future, he should be driven out. But if he quickly feels remorse, thinking, 'I have acted wrongly,' and wishes to maintain restraint again, there is no need for the act of removing the outward signs. The refuges should be given to him just as he is dressed and robed, and a preceptor should be given. The training rules, however, are fulfilled by the going for refuge itself. For novices, going for refuge is indeed similar to the formal act of ordination for monks. Therefore, like the monks' fourfold purity of virtue, by this the ten precepts are also undertaken. Even so, to strengthen them and to establish him in future restraint, they should be given again. If he has taken the refuges again in the first watch, he will receive the rains-residence requisite in the later watch. If he has taken them in the later watch, the gain should be given after an announcement to the Sangha.

Adinnādāne [V 0.0281] tiṇasalākamattenāpi vatthunā, abrahmacariye tīsu maggesu yattha katthaci vippaṭipattiyā, musāvāde hassādhippāyatāyapi musā bhaṇite assamaṇo hoti, nāsetabbataṃ āpajjati. Majjapāne pana bhikkhuno ajānitvāpi bījato paṭṭhāya majjaṃ pivantassa [P 5.1015] pācittiyaṃ. Sāmaṇero jānitvā pivanto sīlabhedaṃ āpajjati, na ajānitvā. Yāni panassa itarāni pañca sikkhāpadāni, tesu bhinnesu na nāsetabbo, daṇḍakammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sikkhāpade pana puna dinnepi adinnepi vaṭṭati. Daṇḍakammena pana pīḷetvā āyatiṃ saṃvare ṭhapanatthāya dātabbameva. Sāmaṇerānaṃ majjapānaṃ sacittakaṃ pārājikavatthu, ayaṃ viseso.

In taking what is not given, even with an object the measure of a blade of grass; in unchastity, by misconduct in any of the three paths; in false speech, even when a lie is spoken with the intention of humor—one becomes a non-ascetic and is to be expelled. Regarding the drinking of intoxicants, however, for a monk who unknowingly drinks an intoxicant that is so from its seed onward, it is a pācittiya offense. A novice who knowingly drinks incurs a breach of virtue, but not if he does so unknowingly. As for his other five training rules, if they are broken, he is not to be expelled, but a disciplinary action should be taken. The training rule, however, is valid whether given again or not. But after he has been corrected through a disciplinary action, it should indeed be given for the purpose of establishing him in restraint in the future. For novices, the intentional drinking of intoxicants is a ground for a pārājika-equivalent offense—this is the distinction.

Avaṇṇabhāsane pana arahaṃ sammāsambuddhotiādīnaṃ paṭipakkhavasena buddhassa vā, svākkhātotiādīnaṃ paṭipakkhavasena dhammassa vā, suppaṭipannotiādīnaṃ paṭipakkhavasena saṅghassa vā avaṇṇaṃ bhāsanto ratanattayaṃ nindanto garahanto ācariyupajjhāyādīhi “mā evaṃ avacā”ti avaṇṇabhāsane ādīnavaṃ dassetvā nivāretabbo. Sace yāvatatiyaṃ vuccamāno na oramati, kaṇṭakanāsanāya nāsetabboti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sace evaṃ vuccamāno taṃ laddhiṃ nissajjati, daṇḍakammaṃ kāretvā accayaṃ desāpetabbo. Sace na nissajjati, tatheva ādāya paggayha [M 0.0297] tiṭṭhati, liṅganāsanāya nāsetabbo”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ yuttaṃ. Ayameva hi nāsanā idha adhippetāti.

However, regarding speaking disparagingly: one who speaks disparagingly of the Buddha in opposition to his qualities such as 'Arahant, Perfectly Self-Enlightened One'; or of the Dhamma in opposition to its qualities such as 'well-expounded'; or of the Sangha in opposition to its qualities such as 'practicing well'—one who speaks thus, reviling and censuring the Triple Gem, should be restrained by his teachers, preceptors, and others. Showing the danger in speaking disparagingly, they should say, 'Do not speak thus.' If, being spoken to up to the third time, he does not desist, he is to be expelled by the 'expulsion of a thorn'; so it is said in the Kurundī. In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, however, it is said: 'If, being spoken to thus, he abandons that view, a disciplinary action should be imposed and he should be made to confess the offense. If he does not abandon it, but persists in taking it up and upholding it, he is to be expelled by the 'expulsion of the outward sign'.' That is fitting. For this very expulsion is intended here.

Micchādiṭṭhikepi eseva nayo. Sassatucchedānañhi aññataradiṭṭhiko sace ācariyādīhi ovadiyamāno nissajjati, daṇḍakammaṃ kāretvā accayaṃ desāpetabbo. Appaṭinissajjantova nāsetabboti. Bhikkhunidūsako cettha kāmaṃ abrahmacāriggahaṇena gahitova abrahmacāriṃ pana āyatiṃ saṃvare ṭhātukāmaṃ saraṇāni datvā upasampādetuṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunidūsako āyatiṃ saṃvare ṭhātukāmopi pabbajjampi na labhati, pageva upasampadanti etamatthaṃ dassetuṃ “bhikkhunidūsako”ti idaṃ visuṃ dasamaṃ aṅgaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

This same method applies to one with wrong view. For if a holder of either eternalist or annihilationist views, being admonished by his teachers and others, abandons that view, a disciplinary action should be imposed and he should be made to confess the offense. One who does not abandon it, however, is to be expelled. And here, a defiler of bhikkhunīs is indeed included by the term 'unchastity'. However, while it is permissible to give the refuges to an unchaste person who wishes to be established in restraint in the future and to give him full ordination, a defiler of bhikkhunīs, even if he wishes to be established in restraint in the future, does not obtain even the going forth, let alone full ordination. To show this meaning, 'defiler of bhikkhunīs' was stated by the Blessed One as this separate, tenth factor. Thus it should be understood.

Anāpucchāvaraṇavatthuādikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discussion on the Grounds for Exclusion Without Asking Permission, and So Forth, is concluded.

Paṇḍakavatthukathā

The Account of the Paṇḍaka

109. Dahare dahareti taruṇe taruṇe. Moḷigalleti thūlasarīre. Hatthibhaṇḍe assabhaṇḍeti hatthigopake ca assagopake ca.

109. ‘Dahare dahare’ means the young ones, the very young. ‘Moḷigalle’ means one with a stout body. ‘Hatthibhaṇḍe assabhaṇḍe’ means elephant keepers and horse keepers.

Paṇḍako [V 0.0282] bhikkhaveti ettha āsittapaṇḍako usūyapaṇḍako opakkamikapaṇḍako pakkhapaṇḍako napuṃsakapaṇḍakoti pañca [P 5.1016] paṇḍakā. Tattha yassa paresaṃ aṅgajātaṃ mukhena gahetvā asucinā āsittassa pariḷāho vūpasammati, ayaṃ āsittapaṇḍako. Yassa paresaṃ ajjhācāraṃ passato usūyāya uppannāya pariḷāho vūpasammati, ayaṃ usūyapaṇḍako. Yassa upakkamena bījāni apanītāni, ayaṃ opakkamikapaṇḍako. Ekacco pana akusalavipākānubhāvena kāḷapakkhe paṇḍako hoti, juṇhapakkhe panassa pariḷāho vūpasammati, ayaṃ pakkhapaṇḍako. Yo pana paṭisandhiyaṃyeva abhāvako uppanno, ayaṃ napuṃsakapaṇḍakoti. Tesu āsittapaṇḍakassa ca usūyapaṇḍakassa ca pabbajjā na vāritā, itaresaṃ tiṇṇaṃ vāritā. Tesupi pakkhapaṇḍakassa yasmiṃ pakkhe paṇḍako hoti, tasmiṃyevassa pakkhe pabbajjā vāritāti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Yassa cettha pabbajjā vāritā, taṃ sandhāya idaṃ vuttaṃ – “anupasampanno na upasampādetabbo upasampanno nāsetabbo”ti. Sopi [M 0.0298] liṅganāsaneneva nāsetabbo. Ito paraṃ “nāsetabbo”ti vuttesupi eseva nayo.

Regarding ‘A paṇḍaka, Bhikkhus’: here there are five kinds of paṇḍakas: the āsittapaṇḍaka, the usūyapaṇḍaka, the opakkamikapaṇḍaka, the pakkhapaṇḍaka, and the napuṃsakapaṇḍaka. Among them, one whose passion is pacified when, having taken another's genitals into his mouth, he is sprinkled with impurity—this is the āsittapaṇḍaka. One whose passion is pacified when, upon seeing the sexual transgression of others, envy arises in him—this is the usūyapaṇḍaka. One whose testicles have been removed by some means—this is the opakkamikapaṇḍaka. Another, through the power of the result of unwholesome kamma, is a paṇḍaka during the waning fortnight, while during the waxing fortnight his passion is pacified—this is the pakkhapaṇḍaka. One who is born without sexual characteristics from conception itself—this is the napuṃsakapaṇḍaka. Among these, the going forth is not forbidden for the āsittapaṇḍaka and the usūyapaṇḍaka, but it is forbidden for the other three. Even among those, for the pakkhapaṇḍaka, the going forth is forbidden only during the fortnight in which he is a paṇḍaka—so it is said in the Kurundī. And it is with reference to one for whom the going forth is forbidden that this was said: ‘One who is not fully ordained should not be given full ordination; one who is fully ordained is to be expelled.’ He too is to be expelled only by the annulment of his outward sign. From this point onward, wherever it is said ‘is to be expelled,’ this same method applies.

Paṇḍavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Paṇḍaka is concluded.

Theyyasaṃvāsakavatthukathā

The Account of One Who Lives in Communion by Theft

110. Purāṇakulaputtoti purāṇassa anukkamena pārijuññaṃ pattassa kulassa putto. Mātipakkhapitipakkhato kolaññā khīṇā vinaṭṭhā matā assāti khīṇakolañño. Anadhigatanti appattaṃ. Phātiṃkātunti vaḍḍhetuṃ. Iṅghāti uyyojanatthe nipāto. Anuyuñjiyamānoti ekamantaṃ netvā kesamassuoropanakāsāyapaṭiggahaṇasaraṇagamanaupajjhāyaggahaṇakammavācānissayadhamme pucchiyamāno. Etamatthaṃ ārocesīti etaṃ sayaṃ pabbajitabhāvaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya ācikkhi.

110. ‘Purāṇakulaputta’ means the son of an ancient family that has successively fallen into decline. ‘Khīṇakolañño’ means one whose relatives from the maternal and paternal side are exhausted, destroyed, and dead. ‘Anadhigataṃ’ means not attained. ‘Phātiṃ kātuṃ’ means to increase. ‘Iṅgha’ is a particle in the sense of urging. ‘Anuyuñjiyamāno’ means being questioned, having been led to a secluded place, about the shaving of hair and beard, the acceptance of the ochre robe, going for refuge, the acceptance of a preceptor, the formal act, and the rules of dependence. ‘Etamatthaṃ ārocesī’ means he explained this state of having gone forth himself, from the beginning.

Theyyasaṃvāsako bhikkhaveti ettha tayo theyyasaṃvāsakā – liṅgatthenako, saṃvāsatthenako, ubhayatthenakoti. Tattha yo sayaṃ pabbajitvā vihāraṃ gantvā na bhikkhuvassāni gaṇeti, na yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyati, na āsanena paṭibāhati, na uposathapavāraṇādīsu sandissati, ayaṃ liṅgamattasseva thenitattā liṅgatthenako nāma.

Regarding ‘One who lives in communion by theft, Bhikkhus’: here there are three kinds of those who live in communion by theft: one who steals the outward sign, one who steals the communion, and one who steals both. Among them, one who, having gone forth by himself, goes to a monastery and does not count the years as a bhikkhu, does not accept homage according to seniority, does not prevent junior monks from taking his seat, and is not present at the Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, and other ceremonies—this one, because of having stolen only the outward sign, is called ‘one who steals the outward sign’.

Yo pana bhikkhūhi pabbājito sāmaṇero samānopi videsaṃ gantvā “ahaṃ dasavasso vā [V 0.0283] vīsativasso vā”ti musā vatvā bhikkhuvassāni gaṇeti, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ [P 5.1017] sādiyati, āsanena paṭibāhati, uposathapavāraṇādīsu sandissati, ayaṃ saṃvāsamattasseva thenitattā saṃvāsatthenako nāma. Bhikkhuvassagaṇanādiko hi sabbopi kiriyabhedo imasmiṃ atthe “saṃvāso”ti veditabbo. Sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya “na maṃ koci jānātī”ti evaṃ paṭipajjantepi eseva nayo.

But one who, though a novice ordained by bhikkhus, goes to another region and, speaking falsely, says, ‘I am of ten years’ standing,’ or ‘I am of twenty years’ standing,’ and counts the years as a bhikkhu, accepts homage according to seniority, obstructs others with his seat, and is seen at the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies and so on—this one, because of having stolen only the communion, is called ‘one who steals the communion.’ Indeed, every kind of action, beginning with the counting of years as a bhikkhu, should be understood in this context as ‘communion.’ Even for one who, having renounced the training, acts thinking, ‘No one knows me,’ this is the same method.

Yo pana sayaṃ pabbajitvā vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhuvassāni gaṇeti, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ vandanaṃ sādiyati, āsanena paṭibāhati, uposathapavāraṇādīsu sandissati, ayaṃ liṅgassa ceva saṃvāsassa ca thenitattā ubhayatthenako nāma. Ayaṃ tividhopi theyyasaṃvāsako anupasampanno na upasampādetabbo, upasampanno nāsetabbo, puna pabbajjaṃ yācantopi na pabbājetabbo.

But one who, having gone forth by himself, goes to a monastery and counts the years as a bhikkhu, accepts homage according to seniority, obstructs others with his seat, and is seen at the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies and so on—this one, because of having stolen both the outward sign and the communion, is called ‘one who steals both.’ This person who lives in communion by theft, of all three types, if not fully ordained, should not be given full ordination; if fully ordained, he should be expelled. Even if requesting the going forth again, he should not be given the going forth.

Ettha [M 0.0299] ca asammohatthaṃ idaṃ pakiṇṇakaṃ veditabbaṃ –

And here, for the sake of non-bewilderment, this miscellaneous teaching should be understood:

“Rājadubbhikkhakantāra-rogaveribhayehi vā;

Cīvarāharaṇatthaṃ vā, liṅgaṃ ādiyatīdha yo.

‘Whoever here takes up the outward sign due to fear of kings, famine, a difficult journey, disease, or enemies, or for the purpose of carrying robes—

Saṃvāsaṃ nādhivāseti, yāva so suddhamānaso;

Theyyasaṃvāsako nāma, tāva esa na vuccatī”ti.

—as long as he, with a pure mind, does not consent to communion, for that long he is not called one who lives in communion by theft.’

Tatrāyaṃ vitthāranayo – idhekaccassa rājā kuddho hoti, so “evaṃ me sotthi bhavissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā palāyati. Taṃ disvā rañño ārocenti. Rājā “sace pabbajito, na taṃ labbhā kiñci kātu”nti tasmiṃ kodhaṃ paṭivineti, so “vūpasantaṃ me rājabhaya”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgato pabbājetabbo. Athāpi “sāsanaṃ nissāya mayā jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ, handa dāni ahaṃ pabbajāmī”ti uppannasaṃvego teneva liṅgena āgantvā āgantukavattaṃ na sādiyati, bhikkhūhi puṭṭho vā apuṭṭho vā yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikatvā pabbajjaṃ yācati, liṅgaṃ apanetvā pabbājetabbo. Sace pana vattaṃ sādiyati, pabbajitālayaṃ dasseti, sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo.

Therein, this is the detailed method: Here, a king is angry with a certain person. That person, thinking, ‘In this way there will be safety for me,’ takes up the outward sign by himself and flees. Seeing him, they inform the king. The king, thinking, ‘If he has gone forth, it is not possible to do anything to him,’ removes his anger towards him. That person, thinking, ‘The danger from the king has subsided for me,’ without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, having reverted to the layman's appearance and then come, should be given the going forth. Furthermore, if, with a sense of spiritual urgency having arisen, thinking, ‘I have gained my life by relying on the Teaching; come now, I shall go forth,’ he comes with that very same outward sign but does not accept the duties of a newcomer, and, whether questioned by the bhikkhus or not, reveals himself as he really is and requests the going forth, then having removed the outward sign, he should be given the going forth. But if he accepts the duties, shows an inclination for the life of one who has gone forth, and follows the entire procedure previously mentioned, distinguished by the counting of years and so on, this one should not be given the going forth.

Idha panekacco dubbhikkhe jīvituṃ asakkonto sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni [V 0.0284] bhuñjanto dubbhikkhe vītivatte saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva[P 5.1018].

But here, a certain person, being unable to make a living during a famine, takes up the outward sign by himself and, while eating the food of all sectarians, when the famine has passed, without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, having reverted to the layman's appearance, he comes to be ordained. In this case, everything is the same as in the previous example.

Aparo mahākantāraṃ nittharitukāmo hoti, satthavāho ca pabbajite gahetvā gacchati. So “evaṃ maṃ satthavāho gahetvā gamissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā satthavāhena saddhiṃ kantāraṃ nittharitvā khemantaṃ patvā saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another person wishes to cross a great, difficult journey, and a caravan leader takes monks along. That person, thinking, ‘In this way, the caravan leader will take me along,’ takes up the outward sign by himself. Having crossed the difficult journey together with the caravan leader and having reached a place of safety, without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, having reverted to the layman's appearance, he comes to be ordained. In this case, everything is the same as in the previous example.

Aparo rogabhaye uppanne jīvituṃ asakkonto sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā sabbapāsaṇḍiyabhattāni bhuñjanto rogabhaye vūpasante saṅghamajjhaṃ [M 0.0300] anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Another person, when a danger from disease has arisen, being unable to live, takes up the outward sign by himself and, while eating the food of all sectarians, when the danger from disease has subsided, without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, having reverted to the layman's appearance, he comes to be ordained. In this case, everything is the same as in the previous example.

Aparassa eko veriko kuddho hoti, ghātetukāmo naṃ vicarati, so “evaṃ me sotthi bhavissatī”ti sayameva liṅgaṃ gahetvā palāyati. Veriko “kuhiṃ so”ti pariyesanto “pabbajitvā palāto”ti sutvā “sace pabbajito, na taṃ labbhā kiñci kātu”nti tasmiṃ kodhaṃ paṭivineti. So “vūpasantaṃ me veribhaya”nti saṅghamajjhaṃ anosaritvāva gihiliṅgaṃ gahetvā āgatoti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

Towards another person, an enemy is angry and wanders about, wishing to kill him. That person, thinking, ‘In this way, there will be safety for me,’ takes up the outward sign by himself and flees. The enemy, searching, ‘Where is he?’ and hearing, ‘He has gone forth and fled,’ dispels his anger towards that person, thinking, ‘If he has gone forth, it is not possible to do anything to him.’ That person, thinking, ‘The danger from my enemy has subsided,’ without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha, having reverted to the layman's appearance, he comes to be ordained. In this case, everything is the same as in the previous example.

Aparo ñātikulaṃ gantvā sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya gihi hutvā “imāni cīvarāni idha vinassissanti, sacepi imāni gahetvā vihāraṃ gamissāmi, antarāmagge maṃ ‘coro’ti gahessanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ kāyaparihāriyāni katvā gaccheyya”nti cīvarāharaṇatthaṃ nivāsetvā ca pārupitvā ca vihāraṃ gacchati. Taṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā sāmaṇerā ca daharā ca abbhuggacchanti, vattaṃ dassenti. So na sādiyati, yathābhūtamattānaṃ āvikaroti. Sace bhikkhū “na dāni mayaṃ taṃ muñcissāmā”ti balakkārena pabbājetukāmā honti, kāsāyāni apanetvā puna pabbājetabbo. Sace pana “nayime mama hīnāyāvattabhāvaṃ jānantī”ti taṃyeva bhikkhubhāvaṃ paṭijānitvā sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo.

Another, having gone to the home of his relatives, having renounced the training and become a layman, thinks: ‘These robes will be ruined here. If I take these robes and go to the monastery, on the way they will seize me as a thief. What if I were to go having made them wearable on the body?’ For the purpose of carrying the robes, having worn the lower robe and draped the upper robe, he goes to the monastery. Seeing him coming from afar, novices and young monks go out to meet him and show him the duties. He does not consent and reveals himself as he really is. If the bhikkhus, saying, ‘Now we will not release you,’ wish to give him the going forth by force, then having removed the saffron robes, he is to be given the going forth again. But if, thinking, ‘These monks do not know of my having returned to the lower state,’ he asserts that very state of a bhikkhu and follows all the previously stated procedure, differentiated by the counting of years and so on, this one is not to be given the going forth.

Aparo mahāsāmaṇero ñātikulaṃ gantvā uppabbajitvā kammantānuṭṭhānena ubbāḷho hutvā puna “dāni ahaṃ samaṇova bhavissāmi, theropi me uppabbajitabhāvaṃ na jānātī”ti tadeva pattacīvaraṃ [V 0.0285] ādāya vihāraṃ āgacchati, nāpi tamatthaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āroceti, sāmaṇerabhāvaṃ paṭijānāti, ayaṃ theyyasaṃvāsakoyeva pabbajjaṃ na labhati. Sacepissa liṅgaggahaṇakāle [P 5.1019] evaṃ hoti, “nāhaṃ kassaci ārocessāmī”ti vihārañca gato āroceti, gahaṇeneva theyyasaṃvāsako. Athāpissa “gahaṇakāle ācikkhissāmī”ti cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, vihārañca gantvā “kuhiṃ tvaṃ āvuso gato”ti vutto “na dāni maṃ ime jānantī”ti vañcetvā nācikkhati, “nācikkhissāmī”ti saha dhuranikkhepena ayampi theyyasaṃvāsakova. Sace panassa gahaṇakālepi “ācikkhissāmī”ti cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, vihāraṃ gantvāpi ācikkhati, ayaṃ puna pabbajjaṃ labhati.

Another, a senior novice, having gone to his relatives’ home and disrobed, being troubled by his lack of exertion in work, thinks again, 'Now I will be a recluse again, and the elder preceptor does not know of my having disrobed.' Taking that very bowl and robes, he comes to the monastery. He does not inform the monks of that matter and claims the state of a novice. This one is indeed one who co-resides by theft; he does not obtain the going-forth. If, at the time of taking the sign, his thought is thus, 'I will not inform anyone,' but having gone to the monastery, he informs them, he is one who co-resides by theft by the very act of taking. Or if, at the time of taking, the thought 'I will inform them' has arisen for him, but having gone to the monastery and being asked, 'Friend, where did you go?' he, thinking, 'Now these ones do not know me,' deceives and does not tell—simultaneously with the abandoning of the effort to tell, this one too is indeed one who co-resides by theft. But if, at the time of taking, the thought 'I will inform them' has arisen for him, and having gone to the monastery he does inform them, this one obtains the going-forth again.

Aparo [M 0.0301] daharasāmaṇero mahanto vā pana abyatto, so purimanayeneva uppabbajitvā ghare vacchakarakkhaṇādīni kammāni kātuṃ na icchati, tamenaṃ ñātakā tāniyeva kāsāyāni acchādetvā thālakaṃ vā pattaṃ vā hatthe datvā “gaccha samaṇova hohī”ti gharā nīharanti. So vihāraṃ gacchati, neva naṃ bhikkhū jānanti “ayaṃ uppabbajitvā puna sayameva pabbajito”ti, nāpi sayaṃ jānāti, “yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotī”ti. Sace taṃ paripuṇṇavassaṃ upasampādenti, sūpasampanno. Sace pana anupasampannakāleyeva vinayavinicchaye vattamāne suṇāti, “yo evaṃ pabbajati, so theyyasaṃvāsako nāma hotī”ti. Tena “mayā evaṃ kata”nti bhikkhūnaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ, evaṃ puna pabbajjaṃ labhati. Sace “na dāni maṃ koci jānātī”ti nāroceti, dhuraṃ nikkhittamatte theyyasaṃvāsako.

Another, a young novice, or one who is senior but unskilled, having disrobed in the previous manner, does not wish to do work at home such as tending calves. His relatives cover him with those very saffron robes, and having given a dish or a bowl into his hand, they send him out from the house, saying, 'Go, be a recluse.' He goes to the monastery. The monks do not know of him, 'This one, having disrobed, has gone forth again by himself,' nor does he himself know, 'Whoever goes forth in this way is called one who co-resides by theft.' If they give him higher ordination when he is of twenty full years, he is well ordained. But if, while still not having received higher ordination, during a Vinaya decision, he hears, 'Whoever goes forth in this way is called one who co-resides by theft,' it should be told to the monks by him, 'It was done thus by me.' In this way, he obtains the going-forth again. If, thinking, 'Now no one knows me,' he does not inform them, as soon as the responsibility is abandoned, he is one who co-resides by theft.

Bhikkhu sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya liṅgaṃ anapanetvā dussīlakammaṃ katvā vā akatvā vā puna sabbaṃ pubbe vuttaṃ vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ paṭipajjati, theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sikkhaṃ appaccakkhāya saliṅge ṭhito methunaṃ paṭisevitvā vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ vidhiṃ āpajjanto theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, pabbajjāmattaṃ labhati. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana eso theyyasaṃvāsakoti vuttaṃ, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ.

A bhikkhu who, having renounced the training without having removed the sign, whether having done an immoral act or not, again follows all the previously stated procedure, differentiated by the counting of rains-residences, etc., is one who co-resides by theft. One who, not having renounced the training, while remaining in his own sign, having engaged in sexual intercourse, then follows the procedure, differentiated by the counting of rains-residences, etc., is not one who co-resides by theft; he obtains only the going-forth. However, in the Andhaka commentary, it is said that this one is one who co-resides by theft; that should not be accepted.

Eko bhikkhu kāsāye saussāhova odātaṃ nivāsetvā methunaṃ paṭisevitvā puna kāsāyāni nivāsetvā vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ vidhiṃ āpajjati, ayampi theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti, pabbajjāmattaṃ labhati. Sace pana [P 5.1020] kāsāye dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā odātaṃ nivāsetvā methunaṃ [V 0.0286] paṭisevitvā puna kāsāyāni nivāsetvā vassagaṇanādibhedaṃ sabbaṃ vidhiṃ āpajjati, theyyasaṃvāsako hoti.

A certain bhikkhu who, while still having effort towards the saffron robes, having worn white clothes and engaged in sexual intercourse, then wears the saffron robes again and follows all the procedure, differentiated by the counting of rains-residences, etc.—this one too is not one who co-resides by theft; he obtains only the going-forth. But if, having abandoned the responsibility for the saffron robes, he wears white clothes, engages in sexual intercourse, then wears the saffron robes again and follows all the procedure, differentiated by the counting of rains-residences, etc.—this one is one who co-resides by theft.

Sāmaṇero saliṅge ṭhito methunādiassamaṇakaraṇadhammaṃ āpajjitvāpi theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti. Sacepi kāsāye saussāhova kāsāyāni apanetvā methunaṃ paṭisevitvā puna kāsāyāni nivāseti, neva theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sace pana kāsāye dhuraṃ nikkhipitvā naggo vā odātanivattho vā methunasevanādīhi assamaṇo [M 0.0302] hutvā kāsāyaṃ nivāseti, theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Sacepi gihibhāvaṃ patthayamāno kāsāvaṃ ovaṭṭikaṃ vā katvā aññena vā ākārena gihinivāsanena nivāseti “sobhati nu kho me gihiliṅgaṃ, na sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ, rakkhati tāva. “Sobhatī”ti sampaṭicchitvā pana puna liṅgaṃ sādiyanto theyyasaṃvāsako hoti. Odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsanasampaṭicchanesupi eseva nayo.

A novice, while remaining in his own sign, even if he commits an act that makes one not a recluse, such as sexual intercourse, is not one who co-resides by theft. Even if, being enthusiastic about the saffron robes, he removes the saffron robes, engages in sexual intercourse, and then puts on the saffron robes again, he is still not one who co-resides by theft. But if, having laid aside the responsibility for the saffron robes, he goes naked or wears white clothes, becomes a non-recluse through engaging in sexual intercourse and the like, and then puts on the saffron robe, he is one who co-resides by theft. Even if, desiring the state of a householder, he wears the saffron robe tucked up or in some other manner like a householder's garment for the purpose of investigating, 'Does the householder's sign suit me, or does it not?', he is protected for the time being. But having accepted, thinking, 'It suits me,' and then delighting in that sign, he becomes one who co-resides by theft. Also in the cases of investigating and accepting after having put on white clothes, this is the same method.

Sace pana nivatthakāsāyassa upari odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsati vā sampaṭicchati vā, rakkhatiyeva. Bhikkhuniyāpi eseva nayo. Sāpi hi gihibhāvaṃ patthayamānā sace kāsāyaṃ gihinivāsanaṃ nivāseti, “sobhati nu kho me gihiliṅgaṃ, na sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ, rakkhati tāva. Sace “sobhatī”ti sampaṭicchati, na rakkhati. Odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsanasampaṭicchanesupi eseva nayo. Nivatthakāsāyassa pana upari odātaṃ nivāsetvā vīmaṃsatu vā sampaṭicchatu vā, rakkhatiyeva.

If, however, having put on white clothes over the saffron robe that is already worn, one investigates or accepts, one is still protected. For a bhikkhunī also, this is the same method. For if she too, desiring the state of a householder, wears the saffron robe as a householder's garment for the purpose of investigating, 'Does the householder's sign suit me, or does it not?', she is protected for the time being. If she accepts, thinking, 'It suits me,' she is not protected. Also in the cases of investigating and accepting after having put on white clothes, this is the same method. But having put on white clothes over the saffron robe that is already worn, whether one investigates or accepts, one is still protected.

Sace koci vuḍḍhapabbajito vassāni agaṇetvā pāḷiyampi aṭṭhatvā ekapassenāgantvā mahāpeḷādīsu kaṭacchunā ukkhitte bhattapiṇḍe pattaṃ upanāmetvā seno viya maṃsapesiṃ gahetvā gacchati, theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti. Bhikkhuvassāni pana gaṇetvā gaṇhanto theyyasaṃvāsako hoti.

If some aged one who has gone forth, without counting the rains-residences and without standing in the line, comes from the side and, when a lump of rice is lifted with a ladle in the great baskets and so on, brings his bowl near and takes it and goes away like a hawk seizing a piece of meat, he is not one who co-resides by theft. But one who takes it while counting the rains-residences of a bhikkhu is one who co-resides by theft.

Sayaṃ sāmaṇerova sāmaṇerapaṭipāṭiyā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā gaṇhanto theyyasaṃvāsako na hoti. Bhikkhu bhikkhupaṭipāṭiyā kūṭavassāni gaṇetvā gaṇhanto bhaṇḍagghena kāretabboti.

A novice himself, who takes offerings by counting fraudulent rains-residences according to the order of novices, is not one who co-resides by theft. A bhikkhu who takes offerings by counting fraudulent rains-residences according to the order of bhikkhus should be made to pay the value of the goods.

Theyyasaṃvāsakavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The discussion on the topic of one who co-resides by theft is concluded.

Titthiyapakkantakakathā

The Discussion of One Gone Over to the Sectarians

Titthiyapakkantako [P 5.1021][V 0.0287] bhikkhaveti ettha pana titthiyesu pakkanto paviṭṭhoti titthiyapakkantako. So na kevalaṃ na upasampādetabbo, atha kho na pabbājetabbopi. Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – upasampanno bhikkhu titthiyo bhavissāmīti saliṅgeneva tesaṃ upassayaṃ gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Tesaṃ liṅge ādinnamatte titthiyapakkantako hoti. Yopi [M 0.0303] sayameva “titthiyo bhavissāmī”ti kusacīrādīni nivāseti, titthiyapakkantako hotiyeva. Yo pana naggo nhāyanto attānaṃ oloketvā “sobhati me ājīvakabhāvo, ājīvako bhavissāmī”ti kāsāyāni anādāya naggova ājīvakānaṃ upassayaṃ gacchati, padavāre padavāre dukkaṭaṃ. Sace panassa antarāmagge hirottappaṃ uppajjati, dukkaṭāni desetvā muccati. Tesaṃ upassayaṃ gantvāpi tehi vā ovadito attanā vā “imesaṃ pabbajjā atidukkhā”ti nivattantopi muccatiyeva.

Herein, regarding 'a bhikkhu who has gone over to the sectarians,' one who has departed to the sectarians, who has entered among them, is a titthiyapakkantaka. He should not only not be given the higher ordination, but indeed, he should not even be given the going-forth. Herein is the ruling: if a fully ordained bhikkhu, thinking, 'I will become a sectarian,' goes to their dwelling with his own sign as a bhikkhu, there is an offense of wrongdoing at every step. The moment their sign is adopted, he becomes one who has gone over to the sectarians. Also, whoever on his own, thinking, 'I will become a sectarian,' puts on kusa-grass garments and so on, he too becomes one who has gone over to the sectarians. But if a bhikkhu, while bathing naked, looks at himself and thinks, 'The state of an Ājīvaka suits me; I will become an Ājīvaka,' and without taking his ochre robes, goes naked to the dwelling of the Ājīvakas, there is an offense of wrongdoing at every step. But if, for him, shame and fear of wrongdoing arise on the way, he is freed after confessing the offenses of wrongdoing. Even having gone to their dwelling, whether being instructed by them or seeing for himself and thinking, 'The going-forth of these is very difficult,' one who turns back is indeed freed.

Sace pana “kiṃ tumhākaṃ pabbajjāya ukkaṭṭha”nti pucchitvā “kesamassuluñcanādīnī”ti vutto ekakesampi luñcāpeti, ukkuṭikappadhānādīni vā vattāni ādiyati, morapiñchādīni vā nivāseti, tesaṃ liṅgaṃ gaṇhāti, “ayaṃ pabbajjā seṭṭhā”ti seṭṭhabhāvaṃ vā upagacchati, na muccati, titthiyapakkantako hoti. Sace pana “sobhati nu kho me titthiyapabbajjā, nanu kho sobhatī”ti vīmaṃsanatthaṃ kusacīrādīni vā nivāseti, jaṭaṃ vā bandhati, khārikājaṃ vā ādiyati, yāva na sampaṭicchati, tāva naṃ laddhi rakkhati, sampaṭicchitamatte titthiyapakkantako hoti. Acchinnacīvaro pana kusacīrādīni nivāsento rājabhayādīhi vā titthiyaliṅgaṃ gaṇhanto laddhiyā abhāvena neva titthiyapakkantako hoti.

But if, having asked, 'What is the most excellent in your going-forth?' and having been told, 'The plucking of hair and beard, and so on,' he has even a single hair plucked; or he undertakes observances such as striving in the squatting posture; or he wears a bundle of peacock feathers and so on; or he takes up their sign; or, thinking 'This going-forth is excellent,' he arrives at the state of it being excellent, he is not freed; he becomes one who has gone over to the sectarians. But if, for the purpose of investigating, 'Does the sectarian going-forth suit me, or does it not suit me?' he wears kusa-grass garments and so on, or ties his hair in a topknot, or takes up a carrying-pole, as long as he does not accept their view, his own view protects him. The moment it is accepted, he becomes one who has gone over to the sectarians. However, a bhikkhu whose robe has been stolen who wears kusa-grass garments and so on, or who takes up the sign of the sectarians due to fear of the king and so on, does not become one who has gone over to the sectarians because of the absence of their view.

Ayañca titthiyapakkantako nāma upasampannabhikkhunā kathito, tasmā sāmaṇero saliṅgena titthāyatanaṃ gatopi puna pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhatīti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ. Purimo pana theyyasaṃvāsako anupasampannena kathito; tasmā upasampanno kūṭavassaṃ gaṇentopi assamaṇo na hoti. Liṅge saussāho pārājikaṃ āpajjitvā bhikkhuvassādīni gaṇentopi theyyasaṃvāsako na hotīti.

And this case of 'one who has gone over to the sectarians' was spoken of in reference to a fully ordained bhikkhu. Therefore, it is said in the Kurundī that a novice, even having gone to a sectarian establishment with his own sign, can again obtain the going-forth and the higher ordination. But the previous case of 'one who co-resides by theft' was spoken of in reference to one not fully ordained. Therefore, a fully ordained one, even when counting a fraudulent rains-residence, does not become a non-ascetic. One who, being zealous about his sign, having fallen into a pārājika offense, even when counting the years as a bhikkhu and so on, does not become one who co-resides by theft.

Titthiyapakkantakakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of One Gone Over to the Sectarians is concluded.

Tiracchānagatavatthukathā

The Exposition on the Account of One Gone to the Animal State

111. Nāgayoniyā [P 5.1022][V 0.0288] aṭṭīyatīti ettha kiñcāpi so pavattiyaṃ kusalavipākena devasampattisadisaṃ issariyasampattiṃ anubhoti, akusalavipākapaṭisandhikassa [M 0.0304] pana tassa sajātiyā methunapaṭisevane ca vissaṭṭhaniddokkamane ca nāgasarīraṃ pātubhavati udakasañcārikaṃ maṇḍūkabhakkhaṃ, tasmā so tāya nāgayoniyā aṭṭīyati. Harāyatīti lajjati. Jigucchatīti attabhāvaṃ jigucchati. Tassa bhikkhuno nikkhanteti tasmiṃ bhikkhusmiṃ nikkhante. Atha vā tassa bhikkhuno nikkhamaneti attho. Vissaṭṭho niddaṃ okkamīti tasmiṃ anikkhante vissarabhayena satiṃ avissajjitvā kapimiddhavaseneva niddāyanto nikkhante satiṃ vissajjitvā vissaṭṭho nirāsaṅko mahāniddaṃ paṭipajji. Vissaramakāsīti bhayavasena samaṇasaññaṃ pahāya virūpaṃ mahāsaddamakāsi.

111. Regarding 'is afflicted by the nāga-womb': Herein, although in the course of his existence, due to the result of wholesome kamma, he experiences a sovereign fortune like that of the devas, yet for him, who has a rebirth-linking that is the result of unwholesome kamma, his nāga body—which moves about in water and has frogs as its food—appears when he engages in sexual intercourse with one of his own kind and when he falls into an abandoned sleep. Therefore, he is afflicted by that nāga-womb. 'He is ashamed' means he feels shame. 'He is disgusted' means he is disgusted with his own existence. 'When that bhikkhu had departed' means when that bhikkhu had departed. Or, it means 'because of the departure of that bhikkhu.' 'He fell into an abandoned sleep' means: while that bhikkhu had not departed, out of fear of making a strange sound, he did not abandon mindfulness and slept only with a drowsiness like that of a monkey; but when the bhikkhu had departed, having abandoned mindfulness, he, with abandon and free from anxiety, entered a deep sleep. 'He made a strange sound' means: due to fear, having abandoned the perception of being an ascetic, he made a deformed, loud sound.

Tumhe khotthāti tumhe kho attha; akārassa lopaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Tumhe kho nāgā jhānavipassanāmaggaphalānaṃ abhabbattā imasmiṃ dhammavinaye aviruḷhidhammā attha, viruḷhidhammā na bhavathāti ayamettha saṅkhepattho. Sajātiyāti nāgiyā eva. Yadā pana manussitthiādibhedāya aññajātiyā paṭisevati, tadā devaputto viya hoti. Ettha ca pavattiyaṃ abhiṇhaṃ sabhāvapātukammadassanavasena “dve paccayā”ti vuttaṃ. Nāgassa pana pañcasu kālesu sabhāvapātukammaṃ hoti – paṭisandhikāle, tacajahanakāle, sajātiyā methunakāle, vissaṭṭhaniddokkamanakāle, cutikāleti.

The phrase tumhe khottha is tumhe kho attha; it is stated thus, having elided the letter 'a'. The concise meaning here is this: 'You nāgas, due to being incapable of jhāna, insight, path, and fruition, are of a nature that does not grow in this Dhamma-Vinaya; you are not of a nature that grows.' 'Of his own kind' means only with a female nāga. But when he engages with one of another kind, such as a human woman, he is then like a deva. And here, 'two conditions' was said by the Blessed One by way of showing the frequent manifestation of his natural state in the course of existence. However, for a nāga, the manifestation of his natural state occurs at five times: at the time of rebirth-linking, at the time of shedding its skin, at the time of sexual intercourse with one of its own kind, at the time of falling into an abandoned sleep, and at the time of death.

Tiracchānagato bhikkhaveti ettha nāgo vā hotu supaṇṇamāṇavakādīnaṃ vā aññataro, antamaso sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ upādāya yo koci amanussajātiyo, sabbova imasmiṃ atthe tiracchānagatoti veditabbo. So neva upasampādetabbo, na pabbājetabbo, upasampannopi nāsetabboti.

Herein, in the phrase 'Bhikkhus, one gone to the animal state': be it a nāga, or another among the supaṇṇa youths and so on, or any non-human being whatsoever, even up to Sakka, king of the devas—all, in this context, are to be understood as 'one gone to the animal state.' Such a one should neither be given the higher ordination nor the going-forth; and if already possessing the higher ordination, he is to be expelled.

Tiracchānagatavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Exposition on the Account of One Gone to the Animal State is concluded.

Mātughātakādivatthukathā

The Exposition on the Account of Matricide and So Forth

112. Mātughātakādivatthūsu – nikkhantiṃ kareyyanti nikkhamanaṃ niggamanaṃ apavāhanaṃ kareyyanti attho. Mātughātako bhikkhaveti ettha yena manussitthibhūtā [M 0.0305] janikā mātā [P 5.1023] sayampi [V 0.0289] manussajātikeneva satā sañcicca jīvitā voropitā, ayaṃ ānantariyena mātughātakakammena mātughātako, etassa pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca paṭikkhittā. Yena pana manussitthibhūtāpi ajanikā posāvanikā mātā vā mahāmātā vā cūḷamātā vā janikāpi vā na manussitthibhūtā mātā ghātitā, tassa pabbajjā na vāritā, na ca ānantariko hoti. Yena sayaṃ tiracchānabhūtena manussitthibhūtā mātā ghātitā, sopi ānantariko na hoti, tiracchānagatattā panassa pabbajjā paṭikkhittā. Sesaṃ uttānameva. Pitughātakepi eseva nayo. Sacepi hi vesiyā putto hoti, “ayaṃ me pitā”ti na jānāti, yassa sambhavena nibbatto, so ce anena ghātito, pitughātakotveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati, ānantariyañca phusati.

112. In the cases of matricide and so forth—‘nikkhantiṃ kareyyanti’ means: should one effect a departure, a leaving, a removal? ‘A matricide, bhikkhus’—herein, one who, being himself of human birth, intentionally deprives of life his own birth mother, who was a human woman, is a matricide by means of the immediately consequential kamma of matricide. For him, both going forth and higher ordination are prohibited. However, for one who kills a mother who, though a human woman, was not his birth mother—such as a foster mother, a grandmother, or an aunt—or a birth mother who was not a human woman, his going forth is not prohibited, nor does he become one who incurs an immediately consequential kamma. One who, being an animal, kills his mother who was a human woman, also does not become one who incurs an immediately consequential kamma; however, his going forth is prohibited on account of his being an animal. The rest is self-evident. In the case of a patricide, this is the same method. For even if he is the son of a prostitute and does not know, ‘This is my father,’ if the one by whose seed he was produced is killed by him, he is reckoned only as a patricide and incurs an immediately consequential kamma.

114. Arahantaghātakopi manussaarahantavaseneva veditabbo.
