Manussajātiyañhi antamaso apabbajitampi khīṇāsavaṃ dārakaṃ dārikaṃ vā sañcicca jīvitā voropento arahantaghātakova hoti, ānantariyañca phusati, pabbajjā cassa vāritā. Amanussajātikaṃ pana arahantaṃ manussajātikaṃ vā avasesaṃ ariyapuggalaṃ ghātetvā ānantariyo na hoti, pabbajjāpissa na vāritā, kammaṃ pana balavaṃ hoti. Tiracchāno manussaarahantampi ghātetvā ānantariyo na hoti, kammaṃ pana bhāriyanti ayamettha vinicchayo. Te vadhāya onīyantīti vadhatthāya onīyanti, māretuṃ nīyantīti attho. Yaṃ pana pāḷiyaṃ “sacā ca maya”nti vuttaṃ, tassa sace mayanti ayamevattho. “Sace”ti hi vattabbe ettha “sacā ca” iti ayaṃ nipāto vutto. “Sace ca” icceva vā pāṭho. Tattha saceti sambhāvanatthe nipāto; ca iti padapūraṇamatte. “Sacajja maya”ntipi pāṭho. Tassa sace ajja mayanti attho.

114. The killer of an Arahant is also to be understood only by way of a human Arahant. For one of human birth who intentionally deprives of life a boy or girl whose taints are destroyed, even one who is, at the very least, not gone forth, is indeed a killer of an Arahant, incurs an immediately consequential kamma, and his going forth is barred. However, by killing a non-human Arahant or a remaining noble person of human birth, one does not incur an immediately consequential kamma, nor is his going forth barred; the kamma, however, is powerful. An animal, by killing even a human Arahant, does not incur an immediately consequential kamma, but the kamma is grave—this is the determination here. ‘Te vadhāya onīyantīti’ means they are led out for the purpose of execution; the meaning is they are led to be killed. As for what is said in the Pāḷi, ‘sacā ca mayaṃ,’ its meaning is simply ‘sace mayaṃ’ (if we). For where ‘sace’ should be said, here this particle ‘sacā ca’ is spoken. Alternatively, the reading is just ‘sace ca.’ Therein, ‘sace’ is a particle in the sense of possibility; ‘ca’ is merely for filling out the line. There is also the reading ‘sacajja mayaṃ.’ Its meaning is ‘sace ajja mayaṃ’ (if today we).

115. Bhikkhunidūsako bhikkhaveti ettha yo pakatattaṃ bhikkhuniṃ tiṇṇaṃ maggānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ dūseti, ayaṃ bhikkhunidūsako nāma. Etassa pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca vāritā. Yo pana kāyasaṃsaggena sīlavināsaṃ pāpeti, tassa pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca na vāritā. Balakkārena odātavatthavasanaṃ katvā anicchamānaṃyeva [P 5.1024] dūsentopi bhikkhunidūsakoyeva. Balakkārena pana odātavatthavasanaṃ katvā icchamānaṃ dūsento bhikkhunidūsako [M 0.0306] na hoti. Kasmā? Yasmā gihibhāve sampaṭicchitamatteyeva sā abhikkhunī hoti. Sakiṃ sīlavipannaṃ pana pacchā dūsento sikkhamānāsāmaṇerīsu ca vippaṭipajjanto neva bhikkhunidūsako hoti, pabbajjampi upasampadampi labhati.

115. ‘A defiler of a bhikkhunī, bhikkhus’—herein, one who defiles a bhikkhunī in good standing in one or another of the three passages is called a defiler of a bhikkhunī. For him, both going forth and higher ordination are barred. However, for one who causes the destruction of virtue through bodily contact, his going forth and higher ordination are not barred. One who defiles an unwilling bhikkhunī after forcibly making her wear white clothes is indeed a defiler of a bhikkhunī. However, one who defiles a willing bhikkhunī after forcibly making her wear white clothes is not a defiler of a bhikkhunī. Why? Because at the very moment of accepting the lay state, she is no longer a bhikkhunī. However, one who afterwards defiles a bhikkhunī whose virtue has already been broken once, and one who misbehaves with female probationers and female novices, is not a defiler of a bhikkhunī at all; he may receive both going forth and higher ordination.

Saṅghabhedako [V 0.0290] bhikkhaveti ettha yo devadatto viya sāsanaṃ uddhammaṃ ubbinayaṃ katvā catunnaṃ kammānaṃ aññataravasena saṅghaṃ bhindati, ayaṃ saṅghabhedako nāma. Etassa pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca vāritā.

‘A schismatic, bhikkhus’—herein, a monk who, like Devadatta, having rendered the Dispensation as non-Dhamma and non-Vinaya, splits the Saṅgha by means of one or another of the four formal acts, is called a schismatic. For him, both going forth and higher ordination are barred.

Lohituppādako bhikkhaveti etthāpi yo devadatto viya duṭṭhacittena vadhakacittena tathāgatassa jīvamānakasarīre khuddakamakkhikāya pivanakamattampi lohitaṃ uppādeti, ayaṃ lohituppādako nāma. Etassa pabbajjā ca upasampadā ca vāritā. Yo pana rogavūpasamanatthaṃ jīvako viya satthena phāletvā pūtimaṃsañca lohitañca nīharitvā phāsuṃ karoti, bahuṃ so puññaṃ pasavatīti.

‘One who causes blood to flow, bhikkhus’—herein also, one who, like Devadatta, with a corrupt mind and a murderous mind, produces on the Tathāgata’s living body blood even to the amount a small fly might drink, is called one who causes blood to flow. For him, both going forth and higher ordination are barred. However, one who, like Jīvaka, for the purpose of curing an illness, makes an incision with a knife, removes putrid flesh and blood, and makes the patient comfortable—he generates much merit.

Mātughātakādivatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Cases of Matricide and So Forth is finished.

Ubhatobyañjanakavatthukathā

The Discourse on the Case of an Ubhatobyañjanaka

116. Ubhatobyañjanako bhikkhaveti itthinimittuppādanakammato ca purisanimittuppādanakammato ca ubhato byañjanamassa atthīti ubhatobyañjanako. Karotīti purisanimittena itthīsu methunavītikkamaṃ karoti. Kārāpetīti paraṃ samādapetvā attano itthinimitte kārāpeti, so duvidho hoti – itthiubhatobyañjanako, purisaubhatobyañjanakoti.

116. ‘An ubhatobyañjanaka, bhikkhus’—one is called an ubhatobyañjanaka because for that person a characteristic exists due to both the kamma that produces the female sign and the kamma that produces the male sign. ‘He does it’ means: he commits a sexual transgression with women by means of the male sign. ‘He causes it to be done’ means: having persuaded another, he causes it to be done in his own female sign. That person is of two kinds: a female ubhatobyañjanaka and a male ubhatobyañjanaka.

Tattha itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthinimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti, purisanimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ, itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Itthiubhatobyañjanakassa itthīsu purisattaṃ karontassa itthinimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, purisanimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Purisaubhatobyañjanakassa purisānaṃ itthibhāvaṃ upagacchantassa purisanimittaṃ paṭicchannaṃ hoti, itthinimittaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti. Itthiubhatobyañjanako sayañca gabbhaṃ gaṇhāti, parañca gaṇhāpeti. Purisaubhatobyañjanako pana sayaṃ na gaṇhāti, paraṃ gaṇhāpetīti, idametesaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana vuttaṃ – “yadi paṭisandhiyaṃ purisaliṅgaṃ [P 5.1025] pavatte itthiliṅgaṃ nibbattati, yadi paṭisandhiyaṃ itthiliṅgaṃ pavatte purisaliṅgaṃ nibbattatī”ti[M 0.0307]. Tattha vicāraṇakkamo vitthārato aṭṭhasāliniyā dhammasaṅgahaṭṭhakathāya veditabbo. Imassa pana duvidhassāpi ubhatobyañjanakassa neva pabbajjā atthi, na upasampadāti idamidha veditabbaṃ.

Among these two, for a female ubhatobyañjanaka, the female sign is manifest and the male sign is concealed. For a male ubhatobyañjanaka, the male sign is manifest and the female sign is concealed. For a female ubhatobyañjanaka who acts as a man among women, the female sign becomes concealed and the male sign becomes manifest. For a male ubhatobyañjanaka who approaches the state of a woman among men, the male sign becomes concealed and the female sign becomes manifest. A female ubhatobyañjanaka both conceives and causes another to conceive. A male ubhatobyañjanaka, however, does not conceive but causes another to conceive. This is the distinction between them. In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is said: 'If at the time of relinking there is the male sex, in the course of existence the female sex arises; if at the time of relinking there is the female sex, in the course of existence the male sex arises.' The method of investigating this should be known in detail from the Aṭṭhasālinī, the commentary to the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. Furthermore, it should be known here that for both these kinds of ubhatobyañjanaka, there is neither the going forth nor the higher ordination.

Ubhatobyajjanakavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Case of an Ubhatobyañjanaka is concluded.

Anupajjhāyakādivatthukathā

The Discourse on the Case of One Without a Preceptor, and Other Topics

117. Tena [V 0.0291] kho pana samayenāti yena samayena bhagavatā sikkhāpadaṃ apaññattaṃ hoti, tena samayena. Anupajjhāyakanti upajjhaṃ agāhāpetvā sabbena sabbaṃ upajjhāyavirahitaṃ. Evaṃ upasampannā neva dhammato na āmisato saṅgahaṃ labhanti, te parihāyantiyeva, na vaḍḍhanti. Na bhikkhave anupajjhāyakoti upajjhaṃ agāhāpetvā nirupajjhāyako na upasampādetabbo. Yo upasampādeyya āpatti dukkaṭassāti sikkhāpadapaññattito paṭṭhāya evaṃ upasampādentassa āpatti hoti; kammaṃ pana na kuppati. Keci kuppatīti vadanti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Saṅghena upajjhāyenātiādīsupi ubhatobyañjanakupajjhāyapariyosānesu eseva nayo.

117. “Now at that time” refers to the time when the Blessed One had not yet laid down the training rule. “Without a preceptor” means entirely without a preceptor, not having had one assigned. Those thus ordained receive neither support in accordance with the Dhamma nor material support; they decline and do not prosper. “Monks, one without a preceptor should not be ordained” means one should not give higher ordination to someone without a preceptor, not having had one assigned. Regarding “Whoever should ordain such a one incurs an offense of wrong conduct”: from the time the training rule was laid down, for one who ordains in this way there is an offense; however, the formal act is not invalidated. Some say it is invalidated, but that should not be accepted. This same principle applies in cases such as “by the Saṅgha, with a preceptor,” and so on, up to the rules concluding with the preceptor who is an ubhatobyañjanaka.

Anupajjhāyakādivatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Case of One Without a Preceptor, and Other Topics, is concluded.

Apattakādivatthukathā

The Discourse on the Case of One Without a Bowl, etc.

118. Hatthesu piṇḍāya carantīti yo hatthesu piṇḍo labbhati, tadatthāya caranti. Seyyathāpi titthiyāti yathā ājīvakanāmakā titthiyā; sūpabyañjanehi missetvā hatthesu ṭhapitapiṇḍameva hi te bhuñjanti. Āpatti dukkaṭassāti evaṃ upasampādentasseva āpatti hoti, kammaṃ pana na kuppati. Acīvarakādivatthūsupi eseva nayo.

118. “They wander for alms in their hands” means: they wander for the sake of the almsfood that is obtained in their hands. “Just as the sectarians” means: just as the sectarians named Ājīvaka; indeed, having mixed it with soup and curries, they eat only the lump of almsfood placed in their hands. “The offense is one of wrong-doing” means: thus, there is an offense only for the one who ordains, but the formal act is not invalidated. In the cases of one without robes, etc., this is the same principle.

Yācitakenāti “yāva upasampadaṃ karoma, tāva dethā”ti yācitvā gahitena; tāvakālikenāti attho. Īdisena hi pattena vā cīvarena vā pattacīvarena vā upasampādentasseva āpatti hoti, kammaṃ pana na kuppati, tasmā paripuṇṇapattacīvarova upasampādetabbo. Sace tassa natthi, ācariyupajjhāyā cassa dātukāmā honti, aññe vā bhikkhū nirapekkhehi nissajjitvā adhiṭṭhānupagaṃ pattacīvaraṃ dātabbaṃ. Pabbajjāpekkhaṃ pana paṇḍupalāsaṃ yācitakenāpi pattacīvarena pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati, sabhāgaṭṭhāne vissāsena gahetvāpi pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

“By what is requested” means by that which is taken after requesting, “Give it for as long as we perform the higher ordination”; the meaning is “for temporary use.” Indeed, with such a bowl, or robe, or bowl and robes, there is an offense only for the one who ordains, but the formal act is not invalidated. Therefore, only one with a complete bowl and robes should be ordained. If he does not have them, and his teacher and preceptor are willing to give them, or other monks are, a bowl and robes fit for determination should be given, after they have become unattached and relinquished them. However, regarding a candidate seeking the going forth, it is allowable to give the going forth even with a requested bowl and robes. It is also allowable to give the going forth after taking them with trust from a place of associates.

Sace pana [P 5.1026] apakkaṃ pattaṃ cīvarūpagāni ca vatthāni gahetvā āgato hoti, yāva patto paccati, cīvarāni ca kariyanti, tāva vihāre vasantassa [M 0.0308] anāmaṭṭhapiṇḍapātaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati, thālake bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, purebhattaṃ sāmaṇerabhāgasamako āmisabhāgo dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Senāsanaggāho [V 0.0292] pana salākabhattauddesabhattanimantanādīni ca na vaṭṭanti. Pacchābhattampi sāmaṇerabhāgasamo telamadhuphāṇitādibhesajjabhāgo vaṭṭati. Sace gilāno hoti, bhesajjamassa kātuṃ vaṭṭati, sāmaṇerassa viya ca sabbaṃ paṭijagganakammanti.

If, however, a candidate arrives having taken an unbaked bowl and cloths suitable for robes, then for as long as the bowl is being baked and the robes are being made, it is allowable to give him, while he is dwelling in the monastery, almsfood of which the first portion has not been set aside. It is allowable for him to eat from a dish. Before the meal, it is allowable to give him a material share equal to that of a novice. However, the taking of a lodging, ticket-food, designated-food, invitations, and so forth are not allowable. After the mealtime, a share of medicines such as oil, honey, and molasses, equal to that of a novice, is allowable. If he is sick, it is allowable to prepare medicine for him, and all attending duties should be performed as for a novice.

Apattakādivatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Case of One Without a Bowl, etc., is concluded.

Hatthacchinnādivatthukathā

The Discourse on the Case of One with a Severed Hand, etc.

119. Hatthacchinnādivatthūsu – hatthacchinnoti yassa hatthatale vā maṇibandhe vā kappare vā yattha katthaci eko vā dve vā hatthā chinnā honti. Pādacchinnoti yassa aggapāde vā gopphakesu vā jaṅghāya vā yattha katthaci eko vā dve vā pādā chinnā honti. Hatthapādacchinnoti yassa vuttappakāreneva catūsu hatthapādesu dve vā tayo vā sabbe vā hatthapādā chinnā honti. Kaṇṇacchinnoti yassa kaṇṇamūle vā kaṇṇasakkhalikāya vā eko vā dve vā kaṇṇā chinnā honti. Yassa pana kaṇṇāviddhe chijjanti, sakkā ca hoti saṅghāṭetuṃ, so kaṇṇaṃ saṅghāṭetvā pabbājetabbo. Nāsacchinnoti yassa ajapadake vā agge vā ekapuṭe vā yattha katthaci nāsā chinnā hoti. Yassa pana nāsikā sakkā hoti sandhetuṃ, so taṃ phāsukaṃ katvā pabbājetabbo. Kaṇṇanāsacchinno ubhayavasena veditabbo. Aṅgulicchinnoti yassa nakhasesaṃ adassetvā ekā vā bahū vā aṅguliyo chinnā honti. Yassa pana suttatantumattampi nakhasesaṃ paññāyati, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Aḷacchinnoti yassa catūsu aṅguṭṭhakesu aṅguliyaṃ vuttanayeneva eko vā bahū vā aṅguṭṭhakā chinnā honti. Kaṇḍaracchinnoti yassa kaṇḍaranāmakā mahānhārū purato vā pacchato vā chinnā honti; yesu ekassapi chinnattā aggapādena vā caṅkamati, mūlena vā caṅkamati, na vā pādaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ sakkoti.

119. In the cases of one with a severed hand and so forth, the decision should be understood thus. “One with a severed hand” is one whose one or two hands are severed at the palm, or at the wrist, or at the elbow, or anywhere whatsoever. “One with a severed foot” is one whose one or two feet are severed at the tip of the foot, or at the ankles, or at the shin, or anywhere whatsoever. “One with severed hands and feet” is one whose two, or three, or all hands and feet out of the four are severed in the manner just stated. “One with a severed ear” is one whose one or two ears are severed at the base of the ear or at the earlobe. If, however, one's pierced ears are torn, and it is possible to join them, he should be given the going forth after joining the ear. “One with a severed nose” is one whose nose is severed at the part shaped like a goat's hoof, or at the tip, or at one nostril, or anywhere whatsoever. If, however, one's nose can be joined, he should be given the going forth after it has been made comfortable. “One with severed ears and nose” should be understood by way of both. “One with a severed finger or toe” is one whose one or many fingers or toes are severed without showing a remnant of the nail. If, however, a remnant of the nail even to the extent of a thread is apparent, it is allowable to give him the going forth. “One with a severed thumb or big toe” is one whose one or many thumbs or big toes out of the four are severed in the manner stated for the finger or toe. “One with a severed tendon” is one whose great sinews called 'kaṇḍara' are severed in the front or in the back; due to the severing of even one of these, one walks on the forefoot, or walks on the heel, or is unable to place the foot down.

Phaṇahatthakoti [P 5.1027] yassa vaggulipakkhakā viya aṅguliyo sambaddhā honti; etaṃ pabbājetukāmena aṅgulantarikāyo phāletvā sabbaṃ antaracammaṃ apanetvā phāsukaṃ katvā pabbājetabbo. Yassapi cha aṅguliyo [M 0.0309] honti, taṃ pabbājetukāmena adhikaaṅguliṃ chinditvā phāsukaṃ katvā pabbājetabbo.

“One with webbed hands” is one whose fingers are connected like a bat's wing. One wishing to give him the going forth should have the spaces between the fingers split, have all the skin in between removed, and after it has been made comfortable, give him the going forth. For one who has six fingers, one wishing to give him the going forth should have the extra finger cut off, and after it has been made comfortable, give him the going forth.

Khujjoti yo urassa vā piṭṭhiyā vā passassa vā nikkhantattā khujjasarīro. Yassa pana [V 0.0293] kiñci kiñci aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ īsakaṃ vaṅkaṃ, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Mahāpuriso eva hi brahmujjugatto, avaseso satto akhujjo nāma natthi.

“A hunchback” is one who has a crooked body due to the protrusion of the chest, or the back, or the side. However, for one whose any major or minor limb is slightly crooked, it is allowable to give him the going forth. Indeed, only a Great Man has a body as straight as Brahmā's; there is no remaining being who is not crooked.

Vāmanoti jaṅghavāmano vā kaṭivāmano vā ubhayavāmano vā. Jaṅghavāmanassa kaṭito paṭṭhāya heṭṭhimakāyo rasso hoti, uparimakāyo paripuṇṇo. Kaṭivāmanassa kaṭito paṭṭhāya uparimakāyo rasso hoti, heṭṭhimakāyo paripuṇṇo. Ubhayavāmanassa ubhopi kāyā rassā honti, yesaṃ rassattā bhūtānaṃ viya parivaṭumo mahākucchighaṭasadiso attabhāvo hoti, taṃ tividhampi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

“A dwarf” is one who is a shin-dwarf, or a waist-dwarf, or a dwarf in both respects. For a shin-dwarf, the lower body from the waist down is short, while the upper body is complete. For a waist-dwarf, the upper body from the waist up is short, while the lower body is complete. For a dwarf in both respects, both parts of the body are short; due to their shortness, their individual existence is round all over like a goblin's and resembles a large-bellied water pot. It is not allowable to give the going forth to any of these three types.

Galagaṇḍīti yassa kumbhaṇḍaṃ viya gale gaṇḍo hoti. Desanāmattameva cetaṃ, yasmiṃ kismiñci pana padese gaṇḍe sati na pabbājetabbo. Tattha vinicchayo – “na bhikkhave pañcahi ābādhehi phuṭṭho pabbājetabbo”ti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Lakkhaṇāhatakasāhatalikhitakesu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ “na bhikkhave lakkhaṇāhato”tiādīsu vuttameva.

“One with a goiter” is one who has a lump on the neck like a gourd. And this is merely an indication; in fact, if there is a lump in any place whatsoever, he should not be given the going forth. The decision in this matter should be understood in the same way as stated in the passage: “Monks, one afflicted with the five diseases should not be given the going forth.” As for what should be said regarding one who is branded, one who has been caned, and one who is an outlaw, that has already been stated in the passages beginning, “Monks, one who is branded,” and so forth.

Sīpadīti bhārapādo vuccati. Yassa pādo thūlo hoti sañjātapiḷako kharo, so na pabbājetabbo. Yassa pana na tāva kharabhāvaṃ gaṇhāti, sakkā hoti upanāhaṃ bandhitvā udakaāvāṭe pavesetvā udakavālikāya pūretvā yathā sirā paññāyanti, jaṅghā ca telanāḷikā viya hoti, evaṃ milāpetuṃ sakkā, tassa pādaṃ īdisaṃ katvā taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace puna vaḍḍhati, upasampādentenāpi tathā katvāva upasampādetabbo.

One with elephantiasis is said to have a heavy foot. Whoever has a foot that is thick, has developed boils, and is rough, should not be given the going forth. However, for one whose foot has not yet become rough, it is possible to treat it by applying a poultice, immersing it in a water pit, and filling it with wet sand until the veins become visible and the shin becomes like an oil tube. If it can be made to shrink in this way, it is permissible to give him the going forth after treating his foot thus. If it swells again, even the one conferring the higher ordination must confer it only after having treated it in such a way.

Pāparogīti arisabhagandarapittasemhakāsasosādīsu yena kenaci rogena niccāturo atekiccharogo jeguccho amanāpo; ayaṃ na pabbājetabbo.

A person with a foul disease is one who is constantly afflicted by some disease such as hemorrhoids, fistula, bilious disorders, phlegm, cough, or consumption; is incurably ill, repulsive, and disagreeable. Such a person should not be given the going forth.

Parisadūsakoti yo attano virūpatāya parisaṃ dūseti; atidīgho vā hoti aññesaṃ sīsappamāṇanābhippadeso, atirasso [M 0.0310] vā ubhayavāmanabhūtarūpaṃ [P 5.1028] viya, atikāḷo vā jhāpitakhette khāṇuko viya, accodāto vā dadhitakkādīhi pamajjitamaṭṭhatambalohavaṇṇo, atikiso vā mandamaṃsalohito aṭṭhisirācammasarīro viya, atithūlo vā bhāriyamaṃso, mahodaro vā mahābhūtasadiso, atimahantasīso vā pacchiṃ sīse katvā ṭhito viya, atikhuddakasīso vā sarīrassa ananurūpena atikhuddakena sīsena samannāgato, kūṭakūṭasīso vā [V 0.0294] tālaphalapiṇḍisadisena sīsena samannāgato, sikharasīso vā uddhaṃ anupubbatanukena sīsena samannāgato, nāḷisīso vā mahāveḷupabbasadisena sīsena samannāgato, kappasīso vā pabbhārasīso vā catūsu passesu yena kenaci passena oṇatena sīsena samannāgato, vaṇasīso vā pūtisīso vā kaṇṇikakeso vā pāṇakehi khāyitakedāre sassasadisehi tahiṃ tahiṃ uṭṭhitehi kesehi samannāgato, nillomasīso vā thūlathaddhakeso vā tālahīrasadisehi kesehi samannāgato, jātipalitehi paṇḍarasīso vā pakatitambakeso vā ādittehi viya kesehi samannāgato, āvaṭṭasīso vā gunnaṃ sarīre āvaṭṭasadisehi uddhaggehi kesāvaṭṭehi samannāgato, sīsalomehi saddhiṃ ekābaddhabhamukalomo vā jālabaddhena viya nalāṭena samannāgato.

One who spoils an assembly is one who spoils an assembly by his own deformity. He may be excessively tall, with his navel region at the level of others’ heads; or excessively short, like the form of a goblin dwarfed in both its upper and lower parts; or excessively dark, like a stump in a burnt field; or excessively pale, with a complexion like polished copper burnished with curd or buttermilk; or excessively thin, with little flesh and blood, like a body of only bone, sinew, and skin; or excessively fat, with heavy flesh; or with a large belly, like a great goblin; or with an excessively large head, as if standing with a basket on his head; or with an excessively small head that is disproportionate to his body; or with a lumpy head, endowed with a head like a cluster of young palm fruits; or with a peaked head, endowed with a head that tapers gradually upwards; or with a tubular head, endowed with a head like a large bamboo joint; or with a forked head or a sloping head, endowed with a head bent on any of its four sides; or with a wounded head or a putrid head; or with hair like a lotus pericarp, endowed with hair growing here and there like crops in a field eaten by insects; or with a hairless head; or with thick, stiff hair, endowed with hair like palm fibers; or with a white head from birth-gray hair; or with naturally red hair, endowed with hair as if on fire; or with a whorled head, endowed with hair whorls whose tips point upwards, like the whorls on the body of cattle; or one whose eyebrow hair is joined as one with the hair of the head, possessing a forehead as if bound by a net.

Sambaddhabhamuko vā nillomabhamuko vā makkaṭabhamuko vā atimahantakkhi vā atikhuddakakkhi vā mahiṃsacamme vāsikoṇena paharitvā katachiddasadisehi akkhīhi samannāgato, visamakkhi vā ekena mahantena ekena khuddakena akkhinā samannāgato, visamacakkalo vā ekena uddhaṃ ekena adhoti evaṃ visamajātehi akkhicakkalehi samannāgato, kekaro vā gambhīrakkhi vā yassa gambhīre udapāne udakatārakā viya akkhitārakā paññāyanti; nikkhantakkhi vā yassa kakkaṭakasseva akkhitārakā nikkhantā honti; hatthikaṇṇo vā mahatīhi kaṇṇasakkhalikāhi samannāgato, mūsikakaṇṇo vā jaṭukakaṇṇo vā khuddikāhi kaṇṇasakkhalikāhi samannāgato, chiddamattakaṇṇo vā yassa vinā kaṇṇasakkhalikāhi [M 0.0311] kaṇṇachiddamattameva [P 5.1029] hoti; aviddhakaṇṇo vā yonakajātiko pana parisadūsako na hoti; sabhāvoyeva hi so tassa kaṇṇabhagandariko vā niccapūtinā kaṇṇena samannāgato, gaṇḍakaṇṇo vā sadāpaggharitapubbena kaṇṇena samannāgato, ṭaṅkitakaṇṇo vā gobhattanāḷikāya aggasadisehi kaṇṇehi samannāgato, atipiṅgalakkhi vā madhupiṅgalaṃ pana pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Nippakhumakkhi vā assupaggharaṇakkhi vā pupphitakkhi vā akkhipākena samannāgatakkhi vā.

Or with connected eyebrows, or with hairless eyebrows, or with monkey-like eyebrows. Or with extremely large eyes. Or with extremely small eyes, endowed with eyes like holes made by striking a buffalo hide with the corner of an adze. Or with uneven eyes, endowed with one large eye and one small eye. Or with uneven pupils, endowed with pupils of uneven position, one up and one down. Or with squinting eyes. Or with deep-set eyes, in which the pupils appear like reflections in the water of a deep well. Or with protruding eyes, whose pupils protrude just like a crab's. Or with elephant-like ears, endowed with large outer ears. Or with mouse-like ears or bat-like ears, endowed with small outer ears. Or with ears that are only holes, for whom there is only an ear-hole without the outer ear. Or with unpierced ears—however, one of Yona birth is not a spoiler of the assembly, for that is indeed his nature. Or with a fistula in the ear, endowed with a constantly putrid ear. Or with a boil on the ear, endowed with an ear from which pus always flows. Or with chiseled ears, endowed with ears like the tip of a tube for feeding cattle. Or with very tawny eyes—however, it is permissible to ordain one with honey-colored eyes. Or with eyes without eyelashes. Or with eyes from which tears constantly flow. Or with flowered eyes (i.e., with cataracts). Or with eyes affected by an eye disease.

Atimahantanāsiko vā atikhuddakanāsiko vā cipiṭanāsiko vā majjhe appatiṭṭhahitvā ekapasse ṭhitavaṅkanāsiko vā, dīghanāsiko vā sukatuṇḍasadisāya jivhāya lehituṃ sakkuṇeyyāya nāsikāya samannāgato, niccapaggharitasiṅghāṇikanāso vā.

Or with an excessively large nose, or an excessively small nose, or a flattened nose, or a crooked nose that is not centered but positioned to one side. Or with a long nose, endowed with a nose that can be licked by a tongue like a parrot's beak. Or with a nose from which mucus constantly flows.

Mahāmukho vā yassa paṭaṅgamaṇḍūkasseva mukhanimittaṃyeva mahantaṃ hoti, mukhaṃ pana lābusadisaṃ [V 0.0295] atikhuddakaṃ, bhinnamukho vā vaṅkamukho vā mahāoṭṭho vā ukkhalimukhavaṭṭisadisehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato, tanukaoṭṭho vā bhericammasadisehi dante pidahituṃ asamatthehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato, mahādharoṭṭho vā tanukauttaroṭṭho vā tanukaadharoṭṭho vā mahāuttaroṭṭho vā oṭṭhachinnako vā eḷamukho vā uppakkamukho vā saṅkhatuṇḍako vā bahisetehi anto atirattehi oṭṭhehi samannāgato, duggandhakuṇapamukho vā.

Or with a large face, whose facial features are large like those of a paṭaṅga frog, but whose mouth-opening is very small like a gourd's. Or with a split mouth, or a crooked mouth. Or with large lips, endowed with lips like the rim of a cooking pot. Or with thin lips, endowed with lips like drum-skin that are unable to cover the teeth. Or with a large lower lip and a thin upper lip. Or with a thin lower lip and a large upper lip. Or with a cut lip. Or with a slobbering mouth. Or with a swollen mouth. Or with lips like a conch-shell, being white on the outside and very red on the inside. Or with a foul-smelling, corpse-like mouth.

Mahādanto vā aṭṭhakadantasadisehi dantehi samannāgato asuradanto vā heṭṭhā vā upari vā bahinikkhantadanto, yassa pana sakkā hoti oṭṭhehi pidahituṃ kathentasseva paññāyati no akathentassa, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Pūtidanto vā niddanto vā yassa pana dantantare kalandakadanto viya sukhumadanto hoti, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Or with large teeth, endowed with teeth like the eight tines of a harrow. Or with demon-like teeth, having teeth protruding outwards, either below or above; however, for one whose teeth can be covered by the lips, and they are apparent only when speaking, not when silent, it is permissible to ordain him. Or with decayed teeth. Or without teeth; however, for one who has a fine tooth between the teeth, like a squirrel's tooth, it is permissible to ordain him.

Mahāhanuko vā gohanusadisena hanunā samannāgato, dīghahanuko vā cipiṭahanuko vā antopaviṭṭhena viya atirassena hanukena samannāgato, bhinnahanuko vā vaṅkahanuko vā nimmassudāṭhiko vā bhikkhunisadisamukho dīghagalo vā bakagalasadisena galena samannāgato, rassagalo vā antopaviṭṭhena [P 5.1030] viya galena samannāgato, bhinnagalo vā bhaṭṭhaaṃsakūṭo vā ahattho vā ekahattho vā atirassahattho [M 0.0312] vā atidīghahattho vā bhinnauro vā bhinnapiṭṭhi vā kacchugatto vā kaṇḍugatto vā daddugatto vā godhāgatto vā, yassa godhāya viya gattato cuṇṇāni patanti, sabbañcetaṃ virūpakaraṇaṃ sandhāya vitthārikavasena vuttaṃ. Vinicchayo panettha “na bhikkhave pañcahi ābādhehī”ti ettha vuttanayeneva veditabbo.

Or one with a large jaw, endowed with a jaw like a cow's jaw; or one with a long jaw; or one with a flat jaw, endowed with an excessively short jaw as if it were sunken in; or one with a broken jaw; or one with a crooked jaw; or one without a beard and canine teeth; or one with a face like a bhikkhunī's; or one with a long neck, endowed with a neck like a heron's; or one with a short neck, endowed with a neck as if it were sunken in; or one with a broken neck; or one with fallen shoulder-blades; or one without a hand; or one with one hand; or one with excessively short hands; or one with excessively long hands; or one with a broken chest; or a broken back; or one with a scabby body; or one with an itchy body; or one with a body afflicted with ringworm; or one with a body like a monitor lizard's, from whose body powder falls as from a monitor lizard's—all this has been stated in detail with reference to that which causes disfigurement. And the decision here should be understood in the same way as stated in the passage: “Bhikkhus, not by five diseases…”

Bhaṭṭhakaṭiko vā mahāānisado vā uddhanakūṭasadisehi ānisadamaṃsehi accuggatehi samannāgato, mahāūruko vā vātaṇḍiko vā mahājāṇuko vā saṅghaṭṭanajāṇuko vā dīghajaṅgho vā yaṭṭhisadisajaṅgho vikaṭo vā paṇho vā ubbaddhapiṇḍiko vā, so duvidho heṭṭhā oruḷhāhi vā upari āruḷhāhi vā mahatīhi jaṅghapiṇḍikāhi samannāgato, mahājaṅgho vā thūlajaṅghapiṇḍiko vā mahāpādo vā mahāpaṇhi vā piṭṭhikapādo vā pādavemajjhato uṭṭhitajaṅgho vaṅkapādo vā so duvidho – anto vā bahi vā parivattapādo gaṇṭhikaṅguli vā siṅgiveraphaṇasadisāhi aṅgulīhi samannāgato, andhanakho vā kāḷavaṇṇehi pūtinakhehi samannāgato, sabbopi esa parisadūsako. Evarūpo parisadūsako na pabbājetabbo.

Or one with a fallen waist; or one with large buttocks, being endowed with excessively raised buttock-flesh like the points of a tripod stove; or one with huge thighs; or one with a hydrocele; or one with massive knees; or one with knocking knees; or one with long shanks, having shanks like a stick; or one with misshapen feet; or one with heels turned backwards; or one with bulging calves—he is of two kinds, being endowed with large calf-muscles that either hang down or rise up; or one with massive shanks; or one with thick calf-muscles; or one with huge feet; or one with massive heels; or one with shanks growing from the instep, that is, whose shanks rise from the middle of the top of the foot; or one with crooked feet—he is of two kinds, having feet that are turned either inward or outward; or one with knotted fingers or toes, being endowed with digits like the hood of a ginger root; or one with blind nails, being endowed with black-colored, putrid nails—every such person is a defiler of the assembly. Such a defiler of the assembly should not be given the going-forth.

Kāṇoti pasannandho vā hotu pupphādīhi vā upahatapasādo. Yo dvīhi vā ekena vā akkhinā [V 0.0296] na passati, so na pabbājetabbo. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana ekakkhikāṇo kāṇoti vutto, dviakkhikāṇo andhena saṅgahito. Mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ jaccandho andhoti vutto, tasmā ubhayampi pariyāyena yujjati. Kuṇīti hatthakuṇī vā pādakuṇī vā aṅgulikuṇī vā; yassa etesu hatthādīsu yaṃkiñci vaṅkaṃ paññāyati, so kuṇī nāma. Khañjoti natajāṇuko vā bhinnajaṅgho vā majjhe saṅkuṭitapādattā kuṇḍapādako vā piṭṭhipādamajjhena caṅkamanto agge saṅkuṭitapādattā kuṇḍapādako vā piṭṭhipādaggena caṅkamanto aggapādeneva caṅkamanakhañjo vā paṇhikāya caṅkamanakhañjo [P 5.1031] vā pādassa bāhirantena caṅkamanakhañjo vā pādassa abbhantarantena caṅkamanakhañjo vā gopphakānaṃ upari bhaggattā sakalena piṭṭhipādena caṅkamanakhañjo vā; sabbopesa khañjoyeva, so na pabbājetabbo.

Kāṇa means one may be blind in the lens or have the lens damaged by cataracts or other things. Whoever cannot see with either two eyes or with one eye, they should not be given the going-forth. In the Mahāpaccariya, however, one who is blind in one eye is called kāṇa, while one who is blind in two eyes is included under andha (blind). In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā, one who is blind from birth is called andha; therefore, both are suitable according to the context. Kuṇī (crippled) means one with a crippled hand, a crippled foot, or crippled fingers or toes; whoever has any crookedness apparent in these—hands and so on—is called kuṇī. Khañja (lame) means one with bent knees, or a broken shin, or, due to having feet contracted in the middle, one with stunted feet who walks on the middle of the instep; or, due to having feet contracted at the tip, one with stunted feet who walks on the tip of the instep; or one who is lame by walking only on the forefoot; or one who is lame by walking on the heel; or one who is lame by walking on the outer edge of the foot; or one who is lame by walking on the inner edge of the foot; or, due to the ankles being broken above, one who is lame by walking on the entire instep. All these are indeed lame; such a one should not be given the going-forth.

Pakkhahatoti [M 0.0313] yassa eko hattho vā pādo vā aḍḍhasarīraṃ vā sukhaṃ na vahati. Chinniriyāpathoti pīṭhasappi vuccati. Jarādubbaloti jiṇṇabhāvena dubbalo attano cīvararajanādikammaṃ kātumpi asamattho. Yo pana mahallakopi balavā hoti, attānaṃ paṭijaggituṃ sakkoti, so pabbājetabbo. Andhoti jaccandho vuccati. Mūgoti yassa vacībhedo nappavattati; yassāpi pavattati, saraṇagamanaṃ pana paripuṇṇaṃ bhāsituṃ na sakkoti, tādisaṃ mammanampi pabbājetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yo pana saraṇagamanamattaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ bhāsituṃ sakkoti, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati.

Pakkhahata (paralyzed) is one whose one hand, or one foot, or half the body does not function with ease. One who moves about on a small wheeled stool is called chinniriyāpatha (one with broken postures). Jarādubbala (weak from old age) means one who, being weak due to old age, is unable even to do one's own tasks such as dyeing robes. But one who, although old, is strong and able to look after oneself, may be given the going-forth. Andha (blind) means one who is blind from birth. Mūga (mute) refers to one whose distinct speech does not occur; and even if it does occur, if one is unable to recite the going for refuge completely, it is not proper to give the going-forth to such a stammerer. But one who is able to recite the going for refuge completely, it is proper to give them the going-forth.

Badhiroti yo sabbena sabbaṃ na suṇāti. Yo pana mahāsaddaṃ suṇāti, taṃ pabbājetuṃ vaṭṭati. Andhamūgādayo ubhayadosavasena vuttā. Yesañca pabbajjā paṭikkhittā, upasampadāpi tesaṃ paṭikkhittāva. Sace pana te saṅgho upasampādeti, sabbepi hatthacchinnādayo sūpasampannā, kārakasaṅgho pana ācariyupajjhāyā ca āpattito na muccanti. Vakkhati ca – “atthi bhikkhave puggalo appatto osāraṇaṃ, tañce saṅgho osāreti, ekacco suosārito, ekacco duosārito”ti tassattho āgataṭṭhāneyeva āvi bhavissatīti.

Badhira (deaf) is one who does not hear at all. However, one who can hear a loud sound, it is proper to give them the going-forth. The blind, the mute, and others are mentioned on account of a twofold fault. And for those whose going-forth is prohibited, their higher ordination is also prohibited. But if the Saṅgha gives them higher ordination, all those such as the one with a severed hand are well-ordained; but the officiating Saṅgha, and the teachers and preceptors, are not freed from an offense. And it will be said: “Bhikkhus, there is a person who has not received rehabilitation; if the Saṅgha rehabilitates them, one is well-rehabilitated, another is badly-rehabilitated.” The meaning of this will become clear in the place where it appears.

Hatthacchinnādivatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The account concerning those with severed hands and so forth is concluded.

Alajjīnissayavatthukathā

The Account of Dependence on the Shameless

120. Alajjīnaṃ nissāya vasantīti upayogatthe sāmivacanaṃ; alajjipuggale nissāya vasantīti [V 0.0297] attho. Yāva bhikkhusabhāgataṃ jānāmīti nissayadāyakassa bhikkhuno bhikkhūhi sabhāgataṃ lajjibhāvaṃ yāva jānāmīti attho. Tasmā navaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatena “ehi bhikkhu, nissayaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti vuccamānenāpi catūhapañcāhaṃ nissayadāyakassa lajjibhāvaṃ upaparikkhitvā nissayo gahetabbo.

120. In the phrase `alajjīnaṃ nissāya vasanti`, the genitive is used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is 'they live in dependence on shameless persons.' The phrase `yāva bhikkhusabhāgataṃ jānāti` means: until one knows the conscientiousness and the fitness, in common with other monks, of the monk who is the dependence-giver. Therefore, a monk who has gone to a new place, even when told, 'Come, monk, take dependence,' should take dependence only after investigating the dependence-giver’s conscientiousness for four or five days.

Sace “thero lajjī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ santike sutvā āgatadivaseyeva gahetukāmo hoti, thero pana “āgamehi tāva, vasanto jānissasī”ti katipāhaṃ ācāraṃ upaparikkhitvā nissayaṃ deti, vaṭṭati. Pakatiyā nissayaggahaṇaṭṭhānaṃ [P 5.1032] gatena tadaheva gahetabbo, ekadivasampi parihāro [M 0.0314] natthi. Sace paṭhamayāme ācariyassa okāso natthi, okāsaṃ alabhanto “paccūsasamaye gahessāmī”ti sayati, aruṇaṃ uggatampi na jānāti, anāpatti. Sace pana “gaṇhissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ akatvā sayati, aruṇuggamane dukkaṭaṃ. Agatapubbaṃ ṭhānaṃ gatena dve tīṇi divasāni vasitvā gantukāmena anissitena vasitabbaṃ. “Sattāhaṃ vasissāmī”ti ālayaṃ karontena pana nissayo gahetabbo. Sace thero “kiṃ sattāhaṃ vasantassa nissayenā”ti vadati, paṭikkhittakālato paṭṭhāya laddhaparihāro hoti.

If, having heard from other monks that 'the elder is conscientious,' one wishes to take dependence on the very day of arrival, but the elder says, 'Wait for now; while living here you will come to know,' and gives dependence only after investigating the junior monk's conduct for some days, this is allowable. Ordinarily, by one who has gone to a place for taking dependence, it should be taken on that very day; there is no exemption even for a single day. If in the first watch the teacher is not available, and one, not getting an opportunity, sleeps thinking, 'I will take it in the early morning,' and does not know even when the dawn has arisen, there is no offense. But if one sleeps without making the reflection, 'I will take it,' at the arising of dawn, it is a dukkaṭa offense. By one who has gone to a place not gone to before, and who wishes to leave after staying for two or three days, one may stay without dependence. However, by one making an attachment to the idea, 'I will stay for seven days,' dependence must be taken. If the elder says, 'What is the use of dependence for one staying for seven days?', from the time of refusal, one obtains the exemption.

Alajjīnissayavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of Dependence on the Shameless is concluded.

Gamikādinissayavatthukathā

The Account of Dependence for Travelers and Others

121. Nissayakaraṇīyoti karaṇīyanissayo, karaṇīyo mayā nissayo; gahetabboti attho. Nissayaṃ alabhamānenāti attanā saddhiṃ addhānamaggappaṭipannesu nissayadāyake asati nissayaṃ na labhati nāma. Evaṃ alabhantena anissitena bahūnipi divasāni gantabbaṃ. Sace pubbepi nissayaṃ gahetvā vutthapubbaṃ kañci āvāsaṃ pavisati, ekarattaṃ vasantenāpi nissayo gahetabbo. Antarāmagge vissamanto vā satthaṃ pariyesanto vā katipāhaṃ vasati, anāpatti. Antovasse pana nibaddhavāsaṃ vasitabbaṃ, nissayo ca gahetabbo. Nāvāya gacchantassa pana vassāne āgatepi nissayaṃ alabhantassa anāpatti.

121. `Nissayakaraṇīyo` means one for whom dependence ought to be taken; that is, 'dependence should be taken by me'; the meaning is 'it should be taken.' `Nissayaṃ alabhamānena` (by one not obtaining dependence) means: when there is no dependence-giver among those who have set out on a long road together with oneself, it is called 'not obtaining dependence.' Thus, by one not obtaining it, one may travel for many days without dependence. If one enters any monastery where one has previously dwelt under dependence, dependence must be taken even by one staying for only one night. If one stays for some days while resting on the way or while searching for a caravan, there is no offense. But during the rains-residence, one must dwell in a fixed residence, and dependence must be taken. However, for one going by boat, even if the rains-residence arrives, there is no offense for one not obtaining dependence.

Yāciyamānenāti tena gilānena yāciyamānena anissitena vasitabbaṃ. Sace “yācāhi ma”nti vuccamānopi gilāno mānena na yācati, gantabbaṃ.

`Yāciyamānena` (being requested) means: being requested by that sick person to stay, one may stay without dependence. If, even when told, 'Request me to stay,' the sick person does not request out of conceit, one should go.

Phāsu [V 0.0298] hotīti samathavipassanānaṃ paṭilābhavasena phāsu hoti. Imañhi parihāraṃ neva sotāpanno na sakadāgāmī anāgāmī arahanto labhanti; na thāmagatassa samādhino vā vipassanāya vā lābhī, vissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhāne pana bālaputhujjane kathāva natthi. Yassa kho pana samatho vā vipassanā vā taruṇo hoti, ayaṃ imaṃ parihāraṃ labhati, pavāraṇasaṅgahopi etasseva anuññāto. Tasmā iminā puggalena ācariye pavāretvā gatepi “yadā patirūpo nissayadāyako āgacchissati, tassa nissāya vasissāmī”ti ābhogaṃ katvā puna yāva [M 0.0315] āsāḷhīpuṇṇamā, tāva anissitena vatthuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana āsāḷhīmāse [P 5.1033] ācariyo nāgacchati, yattha nissayo labbhati, tattha gantabbaṃ.

`Phāsu hoti` (it is comfortable) means it is comfortable by way of obtaining serenity and insight. Indeed, this exemption is obtained by neither a stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, nor an arahant; nor by one who has obtained concentration or insight that has reached full strength. As for a foolish worldling whose meditation subject has been abandoned, there is nothing to be said. However, a person whose serenity or insight is tender obtains this exemption, and assistance by way of the pavāraṇā (invitation) is permitted only for this very person. Therefore, by this person, even when the teacher has departed after the pavāraṇā has been made, it is allowable to live without dependence until the full moon of Āsāḷhī, having made the reflection, 'When a suitable dependence-giver arrives, I will live depending on him.' But if in the month of Āsāḷhī the teacher does not come, one should go to where dependence is obtainable.

122. Gottenapi anussāvetunti mahākassapassa upasampadāpekkhoti evaṃ gottaṃ vatvā anussāvetuṃ anujānāmīti attho.

122. `Gottenapi anussāvetuṃ` (to announce by clan name) means: I allow one to announce by stating the clan name thus, 'He is the candidate for higher ordination of Mahākassapa'; this is the meaning.

123. Dve ekānussāvaneti dve ekato anussāvane; ekena ekassa aññena itarassāti evaṃ dvīhi vā ācariyehi ekena vā ekakkhaṇe kammavācaṃ anussāventehi upasampādetuṃ anujānāmīti attho.

123. `Dve ekānussāvane` (two as one announcement) means two announcements made together. The meaning is: I allow the higher ordination to be conferred by those announcing the formal act at the same moment—either by two teachers, one for one candidate and another for the other, or by one teacher for both.

Dve tayo ekānussāvane kātuṃ tañca kho ekena upajjhāyenāti dve vā tayo vā jane purimanayeneva ekato anussāvane kātuṃ anujānāmi; tañca kho anussāvanakiriyaṃ ekena upajjhāyena anujānāmīti attho. Tasmā ekena ācariyena dve vā tayo vā anussāvetabbā. Dvīhi vā tīhi vā ācariyehi visuṃ visuṃ ekena ekassāti evaṃ ekappahāreneva dve tisso vā kammavācā kātabbā. Sace pana nānācariyā nānupajjhāyā honti, tissatthero sumanattherassa saddhivihārikaṃ, sumanatthero tissattherassa saddhivihārikaṃ anussāveti, aññamaññañca gaṇapūrakā honti, vaṭṭati. Sace pana nānāupajjhāyā honti, eko ācariyo hoti, “natveva nānupajjhāyenā”ti paṭikkhittattā na vaṭṭati. Idaṃ sandhāya hi esa paṭikkhepo.

`Dve tayo ekānussāvane kātuṃ tañca kho ekena upajjhāyenā` (to make two or three announcements as one, and that by one preceptor) means: I allow announcements for two or three persons to be made together in the same way as before; and I allow that act of announcement to be with one preceptor; this is the meaning. Therefore, by one teacher, announcements may be made for two or three candidates. Or, by two or three teachers, separately, one for each, thus two or three formal acts may be performed simultaneously. But if there are different teachers and different preceptors—for example, the Elder Tissa announces for the co-resident of the Elder Sumana, and the Elder Sumana announces for the co-resident of the Elder Tissa—and they are quorum-completers for each other, it is allowable. But if there are different preceptors and one teacher, it is not allowable, because it is rejected by the phrase 'but not with different preceptors.' Indeed, this rejection is made with reference to this.

Gamikādinissayavatthukathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of Dependence for Travelers and Others is concluded.

Upasampadāvidhikathā

Discourse on the Procedure for Higher Ordination

126. Paṭhamaṃ [V 0.0299] upajjhaṃ gāhāpetabboti ettha vajjāvajjaṃ upanijjhāyatīti upajjhā, taṃ upajjhaṃ; “upajjhāyo me bhante hohī”ti evaṃ vadāpetvā gāhāpetabbo. Vitthāyantīti vitthaddhagattā honti. Yaṃ jātanti yaṃ tava sarīre jātaṃ nibbattaṃ vijjamānaṃ, taṃ saṅghamajjhe pucchante santaṃ atthīti vattabbantiādi. Ullumpatu manti uddharatu maṃ.

Herein, regarding "Firstly, a preceptor should be taken": because he carefully observes minor and major faults, he is a preceptor. That preceptor should be taken after having the candidate for higher ordination say, "Venerable sir, be my preceptor." As for `vitthāyanti`, it means they have especially stiff bodies. As for "what is born," it means: whatever is born, has arisen, or is present in your body, that, when asked about in the midst of the Saṅgha by an appointed monk, what is present should be stated as "it is," and so forth. As for "May he pull me up," it means: "May he lift me out."

Upasampadāvidhikathā niṭṭhitā.

126. The Discourse on the Procedure for Higher Ordination is concluded.

Cattāronissayādikathā

Discourse on the Four Requisites and so forth

128. Tāvadevāti [M 0.0316] upasampannasamanantarameva. Chāyā metabbāti ekaporisā vā dviporisā vāti chāyā metabbā. Utuppamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabbanti “vassāno hemanto gimho”ti evaṃ utuppamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. Ettha ca utuyeva utuppamāṇaṃ. Sace vassānādayo aparipuṇṇā honti, yattakehi divasehi yassa yo utu aparipuṇṇo, te divase sallakkhetvā so divasabhāgo ācikkhitabbo. Atha vā “ayaṃ nāma utu, so ca kho paripuṇṇo vā aparipuṇṇo vā”ti evaṃ utuppamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ. “Pubbaṇho vā sāyanho vā”ti evaṃ divasabhāgo [P 5.1034] ācikkhitabbo. Saṅgītīti idameva sabbaṃ ekato katvā “tvaṃ kiṃ labhasi, kā te chāyā, kiṃ utuppamāṇaṃ, ko divasabhāgo”ti puṭṭho “idaṃ nāma labhāmi – vassaṃ vā hemantaṃ vā gimhaṃ vā, ayaṃ me chāyā, idaṃ utuppamāṇaṃ, ayaṃ divasabhāgoti vadeyyāsī”ti evaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ.

As for `tāvadeva`, it means just immediately after becoming a monk through higher ordination. As for `chāyā metabbā`, it means a shadow of one man's measure or two men's measure should be measured. As for `utuppamāṇaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ`, it means the measure of the season should be told thus: "the rainy season, the winter season, the hot season." And here, the season itself is the measure of the season. If the rainy season and so forth are not complete, by however many days that season is not complete, having noted those days, that portion of the day of becoming a monk should be told. Or else, the measure of the season should be told thus: "This is the season by name, and it is either complete or incomplete." The portion of the day should be told thus: "It is the forenoon" or "it is the afternoon." As for `saṅgīti`, it means that having put all this together, it should be explained thus: "When asked, 'What do you get? What is your shadow? What is the measure of the season? What is the portion of the day?' you should reply, 'I get this season by name—the rainy season, or the winter season, or the hot season. This is my shadow. This is the measure of the season. This is the portion of the day.'"

129. Ohāyāti chaḍḍetvā. Dutiyaṃ dātunti upasampadamāḷakato pariveṇaṃ gacchantassa dutiyakaṃ dātuṃ anujānāmi, cattāri ca akaraṇīyāni ācikkhitunti attho. Paṇḍupalāsoti paṇḍuvaṇṇo patto. Bandhanā pavuttoti vaṇṭato patito. Abhabbo haritatthāyāti puna harito bhavituṃ abhabbo. Puthusilāti mahāsilā.

128. As for `ohāya`, it means having abandoned. As for `dutiyaṃ dātuṃ`, the meaning is: I allow giving a second companion to a newly ordained monk going from the ordination enclosure to the monastic dwelling, and explaining the four offenses that are not to be done. As for `paṇḍupalāso`, it means a leaf of pale color. As for `bandhanā pavutto`, it means fallen from the stalk. As for `abhabbo haritatthāya`, it means incapable of becoming green again. As for `puthusilā`, it means a great stone.

130. Alabbhamānāya sāmaggiyā anāpatti sambhoge saṃvāseti yāva tassa ukkhepanīyakammakaraṇatthāya sāmaggī na labbhati, tāva tena saddhiṃ sambhoge ca uposathapavāraṇādikaraṇabhede [V 0.0300] saṃvāse ca anāpattīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha mahāvibhaṅge vuttānusārena suviññeyyattā pākaṭamevāti.

130. Regarding 'When harmony is not being obtained, there is no offense in communion and co-residence': so long as harmony is not obtained for the purpose of performing the act of suspension upon that monk, there is no offense in communion of material things and Dhamma with that monk, nor in co-residence which is distinguished by the performance of acts such as Uposatha and Pavāraṇā. The remainder in all cases is indeed clear, as it is easily understood in accordance with the method stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga.

Cattāronissayādikathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Four Requisites and so forth is concluded.

Samantapāsādikāya vinayasaṃvaṇṇanāya

In the Samantapāsādikā, the commentary on the Vinaya,

Dvāsattatiadhikavatthusatapaṭimaṇḍitassa mahākhandhakassa

Of the Mahākhandhaka (Great Chapter), which is adorned with one hundred and seventy-two topics,

Atthavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the meaning is concluded.

Mahākhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Mahākhandhaka (Great Chapter) is concluded.

2. Uposathakkhandhakaṃ

2. The Uposatha Chapter

Sannipātānujānanādikathā

The Discussion on Permission for Assemblies, and So Forth

132. Uposathakkhandhake [M 0.0317][V 0.0301] – aññatitthiyāti ettha titthaṃ vuccati laddhi; aññaṃ titthaṃ aññatitthaṃ; aññatitthaṃ etesaṃ atthīti aññatitthiyā; ito aññaladdhikāti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammaṃ bhāsantīti yaṃ tesaṃ kattabbākattabbaṃ, taṃ kathenti. Te labhantīti te manussā labhanti. Mūgasūkarāti thūlasarīrasūkarā.

132. In the Uposathakkhandhaka: Regarding `aññatitthiyā` (those of other sects), here `tittha` (sect) is said to mean `laddhi` (doctrine); `aññaṃ titthaṃ` is `aññatitthaṃ` (another doctrine); `aññatitthiyā` means 'those for whom there is another doctrine'; this is said to mean 'those who hold a doctrine other than this one'. Regarding `dhammaṃ bhāsanti` (they speak the Dhamma), they explain to those people what should and should not be done. Regarding `te labhanti` (they obtain), it means those people obtain. Regarding `mūgasūkarā`, they are stout-bodied pigs.

135. Anajjhāpanno vā hoti āpajjitvā vā vuṭṭhitoti ettha yaṃ āpattiṃ bhikkhu anajjhāpanno vā hoti, āpajjitvā vā vuṭṭhito, ayaṃ asantī nāma āpattīti evamattho veditabbo. Sampajānamusāvāde kiṃ hotīti yvāyaṃ sampajānamusāvādo assa hotīti vutto, so āpattito kiṃ hoti, katarā āpatti hotīti attho. Dukkaṭaṃ hotīti dukkaṭāpatti hoti; sā ca kho na [P 5.1035] musāvādalakkhaṇena; bhagavato pana vacanena vacīdvāre akiriyasamuṭṭhānā āpatti hotīti veditabbā. Vakkhati hi –

135. Regarding `anajjhāpanno vā hoti āpajjitvā vā vuṭṭhito` (he has not fallen into or, having fallen into, has emerged), here the meaning should be understood thus: an offense which a bhikkhu has not fallen into, or having fallen into, has emerged from, this is called a non-existent offense (`asantī nāma āpatti`). Regarding `sampajānamusāvāde kiṃ hoti` (what is there in the case of a deliberate lie?), the meaning is: that which was spoken of as a deliberate lie, what offense is it? Which offense is it? Regarding `dukkaṭaṃ hoti` (it is a `dukkaṭa`), it is a `dukkaṭa` offense. And it is not due to the characteristic of false speech; rather, it should be known that by the Blessed One's word, it is an offense arising from non-action at the verbal door. For it will be said:

“Anālapanto manujena kenaci,

Vācāgiraṃ no ca pare bhaṇeyya;

Āpajjeyya vācasikaṃ na kāyikaṃ,

Pañhā mesā kusalehi cintitā”ti. (pari. 479);

He who does not speak with any person, and utters no word to others, would fall into a verbal, not a bodily, offense. This problem has been considered by the skillful.

Antarāyikoti antarāyakaro. Kissa phāsu hotīti kimatthāya phāsu hoti. Paṭhamassa jhānassa adhigamāyāti paṭhamassa jhānassa adhigamanatthāya tassa bhikkhuno phāsu hoti sukhaṃ hoti. Esa nayo sabbattha. Iti bhagavā uddesato ca niddesato ca paṭhamaṃ pātimokkhuddesaṃ dassesi.

Regarding `antarāyiko` (obstructive), it means `antarāyakaro` (causing an obstruction). Regarding `kissa phāsu hoti` (for what is it comfortable?), it means `kimatthāya phāsu hoti` (for what purpose is it comfortable?). Regarding `paṭhamassa jhānassa adhigamāya` (for the attainment of the first jhāna), it means it is comfortable (`phāsu`) or easy (`sukhaṃ`) for that bhikkhu for the sake of attaining the first jhāna. This is the method everywhere. Thus the Blessed One first taught the recitation of the Pātimokkha both by way of summary (`uddesa`) and by way of detailed explanation (`niddesa`).

136. Devasikanti [V 0.0302] divase divase. Cātuddase vā pannarase vāti ekassa utuno tatiye ca sattame ca pakkhe dvikkhattuṃ cātuddase avasese chakkhattuṃ pannarase; ayaṃ tāva eko attho. Ayaṃ pana pakaticārittavasena [M 0.0318] vutto “sakiṃ pakkhassa cātuddase vā pannarase vā”ti vacanato pana tathārūpe paccaye sati yasmiṃ tasmiṃ cātuddase vā pannarase vā uddisituṃ vaṭṭati, āvāsikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cātuddaso hoti, āgantukānaṃ pannaraso. Sace āvāsikā bahutarā honti, āgantukehi āvāsikānaṃ anuvattitabba”nti vacanatopi cetaṃ veditabbaṃ.

136. Regarding `devasikaṃ` (daily), it means `divase divase` (day by day). Regarding `cātuddase vā pannarase vā` (on the fourteenth or on the fifteenth), in one season, in the third and seventh fortnights, it is on the fourteenth day twice, and in the remaining six fortnights, it is on the fifteenth; this, for now, is one meaning. This, however, was stated according to normal practice. But, from the statement, 'once a fortnight, on the fourteenth or on the fifteenth,' when there is such a condition, it is allowable to recite on any fourteenth whatsoever or on any fifteenth whatsoever. This can be known also from the statement: 'For the resident bhikkhus it is the fourteenth, for the visiting bhikkhus it is the fifteenth. If the resident bhikkhus are more numerous, the visiting bhikkhus should conform to the residents.'

Sīmānujānanakathā

The Discussion on the Authorization of Boundaries

138. Paṭhamaṃ nimittā kittetabbāti vinayadharena pucchitabbaṃ “puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimitta”nti? Pabbato bhanteti. Puna vinayadharena “eso pabbato nimitta”nti evaṃ nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. “Etaṃ pabbataṃ nimittaṃ karoma, karissāma, nimittaṃ kato, nimittaṃ hotu, hoti bhavissatī”ti evaṃ pana kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pāsāṇādīsupi eseva nayo. Puratthimāya anudisāya, dakkhiṇāya disāya, dakkhiṇāya anudisāya, pacchimāya disāya, pacchimāya anudisāya, uttarāya disāya, uttarāya anudisāya, kiṃ nimittaṃ? Udakaṃ bhante. Etaṃ udakaṃ nimittanti ettha pana aṭṭhatvā puna puratthimāya disāya kiṃ nimittaṃ. Pabbato bhante. Eso pabbato nimittanti evaṃ paṭhamaṃ [P 5.1036] kittitanimittaṃ kittetvāva ṭhapetabbaṃ. Evañhi nimittena nimittaṃ ghaṭitaṃ hoti. Evaṃ nimittāni kittetvā athānantaraṃ vuttāya kammavācāya sīmā sammannitabbā. Kammavācāpariyosāne nimittānaṃ anto sīmā hoti, nimittāni sīmato bahi honti. Tattha nimittāni sakiṃ kittitānipi kittitāneva honti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tikkhattuṃ sīmamaṇḍalaṃ sambandhantena nimittaṃ kittetabbanti vuttaṃ. “Pabbato bhanteti…pe… udakaṃ bhante”ti evaṃ pana upasampanno vā ācikkhatu anupasampanno vā vaṭṭatiyeva.

138. First, the landmarks should be declared. It should be asked by the Vinaya expert: “What is the landmark in the eastern direction?” “Venerable sir, it is a mountain.” Then the Vinaya expert should declare the landmark thus: “This mountain is the landmark.” However, it is not proper to declare it by saying, “We make this mountain the landmark; we will make it the landmark; the landmark has been made; let the landmark be; it is the landmark; it will be the landmark.” This same method applies to stones and so forth. For the southeast intermediate direction, the southern direction, the southwest intermediate direction, the western direction, the northwest intermediate direction, the northern direction, and the northeast intermediate direction, [the questioning proceeds, for example:] “What is the landmark?” “Venerable sir, it is water.” “This water is the landmark.” However, not stopping there, one returns again to the eastern direction: “What is the landmark?” “Venerable sir, it is a mountain.” “This mountain is the landmark.” Thus, only after having declared again the landmark that was first declared, should one stop. For in this way, one landmark is connected to the next. Having declared the landmarks in this manner, the boundary should then be authorized by the formal act as stated. At the conclusion of the formal act, the boundary is within the landmarks, and the landmarks are outside the boundary. Therein, even if the landmarks are declared only once, they are indeed declared. However, in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, it is said that the landmark should be declared three times, connecting the boundary circle. Furthermore, it is permissible for either an ordained person or an unordained person to announce [the landmark], saying, “Venerable sir, it is a mountain… Venerable sir, it is water.”

Idāni pabbatanimittādīsu evaṃ vinicchayo veditabbo – tividho pabbato, suddhapaṃsupabbato, suddhapāsāṇapabbato, ubhayamissakoti. So tividhopi vaṭṭati. Vālikarāsi pana na vaṭṭati. Itaropi hatthippamāṇato omakataro na vaṭṭati. Hatthippamāṇato pana paṭṭhāya sineruppamāṇopi vaṭṭati. Sace catūsu disāsu cattāro tīsu vā tayo pabbatā honti, catūhi vā tīhi vā pabbatanimittehi eva sammannituṃ vaṭṭati. Dvīhi pana nimittehi ekena [M 0.0319] vā sammannituṃ na vaṭṭati. Ito paresu pāsāṇanimittādīsupi eseva nayo. Tasmā pabbatanimittaṃ [V 0.0303] karontena pucchitabbaṃ “ekābaddho na ekābaddho”ti. Sace ekābaddho hoti, na kātabbo. Tañhi catūsu vā aṭṭhasu vā disāsu kittentenāpi ekameva nimittaṃ kittitaṃ hoti, tasmā yo evaṃ cakkasaṇṭhānena vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhito pabbato, taṃ ekadisāya kittetvā aññāsu disāsu taṃ bahiddhā katvā anto aññāni nimittāni kittetabbāni.

Now, the determination regarding mountain landmarks and so forth should be understood thus: a mountain is of three kinds—a mountain of pure earth, a mountain of pure rock, or one mixed with both. All three kinds are permissible. However, a heap of sand is not permissible. Another mountain that is smaller than the size of an elephant is not permissible. However, from the size of an elephant upwards, even one the size of Mount Sineru is permissible. If there are four mountains in the four directions, or three in three directions, it is permissible to authorize the boundary with four or with three mountain landmarks. However, it is not permissible to authorize it with two landmarks or with one. For stone landmarks and so forth subsequent to this, this same method applies. Therefore, when making a mountain landmark, one should ask: “Is it a single continuous range or not?” If it is a single continuous range, it should not be made a landmark. Indeed, for that continuous mountain, even when declaring it in four or eight directions, only one landmark is declared. Therefore, for a mountain that stands encircling the monastery in the shape of a wheel, one should declare it in one direction and, having made it external in the other directions, declare other landmarks inside.

Sace pabbatassa tatiyabhāgaṃ vā upaḍḍhaṃ vā antosīmāya kattukāmā honti, pabbataṃ akittetvā yattakaṃ padesaṃ anto kattukāmā, tassa parato tasmiṃyeva pabbate jātarukkhavammikādīsu aññataraṃ nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. Sace ekayojanadviyojanappamāṇaṃ sabbaṃ pabbataṃ anto kattukāmā honti, pabbatassa parato bhūmiyaṃ jātarukkhavammikādīni nimittāni kittetabbāni.

If they wish to make a third part or half of a mountain internal to the boundary, without declaring the mountain itself, they should declare as a landmark one among such things as a tree that has grown there or a termite mound, on that same mountain beyond the portion they wish to make internal. If they wish to make the entire mountain, one or two yojanas in size, internal, they should declare as landmarks such things as trees that have grown there or termite mounds on the ground beyond the mountain.

Pāsāṇanimitte – ayaguḷopi pāsāṇasaṅkhyameva gacchati, tasmā yo [P 5.1037] koci pāsāṇo vaṭṭati. Pamāṇato pana hatthippamāṇo pabbatasaṅkhyaṃ gato, tasmā so na vaṭṭati. Mahāgoṇamahāmahiṃsappamāṇo pana vaṭṭati. Heṭṭhimaparicchedena dvattiṃsapalaguḷapiṇḍaparimāṇo vaṭṭati. Tato khuddakataro iṭṭhakā vā mahantīpi na vaṭṭati. Animittupagapāsāṇarāsipi na vaṭṭati, pageva paṃsuvālikarāsi. Bhūmisamo khalamaṇḍalasadiso piṭṭhipāsāṇo vā bhūmito khāṇuko viya uṭṭhitapāsāṇo vā hoti, sopi pamāṇupago ce vaṭṭati. Piṭṭhipāsāṇo atimahantopi pāsāṇasaṅkhyameva gacchati, tasmā sace mahato piṭṭhipāsāṇassa ekappadesaṃ antosīmāya kattukāmā honti, taṃ akittetvā tassupari añño pāsāṇo kittetabbo. Sace piṭṭhipāsāṇupari vihāraṃ karonti, vihāramajjhena vā piṭṭhipāsāṇo vinivijjhitvā gacchati, evarūpo piṭṭhipāsāṇo na vaṭṭati. Sace hi taṃ kittenti, nimittassa upari vihāro hoti, nimittañca nāma bahisīmāya hoti, vihāropi bahisīmāyaṃ āpajjati. Vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitapiṭṭhipāsāṇo ekattha kittetvā aññattha na kittetabbo.

Regarding a stone landmark: even a lump of iron is counted as a stone; therefore, any kind of stone is permissible. As for size, however, one the size of an elephant is counted as a mountain; therefore, it is not permissible. But one the size of a large ox or a large buffalo is permissible. By the lower limit, a stone the size of a sugar-lump of thirty-two palas is permissible. One smaller than that is not permissible; and a brick, even a large one, is not permissible. A pile of stones that does not qualify as a landmark is also not permissible, let alone a heap of earth or sand. There may be a flat stone level with the ground, like a threshing floor, or a stone risen from the ground like a tree stump; that too, if it meets the size requirement, is permissible. A flat stone, even if very large, is counted only as a stone. Therefore, if they wish to make one part of a large flat stone internal to the boundary, without declaring it, another stone on top of it should be declared. If they build a monastery on top of a flat stone, or if a flat stone goes piercing through the middle of the monastery, such a kind of flat stone is not permissible. Indeed, if they declare it, the monastery is on top of the landmark; and a landmark, by definition, must be outside the boundary, so the monastery also comes to be outside the boundary. A flat stone that stands encircling the monastery, having been declared in one place, should not be declared in another.

Vananimitte – tiṇavanaṃ vā tacasāratālanāḷikerādirukkhavanaṃ vā na vaṭṭati. Antosārānaṃ pana sākasālādīnaṃ antosāramissakānaṃ vā rukkhānaṃ [M 0.0320] vanaṃ vaṭṭati, tañca kho heṭṭhimaparicchedena catupañcarukkhamattampi tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati, paraṃ yojanasatikampi vaṭṭati. Sace pana vanamajjhe vihāraṃ karonti, vanaṃ na kittetabbaṃ. Ekadesaṃ antosīmāya kattukāmehipi vanaṃ akittetvā tattha rukkhapāsāṇādayo kittetabbā. Vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitavanaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha na kittetabbaṃ.

Regarding a forest landmark: a forest of grass, or a forest of trees with substance only in their bark, such as palmyra palms and coconut trees, is not permissible. However, a forest of trees with inner heartwood, such as teak and sal trees, or one mixed with such trees, is permissible. And that, by the lower limit, must consist of at least four or five trees; less than that is not permissible. Beyond that, even a forest of a hundred yojanas is permissible. However, if they build a monastery in the middle of a forest, the forest should not be declared. Also, by those who wish to make one part of the forest internal to the boundary, without declaring the forest, trees, stones, and so forth should be declared therein. A forest that stands encircling the monastery, having been declared in one place, should not be declared in another.

Rukkhanimitte [V 0.0304] – tacasāro tālanāḷikerādirukkho na vaṭṭati, antosāro jīvamānako antamaso ubbedhato aṭṭhaṅgulo pariṇāhato sūcidaṇḍakappamāṇopi vaṭṭati, tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati, paraṃ dvādasayojano suppatiṭṭhitanigrodhopi vaṭṭati. Vaṃsanaḷakasarāvādīsu bījaṃ ropetvā vaḍḍhāpito pamāṇupagopi na vaṭṭati. Tato apanetvā pana taṅkhaṇampi [P 5.1038] bhūmiyaṃ ropetvā koṭṭhakaṃ katvā udakaṃ āsiñcitvā kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Navamūlasākhāniggamanaṃ akāraṇaṃ. Khandhaṃ chinditvā ropite pana etaṃ yujjati. Kittentena ca “rukkho”tipi vattuṃ vaṭṭati, “sākarukkhotipi sālarukkho”tipi. Ekābaddhaṃ pana suppatiṭṭhitanigrodhasadisaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding a tree landmark: a tree with bark as its heartwood, such as a palmyra palm or coconut palm, is not permissible. A tree with inner heartwood, being alive, at the very least eight finger-breadths in height and the size of a stylus shaft in circumference, is permissible. Less than that is not permissible. Beyond that, even a well-established banyan tree of twelve yojanas is permissible. A tree grown by planting a seed in bamboo joints, reed joints, potsherds, and the like, even if it has reached the required size, is not permissible. However, having removed it from there and planted it in the ground even at that very moment, and having made an earth-mound and poured water, it is permissible to declare it as a landmark. The emergence of new roots and branches is not a factor. But in the case of a tree planted after cutting its trunk, this is suitable. And by the one declaring the landmark, it is permissible to say, “a tree,” or “a teak tree,” or “a sal tree.” However, an interconnected tree, like a well-established banyan tree, having been declared in one place, it is not permissible to declare it in another place.

Magganimitte – araññakhettanadītaḷākamaggādayo na vaṭṭanti, jaṅghamaggo vā sakaṭamaggo vā vaṭṭati, yo nibbijjhitvā dve tīṇi gāmantarāni gacchati. Yo pana jaṅghamaggo sakaṭamaggato okkamitvā puna sakaṭamaggameva otarati, ye vā jaṅghamaggasakaṭamaggā avaḷañjā, te na vaṭṭanti. Jaṅghasatthasakaṭasatthehi vaḷañjiyamānāyeva vaṭṭanti. Sace dve maggā nikkhamitvā pacchā sakaṭadhuramiva ekībhavanti, dvidhā bhinnaṭṭhāne vā sambandhaṭṭhāne vā sakiṃ kittetvā puna na kittetabbā, ekābaddhanimittañhetaṃ hoti.

Regarding a path landmark: paths to a forest, to a field, to a river, to a reservoir, and the like are not permissible. A footpath or a cart track that goes by penetrating through to two or three other villages is permissible. However, a footpath that deviates from a cart track and then descends back to that same cart track, or footpaths and cart tracks that are not in use—these are not permissible. Only those currently being used by foot-traders and cart-traders are permissible. If two paths, having diverged, later become one like a cart-yoke, they should be declared once, either at the place of divergence or at the place of connection, and should not be declared again, for this is a single interconnected landmark.

Sace vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā cattāro maggā catūsu disāsu gacchanti, majjhe ekaṃ kittetvā aparaṃ kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Ekābaddhanimittañhetaṃ hoti. Koṇaṃ nibbijjhitvā gatamaggaṃ pana parabhāge kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Vihāramajjhena nibbijjhitvā gatamaggo pana na kittetabbo. Kittite nimittassa upari vihāro hoti. Sace sakaṭamaggassa antimacakkamaggaṃ nimittaṃ karonti, maggo bahisīmāya hoti. Sace bāhiracakkamaggaṃ nimittaṃ karonti, bāhiracakkamaggova bahisīmāya hoti, sesaṃ antosīmaṃ bhajati. Maggaṃ [M 0.0321] kittentena “maggo pantho patho pajjo”ti dasasu yena kenaci nāmena kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Parikhāsaṇṭhānena vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gatamaggo ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

If four paths go in the four directions encircling a monastery, having declared one of them, it is not allowable to declare another, for this is a single interconnected sign. However, a path that goes by penetrating a corner may be declared in its outer part. But a path that goes by penetrating through the middle of the monastery should not be declared. If it is declared, the monastery is on top of the sign. If they make the inner wheel-track of a cart track the sign, the entire path is outside the sīmā. If they make the outer wheel-track the sign, only the outer wheel-track is outside the sīmā; the remainder falls inside the sīmā. When declaring a path, it is allowable to declare it by any one of the ten names, such as ‘magga,’ ‘pantha,’ ‘patha,’ ‘pajja.’ A path that goes encircling a monastery in the shape of a moat, having been declared in one place, is not allowable to be declared in another.

Vammikanimitte – heṭṭhimaparicchedena taṃ divasaṃ jāto aṭṭhaṅgulubbedho govisāṇappamāṇopi vammiko vaṭṭati, tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati, paraṃ himavantapabbatasadisopi vaṭṭati. Vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā ṭhitaṃ pana ekābaddhaṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati.

Regarding the anthill-sign: by the lower limit, an anthill formed on that very day, being eight finger-breadths in height and even of the size of a cow’s horn, is allowable. Less than that is not allowable. More than that, even one like the Himavanta mountain is allowable. However, an interconnected anthill that stands encircling a monastery, having been declared in one place, is not allowable to be declared in another.

Nadīnimitte [V 0.0305] – yassā dhammikānaṃ [P 5.1039] rājūnaṃ kāle anvaddhamāsaṃ anudasāhaṃ anupañcāhanti evaṃ anatikkamitvā deve vassante valāhakesu vigatamattesu sotaṃ pacchijjati, ayaṃ nadīsaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Yassā pana īdise suvuṭṭhikāle vassānassa cātumāse sotaṃ na pacchijjati, timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādetvā yattha katthaci uttarantiyā bhikkhuniyā antaravāsako temiyati, ayaṃ nadīsaṅkhyaṃ gacchati, sīmaṃ bandhantānaṃ nimittaṃ hoti. Bhikkhuniyā nadīpāragamanepi uposathādisaṅghakammakaraṇepi nadīpārasīmasammannanepi ayameva nadī.

Regarding the river-sign: a river whose current is interrupted as soon as the clouds have dispersed—even when, in the time of righteous kings, the rain falls without fail every half-month, every ten days, or every five days—does not count as a river. However, a river whose current is not interrupted throughout the four months of the rainy season in such a time of good rain, and which, covering the three circles (the two knees and the navel), wets the lower robe of a bhikkhunī crossing it anywhere—this counts as a river and is a sign for those establishing a sīmā. For a bhikkhunī crossing to the other bank of the river, for performing Sangha acts such as the Uposatha, and for authorizing a nadīpārasīmā, this very one is the river.

Yā pana maggo viya sakaṭadhurasaṇṭhānena vā parikhāsaṇṭhānena vā vihāraṃ parikkhipitvā gatā, taṃ ekattha kittetvā aññattha kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Vihārassa catūsu disāsu aññamaññaṃ vinibbijjhitvā gate nadicatukkepi eseva nayo. Asammissanadiyo pana catassopi kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vatiṃ karonto viya rukkhapāde nikhaṇitvā vallipalālādīhi nadisotaṃ rumbhanti, udakañca ajjhottharitvā āvaraṇaṃ pavattatiyeva, nimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā pana udakaṃ nappavattati, evaṃ setumhi kate appavattamānā nadī nimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pavattanaṭṭhāne nadinimittaṃ, appavattanaṭṭhāne udakanimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

However, a river that has gone encircling a monastery like a path, in the shape of a cart-yoke or a moat, having been declared in one place, is not allowable to be declared in another. This same method applies also in the case of a set of four rivers that go in the four directions of the monastery, penetrating one another. But as for non-confluent rivers, it is allowable to declare all four. If, as if making a fence, they drive wooden posts into the ground and block the river's current with creepers, straw, and the like, and the water, overwhelming the barrier, continues to flow as before, it is allowable to make it a sign. But if a dam is made in such a way that the water does not flow, a non-flowing river is not allowable to be made a sign. At a place where it flows, it is allowable to make a river-sign; at a place where it does not flow, it is allowable to make a water-sign.

Yā pana dubbuṭṭhikāle vā gimhe vā nirudakabhāvena nappavattati, sā vaṭṭati. Mahānadito udakamātikaṃ nīharanti, sā kunnadisadisā hutvā tīṇi sassāni sampādentī niccaṃ pavattati, kiñcāpi pavattati, nimittaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yā pana mūle mahānadito niggatāpi kālantarena teneva niggatamaggena [M 0.0322] nadiṃ bhinditvā sayañca gacchati, gacchantī parato susumārādisamākiṇṇā nāvādīhi sañcaritabbā nadī hoti, taṃ nimittaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

However, a river that does not flow in a time of poor rain or in the hot season due to being without water, is allowable. They may lead a water-channel from a great river; that channel, having become like a small river and bringing three crops to completion, flows constantly. Although it flows, it is not allowable to make it a sign. However, a channel which, though at its source it came from a great river, after some time breaks through the original river by that same channel of exit and flows on its own, and flowing on, later becomes a river teeming with crocodiles and the like, and navigable by boats and the like—it is allowable to make that a sign.

Udakanimitte – nirudake ṭhāne nāvāya vā cāṭiādīsu vā udakaṃ pūretvā udakanimittaṃ kittetuṃ na vaṭṭati, bhūmigatameva vaṭṭati[P 5.1040]. Tañca kho appavattanaudakaṃ āvāṭapokkharaṇitaḷākajātassaraloṇisamuddādīsu ṭhitaṃ, aṭṭhitaṃ pana oghanadiudakavāhakamātikādīsu udakaṃ na vaṭṭati. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “gambhīresu āvāṭādīsu ukkhepimaṃ udakaṃ nimittaṃ na kātabba”nti vuttaṃ, taṃ duvuttaṃ attanomatimattameva. Ṭhitaṃ pana antamaso sūkarakhatāyapi gāmadārakānaṃ kīḷanavāpiyampi taṅkhaṇaññeva pathaviyaṃ āvāṭakaṃ katvā kuṭehi āharitvā pūritaudakampi sace yāva kammavācāpariyosānā tiṭṭhati, appaṃ vā hotu bahu vā, vaṭṭati. Tasmiṃ pana ṭhāne nimittasaññākaraṇatthaṃ pāsāṇavālikāpaṃsuādirāsi vā pāsāṇatthambho vā dārutthambho vā kātabbo. Taṃ kātuñca kāretuñca bhikkhussa vaṭṭati. Lābhasīmāyaṃ pana na vaṭṭati[V 0.0306]. Samānasaṃvāsakasīmā kassaci pīḷanaṃ na karoti, kevalaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vinayakammameva sādheti, tasmā ettha vaṭṭati.

Regarding the water-sign: in a place without water, it is not allowable to declare a water-sign by filling a boat or pots and so on with water. Only water that is on the ground is allowable. And that is non-flowing water situated in wells, rectangular ponds, reservoirs, natural lakes, salt-lakes, oceans, and so on. However, water that is not stationary, in places such as overflowing rivers, water-carrying channels, canals, and so on, is not allowable. But in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā it is said, 'In deep wells and so on, water that is drawn up should not be made a sign.' That is poorly said; it is merely a personal opinion. However, still water, even in a pool dug by a pig, or in a play-pond of village children, and even water that has been brought in pots and used to fill a small pit dug in the earth at that very moment—if it remains until the conclusion of the formal act, then whether it be little or much, it is allowable. Furthermore, in that place, for the purpose of marking the sign, a heap of stones, sand, dust, and so on, or a stone pillar, or a wooden pillar should be made. It is allowable for a bhikkhu to make it or to have it made. In a lābhasīmā, however, it is not allowable. A samānasaṃvāsakasīmā does not cause oppression to anyone; it merely accomplishes the Vinaya acts of the bhikkhus. Therefore, herein it is allowable.

Imehi ca aṭṭhahi nimittehi asammissehipi aññamaññaṃ sammissehipi sīmaṃ sammannituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Sā evaṃ sammannitvā bajjhamānā ekena dvīhi vā nimittehi abaddhā hoti, tīṇi pana ādiṃ katvā vuttappakārānaṃ nimittānaṃ satenāpi baddhā hoti. Sā tīhi siṅghāṭakasaṇṭhānā hoti, catūhi caturassā vā siṅghāṭakaaḍḍhacandamudiṅgādisaṇṭhānā vā, tato adhikehi nānāsaṇṭhānā. Taṃ bandhitukāmehi sāmantavihāresu bhikkhū tassa tassa vihārassa sīmāparicchedaṃ pucchitvā, baddhasīmavihārānaṃ sīmāya sīmantarikaṃ, abaddhasīmavihārānaṃ sīmāya upacāraṃ ṭhapetvā disācārikabhikkhūnaṃ nissañcārasamaye sace ekasmiṃ gāmakhette sīmaṃ bandhitukāmā, ye tattha baddhasīmavihārā, tesu bhikkhūnaṃ “mayaṃ ajja sīmaṃ bandhissāma, tumhe sakasīmāparicchedato mā nikkhamitthā”ti pesetabbaṃ. Ye abaddhasīmavihārā, tesu bhikkhū ekajjhaṃ sannipātetabbā, chandārahānaṃ chando āharāpetabbo[P 5.1041]. Sace aññānipi gāmakkhettāni antokātukāmā[M 0.0323], tesu gāmesu ye bhikkhū vasanti, tehipi āgantabbaṃ. Anāgacchantānaṃ chando āharitabboti mahāsumatthero āha. Mahāpadumatthero pana “nānāgāmakhettāni nāma pāṭekkaṃ baddhasīmāsadisāni, na tato chandapārisuddhi āgacchati. Antonimittagatehi pana bhikkhūhi āgantabba”nti vatvā puna āha – “samānasaṃvāsakasīmāsammannanakāle āgamanampi anāgamanampi vaṭṭati. Avippavāsasīmāsammannanakāle pana antonimittagatehi āgantabbaṃ, anāgacchantānaṃ chando āharitabbo”ti.

And it is indeed permissible to establish a sīmā with these eight markers, whether unmixed or mutually mixed. That sīmā, being bound after having been agreed upon in this way, is not bound by one or two markers. However, beginning with three, it is bound even by a hundred of the aforementioned types of markers. When bound by three markers, it has the shape of a three-way crossroads. When bound by four, it is either square or has the shape of a crossroads, a half-moon, a mudiṅga drum, and so on. When bound by more than four, it has various shapes.
