Those who wish to bind it, having asked the bhikkhus in the surrounding monasteries about the boundary-limit of each monastery, should leave a sīmantarika for the sīmā of monasteries with a bound sīmā, and an upacāra for the sīmā of monasteries without a bound sīmā. If, during a time when itinerant bhikkhus are not traveling, they wish to bind a sīmā in a single village-field, a message should be sent to the bhikkhus in those monasteries that have a bound sīmā, saying: 'Today we will bind a sīmā; do not go beyond the limits of your own sīmā.' The bhikkhus in those monasteries that do not have a bound sīmā should be assembled together, and the consent of those eligible to give consent should be brought. If they wish to include other village-fields within, the bhikkhus who reside in those villages should also come. For those not coming, their consent should be brought. Thus said the Elder Mahāsuma. The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: 'Various village-fields are like individually bound sīmās; purity of consent does not come from them. However, the bhikkhus who are within the markers should come.' And having said this, he said again: 'At the time of agreeing upon a samānasaṃvāsakasīmā, both coming and not coming are permissible. But at the time of agreeing upon an avippavāsasīmā, those within the markers must come, and for those not coming, their consent must be brought.'

Evaṃ sannipatitesu pana bhikkhūsu chandārahānaṃ chande āhaṭe tesu tesu maggesu nadītitthagāmadvārādīsu ca āgantukabhikkhūnaṃ sīghaṃ sīghaṃ hatthapāsānayanatthañca bahisīmākaraṇatthañca ārāmike ceva samaṇuddese ca ṭhapetvā bherisaññaṃ vā saṅkhasaññaṃ vā katvā nimittakittanānantaraṃ vuttāya “suṇātu me bhante saṅgho”tiādikāya kammavācāya sīmā bandhitabbā. Kammavācāpariyosāneyeva nimittāni bahi katvā heṭṭhā pathavisandhārakaṃ udakaṃ pariyantaṃ katvā sīmā gatā hoti.

Furthermore, when the bhikkhus have thus assembled and the consent of those eligible for consent has been brought, having stationed monastery attendants and novices on the various paths, at river-fords, village gates, and so on, for the purpose of quickly bringing incoming bhikkhus into hand-reach and for the purpose of keeping them outside the sīmā, and having made a signal with a drum or a conch, immediately after the announcing of the markers, the sīmā should be bound by the formal act beginning with 'Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.' At the very conclusion of the formal act, the markers having been made external, and the earth-supporting water below having been made the limit, the sīmā is established.

Imaṃ pana samānasaṃvāsakasīmaṃ sammannantehi pabbajjupasampadādīnaṃ saṅghakammānaṃ sukhakaraṇatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ khaṇḍasīmā bandhitabbā. Taṃ pana bandhantehi vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Sace hi bodhicetiyabhattasālādīni sabbavatthūni patiṭṭhāpetvā katavihāre bandhanti, vihāramajjhe bahūnaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhāne [V 0.0307] abandhitvā vihārapaccante vivittokāse bandhitabbā. Akatavihāre bandhantehi bodhicetiyādīnaṃ sabbavatthūnaṃ ṭhānaṃ sallakkhetvā yathā patiṭṭhitesu vatthūsu vihārapaccante vivittokāse hoti, evaṃ bandhitabbā. Sā heṭṭhimaparicchedena sace ekavīsati bhikkhū gaṇhāti, vaṭṭati. Tato oraṃ na vaṭṭati, paraṃ bhikkhusahassaṃ gaṇhantīpi vaṭṭati. Taṃ bandhantehi sīmāmāḷakassa samantā nimittupagā pāsāṇā ṭhapetabbā, na khaṇḍasīmāya [P 5.1042] ṭhitehi mahāsīmā bandhitabbā, na mahāsīmāya ṭhitehi khaṇḍasīmā, khaṇḍasīmāyameva pana ṭhatvā khaṇḍasīmā bandhitabbā, mahāsīmāyameva ṭhatvā mahāsīmā.

Furthermore, by those agreeing upon this samānasaṃvāsakasīmā, a khaṇḍasīmā should first be bound for the purpose of easily performing Saṅgha acts such as the going-forth, higher ordination, and so on. Furthermore, those binding it should know the procedure. Indeed, if they bind it in a monastery that has been built, where all structures such as the Bodhi tree, a cetiya, a dining hall, and so on, have been established, it should be bound in a secluded place at the edge of the monastery, not in the middle of the monastery in a place of assembly for many. By those binding it in an unbuilt monastery, having marked the location of all structures such as the Bodhi tree, a cetiya, and so on, it should be bound in such a way that, when the structures are established, the sīmā is in a secluded place at the edge of the monastery. If it holds twenty-one bhikkhus as its minimum capacity, it is permissible. Less than that is not permissible; beyond that, even one holding a thousand bhikkhus is permissible. By those binding it, stones suitable as markers should be placed all around the sīmā-pavilion. A mahāsīmā should not be bound by those standing in a khaṇḍasīmā, nor a khaṇḍasīmā by those standing in a mahāsīmā. Rather, a khaṇḍasīmā should be bound only while standing in a khaṇḍasīmā, and a mahāsīmā only while standing in a mahāsīmā.

Tatrāyaṃ bandhanavidhi – samantā “eso pāsāṇo nimitta”nti evaṃ nimittāni kittetvā kammavācāya sīmā sammannitabbā. Atha tassā eva daḷhīkammatthaṃ avippavāsakammavācā kātabbā. Evañhi sīmaṃ samūhanissāmāti āgatā [M 0.0324] samūhanituṃ na sakkhissanti. Sīmaṃ sammannitvā bahisīmantarikapāsāṇā ṭhapetabbā. Sīmantarikā pacchimakoṭiyā ekaratanappamāṇā vaṭṭati. Vidatthippamāṇāpi vaṭṭatīti kurundiyaṃ, caturaṅgulappamāṇāpi vaṭṭatīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Sace pana vihāro mahā hoti, dvepi tissopi tatuttaripi khaṇḍasīmāyo bandhitabbā.

Herein is the procedure for establishing a boundary: All around, having announced the markers thus, 'This stone is a marker,' the boundary should be agreed upon by means of a kammavācā. Then, for the purpose of making it firm, the avippavāsa-kammavācā should be performed. Indeed, when this is done, those who come thinking, 'We will abolish the boundary,' will not be able to abolish it. Having agreed upon the boundary, sīmantarika stones should be placed outside. The sīmantarika, at its minimum extent, being of the measure of one ratana, is allowable. It is said in the Kurundī that even one of the measure of a vidatthi is allowable, and it is said in the Mahāpaccarī that even one of the measure of four finger-breadths is allowable. However, if the monastery is large, two, three, or even more khaṇḍasīmās should be bound.

Evaṃ khaṇḍasīmaṃ sammannitvā mahāsīmāsammutikāle khaṇḍasīmato nikkhamitvā mahāsīmāya ṭhatvā samantā anupariyāyantehi sīmantarikapāsāṇā kittetabbā. Tato avasesanimittāni kittetvā hatthapāsaṃ avijahantehi kammavācāya samānasaṃvāsakasīmaṃ sammannitvā tassā daḷhīkammatthaṃ avippavāsakammavācāpi kātabbā. Evañhi “sīmaṃ samūhanissāmā”ti āgatā samūhanituṃ na sakkhissanti. Sace pana khaṇḍasīmāya nimittāni kittetvā tato sīmantarikāya nimittāni kittetvā mahāsīmāya nimittāni kittenti, evaṃ tīsu ṭhānesu nimittāni kittetvā yaṃ sīmaṃ icchanti, taṃ paṭhamaṃ bandhituṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ santepi yathāvuttenayena khaṇḍasīmatova paṭṭhāya bandhitabbā. Evaṃ baddhāsu pana sīmāsu khaṇḍasīmāya ṭhitā bhikkhū mahāsīmāya kammaṃ karontānaṃ na kopenti, mahāsīmāya vā ṭhitā khaṇḍasīmāya kammaṃ karontānaṃ sīmantarikāya pana ṭhitā ubhinnampi na kopenti. Gāmakhette ṭhatvā kammaṃ karontānaṃ pana sīmantarikāya ṭhitā kopenti. Sīmantarikā hi gāmakhettaṃ bhajati.

Having thus agreed upon the partial boundary, at the time of agreeing upon the great boundary, having gone out from the partial boundary and stood in the great boundary, while circumambulating all around, the sīmantarika stones should be announced. Then, having announced the remaining markers, without abandoning hand's reach, the great boundary for common communion should be agreed upon by means of a kammavācā, and for the purpose of making it firm, the avippavāsa-kammavācā should also be performed. Indeed, when this is done, those who come thinking, 'We will abolish the boundary,' will not be able to abolish it. However, if they announce the markers of the partial boundary, then announce the markers of the sīmantarika, and then announce the markers of the great boundary, having thus announced the markers in three places, it is allowable to establish first whichever boundary they wish. Even so, it should be established starting from the partial boundary by the method already stated. However, among the boundaries thus established, monks standing in the partial boundary do not invalidate the act of those performing it in the great boundary, nor do those standing in the great boundary invalidate the act of those performing it in the partial boundary. Moreover, those standing in the sīmantarika do not invalidate the act of either of the two. However, those standing in the sīmantarika do invalidate the act of those performing it while standing in a village-field. Indeed, the sīmantarika partakes of the village-field.

Sīmā ca nāmesā na kevalaṃ pathavitaleyeva baddhā baddhā nāma hoti. Atha kho piṭṭhipāsāṇepi kuṭigehepi leṇepi pāsādepi [P 5.1043] pabbatamatthakepi baddhā baddhāyeva hoti. Tattha piṭṭhipāsāṇe bandhantehi pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ rājiṃ vā koṭṭetvā udukkhalaṃ vā khaṇitvā nimittaṃ na kātabbaṃ[V 0.0308], nimittupagapāsāṇe ṭhapetvā nimittāni kittetabbāni. Kammavācāpariyosāne sīmā pathavisandhārakaṃ udakaṃ pariyantaṃ katvā otarati. Nimittapāsāṇā yathāṭhāne na tiṭṭhanti, tasmā samantato rāji vā uṭṭhāpetabbā, catūsu vā koṇesu pāsāṇā vijjhitabbā, “ayaṃ sīmāparicchedo”ti vatvā akkharāni vā chinditabbāni. Keci usūyakā sīmaṃ jhāpessāmāti aggiṃ denti, pāsāṇāva jhāyanti, na sīmā.

And this, which is called a boundary, is not what is called 'established' when established only on the surface of the earth. Rather, when established on a rock slab, in a hut-house, in a cave, in a multi-storied building, or on a mountain peak, it is indeed established. Therein, by those establishing it on a rock slab, a marker should not be made by carving a line or digging a mortar on the rock slab; having placed stones suitable for markers, the markers should be announced. At the conclusion of the kammavācā, the boundary descends, having made the earth-supporting water its limit. The marker stones do not remain in their proper place; therefore, a line should be made to appear all around, or stones should be pierced at the four corners, or having said, 'This is the boundary's demarcation,' letters should be carved. Some envious persons, thinking, 'We will burn the boundary,' set fire, but only the stones burn, not the boundary.

Kuṭigehepi [M 0.0325] bandhantehi bhittiṃ akittetvā ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāsaṭṭhānaṃ anto karitvā pāsāṇanimittāni ṭhapetvā sīmā sammannitabbā, antokuṭṭameva sīmā hoti. Sace antokuṭṭe ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāso natthi, pamukhe nimittapāsāṇe ṭhapetvā sammannitabbā. Sace evampi nappahoti, bahinibbodakapatanaṭṭhānepi nimittāni ṭhapetvā sammannitabbā. Evaṃ sammatāya pana sabbaṃ kuṭigehaṃ sīmaṭṭhameva hoti.

Also, when establishing a boundary in a hut-house, without announcing the wall, having made a space inside for twenty-one monks and having placed stone markers, the boundary should be agreed upon; only the interior of the wall becomes the boundary. If there is no space for twenty-one monks inside the wall, it should be agreed upon by placing marker stones in the porch. If even this is not sufficient, it should be agreed upon by also placing markers outside at the place where the rainwater from the eaves falls. However, when it is agreed upon thus, the entire hut-house is situated within the boundary.

Catubhittiyaleṇepi bandhantehi kuṭṭaṃ akittetvā pāsāṇāva kittetabbā. Sace anto okāso natthi, pamukhepi nimittāni ṭhapetabbāni. Sace nappahoti, bahi nibbodakapatanaṭṭhānepi nimittapāsāṇe ṭhapetvā nimittāni kittetvā sīmā sammannitabbā. Evaṃ leṇassa anto ca bahi ca sīmā hoti.

Also, when establishing a boundary in a four-walled cave, without announcing the wall, only the stones should be announced. If there is no space inside, markers should also be placed in the porch. If this is not sufficient, having placed marker stones also outside at the place where the rainwater from the eaves falls and having announced the markers, the boundary should be agreed upon. Thus, the boundary comes to be both inside and outside the cave.

Uparipāsādepi bhittiṃ akittetvā anto pāsāṇe ṭhapetvā sīmā sammannitabbā. Sace nappahoti, pamukhepi pāsāṇe ṭhapetvā sammannitabbā. Evaṃ sammatā uparipāsādeyeva hoti, heṭṭhā na otarati. Sace pana bahūsu thambhesu tulānaṃ upari katapāsādassa heṭṭhimatale [P 5.1044] kuṭṭo yathā nimittānaṃ anto hoti, evaṃ uṭṭhahitvā tulārukkhehi ekasambaddho ṭhito, heṭṭhāpi otarati. Ekathambhapāsādassa pana uparimatale baddhā sīmā sace thambhamatthake ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāso hoti, heṭṭhā otarati. Sace pāsādabhittito niggatesu niyyūhakādīsu pāsāṇe ṭhapetvā sīmaṃ bandhanti, pāsādabhitti antosīmāyaṃ hoti. Heṭṭhā panassā otaraṇānotaraṇaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Heṭṭhāpāsāde kittentehipi bhitti ca rukkhatthambhā ca na kittetabbā. Bhittilagge pana pāsāṇatthambhe kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Evaṃ kittitā sīmā heṭṭhā pāsādassa pariyantathambhānaṃ antoyeva hoti. Sace pana heṭṭhāpāsādassa kuḍḍo uparimatalena sambaddho hoti, uparipāsādampi abhiruhati. Sace pāsādassa bahi nibbodakapatanaṭṭhāne nimittāni karonti, sabbo pāsādo sīmaṭṭho hoti.

Also on the upper story of a multi-storied building, without announcing the wall, having placed stones inside, the boundary should be agreed upon. If this is not sufficient, it should be agreed upon by also placing stones in the porch. A boundary agreed upon thus is only on the upper story; it does not descend below. However, if, in a building made upon beams on many pillars, a wall on the lower floor rises up in such a way that it is inside the markers and stands connected as one with the wooden beams, it also descends below. Furthermore, in the case of a single-pillared building, if a boundary established on the upper floor has space for twenty-one monks on top of the pillar, it descends below. If they establish a boundary by placing stones on projections, such as brackets, etc., extending from the building's wall, the building's wall is inside the boundary. However, its descending or not descending below should be understood only by the method already stated. Also by those announcing markers below the building, the wall and wooden pillars should not be announced. However, it is allowable to announce stone pillars attached to the wall. A boundary thus announced is, below, only inside the perimeter pillars of the building. However, if a wall of the lower building is connected with the upper floor, it also ascends to the upper building. If they make markers outside the building at the place where the rainwater from the eaves falls, the entire building is situated within the boundary.

Pabbatamatthake [M 0.0326][V 0.0309] talaṃ hoti ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāsārahaṃ, tattha piṭṭhipāsāṇe viya sīmaṃ bandhanti. Heṭṭhāpabbatepi teneva paricchedena sīmā otarati. Tālamūlakapabbatepi upari sīmā baddhā heṭṭhā otarateva. Yo pana vitānasaṇṭhāno hoti, upari ekavīsatiyā bhikkhūnaṃ okāso atthi, heṭṭhā natthi, tassa upari baddhā sīmā heṭṭhā na otarati. Evaṃ mudiṅgasaṇṭhāno vā hotu paṇavasaṇṭhāno vā, yassa heṭṭhā vā majjhe vā sīmappamāṇaṃ natthi, tassupari baddhā sīmā heṭṭhā neva otarati. Yassa pana dve kūṭāni āsanne ṭhitāni, ekassapi upari sīmappamāṇaṃ nappahoti, tassa kūṭantaraṃ cinitvā vā pūretvā vā ekābaddhaṃ katvā upari sīmā sammannitabbā.

On the summit of a mountain, if there is a flat area suitable for twenty-one monks, they may establish the boundary there as if on a flat rock. Below the mountain also, the boundary descends following the same demarcation. On a mountain shaped like a palm root, a boundary established above certainly descends below. But for a mountain that is canopy-shaped, where there is space for twenty-one monks above but not below, a boundary established above does not descend below. Similarly, whether it is shaped like a mudiṅga-drum or a paṇava-drum, if there is no boundary-sized area below or in the middle, a boundary established above certainly does not descend below. However, for a mountain which has two peaks standing close together, where there is not sufficient boundary-sized area on top of even one, the space between the peaks should be built up or filled in, making it a single connected area, and the boundary should be established above.

Eko sappaphaṇasadiso pabbato, tassupari sīmappamāṇassa atthitāya sīmaṃ bandhanti, tassa ce heṭṭhā ākāsapabbhāraṃ hoti, sīmā na otarati. Sace panassa vemajjhe sīmappamāṇo susirapāsāṇo hoti, otarati. So ca pāsāṇo sīmaṭṭhoyeva hoti. Athāpissa heṭṭhā leṇassa kuṭṭo aggakoṭiṃ āhacca tiṭṭhati[P 5.1045], otarati, heṭṭhā ca upari ca sīmāyeva hoti. Sace pana heṭṭhā uparimassa sīmāparicchedassa pārato anto-leṇaṃ hoti, bahi sīmā na otarati. Athāpi uparimassa sīmāparicchedassa orato bahileṇaṃ hoti, anto sīmā na otarati. Athāpi upari sīmāya paricchedo khuddako, heṭṭhā leṇaṃ mahantaṃ sīmāparicchedamatikkamitvā ṭhitaṃ, sīmā upariyeva hoti, heṭṭhā na otarati. Yadi pana leṇaṃ khuddakaṃ sabbapacchimasīmāparimāṇaṃ, upari sīmā mahatī taṃ ajjhottharitvā ṭhitā, sīmā otarati. Atha leṇaṃ atikhuddakaṃ sīmappamāṇaṃ na hoti, sīmā upariyeva hoti, heṭṭhā na otarati. Sace tato upaḍḍhaṃ bhijjitvā patati, sīmappamāṇaṃ cepi hoti, bahi patitaṃ asīmā. Apatitaṃ pana yadi sīmappamāṇaṃ, sīmā hotiyeva.

There is a certain mountain like a cobra's hood; on top of it, because there is a boundary-sized area, they establish a boundary. If below it there is an open precipice, the boundary does not descend. But if in its middle there is a hollow rock of boundary-size, it descends. And that rock is indeed within the boundary. Furthermore, if below it the wall of a cave stands touching the highest point, it descends, and it is the boundary both below and above. However, if below, there is an inner cave beyond the demarcation of the upper boundary, the boundary does not descend outside. Furthermore, if there is an outer cave on this side of the demarcation of the upper boundary, the boundary does not descend inside. Furthermore, if the demarcation of the boundary above is small, and below a large cave stands having transgressed the boundary demarcation, the boundary is only above; it does not descend below. But if the cave is small, having the minimum measure for a boundary, and the boundary above is large, standing covering it, the boundary descends. If the cave is very small and is not of boundary-size, the boundary is only above; it does not descend below. If half of it, having broken off, falls, even if it is of boundary-size, the part that has fallen outside is not a boundary. But if the part that has not fallen is of boundary-size, it is indeed a boundary.

Khaṇḍasīmā nīcavatthukā hoti, taṃ pūretvā uccavatthukaṃ karonti, sīmāyeva. Sīmāya gehaṃ karonti, sīmaṭṭhakameva hoti. Sīmāya pokkharaṇiṃ khaṇanti, sīmāyeva. Ogho sīmāmaṇḍalaṃ ottharitvā gacchati, sīmāmāḷake aṭṭaṃ bandhitvā kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sīmāya heṭṭhā umaṅganadī hoti, iddhimā bhikkhu tattha nisīdati, sace sā nadī paṭhamaṃ gatā, sīmā pacchā baddhā[M 0.0327], kammaṃ na kopeti. Atha paṭhamaṃ sīmā baddhā, pacchā nadī gatā, kammaṃ kopeti. Heṭṭhāpathavitale ṭhito pana kopetiyeva.

If a khaṇḍasīmā is low-lying, and they, having filled it in, make it high-lying, it is still a boundary. If they build a dwelling within the boundary, it is indeed within the boundary. If they dig a pond within the boundary, it is still a boundary. If a flood covers the boundary circle, it is permissible to perform a formal act by constructing a platform in the boundary enclosure. Below the boundary there is an underground river; a monk with psychic power sits there. If that river flowed first, and the boundary was established afterwards, it does not invalidate the formal act. But if the boundary was established first, and the river flowed afterwards, it invalidates the formal act. However, one standing below on the earth's surface certainly invalidates it.

Sīmāmāḷake vaṭarukkho hoti, tassa sākhā vā tato niggatapāroho vā mahāsīmāya pathavitalaṃ [V 0.0310] vā tatthajātarukkhādīni vā āhacca tiṭṭhati, mahāsīmaṃ sodhetvā vā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, te vā sākhāpārohā chinditvā bahiṭṭhakā kātabbā. Anāhacca ṭhitasākhādīsu āruḷhabhikkhu hatthapāsaṃ ānetabbo. Evaṃ mahāsīmāya jātarukkhassa sākhā vā pāroho vā vuttanayeneva sīmāmāḷake patiṭṭhāti, vuttanayeneva sīmaṃ sodhetvā vā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ, te vā sākhāpārohā chinditvā bahiṭṭhakā kātabbā.

In the boundary enclosure there is a banyan tree. If its branch or an aerial root coming from it stands touching either the ground of the great boundary or trees and so on grown there, the formal act should be done either after clearing the great boundary, or those branches and aerial roots should be cut off and made to be outside. A monk who has climbed on branches and so on that stand without touching should be brought into hand's reach. Similarly, if a branch or an aerial root of a tree grown in the great boundary is established in the boundary enclosure in the way just mentioned, then in the way just mentioned, the formal act should be done either after clearing the boundary, or those branches and aerial roots should be cut off and made to be outside.

Sace sīmāmāḷake kamme kariyamāne koci bhikkhu sīmāmāḷakassa anto pavisitvā vehāsaṭṭhitasākhāya nisīdati[P 5.1046], pādā vāssa bhūmigatā honti, nivāsanapārupanaṃ vā bhūmiṃ phusati, kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Pāde pana nivāsanapārupanañca ukkhipāpetvā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Idañca lakkhaṇaṃ purimanayepi veditabbaṃ. Ayaṃ pana viseso – tatra ukkhipāpetvā kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, hatthapāsameva ānetabbo. Sace antosīmato pabbato abbhugacchati, tatraṭṭho bhikkhu hatthapāsaṃ ānetabbo. Iddhiyā antopabbataṃ paviṭṭhepi eseva nayo. Bajjhamānā eva hi sīmā pamāṇarahitaṃ padesaṃ na otarati. Baddhasīmāya jātaṃ yaṃkiñci yattha katthaci ekasambaddhena gataṃ sīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchatīti.

If, while a formal act is being performed in a boundary enclosure, some monk, having entered inside the boundary enclosure, sits on a branch standing in the air, and either his feet are on the ground, or his lower or upper robe touches the ground, it is not permissible to perform the formal act. However, it is permissible to perform the act after having his feet and his lower and upper robes lifted up. And this characteristic should be understood in the previous case as well. But this is the difference: in that case, it is not permissible to perform the act after having them lifted up; he must be brought only into hand's reach. If a mountain rises up from within the boundary, a monk standing there must be brought into hand's reach. This same rule applies even to one who has entered inside a mountain by psychic power. For a boundary that is being established does not descend into an area lacking the required measure. Whatever has arisen within an established boundary, having gone anywhere whatsoever by a single connection, it comes to be counted as the boundary.

140. Tiyojanaparamanti ettha tiyojanaṃ paramaṃ pamāṇametissāti tiyojanaparamā; taṃ tiyojanaparamaṃ. Sammannantena pana majjhe ṭhatvā yathā catūsupi disāsu diyaḍḍhadiyaḍḍhayojanaṃ hoti, evaṃ sammannitabbā. Sace pana majjhe ṭhatvā ekekadisato tiyojanaṃ karonti, chayojanaṃ hotīti na vaṭṭati. Caturassaṃ vā tikoṇaṃ vā sammannantena yathā koṇato koṇaṃ tiyojanaṃ hoti, evaṃ sammannitabbā. Sace hi yena kenaci pariyantena kesaggamattampi tiyojanaṃ atikkāmeti, āpattiñca āpajjati sīmā ca asīmā hoti.

140. Herein, regarding 'extending up to three leagues': 'three leagues is the maximum measure of this boundary'; thus, it is 'extending up to three leagues.' However, one who is establishing it should stand in the middle and do so in such a way that in all four directions it is one and a half leagues each. If, however, standing in the middle, they make it three leagues from each single direction, it becomes six leagues, and therefore it is not permissible. When establishing a square or a triangular boundary, it should be established in such a way that from corner to corner it is three leagues. For if, at any extremity, it exceeds three leagues by even a hair’s breadth, one incurs an offense and the boundary becomes not a boundary.

Nadīpāranti ettha pārayatīti pārā. Kiṃ pārayati? Nadiṃ. Nadiyā pārā nadīpārā, taṃ nadīpāraṃ; nadiṃ ajjhottharamānanti attho. Ettha ca nadiyā lakkhaṇaṃ [M 0.0328] nadīnimitte vuttanayameva. Yatthassa dhuvanāvā vāti yattha nadiyā sīmābandhanaṭṭhānagatesu titthesu niccasañcaraṇanāvā assa, yā sabbantimena paricchedena pājanapurisena saddhiṃ tayo jane vahati. Sace pana sā nāvā uddhaṃ vā adho vā kenacideva karaṇīyena puna āgamanatthāya nītā, corehi vā haṭā, avassaṃ labbhaneyyā, yā pana vātena vā chinnabandhanā vīcīhi nadimajjhaṃ nītā avassaṃ āharitabbā, puna dhuvanāvāva [P 5.1047] hoti. Udake ogate thalaṃ ussāritāpi sudhākasaṭādīhi pūretvā ṭhapitāpi dhuvanāvāva. Sace bhinnā vā visaṅkhatapadarā vā na vaṭṭati. Mahāpadumatthero panāha – “sacepi tāvakālikaṃ nāvaṃ ānetvā sīmābandhanaṭṭhāne [V 0.0311] ṭhapetvā nimittāni kittenti, dhuvanāvāva hotī”ti. Tatra mahāsumatthero āha – “nimittaṃ vā sīmā vā kammavācāya gacchati na nāvāya. Bhagavatā ca dhuvanāvā anuññātā, tasmā nibaddhanāvāyeva vaṭṭatī”ti.

Herein, regarding `nadīpāra`: because it crosses over (`pārayati`), it is called `pārā`. What does it cross over? The river. The `pārā` of the river is `nadīpārā`; that `nadīpāraṃ` means 'crossing over the river.' And here, the characteristic of a river is just as stated in the section on the river-mark. As for 'where there is a permanent boat': this means where, at the landing places situated at the spot for binding the sīmā of a river, there is a boat that regularly travels, one that carries three persons, including the boatman, as its final capacity. If, however, that boat is taken upstream or downstream for some necessary task for the purpose of returning, or is taken by thieves but is certainly retrievable, or if, its mooring rope having been broken by the wind, it is carried to the middle of the river by waves but must certainly be brought back, it is still a permanent boat. Even if, when the water recedes, it is raised onto dry land, or it is filled with plaster, astringent decoctions, and so forth, and set aside, it is still a permanent boat. If it is broken or has unrepaired planks, it is not allowable. The Elder Mahāpaduma, however, said: “Even if they bring a temporary boat, place it at the spot for binding the sīmā, and announce the marks, it is still a permanent boat.” Therein, the Elder Mahāsuma said: “The mark or the sīmā comes to be through the formal act, not through the boat. And a permanent boat was allowed by the Blessed One; therefore, only a fixed boat is allowable.”

Dhuvasetu vāti yattha rukkhasaṅghāṭamayo vā padarabaddho vā jaṅghasatthasetu vā hatthissādīnaṃ sañcaraṇayoggo mahāsetu vā atthi; antamaso taṅkhaṇaññeva rukkhaṃ chinditvā manussānaṃ sañcaraṇayoggo ekapadikasetupi dhuvasetutveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Sace pana upari baddhāni vettalatādīni hatthena gahetvāpi na sakkā hoti tena sañcarituṃ, na vaṭṭati.

As for 'a permanent bridge': this is where there is a bridge made of a collection of logs, or one constructed with planks, or a bridge for foot-travelers and caravans, or a great bridge suitable for the passage of elephants, horses, and so forth. At the very least, even a single-footstep bridge suitable for human passage, made by felling a tree at that very moment, is counted as a permanent bridge. If, however, it is not possible to travel on it even while holding by hand onto rattan, creepers, and so forth, tied above, it is not allowable.

Evarūpaṃ nadīpārasīmaṃ sammannitunti yatthāyaṃ vuttappakārā dhuvanāvā vā dhuvasetu vā abhimukhatittheyeva atthi, evarūpaṃ nadīpārasīmaṃ sammannituṃ anujānāmīti attho. Sace dhuvanāvā vā dhuvasetu vā abhimukhatitthe natthi, īsakaṃ uddhaṃ abhiruhitvā adho vā orohitvā atthi, evampi vaṭṭati. Karavīkatissatthero pana “gāvutamattabbhantarepi vaṭṭatī”ti āha.

'To establish such a nadīpāra sīmā' means: 'I allow a nadīpāra sīmā of such a kind to be established where this permanent boat or permanent bridge of the type described exists at the very landing place opposite.' If a permanent boat or permanent bridge does not exist at the landing place opposite, but one exists by going slightly upstream or descending slightly downstream, even so, it is allowable. The Elder Karavīkatissa, however, said: “It is allowable even if it is within the distance of a gāvuta.”

Imañca pana nadīpārasīmaṃ sammannantena ekasmiṃ tīre ṭhatvā uparisote nadītīre nimittaṃ kittetvā tato paṭṭhāya attānaṃ parikkhipantena yattakaṃ paricchedaṃ icchati, tassa pariyosāne adhosotepi nadītīre nimittaṃ kittetvā paratīre sammukhaṭṭhāne nadītīre nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya yattakaṃ paricchedaṃ icchati, tassa vasena yāva uparisote paṭhamakittitanimittassa sammukhā nadītīre nimittaṃ, tāva kittetvā paccāharitvā paṭhamakittitanimittena [M 0.0329] saddhiṃ ghaṭetabbaṃ. Atha sabbanimittānaṃ anto ṭhite bhikkhū hatthapāsagate katvā kammavācāya sīmā sammannitabbā. Nadiyaṃ ṭhitā anāgatāpi kammaṃ na kopenti. Sammutipariyosāne ṭhapetvā nadiṃ nimittānaṃ anto pāratīre ca orimatīre ca ekasīmā hoti. Nadī [P 5.1048] pana baddhasīmāsaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati, visuṃ nadisīmā eva hi sā.

Furthermore, when establishing this nadīpāra sīmā, one should stand on one bank and announce a mark on the riverbank upstream. Starting from there, enclosing oneself to the desired extent, at its end, one should announce a mark on the riverbank downstream as well. Then, on the opposite bank, at a place directly facing, a mark should be announced on the riverbank. Starting from there, according to the desired extent, one should announce marks up to the point on the riverbank directly opposite the first-announced mark upstream, and then bring it back and connect it with the first-announced mark. Then, having brought the bhikkhus standing inside all the marks to be within hand's reach, the sīmā should be established by a formal act. Those standing in the river, even if they have not come, do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, the area within the marks on the far bank and the near bank becomes a single sīmā. The river, however, is not counted as a bound sīmā, for it is indeed a separate river-sīmā.

Sace antonadiyaṃ dīpako hoti, taṃ antosīmāya kātukāmena purimanayeneva attanā ṭhitatīre nimittāni kittetvā dīpakassa orimante ca pārimante ca nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. Atha paratīre nadiyā orimatīre nimittassa sammukhaṭṭhāne nimittaṃ kittetvā tato paṭṭhāya purimanayeneva yāva uparisote paṭhamakittitanimittassa sammukhā nimittaṃ, tāva kittetabbaṃ. Atha dīpakassa pārimante ca orimante ca nimittaṃ kittetvā paccāharitvā paṭhamakittitanimittena [V 0.0312] saddhiṃ ghaṭetabbaṃ. Atha dvīsu tīresu dīpake ca bhikkhū sabbeva hatthapāsagate katvā kammavācāya sīmā sammannitabbā. Nadiyaṃ ṭhitā anāgacchantāpi kammaṃ na kopenti. Sammutipariyosāne ṭhapetvā nadiṃ nimittānaṃ anto tīradvayañca dīpako ca ekasīmā hoti, nadī pana nadisīmāyeva.

If there is a small island in the river, one who wishes to include it within the sīmā should, in the same way as before, having announced the marks on the bank where he stands, announce a mark on the near edge and the far edge of the small island. Then, on the opposite bank, at a place directly facing the mark on the near bank of the river, a mark should be announced. Starting from there, in the same way as before, marks should be announced up to the point opposite the first-announced mark upstream. Then, having announced the mark on the far edge and the near edge of the island, it should be brought back and connected with the first-announced mark. Then, having brought all the bhikkhus on the two banks and on the island to be within hand's reach, the sīmā should be established by a formal act. Those standing in the river, even if they do not come, do not invalidate the formal act. At the conclusion of the establishment, excluding the river, the two banks and the island within the marks become a single sīmā; the river, however, remains a river-sīmā.

Sace pana dīpako vihārasīmāparicchedato uddhaṃ vā adho vā adhikataro hoti, atha vihārasīmāparicchedanimittassa ujukameva sammukhibhūte dīpakassa sorimante nimittaṃ kittetvā tato paṭṭhāya dīpakasikharaṃ parikkhipantona puna dīpakassa sorimante nimittasammukhe pārimante nimittaṃ kittetabbaṃ. Tato paraṃ purimanayeneva pāratīre sammukhanimīttamādiṃkatvā pāratīranimittāni ca dīpakassa pārimantasorimantanimittāni ca kittetvā paṭhamakittitanimittena saddhiṃ ghaṭanā kātabbā. Evaṃ kittetvā sammatā sīmā pabbatasaṇḍānā hoti.

If, however, the small island extends further upstream or downstream than the monastery-sīmā demarcation, then, having announced a mark on the near edge of the island directly opposite the monastery-sīmā demarcation mark, and starting from there, encircling the peak of the small island, a mark should again be announced on the far edge opposite the mark on the near edge. Thereafter, in the same way as before, beginning with the facing mark on the opposite bank, having announced the marks on the opposite bank and the marks on the far and near edges of the island, a connection should be made with the first-announced mark. The sīmā, having been announced and established in this way, has the shape of a mountain.

Sace pana dīpako vihārasīmāparicchedato uddhampi adhopi adhikataro hoti. Purimanayeneva dīpakassa ubhopi sīkharāni parikkhipitvā nimittāni kittentena nimittaghaṭanā kātabbā. Evaṃ kittetvā sammatā sīmā mudiṅgasaṇṭhānā hoti.

If, however, the small island extends further both upstream and downstream than the monastery-sīmā demarcation, then, in the same way as before, by encircling both peaks of the island and announcing the marks, a connection of the marks should be made. The sīmā, having been announced and established in this way, has the shape of a mudiṅga drum.

Sace [M 0.0330] dīpako vihārasīmāparicchedassa anto khuddako hoti, sabbapaṭhamanayena dīpake nimittāni kittetabbāni. Evaṃ kittetvā sammatā sīmā paṇavasaṇṭhānā hoti.

If the island within the monastery boundary demarcation is small, the signs should be proclaimed on the island according to the very first method. Having been proclaimed thus, the designated boundary has the shape of a drum.

Sīmānujānanakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Discourse on the Authorization of Boundaries is concluded.

Uposathāgārādikathā

The Discourse on the Uposatha Hall and so forth

141. Anupariveṇiyanti ekasīmamahāvihāre tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pariveṇe. Asaṅketenāti [P 5.1049] saṅketaṃ akatvā. Ekaṃ samūhanitvāti kammavācāya samūhanitvā.

141. “Anupariveṇiya” means in each and every precinct of the great monastery with a single boundary. “Asaṅketena” means without making an appointment. “Ekaṃ samūhanitvā” means having removed by means of a formal act.

142. Yato pātimokkhaṃ suṇātīti yattha katthaci bhikkhūnaṃ hatthapāse nisinno yasmā pātimokkhaṃ suṇāti; katovassa uposathoti attho. Idañca vatthuvasena vuttaṃ, hatthapāse nisinnassa pana asuṇantassāpi katova hoti uposatho. Nimittā kittetabbāti uposathapamukhassa khuddakāni vā mahantāni vā pāsāṇaiṭṭhakadārukhaṇḍadaṇḍakādīni yāni kānici [V 0.0313] nimittāni abbhokāse vā māḷakādīsu vā yattha katthaci saññaṃ katvā kittetuṃ vaṭṭati. Atha vā nimittā kittetabbāti nimittupagā vā animittupagā vā paricchedajānanatthaṃ kittetabbā.

142. “Since he hears the Pātimokkha”: Wherever, being seated within arm’s reach of the monks, because he hears the Pātimokkha, his Uposatha is indeed performed; this is the meaning. And this was said by the Blessed One according to the story. However, for one seated within arm’s reach, even if not hearing, the Uposatha is indeed performed. “The signs should be proclaimed”: Whether small or large, whatever signs there may be—such as stones, bricks, pieces of wood, sticks, and so on—it is proper to proclaim them after making a designation, whether in an open space or in pavilions and so forth, in any place whatsoever. Alternatively, “The signs should be proclaimed” means: whether suitable as signs or unsuitable as signs, stones and so forth should be proclaimed for the purpose of knowing the boundary.

Therehi bhikkhūhi paṭhamataraṃ sannipatitunti ettha sace mahāthero paṭhamataraṃ na āgacchati, dukkaṭaṃ. Sabbeheva ekajjhaṃ sannipatitvā uposatho kātabboti ettha sace porāṇako āvāso majjhe vihārassa hoti, pahoti cettha bhikkhūnaṃ nisajjaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha sannipatitvā uposatho kātabbo. Sace porāṇako paridubbalo ceva sambādho ca añño pacchā uṭṭhitāvāso asambādho, tattha uposatho kātabbo.

Regarding “The elder monks should assemble first”: Here, if the great elder does not arrive first, it is a dukkaṭa offense. Regarding “The Uposatha should be performed by all having assembled together”: Here, if the ancient dwelling is in the middle of the monastery, and there is sufficient seating space for the monks, the Uposatha should be performed there, having assembled. If the ancient dwelling is both very dilapidated and cramped, and another dwelling that arose later is spacious, the Uposatha should be performed there.

Yattha vā pana thero bhikkhu viharatīti etthāpi sace therassa vihāro sabbesaṃ pahoti, phāsuko hoti, tattha uposatho kātabbo. Sace pana so paccante visamappadese hoti, therassa vattabbaṃ – “bhante, tumhākaṃ vihāro aphāsukadeso, natthi ettha sabbesaṃ okāso[M 0.0331], asukasmiṃ nāma āvāse okāso atthi, tattha gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sace thero nāgacchati, tassa chandapārisuddhiṃ ānetvā sabbesaṃ pahonake phāsukaṭṭhāne uposatho kātabbo.

Also regarding “Or wherever the elder monk dwells”: Here, if the elder’s dwelling is sufficient for all and is comfortable, the Uposatha should be performed there. But if it is at the edge, in an uneven place, the elder should be told: “Venerable sir, your dwelling is an uncomfortable place; there is no space here for all. In such-and-such a dwelling there is space; it is proper to go there.” If the elder does not come, having brought his consent and purity, the Uposatha should be performed in a comfortable place sufficient for all.

Avippavāsasīmānujānanakathā

The Account of the Authorization of the Non-Separation Boundary

143. Andhakavindāti rājagahato gāvutattaye andhakavindaṃ nāma, taṃ upanissāya thero vasati; tato rājagahaṃ uposathaṃ āgacchanto. Rājagahañhi parikkhipitvā aṭṭhārasa mahāvihārā sabbe ekasīmā, dhammasenāpatinā nesaṃ sīmā baddhā, tasmā veḷuvane saṅghassa sāmaggīdānatthaṃ āgacchantoti attho. Nadiṃ tarantoti sippiniyaṃ nāma nadiṃ atikkamanto. Manaṃ vuḷho ahosīti īsakaṃ appattavuḷhabhāvo ahosi. Sā kira nadī gijjhakūṭato otaritvā [P 5.1050] caṇḍena sotena vahati. Tattha vegena āgacchantaṃ udakaṃ amanasikaronto thero manaṃ vuḷho ahosi, na pana vuḷho, udakabbhāhatānissa cīvarāni allāni jātāni.

143. Andhakavinda—this is a village named Andhakavinda, at a distance of three gāvutas from Rājagaha. The elder lived relying on it and was coming to Rājagaha for the Uposatha. Indeed, surrounding Rājagaha, there are eighteen great monasteries, all within a single boundary; their boundary was established by the General of the Dhamma. Therefore, the meaning is that he was coming to the Bamboo Grove for the purpose of providing harmony to the Saṅgha. Crossing the river means he was crossing a river named Sippinī. He was slightly carried away means he was slightly carried away, but did not reach a state of being fully carried away. It is said that this river, descending from Vulture’s Peak, flows with a fierce current. There, not paying attention to the water approaching with swiftness, the elder was slightly carried away, but not truly carried away; his robes, struck by the water, became wet.

144. Sammatā sā sīmā saṅghena ticīvarena avippavāsā ṭhapetvā gāmañca gāmūpacārañcāti imissā kammavācāya uppannakālato paṭṭhāya bhikkhūnaṃ purimakammavācā na vaṭṭati. Ayameva hi thāvarā hoti. Bhikkhunīnaṃ pana ayaṃ na vaṭṭati, purimāyeva vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Bhikkhunisaṅgho hi antogāme vasati. Yadi evaṃ siyā, so etāya kammavācāya ticīvaraparihāraṃ [V 0.0314] na labheyya, atthi cassa parihāro, tasmā purimāyeva vaṭṭati. Bhikkhunisaṅghassa hi dvepi sīmāyo labbhanti. Tattha bhikkhūnaṃ sīmaṃ ajjhottharitvāpi tassā antopi bhikkhunīnaṃ sīmaṃ sammannituṃ vaṭṭati. Bhikkhūnampi bhikkhunisīmāya eseva nayo. Na hi te aññamaññassa kamme gaṇapūrakā honti, na kammavācaṃ vaggaṃ karonti. Ettha ca nigamanagarānampi gāmeneva saṅgaho veditabbo.

144. That boundary was agreed upon by the Saṅgha as a non-separation boundary for the three robes, excluding the village and its environs. From the time this formal act was declared, the previous formal act for the bhikkhus is no longer valid. Indeed, this alone is permanent. For the bhikkhunīs, however, this is not valid; only the previous one is valid. Why? Because the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha dwells within the village. If it were so, they would not obtain the exemption regarding the three robes with this formal act; but since they have that exemption, the previous one alone is valid. Indeed, two boundaries are obtainable for the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. There, even if it overlaps the bhikkhus' boundary, it is valid to establish a bhikkhunīs' boundary within it. The same principle applies to the bhikkhus regarding the bhikkhunīs' boundary. For they do not serve to complete the quorum in each other’s acts, nor do they render each other’s formal acts incomplete. And here, market towns and cities should be understood to be included by the word 'village'.

Gāmūpacāroti parikkhittassa parikkhepo, aparikkhittassa parikkhepokāso. Tesu adhiṭṭhitatecīvariko bhikkhu parihāraṃ na labhati. Iti [M 0.0332] bhikkhūnaṃ avippavāsasīmā gāmañca gāmūpacārañca na ottharati, samānasaṃvāsakasīmāva ottharati. Samānasaṃvāsakasīmā cettha attano dhammatāya gacchati. Avippavāsasīmā pana yattha samānasaṃvāsakasīmā, tattheva gacchati. Na hi tassā visuṃ nimittakittanaṃ atthi, tattha sace avippavāsāya sammutikāle gāmo atthi, taṃ sā na ottharati. Sace pana sammatāya sīmāya pacchā gāmo nivisati, sopi sīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Yathā ca pacchā niviṭṭho, evaṃ paṭhamaṃ niviṭṭhassa pacchā vaḍḍhitappadesopi sīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Sacepi sīmāsammutikāle gehāni katāni, pavisissāmāti ālayopi atthi, manussā pana appaviṭṭhā, porāṇakagāmaṃ vā sagehameva chaḍḍetvā aññattha gatā, agāmoyeva esa, sīmā ottharati[P 5.1051]. Sace pana ekampi kulaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ vā āgataṃ vā atthi, gāmoyeva sīmā na ottharati.

The village environs (gāmūpacāra) means the enclosure for an enclosed village, and the place suitable for an enclosure for an unenclosed village. In these places, a bhikkhu who has determined his three robes does not receive the allowance. Thus, the non-separation boundary of the bhikkhus does not extend over the village and its environs; only the common-communion boundary extends over them. Here, the common-communion boundary proceeds by its own nature. However, the non-separation boundary goes only where the common-communion boundary goes, for it has no separate declaration of markers. If, at the time of the agreement for the non-separation boundary, a village exists there, that boundary does not extend over it. But if a village is established after the boundary has been agreed upon, it too falls within the boundary's scope. And just as a later-established village falls within it, so too an area of a previously established village that is expanded later also falls within the boundary's scope. Even if, at the time of the boundary agreement, houses were built and there was the intention, “We will move in,” but people had not yet moved in; or if they abandoned an old village, together with its houses, and went elsewhere, it is not a village, and the boundary extends over it. However, if even a single family has moved in or has not yet left, it is a village, and the boundary does not extend over it.

Evañca pana bhikkhave ticīvarena avippavāso samūhantabboti ettha samūhanantena bhikkhunā vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tatridaṃ vattaṃ – khaṇḍasīmāya ṭhatvā avippavāsasīmā na samūhantabbā, tathā avippavāsasīmāya ṭhatvā khaṇḍasīmāpi. Khaṇḍasīmāyaṃ pana ṭhitena khaṇḍasīmāva samūhanitabbā, tathā itarāya ṭhitena itarā. Sīmaṃ nāma dvīhi kāraṇehi samūhananti pakatiyā khuddakaṃ puna āvāsavaḍḍhanatthāya mahatiṃ vā kātuṃ; pakatiyā mahatiṃ puna aññesaṃ vihārokāsadānatthāya khuddakaṃ vā kātuṃ. Tattha sace khaṇḍasīmañca avippavāsasīmañca jānanti, samūhanituñceva bandhituñca sakkhissanti. Khaṇḍasīmaṃ pana jānantā avippavāsaṃ ajānantāpi samūhanituñceva bandhituñca sakkhissanti. Khaṇḍasīmaṃ ajānantā avippavāsaṃyeva jānantā cetiyaṅgaṇabodhiyaṅgaṇauposathāgārādīsu nirāsaṅkaṭṭhānesu ṭhatvā appeva nāma samūhanituṃ sakkhissanti, paṭibandhituṃ pana na sakkhissanteva. Sace bandheyyuṃ, sīmāsambhedaṃ katvā vihāraṃ avihāraṃ kareyyuṃ, tasmā na samūhanitabbā. Ye pana ubhopi na jānanti, teneva samūhanituṃ na bandhituṃ sakkhissanti. Ayañhi sīmā nāma kammavācāya vā asīmā hoti sāsanantaradhānena [V 0.0315] vā, na ca sakkā sīmaṃ ajānantehi kammavācā kātuṃ, tasmā na samūhanitabbā. Sādhukaṃ pana ñatvāyeva samūhanitabbā ca bandhitabbā cāti.

And thus, bhikkhus, regarding the abolishment of the boundary for non-separation from the three robes, in this connection, a bhikkhu who is abolishing it should know the procedure. Herein, this is the procedure: standing within a fragmentary boundary, the boundary for non-separation should not be abolished; likewise, standing within the boundary for non-separation, the fragmentary boundary should not be abolished. However, one standing within the fragmentary boundary should abolish only the fragmentary boundary; and one standing within the other should abolish only the other. A boundary is abolished for two reasons: either to make a naturally small one large for the sake of expanding a residence, or to make a naturally large one small for the sake of providing space for other monasteries. In this regard, if they know both the fragmentary boundary and the boundary for non-separation, they will be able to abolish and establish them. Even if they know the fragmentary boundary but not the boundary for non-separation, they will still be able to abolish and establish it. But if they do not know the fragmentary boundary and only know the boundary for non-separation, standing in places free of doubt—such as shrine courtyards, bodhi tree courtyards, or Uposatha halls—they might be able to abolish it, but they will certainly not be able to re-establish it. If they were to establish it, they would create a confusion of boundaries, making a monastery a non-monastery. Therefore, it should not be abolished. Those who know neither will be able to neither abolish nor establish it. For this boundary becomes a non-boundary either by a formal act or by the disappearance of the Dispensation, and it is not possible for those who do not know the boundary to perform the formal act. Therefore, it should not be abolished. Only after knowing well should one abolish and establish it. This is the procedure.

Gāmasīmādikathā

The Discourse on Village Boundaries, etc.

147. Evaṃ [M 0.0333] baddhasīmāvasena samānasaṃvāsañca ekūposathabhāvañca dassetvā idāni abaddhasīmesupi okāsesu taṃ dassento “asammatāya, bhikkhave, sīmāya aṭṭhapitāyā”tiādimāha. Tattha aṭṭhapitāyāti aparicchinnāya. Gāmaggahaṇena cettha nagarampi gahitameva hoti. Tattha yattake padese tassa gāmassa bhojakā baliṃ labhanti, so padeso appo vā hotu mahanto vā, gāmasīmātveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Nagaranigamasīmāsupi eseva nayo. Yampi ekasmiṃyeva [P 5.1052] gāmakhette ekaṃ padesaṃ “ayaṃ visuṃ gāmo hotū”ti paricchinditvā rājā kassaci deti, sopi visuṃgāmasīmā hotiyeva. Tasmā sā ca itarā ca pakatigāmanagaranigamasīmā baddhasīmāsadisāyeva honti, kevalaṃ pana ticīvaravippavāsaparihāraṃ na labhanti.

147. Thus, having shown common communion and the state of having a single Uposatha by means of a consecrated boundary, now, wishing to show the same in places that are unconsecrated boundaries, He spoke the passage beginning with, “Monks, in a territory that is unconsecrated, whose boundary is not established…” Therein, `aṭṭhapitāya` means ‘undemarcated.’ And here, by the taking of ‘village,’ a city is also taken. Therein, in whatever extent of a region the rulers of that village receive tribute, that region, whether it be small or large, is reckoned as the village boundary. This is the same method for the boundaries of cities and market towns. And also, when a king, having demarcated a certain region within a single village-field, gives it to someone, saying, “Let this be a separate village,” that too becomes a separate village boundary. Therefore, both that and the other natural boundaries of villages, cities, and market towns are indeed like a consecrated boundary; however, they do not afford the protection from separation from the three robes.

Evaṃ gāmantavāsīnaṃ sīmāparicchedaṃ dassetvā idāni āraññakānaṃ sīmāparicchedaṃ dassento “agāmake ce”tiādimāha. Tattha agāmake ceti gāmanigamanagarasīmāhi aparicchinne aṭavippadese. Atha vā agāmake ceti vijjhāṭavisadise araññe bhikkhu vasati, athassa ṭhitokāsato samantā sattabbhantarā samānasaṃvāsakasīmāti attho. Ayaṃ sīmā ticīvaravippavāsaparihārampi labhati. Tattha ekaṃ abbhantaraṃ aṭṭhavīsati hatthappamāṇaṃ hoti. Majjhe ṭhitassa samantā sattabbhantarā vinibbedhena cuddasa honti. Sace dve saṅghā visuṃ vinayakammāni karonti, dvinnaṃ sattabbhantarānaṃ antare aññaṃ ekaṃ sattabbhantaraṃ upacāratthāya ṭhapetabbaṃ. Sesā sattabbhantarasīmakathā mahāvibhaṅge udositasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttanayena gahetabbā.

Thus, having shown the boundary demarcation for monks dwelling near a village, now, wishing to show the boundary demarcation for forest-dwelling monks, He spoke the passage beginning with, “And if in a village-less place…” Therein, `agāmake ce` refers to a forest region not demarcated by the boundaries of a village, market town, or city. Or alternatively, `agāmake ce` means if a monk dwells in a great forest similar to the Vindhya forest; then, for that monk, the boundary for common communion is seven `abbhantaras` all around from the place where he stays. This is the meaning. This boundary also affords the protection from separation from the three robes. Therein, one `abbhantara` has the measure of twenty-eight cubits. For one standing in the middle, the seven `abbhantaras` all around become fourteen `abbhantaras` diametrically. If two communities perform Vinaya acts separately, another single seven-`abbhantara` boundary should be established in between the two seven-`abbhantara` boundaries for the purpose of an intervening space. The remaining discourse on the seven-`abbhantara` boundary should be understood according to the method stated in the Mahāvibhaṅga, in the explanation of the Udosita training rule.

Sabbā bhikkhave nadī asīmāti yā kāci nadīlakkhaṇappattā nadī nimittāni kittetvā “etaṃ baddhasīmaṃ karomā”ti katāpi asīmāva hoti, sā pana attano sabhāveneva baddhasīmāsadisā, sabbamettha saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Samuddajātassaresupi eseva nayo. Ettha ca jātassaro nāma yena kenaci khaṇitvā akato sayaṃjātasobbho samantato āgatena udakena pūrito tiṭṭhati.

“Monks, every river is an unconsecrated boundary” means: any river whatsoever that has the characteristic of a river, even if it is made a boundary by declaring markers and thinking, “Let us make this a consecrated boundary,” it is indeed not a consecrated boundary. However, by its own nature, it is like a consecrated boundary; it is permissible to perform all Sangha acts therein. This is the same method for oceans and natural lakes. And here, what is called a `jātassara` (natural lake) is a naturally arisen pool, not made by being dug by anyone whatsoever, which stands filled with water that has come from all around.

Evaṃ [M 0.0334][V 0.0316] nadīsamuddajātassarānaṃ baddhasīmābhāvaṃ paṭikkhipitvā puna tattha abaddhasīmāpaacchedaṃ dassento “nadiyā vā bhikkhave”tiādimāha. Tattha yaṃ majjhimassa purisassa samantā udakukkhepāti yaṃ ṭhānaṃ majjhimassa purisassa samantato udakukkhepena paricchinnaṃ. Kathaṃ pana udakaṃ ukkhipitabbaṃ? Yathā akkhadhuttā dāruguḷaṃ khipanti, evaṃ udakaṃ vā vālikaṃ vā hatthena gahetvā thāmamajjhimena purisena sabbathāmena khipitabbaṃ. Yattha evaṃ khittaṃ udakaṃ vā vālikā vā patati, ayameko udakukkhepo. Tassa anto hatthapāsaṃ [P 5.1053] vijahitvā ṭhito kammaṃ kopeti. Yāva parisā vaḍḍhati, tāva sīmāpi vaḍḍhati. Parisapariyantato udakukkhepoyeva pamāṇaṃ. Jātassarasamuddesupi eseva nayo.

Thus, having rejected the state of rivers, oceans, and natural lakes being consecrated boundaries, and again wishing to show the demarcation of an unconsecrated boundary therein, He spoke the passage beginning with, “Or, monks, in a river…” Therein, `yaṃ majjhimassa purisassa samantā udakukkhepa` means the place that is demarcated all around by the water-throw of a man of medium strength. But how should the water be thrown? Just as dice-players throw a wooden ball, so should water or sand be taken in the hand and thrown with all one's strength by a man of medium strength. Where the water or sand thus thrown falls, this is one water-throw. One standing inside it, but having gone beyond hand's reach, spoils the act. As the assembly increases, so too does the boundary increase. The water-throw from the edge of the assembly is the measure. This is the same method for natural lakes and oceans.

Ettha ca sace nadī nātidīghā hoti, pabhavato paṭṭhāya yāva mukhadvārā sabbattha saṅgho nisīdati, udakukkhepasīmākammaṃ natthi, sakalāpi nadī etesaṃyeva bhikkhūnaṃ pahoti. Yaṃ pana mahāsumattherena vuttaṃ “yojanaṃ pavattamānāyeva nadī, tatrāpi upari addhayojanaṃ pahāya heṭṭhā addhayojane kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti, taṃ mahāpadumatthereneva paṭikkhittaṃ. Bhagavatā hi “timaṇḍalaṃ paṭicchādetvā yattha katthaci uttarantiyā bhikkhuniyā antaravāsako temiyatī”ti idaṃ nadiyā pamāṇaṃ vuttaṃ, na yojanaṃ vā addhayojanaṃ vā. Tasmā yā imassa suttassa vasena pubbe vuttalakkhaṇā nadī, tassā pabhavato paṭṭhāya saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti. Sace panettha bahū bhikkhū visuṃ visuṃ kammaṃ karonti, sabbehi attano ca aññesañca udakukkhepaparicchedassa antarā añño udakukkhepo sīmantarikatthāya ṭhapetabbo. Tato adhikaṃ vaṭṭatiyeva, ūnakaṃ pana na vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Jātassarasamuddesupi eseva nayo.

And here, if a river is not too long, and the Sangha sits everywhere from its source up to its mouth, there is no need to perform the act of demarcating a water-throw boundary; the entire river is sufficient for just these monks. However, as to what was said by the Elder Mahāsuma, “A river is one that flows for a yojana, and even there, it is permissible to perform the act in the lower half-yojana, having disregarded the upper half-yojana,” that was rejected by the Elder Mahāpaduma himself. Indeed, the Blessed One has stated this measure of a river: “The inner robe of a bhikkhunī crossing anywhere gets wet after she has covered the three circles (the two kneecaps and the navel).” A yojana or half a yojana was not stated. Therefore, for a river that has the previously stated characteristic according to this Sutta, it is permissible to perform a Sangha act starting from its source. If many monks here perform acts separately, another water-throw must be established by all of them in between their own water-throw demarcation and that of the others for the purpose of an intervening boundary. More than that is permissible, but less is not permissible, it is said. This is the same method for natural lakes and oceans.

Nadiyā pana kammaṃ karissāmāti gatehi sace nadī paripuṇṇā hoti samatittikā, udakasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvāpi antonadiyaṃyeva kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace na sakkonti, nāvāyapi ṭhatvā kātabbaṃ. Gacchantiyā pana nāvāya kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Kasmā? Udakukkhepamattameva hi sīmā, taṃ nāvā sīghameva atikkāmeti. Evaṃ sati aññissā sīmāya ñatti aññissā anusāvanā hoti, tasmā nāvaṃ arittena vā ṭhapetvā pāsāṇe vā lambitvā [M 0.0335] antonadiyaṃ jātarukkhe vā bandhitvā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Antonadiyaṃ baddhaaṭṭakepi antonadiyaṃ jātarukkhepi ṭhitehi kātuṃ vaṭṭati.

However, for those who have gone thinking, “We will perform an act in the river,” if the river is full to the banks, the act should be done right within the river, even after putting on a bathing cloth. If they are not able, it should be done while standing on a boat. However, it is not permissible to perform the act on a moving boat. Why? Because the boundary is only the extent of the water-throw, and a boat quickly passes beyond it. This being so, the motion (ñatti) would be in one boundary, and the proclamations (anussāvanā) in another. Therefore, the act should be done having stopped the boat with a pole, or having lowered rocks, or having tied it to a tree growing in the river. It is permissible to perform the act while standing on a platform constructed in the river or on a tree growing in the river.

Sace pana rukkhassa sākhā vā tato nikkhantapāroho [P 5.1054] vā bahinadītīre vihārasīmāya vā gāmasīmāya vā patiṭṭhito, sīmaṃ vā sodhetvā sākhaṃ vā chinditvā kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Bahinadītīre [V 0.0317] jātarukkhassa antonadiyaṃ paviṭṭhasākhāya vā pārohe vā nāvaṃ bandhitvā kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Karontehi sīmā vā sodhetabbā, chinditvā vāssa bahipatiṭṭhitabhāvo nāsetabbo. Nadītīre pana khāṇukaṃ koṭṭetvā tattha baddhanāvāya na vaṭṭatiyeva.

Furthermore, if a branch of a tree or a shoot extending from it is established on the outer riverbank, within a monastery boundary or a village boundary, the act should be performed after either clearing the boundary or cutting the branch. For a tree growing on the outer riverbank, it is not permissible to perform the act by tying a boat to its branch or shoot that has entered into the river. Those performing the act should either clear the boundary or, by cutting it, destroy its state of being established outside. Furthermore, on the riverbank, it is not permissible at all to perform the act on a boat tied to a stake that has been driven in there.

Nadiyaṃ setuṃ karonti, sace antonadiyaṃyeva setu vā setupādā vā, setumhi ṭhitehi kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana setu vā setupādā vā bahitīre patiṭṭhitā, kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, sīmaṃ sodhetvā kātabbaṃ. Atha setupādā anto, setu pana ubhinnampi tīrānaṃ upariākāse ṭhito, vaṭṭati. Antonadiyaṃ pāsāṇo vā dīpako vā hoti, tassa yattakaṃ padesaṃ pubbe vuttappakāre pakativassakāle vassānassa catūsu māsesu udakaṃ ottharati, so nadīsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Ativuṭṭhikāle pana oghena otthaṭokāso na gahetabbo, so hi gāmasīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati.

They make a bridge in the river. If the bridge or its supports are within the river itself, it is permissible for those standing on the bridge to perform the act. But if the bridge or its supports are established on the outer bank, it is not permissible to perform the act; it should be done after clearing the boundary. Or, if the bridge supports are inside, but the bridge stands in the air above both banks, it is permissible. Within the river, there may be a rock or an islet. Whatever area of it the water covers during the four months of the rainy season in a normal rainy season, in the manner previously stated, that area is reckoned only as 'river'. But during a time of excessive rain, the area covered by the flood should not be taken, for that is reckoned only as 'village boundary'.

Nadito mātikaṃ nīharantā nadiyaṃ āvaraṇaṃ karonti, tañce ottharitvā vā vinibbijjhitvā vā udakaṃ gacchati, sabbattha pavattanaṭṭhāne kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana āvaraṇena vā koṭṭakabandhanena vā sotaṃ pacchijjati, udakaṃ nappavattati, appavattanaṭṭhāne kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Āvaraṇamatthakepi kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Sace koci āvaraṇappadeso pubbe vuttapāsāṇadīpakappadeso viya udakena ajjhotthariyati, tattha vaṭṭati. So hi nadīsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Nadiṃ vināsetvā taḷākaṃ karonti, heṭṭhā pāḷi baddhā, udakaṃ āgantvā taḷākaṃ pūretvā tiṭṭhati, ettha kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Upari pavattanaṭṭhāne heṭṭhā ca chaḍḍitamodakaṃ nadiṃ ottharitvā sandanaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya vaṭṭati. Deve avassante hemantagimhesu vā sukkhanadiyāpi vaṭṭati. Nadito nīhaṭamātikāya na vaṭṭati. Sace [M 0.0336] sā kālantarena bhijjitvā nadī hoti, vaṭṭati. Kāci nadī kālantarena uppatitvā gāmanigamasīmaṃ ottharitvā pavattati, nadīyeva hoti, kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana vihārasīmaṃ ottharati, vihārasīmātveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

Those drawing a channel from a river make a dam in the river. If the water flows by overflowing or breaching it, it is permissible to perform the act in every place where it flows. But if the current is cut off by the dam or by an embankment and the water does not flow, it is not permissible to perform the act in the place where it does not flow. It is also not permissible to perform it on top of the dam. If some part of the dam is covered by water like the previously mentioned area of a rock or islet, it is permissible there, for that is reckoned only as 'river'. They destroy a river and make a reservoir; a dike is built below, and water comes, fills the reservoir, and stays; here it is not permissible to perform the act. It is permissible in the place where it flows above, and also below, starting from the place where the discharged water, having descended into the river, flows. When the sky does not rain, or in the winter and summer seasons, it is permissible even in a dry river. It is not permissible in a channel drawn from the river. If that, in time, breaks and becomes a river, it is permissible. A certain river, in time, having risen up, overflows the village or town boundary and flows; it is still a river, and it is permissible to perform the act. But if it overflows a monastery boundary, it is reckoned only as 'monastery boundary'.

Samuddepi [P 5.1055] kammaṃ karontehi yaṃ padesaṃ uddhaṃ vaḍḍhanaudakaṃ vā pakativīci vā vegena āgantvā ottharati, tattha kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Yasmiṃ pana padese pakativīciyo ottharitvā saṇṭhahanti, so udakantato paṭṭhāya antosamuddo nāma, tattha ṭhitehi kammaṃ kātabbaṃ. Sace ūmivego bādhati, nāvāya vā aṭṭake vā ṭhatvā kātabbaṃ. Tesu vinicchayo nadiyaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Samudde piṭṭhipāsāṇo hoti, taṃ kadāci ūmiyo āgantvā ottharanti[V 0.0318], kadāci na ottharanti, tattha kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati, so hi gāmasīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Sace pana vīcīsu āgatāsupi anāgatāsupi pakatiudakeneva otthariyati, vaṭṭati. Dīpako vā pabbato vā hoti, so ce dūre hoti macchabandhānaṃ agamanapathe, araññasīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Tesaṃ gamanapariyantassa orato pana gāmasīmāsaṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Tattha gāmasīmaṃ asodhetvā kammaṃ kātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Samuddo gāmasīmaṃ vā nigamasīmaṃ vā ottharitvā tiṭṭhati, samuddova hoti, tattha kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana vihārasīmaṃ ottharati, vihārasīmātveva saṅkhyaṃ gacchati.

Even in the ocean, for those performing an act, in whatever area the rising water or the normal waves come with force and cover it, it is not permissible to perform the act there. But in whatever area the normal waves, having covered it, settle, that area, starting from the water's edge, is called the inner ocean; the act should be performed by those standing there. If the force of the waves is oppressive, it should be done standing on a boat or a platform. The ruling on these should be understood by the same method as stated for a river. In the ocean, there may be a flat rock. Sometimes waves come and cover it, and sometimes they do not; it is not permissible to perform an act there, for that is reckoned only as 'village boundary'. But if, whether the waves have come or not, it is covered by the normal water, it is permissible. There may be an islet or a mountain. If it is far away, on a path not traveled by fishermen, it is reckoned only as 'wilderness boundary'. But on this side of the limit of their travel, it is reckoned as 'village boundary'. There, it is not permissible to perform an act without clearing the village boundary. If the ocean covers a village or town boundary and remains, it is still the ocean; it is permissible to perform an act there. But if it covers a monastery boundary, it is reckoned only as 'monastery boundary'.

Jātassare kammaṃ karontehipi yattha pubbe vuttappakāre vassakāle vasse pacchinnamatte pivituṃ vā hatthapāde vā dhovituṃ udakaṃ na hoti, sukkhati, ayaṃ na jātassaro, gāmakhettasaṅkhyameva gacchati, tattha kammaṃ na kātabbaṃ. Yattha pana vuttappakāre vassakāle udakaṃ santiṭṭhati, ayameva jātassaro. Tassa yattake padese vassānaṃ cātumāse udakaṃ tiṭṭhati, tattha kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace gambhīraṃ udakaṃ, aṭṭakaṃ bandhitvā tattha ṭhitehipi jātassarassa anto jātarukkhamhi baddhaaṭṭakepi kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Piṭṭhipāsāṇadīpakesu panettha nadiyaṃ vuttasadisova vinicchayo. Samavassadevakāle pahonakajātassaro pana sacepi dubbuṭṭhikāle vā gimhahemantesu vā sukkhati, nirudako hoti, tattha saṅghakammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ “sabbo jātassaro sukkho anodako[M 0.0337], gāmakhettaṃyeva bhajatī”ti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Sace panettha udakatthāya āvāṭaṃ vā pokkharaṇīādīni [P 5.1056] vā khaṇanti, taṃ ṭhānaṃ ajātassaro hoti, gāmasīmāsaṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Lābutipusakādivappe katepi eseva nayo.

Even by those performing an act in a natural lake, where, during the rainy season in the manner previously stated, just when the rain has ceased, there is no water to drink or to wash hands and feet, and it dries up—this is not a natural lake; it is reckoned only as 'village-field', and an act should not be performed there. But where, in the stated manner, water remains during the rainy season, this itself is a natural lake. In whatever area of it water stands during the four months of the rains, it is permissible to perform an act there. If the water is deep, it is permissible to perform it even by those standing on a platform after building it, or on a platform tied to a tree that has grown within the natural lake. Here, regarding flat rocks and islets, the ruling is just like that stated for a river. Furthermore, a natural lake that is sufficient during a time of even rainfall, even if it dries up during a time of drought or in the summer and winter seasons and becomes waterless, it is still permissible to perform a Saṅgha act there. The statement in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, 'Every natural lake, being dry and waterless, reverts to being only village-field,' should not be accepted. If here, for the sake of water, they dig a pit or ponds and so on, that place becomes not a natural lake and is reckoned as 'village boundary'. Even when the planting of gourds, cucumbers, and so on is done, this is the same method.

Sace pana taṃ pūretvā thalaṃ vā karonti, ekasmiṃ disābhāge pāḷiṃ bandhitvā sabbameva taṃ mahātaḷākaṃ vā karonti, sabbopi ajātassaro hoti, gāmasīmāsaṅkhyameva gacchati. Loṇīpi jātassarasaṅkhyameva gacchati. Vassike cattāro māse udakaṭṭhānokāse kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti.

But if they fill it and make it dry land, or if they build a bank in one direction and make the whole of it a great reservoir, the whole of it is no longer a natural lake and is reckoned only as 'village boundary'. A salt stream is also reckoned only as a natural lake. During the four months of the rainy season, it is permissible to perform an act in the place where water stands.

148. Sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindantīti attano sīmāya paresaṃ baddhasīmaṃ sambhindanti. Sace hi porāṇakassa vihārassa puratthimāya disāya ambo ceva jambū cāti dve rukkhā aññamaññaṃ saṃsaṭṭhaviṭapā honti, tesu ambassa pacchimadisābhāge jambū. Vihārasīmā ca jambuṃ anto katvā ambaṃ kittetvā baddhā hoti, atha pacchā tassa vihārassa puratthimāya disāya vihāraṃ katvā sīmaṃ bandhantā taṃ ambaṃ anto katvā jambuṃ kittetvā bandhanti, sīmāya [V 0.0319] sīmā sambhinnā hoti. Evaṃ chabbaggiyā akaṃsu, tenāha – “sīmāya sīmaṃ sambhindantī”ti.

148. 'They intermingle a boundary with a boundary' means they intermingle another's established boundary with their own boundary. For instance, if in the eastern direction of an ancient monastery there are two trees—a mango and a rose-apple—with intertwined branches, and among them, the rose-apple is in the western direction of the mango, and the monastery boundary was established by including the rose-apple within and proclaiming the mango; then afterwards, having built a monastery in the eastern direction of that monastery, the monks establishing the boundary establish it by including that mango within and proclaiming the rose-apple, then a boundary is intermingled with a boundary. The monks of the group of six did so, therefore it was said: 'They intermingle a boundary with a boundary'.

Sīmāya sīmaṃ ajjhottharantīti attano sīmāya paresaṃ baddhasīmaṃ ajjhottharanti;

'They overlap a boundary with a boundary' means they overlap another's established boundary with their own boundary;

Paresaṃ baddhasīmaṃ sakalaṃ vā tassā padesaṃ vā anto katvā attano sīmaṃ bandhanti. Sīmantarikaṃ ṭhapetvā sīmaṃ sammannitunti ettha sace paṭhamataraṃ katassa vihārassa sīmā asammatā hoti, sīmāya upacāro ṭhapetabbo. Sace sammatā hoti, pacchimakoṭiyā hatthamattā sīmantarikā ṭhapetabbā. Kurundiyaṃ vidatthimattampi, mahāpaccariyaṃ caturaṅgulamattampi vaṭṭatīti vuttaṃ. Ekarukkhopi ca dvinnaṃ sīmānaṃ nimittaṃ hoti, so pana vaḍḍhanto sīmāsaṅkaraṃ karoti, tasmā na kātabbo.

They establish their own boundary by including either the whole of another's established boundary or a part of it. Regarding the authorization of a boundary after leaving an intervening space, if the boundary of the monastery built first is unauthorized, the precincts of the boundary should be left. If it is authorized, an intervening space of a cubit's measure should be left at the final edge. In the Kurundī commentary, it is said that even a span's measure is permissible; in the Mahāpaccarī commentary, even four finger-breadths' measure is permissible. And a single tree can be a marker for two boundaries, but as it grows, it causes a confusion of boundaries; therefore, it should not be made so.

Uposathabhedādikathā

Discourse on the Breaking of the Uposatha, etc.

149. Cātuddasiko ca pannarasiko cāti ettha cātuddasikassa pubbakicce “ajjuposatho cātuddaso”ti vattabbaṃ.

149. Herein, regarding 'the fourteenth and the fifteenth', for the preliminary duty of the fourteenth-day Uposatha, it should be said: 'Today is the fourteenth Uposatha'.

Adhammena vaggantiādīsu [M 0.0338] sace ekasmiṃ vihāre catūsu bhikkhūsu vasantesu ekassa chandapārisuddhiṃ āharitvā tayo pārisuddhiuposathaṃ [P 5.1057] karonti, tīsu vā vasantesu ekassa chandapārisuddhiṃ āharitvā dve pātimokkhaṃ uddisanti, adhammena vaggaṃ uposathakammaṃ hoti. Sace pana cattāropi sannipatitvā pārisuddhiuposathaṃ karonti, tayo vā dve vā pātimokkhaṃ uddisanti, adhammena samaggaṃ nāma hoti. Sace catūsu janesu ekassa pārisuddhiṃ āharitvā tayo pātimokkhaṃ uddisanti, tīsu vā janesu ekassa pārisuddhiṃ āharitvā dve pārisuddhiuposathaṃ karonti, dhammena vaggaṃ nāma hoti. Sace pana cattāro ekattha vasantā sabbeva sannipatitvā pātimokkhaṃ uddisanti, tayo pārisuddhiuposathaṃ karonti, dve aññamaññaṃ pārisuddhiuposathaṃ karonti, dhammena samaggaṃ nāma hotīti.

In the cases beginning with 'unlawfully as a divided group,' if, when four monks are dwelling in one monastery, three perform the Uposatha of purity after bringing the purity-by-consent of one, or if, when three are dwelling, two recite the Pātimokkha after bringing the purity-by-consent of one, the Uposatha act is an unlawful one of a divided group. If, however, all four assemble and perform the Uposatha of purity, or if three or two recite the Pātimokkha, it is called an unlawful act of a united group. If, among four persons, three recite the Pātimokkha after bringing the purity of one, or if, among three persons, two perform the Uposatha of purity after bringing the purity of one, it is called a lawful act of a divided group. If, however, four dwelling in one place all assemble and recite the Pātimokkha; or if three perform the Uposatha of purity; or if two perform the Uposatha of purity with each other, it is called a lawful act of a united group.

Pātimokkhuddesakathā

The Discourse on the Recitation of the Pātimokkha

150. Nidānaṃ uddisitvā avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbanti “suṇātu me bhante saṅgho…pe… āvikatā hissa phāsu hotī”ti imaṃ nidānaṃ uddisitvā “uddiṭṭhaṃ kho āyasmanto nidānaṃ, tatthāyasmante pucchāmi – kaccittha parisuddhā, dutiyampi pucchāmi…pe… evametaṃ [V 0.0320] dhārayāmīti. Sutā kho panāyasmantehi cattāro pārājikā dhammā…pe… avivadamānehi sikkhitabba”nti evaṃ avasesaṃ sutena sāvetabbaṃ. Etena nayena sesāpi cattāro pātimokkhuddesā veditabbā.

150. Having recited the introduction, the remainder should be announced by the word 'heard': 'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha listen to me... for when it is declared, there is ease for him.' Having recited this introduction, 'Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited. In that regard, I ask the venerable ones: Are you pure in this matter? A second time I ask... Thus do I remember this.' 'Venerable sirs, you have heard the four Pārājika rules... one should train without disputing.' In this way, the remainder should be announced by the word 'heard'. By this method, the remaining four recitations of the Pātimokkha should also be understood.

Savarabhayanti aṭavimanussabhayaṃ. Rājantarāyotiādīsu sace bhikkhūsu “uposathaṃ karissāmā”ti nisinnesu rājā āgacchati, ayaṃ rājantarāyo. Corā āgacchanti, ayaṃ corantarāyo. Davadāho vā āgacchati, āvāse vā aggi uṭṭhahati, ayaṃ aggantarāyo. Megho vā uṭṭheti, ogho vā āgacchati, ayaṃ udakantarāyo. Bahū manussā āgacchanti, ayaṃ manussantarāyo. Bhikkhuṃ yakkho gaṇhāti, ayaṃ amanussantarāyo. Byagghādayo caṇḍamigā āgacchanti, ayaṃ vāḷantarāyo. Bhikkhuṃ sappādayo ḍaṃsanti, ayaṃ sarīsapantarāyo. Bhikkhu gilāno vā hoti, kālaṃ vā karoti, verino vā taṃ māretukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ [M 0.0339] jīvitantarāyo. Manussā ekaṃ vā bahū vā bhikkhū brahmacariyā cāvetukāmā gaṇhanti, ayaṃ brahmacariyantarāyo. Evarūpesu antarāyesu saṃkhittena pātimokkho uddisitabbo[P 5.1058], paṭhamo vā uddeso uddisitabbo, ādimhi dve tayo cattāro vā. Ettha ca dutiyādīsu uddesesu yasmiṃ apariyosite antarāyo hoti, sopi suteneva sāvetabbo.

The danger from the Savara tribe means the danger from forest-dwelling people. Among dangers such as from a king and so on: if, while the monks are seated intending to perform the Uposatha, a king arrives, this is a danger from a king. If thieves arrive, this is a danger from thieves. If a forest fire approaches or a fire breaks out in the monastery, this is a danger from fire. If a cloud arises or a flood comes, this is a danger from water. If many people arrive, this is a danger from humans. If a yakkha seizes a monk, this is a danger from non-humans. If fierce beasts like tigers come, this is a danger from wild animals. If snakes or other reptiles bite a monk, this is a danger from reptiles. If a monk falls ill or dies, or enemies seize him wishing to kill him, this is a danger to life. If people seize one or many monks wishing to make them fall away from the holy life, this is a danger to the holy life. In such dangers, the Pātimokkha should be recited in brief; or the first section should be recited; or at the beginning, two, three, or four sections. And among these, in the second and subsequent sections, if a danger arises before one is finished, that section also should be announced by the word 'heard'.

Anajjhiṭṭhāti anāṇattā ayācitā vā. Ajjhesanā cettha saṅghena sammatadhammajjhesakāyattā vā saṅghattherāyattā vā, tasmiṃ dhammajjhesake asati saṅghattheraṃ āpucchitvā vā tena yācito vā bhāsituṃ labhati. Saṅghattherenāpi sace vihāre bahū dhammakathikā honti, vārapaṭipāṭiyā vattabbā – “tvaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇa, dhammaṃ kathehi, dhammadānaṃ dehī”ti vā vuttena tīhipi vidhīhi dhammo bhāsitabbo. “Osārehī”ti vutto pana osāretumeva labhati, “kathehī”ti vutto kathetumeva, “sarabhaññaṃ bhaṇāhī”ti vutto sarabhaññameva. Saṅghattheropi ca uccatare āsane nisinno yācituṃ na labhati. Sace upajjhāyo ceva saddhivihāriko ca honti, upajjhāyo ca naṃ uccāsane nisinno “bhaṇāhī”ti vadati, sajjhāyaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā bhaṇitabbaṃ. Sace panettha daharā bhikkhū honti, tesaṃ “bhaṇāmī”ti bhaṇitabbaṃ.

'Unrequested' means not being commanded or not being asked. And here, the request is dependent on one designated by the Saṅgha to make the request for Dhamma, or it is dependent on the Saṅgha's elder. In the absence of that designated person, one may speak after asking the Saṅgha's elder or having been requested by him. If there are many Dhamma-speakers in the monastery, the Saṅgha's elder should address them in turn, saying: 'You, recite the Dhamma,' or 'You, explain the Dhamma,' or 'You, give the gift of the Dhamma.' The one who has been addressed should speak the Dhamma in any of these three ways. However, one who is told, 'Recite the Pāḷi,' may only recite the Pāḷi. One who is told, 'Explain the meaning,' may only explain the meaning. One who is told, 'Recite with intonation,' may only recite with intonation. And the Saṅgha's elder, sitting on a higher seat, does not have the right to make the request. If there is a preceptor and his co-resident, and the preceptor, sitting on a higher seat, says to him, 'Speak,' it should be spoken after having undertaken a recitation. If there are junior monks here, one should speak with the thought, 'I will speak for them.'

Sace vihāre saṅghatthero attanoyeva nissitake bhaṇāpeti, aññe madhurabhāṇakepi nājjhesati, so aññehi vattabbo – “bhante asukaṃ nāma bhaṇāpemā”ti. Sace “bhaṇāpethā”ti vā vadati, tuṇhī vā hoti, bhaṇāpetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana paṭibāhati, na bhaṇāpetabbaṃ. Yadi anāgateyeva saṅghatthere dhammasavanaṃ āraddhaṃ, puna āgate ṭhapetvā āpucchanakiccaṃ [V 0.0321] natthi. Osāretvā pana kathentena āpucchitvā vā aṭṭhapetvāyeva vā kathetabbaṃ, kathentassa puna āgatepi eseva nayo.

If in the monastery the Saṅgha's elder has only his own dependents recite and does not invite other eloquent speakers, he should be told by others: 'Venerable sir, let us have so-and-so recite.' If he says, 'Let them recite,' or if he is silent, it is proper to have them recite. But if he forbids it, they should not be made to recite. If the listening to the Dhamma had already begun before the Saṅgha's elder arrived, there is no duty to stop and ask permission when he arrives. However, one who is explaining the meaning after having recited the Pāḷi text should explain either after asking permission or without stopping. If the Saṅgha's elder arrives again while one is explaining, this same principle applies.

Upanisinnakathāyapi saṅghattherova sāmī, tasmā tena sayaṃ vā kathetabbaṃ, añño vā bhikkhu “kathehī”ti vattabbo, no ca kho uccatare āsane nisinnena. Manussānaṃ pana “bhaṇāhī”ti vattuṃ vaṭṭati. Manussā attano jānanakabhikkhuṃ āpucchanti, tena theraṃ āpucchitvā kathetabbaṃ. Sace saṅghatthero “bhante ime pañhaṃ pucchantī”ti puṭṭho “kathehī”ti [M 0.0340] vā bhaṇati, tuṇhī vā hoti, kathetuṃ vaṭṭati. Antaraghare anumodanādīsupi eseva nayo. Sace saṅghatthero vihāre vā antaraghare vā “maṃ anāpucchitvāpi [P 5.1059] katheyyāsī”ti anujānāti, laddhakappiyaṃ hoti, sabbattha vattuṃ vaṭṭati.

Even in a talk given to those sitting near, the Saṅgha's elder is the authority. Therefore, he should either speak himself or another monk should be told by him, 'Speak'; but this should not be said by one sitting on a higher seat. However, it is proper to say, 'Speak to the laypeople.' If laypeople ask a monk whom they know, he should speak after asking the elder. If the Saṅgha's elder, having been informed, 'Venerable sir, these people are asking a question,' says, 'Speak,' or is silent, it is proper to speak. This same principle applies in a house for the giving of blessings after a meal and so on. If the Saṅgha's elder, whether in the monastery or in a house, gives permission, saying, 'You may speak even without asking me,' it becomes permissible, and it is proper to speak in all circumstances.

Sajjhāyaṃ karontenāpi thero āpucchitabboyeva. Ekaṃ āpucchitvā sajjhāyantassa aparo āgacchati, puna āpucchanakiccaṃ natthi. Sace vissamissāmīti ṭhapitassa āgacchati, puna ārabhantenāpi āpucchitabbaṃ. Saṅghatthere anāgateyeva āraddhaṃ sajjhāyantassāpi eseva nayo. Ekena saṅghattherena “maṃ anāpucchāpi yathāsukhaṃ sajjhāyāhī”ti anuññāte yathāsukhaṃ sajjhāyituṃ vaṭṭati. Aññasmiṃ pana āgate taṃ āpucchitvāva sajjhāyitabbaṃ.
