Bhavanetti samūhatāti bhavato bhavagamanā sandhāvanā taṇhārajju suṭṭhu hatā chinnā appavattikatā.

287. 'Through not understanding' means because of not knowing. 'We have run on' means we have run on continuously by way of going from one existence to another. 'We have transmigrated' means we have transmigrated by way of going again and again. 'Of both me and of you' means by me and by you. Or alternatively, in this passage beginning with `sandhāvitaṃ`, the meaning should be understood thus: the running on and the transmigrating was of me and of you. `Saṃsitaṃ` means transmigrated. 'The guide to existence is uprooted' means the rope of craving—which is the running on, the cause of going from one existence to another—has been well destroyed, cut off, and made non-recurrent.

289. Nīlāti [V 0.0357] idaṃ sabbasaṅgāhakaṃ. Nīlavaṇṇātiādi tasseva vibhāgadassanatthaṃ. Tattha na tesaṃ pakativaṇṇā nīlā, nīlavilepanānaṃ [P 5.1097] vicittatāvasenetaṃ vuttaṃ. Paṭivaṭṭesīti pahāresi. Sāhāraṃ dajjeyyāthāti sajanapadaṃ dadeyyātha. Aṅguliṃ phoṭesunti aṅguliṃ cālesuṃ. Ambakāyāti itthikāya. Olokethāti passatha. Apalokethāti punappunaṃ passatha. Upasaṃharathāti upanetha. Imaṃ licchaviparisaṃ tumhākaṃ cittena tāvatiṃsaparisaṃ haratha, tāvatiṃsassa samakaṃ katvā passathāti attho.

289. `Nīla` (blue): This word is all-inclusive. 'Of blue color,' etc., is for the purpose of showing its distinctions. Therein, their natural color is not blue; this was said by way of the variety of blue unguents. `Paṭivaṭṭesi` means: he struck. `Sāhāraṃ dajjeyyātha` means: you should give it together with its countryside. `Aṅguliṃ phoṭesuṃ` means: they moved their fingers. `Ambakāya` means: by a woman. `Oloketha` means: see. `Apaloketha` means: see again and again. `Upasaṃharatha` means: bring near. The meaning is: 'In your minds, compare this assembly of Licchavis to the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods; see them as being equal to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.'

Sīhasenāpativatthuādikathā

The Discourse Beginning with the Story of General Sīha

290. Dhammassa ca anudhammaṃ byākarontīti bhagavatā vuttakāraṇassa anukāraṇaṃ kathenti. Sahadhammiko vādānuvādoti aparehi vuttakāraṇena sakāraṇo hutvā tumhākaṃ vādo viññugarahitabbaṃ kāraṇaṃ koci appamattakopi kiṃ na āgacchati. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti “kiṃ sabbakārenāpi tumhākaṃ vāde gārayhakāraṇaṃ natthī”ti. Anabbhakkhātukāmāti abhibhavitvā na ācikkhitukāmā.

290. `Dhammassa ca anudhammaṃ byākaronti` (they explain the teaching that is in accordance with the Teaching) means: they state a reason that is in accordance with the reason spoken by the Blessed One. `Sahadhammiko vādānuvādo` (a statement and counter-statement in accordance with the Teaching) means: Does your initial statement, being supported by a reason in line with what was stated by others, not become liable to any reason, even a very slight one, that is censurable by the wise? This is what is said: 'Is there no censurable point in your statement in any way whatsoever?' `Anabbhakkhātukāmā` (not wishing to slander) means: not wishing to speak having overwhelmed, or not wishing to falsely accuse.

293. Anuviccakāranti anuviditvā cintetvā tulayitvā kātabbaṃ karohīti vuttaṃ hoti. Ñātamanussānanti loke pākaṭānaṃ. Sādhu hotīti [M 0.0379] sundaraṃ hoti. Paṭākaṃ parihareyyunti paṭākaṃ ukkhipitvā nagare ghosantā āhiṇḍeyyuṃ. Kasmā? “Evaṃ no amhākaṃ mahantabhāvo bhavissatī”ti. Opānabhūtanti paṭiyattaudapāno viya ṭhitaṃ. Kulanti nivesanaṃ. Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsīti mā imesaṃ deyyadhammaṃ upacchindittha, sampattānañhi dātabbamevāti ovadati. Okāroti avakāro lāmakabhāvo. Sāmukkaṃsikāti attanāyeva uddharitvā gahitā; asādhāraṇaṃ aññesanti attho. Uddissa katanti uddisitvā kataṃ.

293. `Anuviccakāram` (acting after careful consideration) means: it is said, 'Having known accordingly, having considered, and having weighed, do what should be done.' `Ñātamanussānam` (of well-known people) means: of those who are renowned in the world. `Sādhu hoti` (it is good) means: it is excellent. `Paṭākaṃ parihareyyum` (they would carry a banner around) means: having raised a banner, they would wander in the city proclaiming. Why? Because, 'Thus our greatness will come to be.' `Opānabhūtam` (having become like a well) means: standing like a prepared water-well. `Kulam` (family) means: a house. `Dātabbaṃ maññeyyāsi` (you should consider it should be given) means: He advises, 'Do not cut off the alms-food for these ones; indeed, it should be given to those who have arrived.' `Okāro` means: an inferior state, a state of baseness. `Sāmukkaṃsikā` means: taken up, having been extracted by oneself alone; the meaning is that it is not shared with others. `Uddissa katam` (made having specified) means: made having aimed at or specified someone.

294. Paṭiccakammanti attānaṃ paṭicca katanti attho. Atha vā paṭiccakammanti nimittakammassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, taṃ paṭiccakammaṃ ettha atthīti maṃsampi paṭiccakammanti vuttaṃ. Yo hi evarūpaṃ maṃsaṃ paribhuñjati, sopi tassa kammassa dāyādo hoti, vadhakassa viya tassāpi pāṇaghātakammaṃ hotīti adhippāyo[P 5.1098]. Jiridantiti jiranti abbhācikkhantā na jiranti, abbhakkhānassa antaṃ na gacchantīti attho. Tikoṭiparisuddhakathā saṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanāyaṃ vuttā.

294. `Paṭiccakamma` means: an act done in relation to oneself. Alternatively, `paṭiccakamma` is a designation for `nimittakamma` (an act done on a sign or hint). Because that `paṭiccakamma` is present in it, even the meat is called `paṭiccakamma`. For whoever consumes such meat becomes an heir to that kamma; just like the killer, for that person too there is the kamma of destroying life—this is the intention of the Nigaṇṭhas. `Jiridanti` means: they wear out. Those who slander do not wear out; the meaning is that they do not reach the end of their slandering. The discourse on the threefold purity was spoken by me in the explanation of the training rule on schism in the Saṅgha.

Kappiyabhūmianujānanakathā

The Discourse on the Allowance of Suitable Ground

295. Sakaṭaparivaṭṭanti [V 0.0358] sakaṭehi parikkhepaṃ viya katvā acchanti. Paccantimanti abhilāpamattametaṃ “yaṃ saṅgho ākaṅkhatī”ti vuttattā pana dhuravihāropi sammannituṃ vaṭṭati, kammavācaṃ avatvā apalokanenāpi vaṭṭatiyeva. Kākoravasaddanti tattha tattha paviṭṭhānaṃ āmisakhādanatthāya anuppageyeva sannipatitānaṃ kākānaṃ oravasaddaṃ. Yasojo nāma kapilasuttapariyosāne pabbajitānaṃ pañcannaṃ satānaṃ aggapuriso.

295. `Sakaṭaparivaṭṭa` means: they stay, having made something like an enclosure with carts. `Paccantima` is merely a term of speech; but since it was said, 'whatever the Saṅgha desires,' it is allowable to designate even a main monastery, and it is indeed allowable to do so even by simple announcement, without reciting the formal act. `Kākoravasadda` means: the loud sound of crows that have gathered early for the purpose of eating flesh, having entered here and there. The one named Yasoja was the chief person among the five hundred men who had gone forth at the conclusion of the Kapila Sutta.

Ussāvanantikantiādīsu ussāvanantikā tāva evaṃ kattabbā. Yo thambhānaṃ vā upari bhittipāde vā nikhanitvā vihāro kariyati, tassa heṭṭhā thambhapaṭicchakā pāsāṇā bhūmigatikā eva. Paṭhamathambhaṃ pana paṭhamabhittipādaṃ vā patiṭṭhāpentehi bahūhi samparivāretvā “kappiyakuṭiṃ karoma, kappiyakuṭiṃ karomā”ti vācaṃ nicchārentehi manussesu ukkhipitvā patiṭṭhāpentesu āmasitvā vā sayaṃ ukkhipitvā vā thambhe vā bhittipādo vā patiṭṭhāpetabbo. Kurundimahāpaccarīsu pana “kappiyakuṭi kappiyakuṭī”ti vatvā patiṭṭhāpetabbanti vuttaṃ. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “saṅghassa kappiyakuṭiṃ adhiṭṭhāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Taṃ pana avatvāpi aṭṭhakathāsu vuttanayena vutte [M 0.0380] doso natthi. Idaṃ panettha sādhāraṇalakkhaṇaṃ, thambhapatiṭṭhānañca vacanapariyosānañca samakālaṃ vaṭṭati. Sace hi aniṭṭhite vacane thambho patiṭṭhāti, appatiṭṭhite vā tasmiṃ vacanaṃ niṭṭhāti, akatā hoti kappiyakuṭi. Teneva mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ – “bahūhi samparivāretvā vattabbaṃ, avassañhi ettha ekassapi vacananiṭṭhānañca thambhapatiṭṭhānañca ekato bhavissatī”ti.

Regarding `ussāvanantikā` and so on, first, an `ussāvanantikā` hut should be made thus. For a monastery that is made either on top of posts or by digging in wall-foundations, the stones underneath it that support the posts are just like the ground itself. But when establishing the first post or the first wall-foundation, it should be done by many monks surrounding it and uttering the words, 'We are making a suitable hut, we are making a suitable hut.' While laypeople are lifting and establishing it, the post or wall-foundation should be established by the monks either touching it or lifting it themselves. In the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said that it should be established after saying, 'A suitable hut, a suitable hut.' In the Andhaka Commentary it is said, 'I determine this as a suitable hut for the Saṅgha.' But even without saying that, there is no fault if it is done according to the method stated in the ancient commentaries. Herein, this is the general characteristic: it is proper for the establishing of the post and the conclusion of the utterance to be simultaneous. For if the post is established while the utterance is unfinished, or if the utterance is finished while the post is not yet established, the suitable hut is not properly made. For that very reason it was said in the Mahāpaccarī: 'It should be said by many having surrounded it, for in this way the conclusion of the utterance of at least one person and the establishing of the post will certainly occur together.'

Iṭṭhakasilāmattikākuṭṭikāsu pana kuṭīsu heṭṭhā cayaṃ bandhitvā vā abandhitvā vā karontu, yato paṭṭhāya bhittiṃ uṭṭhāpetukāmā [P 5.1099] honti, taṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ vā silaṃ vā mattikāpiṇḍaṃ vā gahetvā vuttanayeneva kappiyakuṭi kātabbā. Iṭṭhakādayo hi bhittiyā paṭhamiṭṭhakādīnaṃ heṭṭhā na vaṭṭanti, thambhā pana upari uggacchanti, tasmā vaṭṭanti. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “thambhehi kariyamāne catūsu koṇesu cattāro thambhā iṭṭhakādikuṭṭe catūsu koṇesu dve tisso iṭṭhakā adhiṭṭhātabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā pana akatāyapi doso natthi, aṭṭhakathāsu hi vuttameva pamāṇaṃ.

Now, in huts with walls of brick, stone, or clay, let them build, either having constructed a foundation mound underneath or not. From whatever point they wish to start raising the wall, taking that very first brick, stone, or lump of clay, the permissible hut should be made in the manner already described. For bricks and so on are not allowable underneath the first bricks, etc., of the wall. Posts, however, rise upwards; therefore, they are allowable. In the Andhaka Commentary it is said: 'When it is being made with posts, four posts should be determined at the four corners; in a hut with walls of brick and so on, two or three bricks should be determined at the four corners.' However, even if it is not done so, there is no fault, for what is stated in the commentaries is the authority.

Gonisādikā duvidhā – ārāmagonisādikā, vihāragonisādikāti. Tāsu yattha neva ārāmo [V 0.0359] na senāsanāni parikkhittāni honti, ayaṃ “ārāmagonisādikā” nāma. Yattha senāsanāni sabbāni vā ekaccāni vā parikkhittāni, ārāmo aparikkhitto, ayaṃ “vihāragonisādikā” nāma. Iti ubhayatrāpi ārāmassa aparikkhittabhāvoyeva pamāṇaṃ. Ārāmo pana upaḍḍhaparikkhittopi bahutaraṃ parikkhittopi parikkhittoyeva nāmāti kurundimahaāpaccariyādīsu vuttaṃ. Ettha kappiyakuṭiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati.

The `gonisādikā` is twofold: the `ārāmagonisādikā` and the `vihāragonisādikā`. Among these, where neither the monastery park nor the lodgings are enclosed, this is called the `ārāmagonisādikā`. Where all or some of the lodgings are enclosed, but the monastery park is unenclosed, this is called the `vihāragonisādikā`. Thus, in both cases, the very state of the monastery park being unenclosed is the standard. But a monastery park, even if half-enclosed or mostly enclosed, is still called 'enclosed'—so it is said in the Kurundī, Mahāpaccarī, and other texts. Herein, it is allowable to obtain a permissible hut.

Gahapatīti manussā āvāsaṃ katvā “kappiyakuṭiṃ dema, paribhuñjathā”ti vadanti, esā gahapati nāma. “Kappiyakuṭiṃ kātuṃ demā”ti vuttepi vaṭṭatiyeva. Andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “yasmā bhikkhuṃ ṭhapetvā sesasahadhammikānaṃ sabbesañca devamanussānaṃ hatthato paṭiggaho ca sannidhi ca antovutthañca tesaṃ santakaṃ bhikkhussa vaṭṭati, tasmā tesaṃ gehāni vā tehi dinnā kappiyakuṭi vā gahapatīti vuccatī”ti vuttaṃ. Punapi vuttaṃ – “bhikkhusaṅghassa vihāraṃ ṭhapetvā bhikkhunupassayo vā ārāmikānaṃ vā titthiyānaṃ vā devatānaṃ vā nāgānaṃ vā api brahmānaṃ vimānaṃ kappiyakuṭi hotī”ti, taṃ suvuttaṃ; saṅghasantakameva [M 0.0381] hi bhikkhusantakaṃ vā gehaṃ gahapatikuṭikā na hoti. Sammutikā nāma kammavācaṃ sāvetvā katāti.

Regarding the `gahapati` hut: when people, having made a dwelling, say, 'We give a permissible hut; please use it,' this is called a `gahapati`. Even if it is said, 'We give [this] to make a permissible hut,' it is indeed permissible. In the Andhaka Commentary, however, it is said: 'Because, for a monk, it is permissible to receive from the hand, to store, and to have food kept overnight that is the property of the remaining fellow practitioners and all devas and humans—setting aside [the property of another] monk—therefore, their houses or a permissible hut given by them is called a `gahapati`.' Furthermore, it is said: 'Excepting a monastery of the Saṅgha of monks, a nun's residence, a house of monastery attendants, a dwelling of heretics, or a mansion of devas, of nāgas, or even of Brahmās, is a permissible hut.' That is well said; for indeed, a dwelling that is the property of the Saṅgha or the personal property of a monk is not a `gahapatikuṭikā`. A `sammutikā` is a hut made after having announced the formal act.

Yaṃ imāsu catūsu kappiyabhūmīsu vutthaṃ āmisaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ antovutthasaṅkhyaṃ na gacchati. Bhikkhūnañca bhikkhunīnañca antovutthaantopakkamocanatthañhi kappiyakuṭiyo anuññātā. Yaṃ pana akappiyabhūmiyaṃ [P 5.1100] sahaseyyappahonake gehe vutthaṃ saṅghikaṃ vā puggalikaṃ vā bhikkhussa bhikkhuniyā vā santakaṃ ekarattampi ṭhapitaṃ, taṃ antovutthaṃ; tattha pakkañca antopakkaṃ nāma hoti, etaṃ na kappati. Sattāhakālikaṃ pana yāvajīvikañca vaṭṭati.

Whatever foodstuffs are kept in these four permissible grounds, none of it falls under the category of 'kept overnight'. Indeed, permissible huts were allowed for monks and nuns for the purpose of being freed from the offenses of 'kept overnight' and 'cooked inside'. However, whatever property belonging to the Saṅgha or to an individual monk or nun is placed even for a single night in an impermissible ground, in a dwelling suitable for co-residence, that is 'kept overnight'; and what is cooked there is called 'cooked inside'. This is not permissible. Seven-day and lifetime requisites, however, are permissible.

Tatrāyaṃ vinicchayo – sāmaṇero bhikkhussa taṇḍulādikaṃ āmisaṃ āharitvā kappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhipitvā punadivase pacitvā deti, antovutthaṃ na hoti. Tattha akappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhittasappiādīsu yaṃkiñci pakkhipitvā deti, mukhasannidhi nāma hoti. Mahāpaccariyaṃ pana “antovutthaṃ hotī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha nāmamattameva nānākaraṇaṃ. Bhikkhu akappiyakuṭiyaṃ ṭhapitasappiñca yāvajīvikapaṇṇañca ekato pacitvā paribhuñjati, sattāhaṃ nirāmisaṃ vaṭṭati. Sace āmisasaṃsaṭṭhaṃ katvā paribhuñjati, antovutthañceva sāmaṃpākañca hoti. Etenupāyena sabbasaṃsaggā veditabbā.

Herein, this is the ruling: a novice brings foodstuffs such as rice for a monk, places it in a permissible hut, and on the next day, cooks and gives it; it is not 'kept overnight'. In that situation, if he adds anything from among ghee and so forth that was placed in an impermissible hut and gives it, it is called `mukhasannidhi` (stored in proximity to the mouth). In the Mahāpaccarī, however, it is said, 'It is `antovuttha`.' In this case, the difference is only in name. If a monk cooks together ghee placed in an impermissible hut and a lifetime-requisite leaf and consumes it, it is permissible for seven days, provided it is without other foodstuffs. If he consumes it having mixed it with other foodstuffs, it becomes both 'kept overnight' and 'self-cooked'. By this method, all such mixtures should be understood.

Imā pana kappiyakuṭiyo kadā jahitavatthukā honti? Ussāvanantikā tāva yā thambhānaṃ [V 0.0360] upari bhittipāde vā nikhaṇitvā katā, sā sabbesu thambhesu ca bhittipādesu ca apanītesu jahitavatthukā hoti. Sace pana thambhe vā bhittipāde vā parivattenti, yo yo ṭhito tattha tattha patiṭṭhāti, sabbesupi parivattitesu ajahitavatthukāva hoti. Iṭṭhakādīhi katā cayassa upari bhittiatthāya ṭhapitaṃ iṭṭhakaṃ vā silaṃ vā mattikāpiṇḍaṃ vā ādiṃkatvā vināsitakāle jahitavatthukā hoti. Yehi pana iṭṭhakādīhi adhiṭṭhitā, tesu apanītesupi tadaññāsu patiṭṭhitāsu ajahitavatthukāva hoti.

Now, when do these permissible huts become 'abandoned as to their site'? Firstly, the `ussāvanantikā` which is made on top of posts or by digging in wall-bases becomes 'abandoned as to its site' when all the posts and wall-bases are removed. But if they replace the posts or the wall-bases, on whichever one remains standing, there it is established; even when all are replaced, it is still 'not abandoned as to its site'. A hut made with bricks and so forth becomes 'abandoned as to its site' at the time of destruction, starting from the first brick, stone, or lump of clay that was placed on top of the foundation mound for the purpose of a wall. But if, after the bricks and so forth on which it was founded have been removed, it is established on other ones, it is still 'not abandoned as to its site'.

Gonisādikā pākārādīhi parikkhepe kate jahitavatthukā hoti. Puna tasmiṃ ārāme kappiyakuṭi laddhuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace pana punapi pākārādayo tattha tattha khaṇḍā honti, tato tato gāvo pavisanti, puna kappiyakuṭi hoti. Itarā pana dve gopānasīmattaṃ ṭhapetvā [M 0.0382] sabbasmiṃ chadane vinaṭṭhe jahitavatthukā honti. Sace gopānasīnaṃ upari ekampi pakkhapāsakamaṇḍalaṃ atthi, rakkhati.

A `gonisādikā` becomes 'abandoned as to its site' when an enclosure is made with a wall or the like. Then, in that monastery park, it is allowable to obtain a permissible hut. But if the wall or the like again becomes broken here and there, and cattle enter from those places, it again becomes a permissible hut. The other two, however, become 'abandoned as to their site' when the entire roof is destroyed, excepting the extent of the rafters. If there is even one gable-end section above the rafters, it protects its status.

Yatra panimā catassopi kappiyabhūmiyo natthi, tattha kiṃ kātabbaṃ? Anupasampannassa [P 5.1101] datvā tassa santakaṃ katvā paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Tatridaṃ vatthu – karavikatissatthero kira vinayadharapāmokkho mahāsīvattherassa santikaṃ agamāsi. So dīpālokena sappikumbhaṃ passitvā “bhante kimeta”nti pucchi. Thero “āvuso gāmato sappikumbho ābhato, lūkhadivase sappinā bhuñjanatthāyā”ti āha. Tato naṃ tissatthero “na vaṭṭati bhante”ti āha. Thero punadivase pamukhe nikkhipāpesi. Tissatthero puna ekadivase āgato taṃ disvā tatheva pucchitvā “bhante sahaseyyappahonakaṭṭhāne ṭhapetuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti āha. Thero punadivase bahi nīharāpetvā nikkhipāpesi, taṃ corā hariṃsu. So puna ekadivasaṃ āgataṃ tissattheraṃ āha – “āvuso tayā ‘na vaṭṭatī’ti vutto so kumbho bahi nikkhitto corehi avahato”ti. Tato naṃ tissatthero āha – “nanu bhante anupasampannassa dātabbo assa, anupasampannassa hi datvā tassa santakaṃ katvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

Further, where these four permissible grounds do not exist, what is to be done? It should be given to one who is not fully ordained, made their property, and then consumed. Herein, this is the story: The Elder Karavika-Tissa, it is said, a foremost expert in the Vinaya, went to the Elder Mahāsīva. Seeing a pot of ghee by lamplight, he asked, 'Venerable sir, what is this?' The Elder replied, 'Friend, a pot of ghee was brought from the village for the purpose of eating with ghee on a day of plain food.' Then the Elder Tissa said to him, 'Venerable sir, it is not permissible.' On the next day, the Elder had it placed in the porch. The Elder Tissa, having come again one day, saw it, asked in the same way, and said, 'Venerable sir, it is not permissible to place it in a location suitable for co-residence.' On the next day, the Elder had it taken outside and placed there. Thieves took it. He said to the Elder Tissa who had come again one day, 'Friend, that pot which you said was "not permissible," was placed outside and has been carried off by thieves.' Then the Elder Tissa said to him, 'Venerable sir, should it not have been given to one who is not fully ordained? For, having given it to one who is not fully ordained and made it their property, it is permissible to consume it.'

296-9. Meṇḍakavatthu uttānameva. Api cettha anujānāmi bhikkhave pañca goraseti ime pañca gorase visuṃ paribhogena paribhuñjitumpi anujānāmīti attho. Pātheyyaṃ pariyesitunti ettha sace keci sayameva ñatvā denti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce denti, ñātipavāritaṭṭhānato vā bhikkhācāravattena vā pariyesitabbaṃ. Tathā alabhantena aññātikaapavāritaṭṭhānato [V 0.0361] yācitvāpi gahetabbaṃ. Ekadivasena gamanīye magge ekabhattatthāya pariyesitabbaṃ. Dīghe addhāne yattakena kantāraṃ nittharati, tattakaṃ pariyesitabbaṃ.

296-9. The story of Meṇḍaka is self-evident. However, in this connection, regarding the text, 'Monks, I allow the five products of a cow,' the meaning is: I allow these five products of a cow to be consumed even as a separate meal. Regarding the text, 'One should seek provisions for a journey': here, if some people, knowing for themselves, give, this is wholesome; if they do not give, provisions should be sought from relatives or those who have given an invitation, or by the practice of the alms-round. Not obtaining them in that way, a monk may take them even by asking from those who are not relatives and have not given an invitation. On a road that can be travelled in one day, provisions should be sought for the sake of one meal. On a long journey, as many provisions as are needed to cross the wilderness should be sought.

Keṇiyajaṭilavatthukathā

The Discourse on the Story of Keṇiya the Matted-Hair Ascetic

300. Kājehi gāhāpetvāti pañcahi kājasatehi susaṅkhatassa badarapānassa kuṭasahassaṃ gāhāpetvā. Etasmiṃ nidāne etasmiṃ pakaraṇe dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvāti “sādhu bhikkhave pānaṃ apivantā samaṇassa gotamassa [M 0.0383] sāvakā paccayabāhullikāti vādaṃ na uppādayittha, mayi ca gāravaṃ akattha, mama ca tumhesu gāravaṃ janayittha, iti vo ahaṃ iminā kāraṇena suṭṭhu pasanno”tiādinā nayena dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā anujānāmi bhikkhave aṭṭha pānānītiādimāha.

300. ‘Having it carried by means of carrying-poles’ means having a thousand jars of well-prepared jujube drink carried by means of five hundred carrying-poles. ‘On this occasion, in this context, having given a talk on the Dhamma’ means having given a talk on the Dhamma in this way: “Good, monks! You, by not drinking the beverage, did not give rise to the talk that ‘the disciples of the ascetic Gotama strive for an abundance of requisites.’ And you have shown respect for me, and you have generated respect in me for you. For this reason, I am very pleased with you,” and so on, he then said, “Monks, I allow eight kinds of drinks,” etc.

Tattha ambapānanti āmehi vā pakkehi vā ambehi katapānaṃ. Tattha [P 5.1102] āmehi karontena ambataruṇāni bhinditvā udake pakkhipitvā ātape ādiccapākena pacitvā parissāvetvā tadahupaṭiggahitehi madhusakkarakappūrādīhi yojetvā kātabbaṃ. Evaṃ kataṃ purebhattameva kappati. Anupasampannehi kataṃ labhitvā pana purebhattaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ purebhattaṃ sāmisaparibhogenāpi vaṭṭati, pacchābhattaṃ nirāmisaparibhogena yāva aruṇuggamanā vaṭṭatiyeva. Esa nayo sabbapānesu.

Therein, 'mango drink' means a drink made with mangoes, whether unripe or ripe. Therein, when making it with unripe mangoes, one should break up young mangoes, put them in water, cook them in the sun by sun-heat, strain them, and mix them with honey, sugar, camphor, and so on, that have been received on that day. Made in this way, it is allowable only in the forenoon. However, having received a drink made by those not fully ordained, if it is accepted in the forenoon, it is allowable in the forenoon even with food; in the afternoon, it is allowable without food until the rising of the dawn. This is the principle for all drinks.

Tesu pana jambupānanti jambuphalehi katapānaṃ. Cocapānanti aṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Mocapānanti anaṭṭhikehi kadaliphalehi katapānaṃ. Madhukapānanti madhukānaṃ jātirasena katapānaṃ; taṃ pana udakasambhinnaṃ vaṭṭati, suddhaṃ na vaṭṭati. Muddikapānanti muddikā udake madditvā ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Sālūkapānanti rattuppalanīluppalādīnaṃ sālūke madditvā katapānaṃ. Phārusakapānanti phārusakaphalehi ambapānaṃ viya katapānaṃ. Imāni aṭṭha pānāni sītānipi ādiccapākānipi vaṭṭanti, aggipākāni na vaṭṭanti. Dhaññaphalarasanti sattannaṃ dhaññānaṃ phalarasaṃ. Ḍākarasanti pakkaḍākarasaṃ. Yāvakālikapattānañhi purebhattaṃyeva raso kappati. Yāvajīvikānaṃ paṭiggahetvā ṭhapitasappiādīhi saddhiṃ pakkānaṃ sattāhaṃ kappati. Sace pana suddhaudakena pacati, yāvajīvampi vaṭṭati. Khīrādīhi pana saddhiṃ pacituṃ na vaṭṭati. Aññehi pakkampi ḍākarasasaṅkhyameva gacchati. Kurundiyaṃ pana “yāvakālikapattānampi sītodakena madditvā kataraso vā ādiccapāko vā vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Ṭhapetvā madhukapuppharasanti ettha madhukapuppharaso aggipāko vā hotu ādiccapāko vā, pacchābhattaṃ [V 0.0362] na vaṭṭati. Purebhattampi yaṃ pānaṃ gahetvā majjaṃ karonti, so ādito paṭṭhāya na vaṭṭati. Madhukapupphaṃ pana allaṃ vā sukkhaṃ vā bhajjitaṃ vā tena [P 5.1103] kataphāṇitaṃ vā yato paṭṭhāya majjaṃ na karonti, taṃ sabbaṃ purebhattaṃ vaṭṭati. Ucchuraso nikasaṭo pacchābhattaṃ vaṭṭati[M 0.0384]. Iti pānāni anujānantena imepi cattāro rasā anuññātāti. Aggihuttamukhā yaññātiādīsu aggihutaṃ seṭṭhaṃ, aggihutaṃ mukhanti vuttaṃ hoti.

Among these, 'jambu drink' is a drink made with jambu fruits. 'Coca drink' is a drink made with seeded wild banana fruits. 'Moca drink' is a drink made with seedless cultivated banana fruits. 'Madhuka drink' is a drink made with the natural juice of madhuka fruits; it is allowable when mixed with water, but not when pure. 'Muddikā drink' is a drink made by crushing grapes in water, like mango drink. 'Sālūka drink' is a drink made by crushing the edible rootstalks of red and blue lotuses, and so on. 'Phārusaka drink' is a drink made with phārusaka fruits, like mango drink. These eight drinks are allowable if made with cold water or cooked by the sun; they are not allowable if cooked by fire. 'Juice of grain-fruit' means the juice from the fruit of the seven kinds of grain. 'Juice of greens' means the juice of cooked greens. Indeed, the juice of yāvakālika leaves is allowable only in the forenoon. The juice of leaves cooked together with yāvajīvika items such as ghee, which have been received and stored, is allowable for seven days. But if one cooks it with plain water, it is allowable for a lifetime. However, it is not allowable to cook it with milk and so on. The juice of leaves cooked with other items is also counted as 'juice of greens'. But in the Kurundī commentary it is said: “For yāvakālika leaves, the juice made by crushing them with cold water or that which is sun-cooked is also allowable.” Regarding “Excluding the juice of madhuka flowers”: herein, the juice of madhuka flowers, whether cooked by fire or by the sun, is not allowable in the afternoon. Even in the forenoon, any drink that is used to make intoxicants is not allowable from the very beginning. However, madhuka flowers—whether fresh, dried, or roasted—or molasses made from them, from the point that they are no longer used to make intoxicants, all of that is allowable in the forenoon. Sugarcane juice that is without dregs is allowable in the afternoon. Thus, by allowing drinks, these four kinds of juices were also allowed. In texts such as 'Sacrifices are headed by the fire-oblation,' it means that the fire-oblation is the best, the fire-oblation is the foremost.

Rojamallādivatthukathā

The Discourse on the Story of Roja the Malla and Others

301-2. Rojavatthu uttānatthameva. Tattha saṅkaraṃ akaṃsūti katikaṃ akaṃsu. Uḷāraṃ kho te idanti sundaraṃ kho te idaṃ. Nāhaṃ bhante ānanda bahukatoti nāhaṃ buddhādigatapasādabahumānena idhāgatoti dasseti. Sabbañca ḍākanti sappiādīhi pakkaṃ vā apakkaṃ vā yaṃkiñci ḍākaṃ. Piṭṭhakhādanīyanti piṭṭhamayaṃ khādanīyaṃ; rojo kira idaṃ ubhayampi satasahassaṃ vayaṃ katvā paṭiyādāpesi.

301-2. The story of Roja is of clear meaning. Therein, `saṅkaraṃ akaṃsu` means: they made an agreement. `Uḷāraṃ kho te idaṃ` means: this welcoming of the Blessed One by you is indeed excellent. The passage `Nāhaṃ bhante ānanda bahukato` shows this meaning: 'I have not come here out of faith and great esteem for the Buddha and others.' `Sabbañca ḍākaṃ` means: any kind of vegetable whatsoever, whether cooked with ghee and so on, or uncooked. `Piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ` means: an edible made of flour. Indeed, Roja, having made an expenditure of a hundred thousand, had both of these prepared.

303. Mañjukāti madhuravacanā. Paṭibhāneyyakāti sake sippe paṭibhānasampannā. Dakkhāti chekā, analasā vā. Pariyodātasippāti niddosasippā. Nāḷiyāvāpakenāti nāḷiyā ca āvāpakena ca. Āvāpako nāma yattha laddhaṃ laddhaṃ āvapanti, pakkhipantīti vuttaṃ hoti. Na ca bhikkhave nahāpitapubbena khurabhaṇḍanti ettha gahetvā pariharitumeva na vaṭṭati, aññassa santakena kese chedetuṃ vaṭṭati. Sace vetanaṃ gahetvā chindati, na vaṭṭati. Yo anahāpitapubbo tassa pariharitumpi vaṭṭati, taṃ vā aññaṃ vā gahetvā kese chedetumpi vaṭṭati.

303. `Mañjukā` means: they have sweet speech. `Paṭibhāneyyakā` means: they are endowed with ready wit in their own craft. `Dakkhā` means: they are skilled, or, they are not lazy. `Pariyodātasippā` means: they have a flawless craft. `Nāḷiyāvāpakenā` means: with a `nāḷi` and with an `āvāpaka`. An `āvāpaka` is the name for that into which they put whatever is received; it means they insert it. In the passage, `Na ca, bhikkhave, ... nahāpitapubbena khurabhaṇḍaṃ`, it is not allowable for him to take it and carry it around for his own use; it is allowable to cut hair with razor equipment that is the property of another. If one cuts hair having taken a wage, it is not allowable. For one who was not formerly a barber, it is allowable even to carry it around. It is also allowable for him to cut hair, having taken that razor or another one.

304. Bhāgaṃ datvāti dasamabhāgaṃ datvā; idaṃ kira jambudīpe porāṇakacārittaṃ, tasmā dasakoṭṭhāse katvā eko koṭṭhāso bhūmisāmikānaṃ dātabbo.

304. `Bhāgaṃ datvā` means: having given the tenth part. This, it is said, is an ancient custom in Jambudīpa. Therefore, having made ten portions, one portion should be given to the landowners.

Catumahāpadesakathā

The Discourse on the Four Great Standards

305. Yaṃ bhikkhave mayā idaṃ na kappatīti ime cattāro mahāpadese bhagavā bhikkhūnaṃ nayaggahaṇatthāya āha. Tattha dhammasaṅgāhakattherā suttaṃ gahetvā parimaddantā idaṃ addasaṃsu. Ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasanti sattadhaññarasāni pacchābhattaṃ na kappantīti paṭikkhittāni. Tālanāḷikerapanasalabujaalābukumbhaṇḍapussaphalatipusaphalaeḷālukāni[P 5.1104][V 0.0363], nava mahāphalāni sabbañca aparaṇṇaṃ, dhaññagatikameva. Taṃ kiñcāpi na paṭikkhittaṃ, atha kho akappiyaṃ anulometi, tasmā pacchābhattaṃ na kappati. Aṭṭha [M 0.0385] pānāni anuññātāni. Avasesāni vettatintiṇikamātuluṅgakapitthakosambakaramandādikhuddakaphalapānāni aṭṭhapānagatikāneva, tāni kiñcāpi na anuññātāni, atha kho kappiyaṃ anulomenti, tasmā kappanti. Ṭhapetvā hi sānulomaṃ dhaññaphalarasaṃ aññaṃ phalapānaṃ nāma akappiyaṃ natthi, sabbaṃ yāmakālikaṃyevāti kurundiyaṃ vuttaṃ.

305. The Blessed One spoke these four great standards, beginning with `Yaṃ, bhikkhave, mayā... “idaṃ na kappati”`, to the monks for the purpose of grasping the method. Therein, the Elder Compilers of the Dhamma, taking the Sutta and examining it, saw this. By the passage `ṭhapetvā dhaññaphalarasaṃ`, the seven grain-juices were rejected as not being allowable after midday. The nine great fruits—tāla-palm, coconut, breadfruit, `labuja`, gourd, pumpkin, `pussaphala` cucumber, `tipusaphala` cucumber, and `eḷāluka` cucumber—and all pulses are of the same nature as grain. Although these were not directly rejected, they nevertheless conform to what is unallowable; therefore, they are not allowable after midday. Eight kinds of drinks were allowed. The remaining drinks from small fruits—such as `vetta`, tamarind, citron, wood-apple, `kosamba`, and `karamanda`—are of the same nature as the eight drinks. Although these were not directly allowed, they nevertheless conform to what is allowable; therefore, they are allowable. Indeed, setting aside the juice of grain-fruit along with that which conforms to it, there is no other fruit drink that is unallowable; all are `yāmakālika`. Thus it is said in the Kurundī commentary.

Bhagavatā cha cīvarāni anuññātāni. Dhammasaṅgāhakattherehi tesaṃ anulomāni dukūlaṃ, pattuṇṇaṃ, cīnapaṭṭaṃ, somārapaṭṭaṃ, iddhimayikaṃ, devadattiyanti aparāni cha anuññātāni. Tattha “pattuṇṇa”nti pattuṇṇadese pāṇakehi sañjātavatthaṃ. Dve paṭā desanāmeneva vuttā. Tāni tīṇi koseyyassānulomāni. Dukūlaṃ sāṇassa, itarāni dve kappāsikassa vā sabbesaṃ vā.

Six robes were allowed by the Blessed One. The Elder Compilers of the Dhamma allowed another six robes that conform to them: `dukūla` cloth, `pattuṇṇa` cloth, Chinese silk, Somāra silk, cloth created by psychic power, and cloth given by deities. Therein, `pattuṇṇa` is cloth produced from small creatures in the Pattuṇṇa country. Two cloths are mentioned simply by the name of their country. Those three—`pattuṇṇa`, Chinese silk, and Somāra silk—conform to silk cloth. `Dukūla` cloth conforms to hemp cloth. The other two conform to cotton cloth or to all of them.

Bhagavatā ekādasa patte paṭikkhipitvā dve pattā anuññātā – lohapatto ceva mattikāpatto ca. Lohathālakaṃ, mattikāthālakaṃ, tambalohathālakanti tesaṃyeva anulomāni. Bhagavatā tayo tumbā anuññātā – lohatumbo, kaṭṭhatumbo, phalatumboti. Kuṇḍikā, kañcanako, udakatumboti tesaṃyeva anulomāni. Kurundiyaṃ pana “pānīyasaṅkhapānīyasarāvakāni etesaṃ anulomānī”ti vuttaṃ. Paṭṭikā, sūkarantanti dve kāyabandhanāni anuññātāni, dussapaṭṭena rajjukena ca katakāyabandhanāni tesaṃ anulomāni. Setacchattaṃ, kilañjacchattaṃ, paṇṇacchattanti tīṇi chattāni anuññātāni. Ekapaṇṇacchattaṃ tesaṃyeva anulomanti iminā nayena pāḷiñca aṭṭhakathañca anupekkhitvā aññānipi kappiyākappiyānaṃ anulomāni veditabbāni.

The Blessed One, having rejected eleven kinds of bowls, allowed two bowls: an iron bowl and a clay bowl. An iron dish, a clay dish, and a copper dish conform to these. The Blessed One allowed three kinds of gourds: an iron gourd, a wooden gourd, and a fruit-gourd. A water-pot, a basin, and a water-gourd conform to these. In the Kurundī commentary, however, it is said: 'Conch-shells for drinking water and small cups for drinking water conform to these.' Two kinds of waist-bands were allowed: a flat band and one shaped like a pig's intestine. Waist-bands made from a strip of cloth or from a small rope conform to these. Three umbrellas were allowed: a white umbrella, a woven-mat umbrella, and a leaf umbrella. A single-leaf umbrella conforms to these. Thus, by this method, having repeatedly examined the Pāḷi and the Aṭṭhakathā, other things that conform to the allowable and the unallowable should be understood.

Tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ kāle kappatītiādi sabbaṃ sambhinnarasaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Sace hi challimpi anapanetvā sakaleneva nāḷikeraphalena saddhiṃ pānakaṃ paṭiggahitaṃ hoti[P 5.1105], nāḷikeraṃ apanetvā taṃ vikālepi kappati. Upari sappipiṇḍaṃ ṭhapetvā sītalapāyāsaṃ denti, yaṃ pāyāsena asaṃsaṭṭhaṃ sappi, taṃ apanetvā sattāhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati. Baddhamadhuphāṇitādīsupi eseva nayo. Takkolajātiphalādīhi alaṅkaritvā piṇḍapātaṃ denti, tāni uddharitvā dhovitvā yāvajīvaṃ paribhuñjitabbāni. Yāguyaṃ pakkhipitvā dinnasiṅgiverādīsupi telādīsu pakkhipitvā dinnalaṭṭhimadhukādīsupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ asambhinnarasaṃ hoti, taṃ taṃ ekato paṭiggahitampi [V 0.0364] yathā [M 0.0386] suddhaṃ hoti, tathā dhovitvā vā tacchetvā vā tassa tassa kālavasena paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati.

The entire passage beginning, `Tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ kāle kappati`, was spoken with reference to things of mixed flavor. Indeed, if a drink is received together with a whole coconut without even removing the husk, then after removing the coconut, that drink is allowable even at the wrong time. They give cool milk-rice with a lump of ghee placed on top; the ghee that is unmixed with the milk-rice may be removed and consumed for seven days. This is the same method for solidified honey, molasses, and so on. They give almsfood decorated with `takkola`, nutmeg, and so on; these should be lifted out, washed, and may be consumed for life. This is the same method for ginger and so on, given after being put into gruel, and for licorice and so on, given after being put into oil. Thus, whatever thing is of unmixed flavor, even though it was received together with another, it is allowable to consume it according to the time-period of that specific item, after washing it or scraping it in such a way that it becomes pure.

Sace pana sambhinnarasaṃ hoti saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, na vaṭṭati. Yāvakālikañhi attanā saddhiṃ sambhinnarasāni tīṇipi yāmakālikādīni attano sabhāvaṃ upaneti, yāmakālikaṃ dvepi sattāhakālikādīni attano sabhāvaṃ upaneti, sattāhakālikampi attanā saddhiṃ saṃsaṭṭhaṃ yāvajīvikaṃ attano sabhāvaññeva upaneti; tasmā tena tadahupaṭiggahitena saddhiṃ tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ vā purepaṭiggahitaṃ vā yāvajīvikaṃ sattāhaṃ kappati dvīhapaṭiggahitena chāhaṃ, tīhapaṭiggahitena pañcāhaṃ…pe… sattāhapaṭiggahitena tadaheva kappatīti veditabbaṃ. Tasmāyeva hi “sattāhakālikena bhikkhave yāvajīvikaṃ tadahupaṭiggahita”nti avatvā “paṭiggahitaṃ sattāhaṃ kappatī”ti vuttaṃ.

But if it is blended such that the tastes are mixed, it is not allowable. For a yāvakālika brings to its own nature the three kinds of items beginning with yāmakālika that are mixed with it and have blended tastes; a yāmakālika brings to its own nature the two kinds of items beginning with sattāhakālika; and a sattāhakālika brings to its own nature a yāvajīvika that is blended with it. Therefore, a yāvajīvika received on that day or received previously, when mixed with a sattāhakālika received on that day, is allowable for seven days. With one received two days ago, it is allowable for six days; with one received three days ago, it is allowable for five days... and so on... with one received seven days ago, it is allowable only on that very day. This should be understood. For this very reason, the Blessed One did not say, 'Bhikkhus, a yāvajīvika with a sattāhakālika is to be received for that day,' but rather said, 'What is received is allowable for seven days.'

Kālayāmasattāhātikkamesu cettha vikālabhojanasannidhibhesajjasikkhāpadānaṃ vasena āpattiyo veditabbā. Imesu ca pana catūsu kālikesu yāvakālikaṃ yāmakālikanti idameva dvayaṃ antovutthakañceva sannidhikārakañca hoti, sattāhakālikañca yāvajīvikañca akappiyakuṭiyaṃ nikkhipitumpi vaṭṭati, sannidhimpi na janetīti. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

And here, in cases of exceeding the time limits for the day, the watch, and the seven days, offenses should be understood by way of the training rules on eating at the wrong time, storing, and medicines. Furthermore, among these four kālika items, only these two—the yāvakālika and the yāmakālika—can cause an offense for being kept inside an unsuitable dwelling and can cause a storing offense. As for the sattāhakālika and the yāvajīvika, it is allowable to place them in an unsuitable dwelling, and they do not cause a storing offense. The rest is clear everywhere.

Bhesajjakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on Medicines is concluded.

7. Kathinakkhandhakaṃ

7. The Chapter on the Kaṭhina

Kathinānujānanakathā

The Discourse on the Allowance of the Kaṭhina

306. Kathinakkhandhake [M 0.0387][V 0.0365] – pāveyyakāti pāveyyaraṭṭhavāsino. Pāveyyaṃ nāma kosalesu pacchimadisābhāge raṭṭhaṃ; tattha [P 5.1106] vāsinoti vuttaṃ hoti. Kosalarañño ekapitukabhātūnaṃ bhaddavaggiyattherānaṃ etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tesu sabbajeṭṭhako anāgāmī, sabbapacchimako sotāpanno, ekopi arahā vā puthujjano vā natthi. Āraññikāti dhutaṅgasamādānavasena āraññikā; na araññavāsamattena. Piṇḍapātikādibhāvepi tesaṃ eseva nayo. Sīsavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Ime pana terasāpi dhutaṅgāni samādāyeva vattanti. Udakasaṅgaheti udakena saṅgahite ghaṭite saṃsaṭṭhe; thale ca ninne ca ekodakībhūteti attho.

306. In the Chapter on the Kaṭhina: 'Those from Pāveyyaka' means residents of the country of Pāveyyaka. Pāveyyaka is a country in the western part of Kosala; 'those who dwell there' is what is said. This is a designation for the Bhaddavaggiya elders, who were brothers of the king of Kosala by the same father. Among them, the very eldest was a non-returner, and the very youngest was a stream-enterer; there was not a single one who was an Arahant or a worldling. 'Forest-dwellers' means they were forest-dwellers by way of undertaking the ascetic practices, not merely by living in the forest. This same method applies to their being alms-food eaters and so on. And this was stated by way of a heading. But in fact, they lived having undertaken all thirteen ascetic practices. 'Gathered by water' means gathered, connected, and mixed by water; the meaning is that on high ground and low ground, it had become a single body of water.

Udakacikkhalleti akkantaakkantaṭṭhāne udakacikkhallo uṭṭhahitvā yāva ānisadā paharati, īdise cikkhalleti attho. Okapuṇṇehīti udakapuṇṇehi. Tesaṃ kira cīvarāni ghanāni, tesu patitaṃ udakaṃ na paggharati ghanattā puṭabaddhaṃ viya tiṭṭhati. Tena vuttaṃ – “okapuṇṇehi cīvarehī”ti. “Oghapuṇṇehī”tipi pāṭho.

'In watery mud' means in such mud where, in every place one steps, watery mud rises up and strikes as far as the buttocks; this is the meaning. 'Filled with water' means filled with water. It seems their robes were dense; water that fell on them did not flow out. Due to the density, it stayed as if bound in a parcel. Therefore it was said, 'with robes full of water.' There is also the reading 'filled with a flood.'

Avivadamānā vassaṃ vasimhāti ettha āgantukaṭṭhāne senāsanaphāsutāya abhāvena ca bhagavato dassanālābhena ukkaṇṭhitatāya ca te bhikkhū phāsuṃ na vasiṃsu, tasmā “avivadamānā phāsukaṃ vassaṃ vasimhā”ti nāvocuṃ. Dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvāti bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ anamataggiyakathaṃ kathesi. Te sabbepi kathāpariyosāne arahattaṃ pāpuṇitvā nisinnaṭṭhānatoyeva ākāse uppatitvā agamaṃsu, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā”ti. Tato bhagavā “sace kathinatthāro paññatto abhavissa, ete bhikkhū ekaṃ cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā santaruttarena āgacchantā na evaṃ kilantā assu, kathinatthāro ca nāmesa sabbabuddhehi anuññāto”ti cintetvā kathinatthāraṃ anujānitukāmo bhikkhū āmantesi, āmantetvā ca pana “anujānāmi bhikkhave”tiādimāha.

Regarding 'We spent the rains without dispute': here, because there was no comfort in the lodgings in the place for visitors, and because they were discontented from not getting to see the Blessed One, those monks did not live comfortably. Therefore, they did not say, 'We spent the rains without dispute and comfortably.' Regarding 'having given a Dhamma talk': the Blessed One gave those monks a talk on the beginningless nature of saṃsāra. At the end of the talk, all of them attained Arahantship, and rising up into the sky from the very place they were sitting, they departed. It was with reference to this that it was said, 'having given a Dhamma talk.' Then, the Blessed One, thinking, 'If the spreading of the Kaṭhina had been laid down, these monks, having left one robe behind and coming with only an under-robe and an upper-robe, would not have been so weary. And this spreading of the Kaṭhina has been allowed by all Buddhas,' and wishing to allow the spreading of the Kaṭhina, addressed the monks. And having addressed them, he said, 'I allow, monks,' and so on.

Tattha [M 0.0388][V 0.0366] atthatakathinānaṃ voti nipātamattaṃ vokāro; atthatakathinānanti attho. Evañhi sati parato “so nesaṃ bhavissatī”ti yujjati. Atha vā voti sāmivacanamevetaṃ. So nesanti ettha pana so cīvaruppādo ye atthatakathinā, tesaṃ bhavissatīti attho.

Therein, in the phrase `atthatakathinānaṃ vo`, the word `vo` is a mere particle; the meaning is 'of those who have spread the kaṭhina.' For if this is so, then what follows, `so nesaṃ bhavissati` ('it will be for them'), is fitting. Alternatively, this word `vo` is indeed a word in the possessive case. In the phrase `so nesaṃ`, however, the meaning is: that arising of robes will be for them, that is, for those who have spread the kaṭhina.

Tattha anāmantacāroti yāva kathinaṃ na uddhariyati, tāva anāmantetvā caraṇaṃ kappissati[P 5.1107], cārittasikkhāpadena anāpatti bhavissatīti attho. Asamādānacāroti ticīvaraṃ asamādāya caraṇaṃ; cīvaravippavāso kappissatīti attho. Gaṇabhojananti gaṇabhojanampi kappissati. Yāvadatthacīvaranti yāvattakena cīvarena attho, tāvattakaṃ anadhiṭṭhitaṃ avikappitaṃ kappissatīti attho. Yo ca tattha cīvaruppādoti tattha kathinatthatasīmāyaṃ matakacīvaraṃ vā hotu saṅghaṃ uddissa dinnaṃ vā saṅghikena tatruppādena ābhataṃ vā, yena kenaci ākārena yaṃ saṅghikacīvaraṃ uppajjati, taṃ tesaṃ bhavissatīti attho.

Therein, 'going about without asking leave' means that for as long as the Kaṭhina has not been taken up, it will be allowable to go about without asking leave; the meaning is that there will be no offense under the training rule on conduct. 'Going about without the set of robes' means going about without taking the three robes; the meaning is that separation from one's robes will be allowable. 'A group meal' means that a group meal will also be allowable. 'As much robe-cloth as is needed' means that whatever amount of robe-cloth is needed, that amount will be allowable even if it is not determined or shared; this is the meaning. 'And whatever arising of robes there is there' means that within the boundary where the Kaṭhina has been spread, whether it be the robe of one who has died, or given with the Sangha as the designation, or brought with what has arisen there as property of the Sangha, whatever robe-cloth belonging to the Sangha arises in any way whatsoever, that will be for them; this is the meaning.

Evañca pana bhikkhave kathinaṃ attharitabbanti ettha kathinatthāraṃ ke labhanti, ke na labhantīti? Gaṇanavasena tāva pacchimakoṭiyā pañca janā labhanti, uddhaṃ satasahassampi, pañcannaṃ heṭṭhā na labhanti. Vutthavassavasena purimikāya vassaṃ upagantvā paṭhamapavāraṇāya pavāritā labhanti, chinnavassā vā pacchimikāya upagatā vā na labhanti, aññasmiṃ vihāre vutthavassāpi na labhantīti mahāpaccariyaṃ vuttaṃ. Purimikāya upagatānaṃ pana sabbe gaṇapūrakā honti, ānisaṃsaṃ na labhanti, ānisaṃso itaresaṃyeva hoti. Sace purimikāya upagatā cattāro vā honti tayo vā dve vā eko vā, itare gaṇapūrake katvā kathinaṃ attharitabbaṃ. Atha cattāro bhikkhū upagatā, eko paripuṇṇavasso sāmaṇero, so ce pacchimikāya upasampajjati, gaṇapūrako ceva hoti, ānisaṃsañca labhati. Tayo bhikkhū dve sāmaṇerā, dve bhikkhū tayo sāmaṇerā, eko bhikkhu cattāro sāmaṇerāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sace purimikāya upagatā kathinatthārakusalā na honti, atthārakusalā khandhakabhāṇakatherā pariyesitvā ānetabbā. Kammavācaṃ sāvetvā kathinaṃ attharāpetvā dānañca bhuñjitvā gamissanti. Ānisaṃso pana itaresaṃyeva hoti.

Herein, regarding 'And how, O bhikkhus, is the Kaṭhina to be spread?': Who obtains the spreading of the Kaṭhina, and who does not? First, by way of number, at the minimum limit, five persons obtain it, and upwards even a hundred thousand; but fewer than five do not obtain it. By way of having completed the rains-residence, those who, having entered the rains-residence in the earlier period, have performed the Pavāraṇā on the first Pavāraṇā day, obtain it; those with a broken rains-residence, or who entered in the later period, do not obtain it; even those who have completed the rains-residence in another monastery do not obtain it, thus it is said in the Mahāpaccarī. However, all who entered the rains-residence in the earlier period serve as group-completers; they do not obtain the benefit, for the benefit belongs only to the others. If those who entered in the earlier period are four, or three, or two, or one, the Kaṭhina should be spread after making the others group-completers. Or, if four bhikkhus have entered the rains-residence, and one novice of twenty years of age has also entered, should he be ordained in the later period, he is both a group-completer and obtains the benefit. If there are three bhikkhus and two such novices, two bhikkhus and three such novices, or one bhikkhu and four such novices, here too, this is the same method. If those who entered in the earlier period are not skilled in spreading the Kaṭhina, elders skilled in spreading the Kaṭhina who are reciters of the Khandhaka should be sought and brought. Having made the formal act proclamation heard, having caused the Kaṭhina to be spread, and having eaten the almsfood, they will depart. However, the benefit belongs only to the others.

Kathinaṃ [M 0.0389] kena dinnaṃ vaṭṭati? Yena kenaci devena vā manussena vā pañcannaṃ vā sahadhammikānaṃ aññatarena dinnaṃ vaṭṭati. Kathinadāyakassa vattaṃ atthi, sace so taṃ ajānanto pucchati – “bhante kathaṃ kathinaṃ dātabba”nti tassa evaṃ ācikkhitabbaṃ – “tiṇṇaṃ cīvarānaṃ aññatarappahonakaṃ sūriyuggamanasamaye vatthaṃ ‘kathinacīvaraṃ demā’ti dātuṃ vaṭṭati[P 5.1108], tassa parikammatthaṃ [V 0.0367] ettakā nāma sūciyo, ettakaṃ suttaṃ, ettakaṃ rajanaṃ, parikammaṃ karontānaṃ ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāgubhattañca dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

By whom given is the Kaṭhina valid? It is valid when given by any deva or human whatsoever, or by any one of the five co-religionists. There is a duty for the Kaṭhina donor. If he, not knowing it, asks, 'Venerable sir, how should the Kaṭhina be given?' he should be told thus: 'At the time of sunrise, it is proper to give cloth sufficient for any one of the three robes, saying, "We give the Kaṭhina-robe-cloth." For the purpose of its preparation, it is proper to give such-and-such a number of needles, so much thread, so much dye, and gruel and food for such-and-such a number of bhikkhus who are doing the preparation.'

Kathinatthārakenāpi dhammena samena uppannaṃ kathinaṃ attharantena vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tantavāyagehato hi ābhatasantāneneva khalimakkhitasāṭako na vaṭṭati, malīnasāṭakopi na vaṭṭati, tasmā kathinatthārasāṭakaṃ labhitvā suṭṭhu dhovitvā sūciādīni cīvarakammūpakaraṇāni sajjetvā bahūhi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ tadaheva sibbitvā niṭṭhitasūcikammaṃ rajitvā kappabinduṃ datvā kathinaṃ attharitabbaṃ. Sace tasmiṃ anatthateyeva aññaṃ kathinasāṭakaṃ āharati, aññāni ca bahūni kathinānisaṃsavatthāni deti, yo ānisaṃsaṃ bahuṃ deti, tassa santakeneva attharitabbaṃ. Itaro yathā tathā ovaditvā saññāpetabbo.

Also by the one who is to spread the Kaṭhina, the duty should be known when spreading the Kaṭhina that has arisen righteously and justly. For a cloth just as it is brought from the weaver's house, smeared with rice-gruel starch, is not suitable; a soiled cloth is also not suitable. Therefore, having received the Kaṭhina-spreading cloth, having washed it well, having prepared the requisites for robe-work, such as needles, etc., together with many bhikkhus, having sewn it on that very day, and once the needlework is completed, having dyed it and applied the kappabindu mark, the Kaṭhina should be spread. If, while that has not yet been spread, one brings another Kaṭhina cloth, and also gives many other cloths that are a benefit of the Kaṭhina, it should be spread with the one belonging to the donor who gives many benefit-cloths. The other donor should be instructed in some way or other and made to understand.

Kathinaṃ pana kena attharitabbaṃ? Yassa saṅgho kathinacīvaraṃ deti. Saṅghena pana kassa dātabbaṃ? Yo jiṇṇacīvaro hoti. Sace bahū jiṇṇacīvarā honti, vuḍḍhassa dātabbaṃ. Vuḍḍhesupi yo mahāpariso tadaheva cīvaraṃ katvā attharituṃ sakkoti, tassa dātabbaṃ. Sace vuḍḍho na sakkoti navakataro sakkoti, tassa dātabbaṃ. Apica saṅghena mahātherassa saṅgahaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā “tumhe bhante gaṇhatha, mayaṃ katvā dassāmā”ti vattabbaṃ. Tīsu cīvaresu yaṃ jiṇṇaṃ hoti, tadatthāya dātabbaṃ. Pakatiyā dupaṭṭacīvarassa dupaṭṭatthāyeva dātabbaṃ. Sacepissa ekapaṭṭacīvaraṃ ghanaṃ hoti, kathinasāṭako ca pelavo, sāruppatthāya dupaṭṭappahonakameva dātabbaṃ, “ahaṃ alabhanto ekapaṭṭaṃ pārupāmī”ti vadantassāpi dupaṭṭaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yo pana lobhapakatiko hoti, tassa na dātabbaṃ. Tenāpi “kathinaṃ attharitvā pacchā sibbitvā dve cīvarāni karissāmī”ti na gahetabbaṃ. Yassa pana dīyati, tassa yena vidhinā dātabbaṃ, taṃ [M 0.0390] dassetuṃ “evañca pana bhikkhave kathinaṃ attharitabba”nti ārabhitvā suṇātu me bhantetiādikā dānakammavācā tāva vuttā.

But by whom should the Kaṭhina be spread? By him to whom the Saṅgha gives the Kaṭhina-robe. But to whom should it be given by the Saṅgha? To him who has a worn-out robe. If many have worn-out robes, it should be given to the most senior. Even among the senior ones, to him who has a large retinue and is able to make and spread the robe on that very day, to him it should be given. If the senior one is not able, but a more junior one is able, to him it should be given. Moreover, it is proper for the Saṅgha to give support to the great elder; therefore, it should be said, 'Venerable sir, you accept it; we will make it and give it.' For whichever of the three robes is worn out, for that purpose it should be given. Ordinarily, to one with a double-layered robe, it should be given for the purpose of a double-layered robe. If his single-layered robe is thick, and the Kaṭhina cloth is thin, for the sake of suitability, enough for a double-layered robe should be given. Even to one who says, 'Not receiving a double-layered one, I wear a single-layered one,' it is proper to give a double-layered one. But to one who is of a greedy nature, it should not be given. Also by him, it should not be accepted thinking, 'Having spread the Kaṭhina, I will sew it later and make two robes.' But to whom it is given, to show by what procedure it should be given to him, having begun with 'And how, O bhikkhus, is the Kaṭhina to be spread...', the formal act proclamation for the giving, beginning with 'Venerable sirs, may the Saṅgha hear me,' has first been stated.

Evaṃ dinne pana kathine sace taṃ kathinadussaṃ niṭṭhitaparikammameva hoti[P 5.1109], iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce niṭṭhitaparikammaṃ hoti, “ahaṃ thero”ti vā “bahussuto”ti vā ekenāpi akātuṃ na labbhati, sabbeheva sannipatitvā dhovanasibbanarajanāni niṭṭhāpetabbāni. Idañhi kathinavattaṃ nāma buddhappasatthaṃ. Atīte padumuttaropi bhagavā kathinavattaṃ akāsi. Tassa kira aggasāvako sujātatthero nāma kathinaṃ gaṇhi, taṃ satthā aṭṭhasaṭṭhiyā bhikkhusatasahassehi saddhiṃ nisīditvā akāsi.

But when the Kaṭhina has been given thus, if that Kaṭhina cloth is one with its preparation already completed, this is good. If it is not one with its preparation completed, it is not allowable for even one person—saying 'I am an elder' or 'I am learned'—not to participate; all must gather together and complete the washing, sewing, and dyeing. For this, the Kaṭhina duty, is praised by the Buddhas. In the past, the Blessed One Padumuttara also performed the Kaṭhina duty. It is said his chief disciple, the elder named Sujāta, received the Kaṭhina, and the Teacher, sitting together with six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus, made it.

Katapariyositaṃ [V 0.0368] pana kathinaṃ gahetvā atthārakena bhikkhunā “sace saṅghāṭiyā kathinaṃ attharitukāmo hoti, porāṇikā saṅghāṭi paccuddharitabbā, navā saṅghāṭi adhiṭṭhātabbā. ‘Imāya saṅghāṭiyā kathinaṃ attharāmī’ti vācā bhinditabbā”tiādinā parivāre vuttavidhānena kathinaṃ attharitabbaṃ. Attharitvā ca pana “tena kathinatthārakena bhikkhunā saṅghaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo – ‘atthataṃ bhante saṅghassa kathinaṃ, dhammiko kathinatthāro, anumodathā’ti tehi anumodakehi bhikkhūhi ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā evamassa vacanīyo – ‘atthataṃ āvuso saṅghassa kathinaṃ, dhammiko kathinatthāro, anumodāmā”ti evamādinā parivāre vuttavidhāneneva anumodāpetabbaṃ, itarehi ca anumoditabbaṃ. Evaṃ sabbesaṃ atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ parivāre “dvinnaṃ puggalānaṃ atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ – atthārakassa ca anumodakassa cā”ti (pari. 403). Punapi vuttaṃ – “na saṅgho kathinaṃ attharati, na gaṇo kathinaṃ attharati, puggalo kathinaṃ attharati, saṅghassa anumodanā gaṇassa anumodanā puggalassa atthārā saṅghassa atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ, gaṇassa atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ, puggalassa atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ”ti (pari. 414).

Now, having received the Kathina that has been completed, the monk who wishes to spread it should spread the Kathina according to the procedure stated in the Parivāra, beginning with: 'If he wishes to spread the Kathina with a saṅghāṭi, the old saṅghāṭi should be relinquished, and a new saṅghāṭi should be determined. The declaration, “I spread the Kathina with this saṅghāṭi,” should be made.' And after spreading it, that monk who spread the Kathina should approach the Sangha, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, raise his hands in añjali, and say thus: 'Venerable sirs, the Kathina has been spread for the Sangha; the spreading of the Kathina is lawful; please rejoice.' Those monks who rejoice should arrange their upper robes over one shoulder, raise their hands in añjali, and say thus: 'Friends, the Kathina has been spread for the Sangha; the spreading of the Kathina is lawful; we rejoice.' In this way, they should be made to rejoice according to the procedure stated in the Parivāra, and the others should also rejoice. Thus the Kathina is spread for all. For it has been stated in the Parivāra: 'The Kathina is spread for two individuals—the spreader and the one who rejoices' (Pari. 403). Again it has been stated: 'The Sangha does not spread the Kathina, nor does a group spread the Kathina; an individual spreads the Kathina. By the Sangha's rejoicing, by the group's rejoicing, and by the individual's spreading, the Kathina is spread for the Sangha, the Kathina is spread for the group, and the Kathina is spread for the individual' (Pari. 414).

Evaṃ atthate pana kathine sace kathinacīvarena saddhiṃ ābhataṃ ānisaṃsaṃ dāyakā “yena amhākaṃ kathinaṃ gahitaṃ, tasseva demā”ti denti[M 0.0391], bhikkhusaṅgho anissaro. Atha avicāretvāva datvā gacchanti, bhikkhusaṅgho issaro. Tasmā sace kathinatthārakassa sesacīvarānipi dubbalāni honti, saṅghena apaloketvā tesampi atthāya vatthāni dātabbāni. Kammavācā pana ekāyeva vaṭṭati. Avasese kathinānisaṃse balavavatthāni [P 5.1110] vassāvāsikaṭṭhitikāya dātabbāni, ṭhitikāya abhāve therāsanato paṭṭhāya dātabbāni, garubhaṇḍaṃ na bhājetabbaṃ. Sace pana ekasīmāya bahū vihārā honti, sabbe bhikkhū sannipātetvā ekattha kathinaṃ attharitabbaṃ, visuṃ visuṃ attharituṃ na vaṭṭati.

Now, when the Kathina has been spread in this way, if the donors give the beneficial cloth brought along with the Kathina robe, saying, 'We give this only to the one who received our Kathina,' then the Bhikkhu Sangha has no authority over it. But if they give it without specifying and then leave, the Bhikkhu Sangha has authority. Therefore, if the remaining robes of the monk who spread the Kathina are also worn out, the Sangha, having obtained consent, should provide cloths for his benefit as well. However, only one formal act is permissible. The remaining strong cloths, which are a benefit of the Kathina, should be distributed according to the seniority of the rains-residence. In the absence of such an order of seniority, they should be distributed starting from the seat of the most senior elder. Goods of significant value should not be divided. Furthermore, if there are many monasteries within a single boundary, all the bhikkhus should be assembled, and the Kathina should be spread in one place; it is not permissible to spread it separately.

308. Idāni yathā ca kathinaṃ atthataṃ hoti, yathā ca anatthataṃ, taṃ vidhiṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ evañca pana bhikkhave atthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ evaṃ anatthatanti vatvā akaraṇīyañceva mahābhūmikañca anatthatalakkhaṇaṃ tāva dassento na ullikhitamattenātiādike catuvīsati ākāre dassesi. Tato paraṃ atthatalakkhaṇaṃ dassento ahatena atthatantiādike sattarasa ākāre dassesi. Parivārepi hi “catuvīsatiyā ākārehi anatthataṃ hoti kathinaṃ, sattarasahi ākārehi atthataṃ hoti kathina”nti idameva lakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ.

308. Now, in order to show in detail the procedure by which the Kathina is spread and by which it is not spread, having said, 'In this way, bhikkhus, the Kathina is spread, and in this way, it is not spread,' the Blessed One first showed the characteristics of not being spread—those which are improper and those which are of major significance—in twenty-four aspects, beginning with 'not by merely marking.' Thereafter, showing the characteristics of being spread, He presented seventeen aspects, beginning with 'spread with a new cloth.' For in the Parivāra, this very characteristic is stated: 'The Kathina is not spread in twenty-four ways; the Kathina is spread in seventeen ways.'

Tattha [V 0.0369] ullikhitamattenāti dīghato ca puthulato ca pamāṇaggahaṇamattena. Pamāṇañhi gaṇhanto tassa tassa padesassa sañjānanatthaṃ nakhādīhi vā paricchedaṃ dassento ullikhati, nalāṭādīsu vā ghaṃsati, tasmā taṃ pamāṇaggahaṇaṃ “ullikhitamatta”nti vuccati. Dhovanamattenāti kathinadussadhovanamattena. Cīvaravicāraṇamattenāti “pañcakaṃ vā sattakaṃ vā navakaṃ vā ekādasakaṃ vā hotū”ti evaṃ vicāritamattena. Chedanamattenāti yathāvicāritassa vatthassa chedanamattena. Bandhanamattenāti moghasuttakāropanamattena. Ovaṭṭiyakaraṇamattenāti moghasuttakānusārena dīghasibbitamattena. Kaṇḍusakaraṇamattenāti muddhiyapattabandhanamattena. Daḷhīkammakaraṇamattenāti dve cimilikāyo ekato katvā sibbitamattena. Atha vā paṭhamacimilikā ghaṭetvā ṭhapitā hoti, kathinasāṭakaṃ tassā kucchicimilikaṃ katvā sibbitamattenātipi attho. Mahāpaccariyaṃ [M 0.0392] “pakaticīvarassa upassayadānenā”ti vuttaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana “pakatipattabaddhacīvaraṃ dupaṭṭaṃ kātuṃ kucchicimilikaṃ alliyāpanamattenā”ti vuttaṃ. Anuvātakaraṇamattenāti piṭṭhianuvātāropanamattena. Paribhaṇḍakaraṇamattenāti kucchianauvātāropanamattena. Ovaddheyyakaraṇamattenāti āgantukapattāropanamattena[P 5.1111]. Kathinacīvarato vā pattaṃ gahetvā aññasmiṃ akathinacīvare pattāropanamattena.

Here, 'by merely marking' means by merely taking the measurement in length and width. For when taking a measurement, in order to identify each section, one marks it by scratching with a fingernail or the like, or rubs it on the forehead, etc. Therefore, that taking of a measurement is called 'merely marking.' 'By merely washing' means by merely washing the Kathina cloth. 'By merely planning the robe' means by merely deciding, 'Let it be of five, seven, nine, or eleven panels.' 'By merely cutting' means by merely cutting the cloth that has been planned. 'By merely tacking' means by merely applying a temporary thread. 'By merely sewing the long seams' means by merely sewing lengthwise along the temporary thread. 'By merely attaching the shoulder sections' means by merely fastening the panels for the shoulder straps. 'By merely strengthening' means by merely sewing two layers of cloth together. Alternatively, it also means that a first layer of cloth has been joined and set aside, and then the Kathina cloth is made into an inner lining for it and sewn. In the Mahāpaccarī, it is said: 'by adding a lining to an ordinary robe.' In the Kurundī, however, it is said: 'by merely attaching an inner lining to make a double-layered robe out of an ordinary robe with fastened panels.' 'By merely attaching the outer border' means by merely applying the back lengthwise border. 'By merely attaching the inner border' means by merely applying the inner lengthwise border. 'By merely attaching an extra patch' means by merely applying a reinforcing patch. Or, it means by merely taking a piece from the Kathina robe and applying it as a patch to another, non-Kathina robe.

Kambalamaddanamattenāti ekavāraṃyeva rajane pakkhittena dantavaṇṇena paṇḍupalāsavaṇṇena vā. Sace pana sakiṃ vā dvikkhattuṃ vā rattampi sāruppaṃ hoti, vaṭṭati. Nimittakatenāti “iminā dussena kathinaṃ attharissāmī”ti evaṃ nimittakatena. Ettakameva hi parivāre vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāsu pana “ayaṃ sāṭako sundaro, sakkā iminā kathinaṃ attharitu’nti evaṃ nimittakammaṃ katvā laddhenā”ti vuttaṃ. Parikathākatenāti “kathinaṃ nāma dātuṃ vaṭṭati, kathinadāyako bahuṃ puññaṃ pasavatī”ti evaṃ parikathāya uppāditena. Kathinaṃ nāma atiukkaṭṭhaṃ vaṭṭati, mātarampi viññāpetuṃ na vaṭṭati, ākāsato otiṇṇasadisameva vaṭṭatīti. Kukkukatenāti tāvakālikena. Sannidhikatenāti ettha duvidho sannidhi karaṇasannidhi ca nicayasannidhi ca. Tattha tadaheva akatvā ṭhapetvā karaṇaṃ karaṇasannidhi. Saṅgho ajja kathinadussaṃ labhitvā punadivase deti, ayaṃ nicayasannidhi.

By `kambalamaddanamatta` is meant: it is not valid with a cloth that has been dyed only once by being dipped in dye, having the color of ivory or the color of a pale leaf. However, if, having been dyed once or twice, it is suitable, it is allowable. By `nimittakatena` is meant: it is not valid with a robe that has been marked by a sign thus: 'With this cloth, I will spread the Kathina.' Indeed, only this much was said in the Parivāra. However, in the commentaries it is said: 'It is not valid with a cloth obtained after making a sign thus: "This cloth is beautiful; it is possible to spread the Kathina with this."' By `parikathākatena` is meant: it is not valid with a robe produced by indirect talk thus: 'It is proper to give the Kathina; a donor of the Kathina generates much merit.' A Kathina robe should be most excellent; it is not proper to ask for it even from one's mother; it should be just like a robe that has descended from the sky. By `kukkukatena` is meant: it is not valid with a temporary (i.e., borrowed) robe. Regarding `sannidhikatena`: here, `sannidhi` (storing) is twofold: `karaṇasannidhi` (storing for making) and `nicayasannidhi` (storing by accumulation). Among these, `karaṇasannidhi` is setting it aside without making it on that very day, and then making it. The Saṅgha, having received the Kathina cloth today, gives it on the following day; this is `nicayasannidhi`.

Nissaggiyenāti rattinissaggiyena. Parivārepi vuttaṃ – “nissaggiyaṃ nāma kariyamāne aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahatī”ti. Akappakatenāti anādinnakappabindunā. Aññatra saṅghāṭiyātiādīsu ṭhapetvā saṅghāṭiuttarāsaṅgaantaravāsake aññena paccattharaṇādinā atthataṃ anatthataṃ hotīti. Aññatra pañcakena vā atirekapañcakena vāti pañca vā atirekāni vā khaṇḍāni katvā mahāmaṇḍalaaḍḍhamaṇḍalāni [V 0.0370] dassetvā kateneva vaṭṭati. Evañhi samaṇḍalikataṃ hoti, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññena acchinnakena vā dvatticatukhaṇḍena vā na vaṭṭati. Aññatra puggalassa atthārāti puggalassa atthāraṃ ṭhapetvā na aññena saṅghassa vā gaṇassa vā atthārena atthataṃ hoti. Nissīmaṭṭho anumodatīti bahiupacārasīmāya ṭhito anumodati.

By `nissaggiyena` is meant: it is not valid with a robe that is to be forfeited by passing the night. In the Parivāra also it is said: 'What is called `nissaggiya` is when dawn arises while it is being made.' By `akappakatena` is meant: it is not valid with a robe that has not been marked with a `kappabindu`. Regarding `aññatra saṅghāṭiyā` and so on: excluding the `saṅghāṭi`, `uttarāsaṅga`, and `antaravāsaka`, if it is spread with another cloth such as a bedsheet, it is considered not spread. Regarding `aññatra pañcakena vā atirekapañcakena vā`: it is allowable to spread the Kathina only with a robe made by joining five or more pieces, showing large circles and half-circles. Indeed, when made thus, the robe is considered `samaṇḍalikataṃ`. Excluding that, it is not allowable to spread the Kathina with another uncut robe, or with one of two, three, or four pieces. Regarding `aññatra puggalassa atthārā`: excluding the spreading by an individual, the Kathina is not considered spread by the spreading of a Saṅgha or a group. Regarding `nissīmaṭṭho anumodati`: if a monk standing outside the `upacāra-sīmā` gives approval.

309. Ahatenāti [M 0.0393] aparibhuttena. Ahatakappenāti ahatasadisena ekavāraṃ vā dvikkhattuṃ vā dhotena. Pilotikāyāti hatavatthakasāṭakena[P 5.1112]. Paṃsukūlenāti tevīsatiyā khettesu uppannapaṃsukūlena. Paṃsukūlikabhikkhunā coḷakabhikkhaṃ āhiṇḍitvā laddhacoḷakehi katacīvarenātipi kurundimahāpaccarīsu vuttaṃ. Pāpaṇikenāti āpaṇadvāre patitapilotikaṃ gahetvā kathinatthāya deti, tenāpi vaṭṭatīti attho. Sesaṃ vuttavipallāseneva veditabbaṃ. Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne “saha kathinassa atthārā kati dhammā jāyantī”tiādi bahuaṭṭhakathāsu vuttaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ parivāre pāḷiārūḷhameva, tasmā tattha āgatanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Na hi tena idha avuccamānena kathinatthārakassa kiñci parihāyati.

309. By `ahatena` is meant: with an unused robe. By `ahatakappena` is meant: with a cloth that is like new, having been washed once or twice. By `pilotikāya` is meant: with a piece of old, worn-out cloth. By `paṃsukūlena` is meant: with a rag-robe that has arisen in the twenty-three sources. It is also said in the Kurundī and Mahāpaccarī commentaries that it is valid with a robe made from rags obtained by a `paṃsukūlika` monk after wandering about searching for cloth. Regarding `pāpaṇikena`: the meaning is that if one takes a piece of cloth that has fallen near a shop door and gives it for the purpose of the Kathina, it is also allowable with that. The remainder should be understood as the opposite of what has been said. However, in this place, much has been said in the ancient commentaries, such as 'How many things arise together with the spreading of the Kathina?' All of that has been included in the Pāḷi of the Parivāra. Therefore, it should be understood according to the method that has come down there. For, by that not being stated here, nothing is lost for the one who spreads the Kathina.

310. Evaṃ kathinatthāraṃ dassetvā idāni ubbhāraṃ dassetuṃ kathañca bhikkhave ubbhataṃ hoti kathinantiādimāha. Tattha mātikāti mātaro; janettiyoti attho. Kathinubbhārañhi etā aṭṭha janettiyo. Tāsu pakkamanaṃ anto assāti pakkamanantikā. Evaṃ sesāpi veditabbā.

310. Having thus shown the spreading of the Kathina, now, in order to show its withdrawal, the Blessed One said, 'And how, monks, is the Kathina withdrawn?' and so on. Therein, `mātikā` means `mātaro` (mothers); the meaning is `janettiyo` (progenitresses). Indeed, these eight are the progenitresses of the withdrawal of the Kathina. Among them, `pakkamanantikā` is so called because its end (`anta`) is departure (`pakkamanaṃ`). In the same way, the remaining ones should also be understood.

Ādāyasattakakathā

Discourse on the Heptad of 'Having Taken'

311. Na paccessanti na puna āgamissaṃ. Etasmiṃ pana pakkamanantike kathinuddhāre paṭhamaṃ cīvarapalibodho chijjati, pacchā āvāsapalibodho. Evaṃ pakkamato hi cīvarapalibodho antosīmāyameva chijjati, āvāsapalibodho sīmātikkame. Vuttampi cetaṃ parivāre –

311. [Thinking,] 'I will not return,' I will not come back again. Now, in this withdrawal of the Kathina that has departure as its end, first the robe-impediment is severed, then the residence-impediment. Indeed, for one departing thus, the robe-impediment is severed within the boundary itself; the residence-impediment is severed upon crossing the boundary. And this has been said in the Parivāra:

“Pakkamanantiko kathinuddhāro, vutto ādiccabandhunā;

Etañca tāhaṃ vissajjissaṃ, cīvarapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati;

Pacchā āvāsapalibodho chijjatī”ti. (pari. 415);

The withdrawal of the Kathina that has departure as its end was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun. And this I shall explain to you: first, the robe-impediment is severed; afterwards, the residence-impediment is severed.

Cīvaraṃ ādāyāti akatacīvaraṃ ādāya. Bahisīmagatassāti aññaṃ sāmantavihāraṃ gatassa. Evaṃ hotīti tasmiṃ vihāre senāsanaphāsukaṃ vā sahāyasampattiṃ vā disvā evaṃ hoti[V 0.0371]. Etasmiṃ pana niṭṭhānantike kathinuddhāre āvāsapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati, so hi “na paccessa”nti citte uppannamatteyeva chijjati. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

'Having taken a robe' means having taken an unmade robe. 'Of one who has gone outside the boundary' means of one who has gone to another nearby monastery. 'Thus it occurs' means: having seen either comfort of lodging or the good fortune of companions in that monastery, thus it occurs. However, in this withdrawal of the Kathina that has completion as its end, the residence-impediment is severed first. For it is severed as soon as the thought, 'I will not return,' arises in the mind. And this has been said:

“Niṭṭhānantiko [M 0.0394] kathinuddhāro, vutto ādiccabandhunā;

Etañca tāhaṃ vissajjissaṃ, āvāsapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati;

Cīvare niṭṭhite cīvarapalibodho chijjatī”ti.

The withdrawal of the Kathina that has completion as its end was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun. And this I shall explain to you: first, the residence-impediment is severed; when the robe is completed, the robe-impediment is severed.

Etena [P 5.1113] nayena sesamātikāvibhajanepi attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – “sanniṭṭhānantike dvepi palibodhā nevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessanti citte uppannamatteyeva ekato chijjantīti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

By this method, the meaning should be understood also in the analysis of the remaining matrix-headings. However, this is the distinction: in the withdrawal of the Kathina that has determination as its end, both impediments are severed together as soon as the thought arises, 'I will not have this robe made, and I will not return.' For this has been said:

“Sanniṭṭhānantiko kathinuddhāro, vutto ādiccabandhunā;

Etañca tāhaṃ vissajjissaṃ, dve palibodhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ chijjantī”ti.

The withdrawal of the Kathina that has determination as its end was spoken by the Kinsman of the Sun. And this I shall explain to you: the two impediments are severed neither before nor after.

Evaṃ sabbakathinuddhāresu palibodhupacchedo veditabbo. So pana yasmā iminā ca vuttanayena parivāre ca āgatabhāvena sakkā jānituṃ, tasmā vitthārato na vutto. Ayaṃ panettha saṅkhepo – nāsanantike āvāsapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati, cīvare naṭṭhe cīvarapalibodho chijjati. Yasmā cīvare naṭṭhe cīvarapalibodho chijjati, tasmā “nāsanantiko”ti vuttaṃ.

Thus, in all withdrawals of the Kathina, the severing of the impediments should be understood. But since this can be known both by this method that has been stated and by the fact of its coming in the Parivāra, therefore it has not been stated in detail by me. Herein, this is the summary: In the withdrawal that has loss as its end, the residence-impediment is severed first; when the robe is lost, the robe-impediment is severed. Because the robe-impediment is severed when the robe is lost, therefore it was called 'that which has loss as its end' by the Blessed One.

Savanantike cīvarapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati, tasmā tassa saha savanena āvāsapalibodho chijjati.

In the withdrawal of the Kaṭhina that has hearing as its end, the robe-impediment is severed first. Therefore, for that monk, the residence-impediment is severed together with the hearing.

Āsāvacchedike āvāsapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati. Cīvarāsāya upacchinnāya cīvarapalibodho chijjati. Ayaṃ pana yasmā “anāsāya labhati; āsāya na labhati; tassa evaṃ hoti ‘idhevimaṃ cīvaraṃ kāressaṃ, na paccessa’”ntiādinā nayena itarehi uddhārehi saddhiṃ vomissakadesano anekappabhedo hoti, tasmā parato visuṃ vitthāretvā vutto, idha na vutto. Idha pana savanantikassa anantaraṃ sīmātikkantiko vutto. Tattha cīvarapalibodho paṭhamaṃ chijjati, tassa bahisīme āvāsapalibodho chijjati. Sahubbhāre dve palibodhā apubbaṃ acarimaṃ chijjantīti.

In the withdrawal of the Kaṭhina that has the cutting off of hope as its end, the residence-impediment is severed first. When hope for the robe is cut off, the robe-impediment is severed. However, because this withdrawal, by the method beginning with, 'He obtains without hope; with hope he does not obtain; for him it occurs thus: "I will have this robe made right here; I will not return,"' is a teaching mixed with other withdrawals and is of many kinds, therefore it is spoken of separately and in detail later; it is not spoken of here. Here, however, after the withdrawal with hearing as its end, the withdrawal with crossing the boundary is spoken of. Therein, the robe-impediment is severed first; for that monk, the residence-impediment is severed outside the boundary. In the withdrawal with simultaneous lifting, the two impediments are severed neither before nor after.

316-325. Evaṃ [M 0.0395][V 0.0372] ādāyavāre sattakathinuddhāre dassetvā puna samādāyavārepi vippakatacīvarassa ādāyasamādāyavāresupi yathāsambhavaṃ teyeva dassitā. Tato paraṃ antosīmāyaṃ “paccessaṃ na paccessa”nti imaṃ vidhiṃ anāmasitvāva “na paccessa”nti imameva āmasitvā anadhiṭṭhitenā”tiādinā nayena ca ye ye yujjanti, te te dassitā. Tato paraṃ “cīvarāsāya pakkamatī”tiādinā nayena itarehi saddhiṃ vomissakanayena anekakkhattuṃ āsāvacchedikaṃ dassetvā puna disaṃgamiyavasena ca phāsuvihārikavasena ca niṭṭhānantikesu yujjamānā kathinuddhārā dassitā. Evaṃ [P 5.1114] pabhedato kathinuddhāraṃ dassetvā idāni ye tena tena kathinuddhārena palibodhā chijjantīti vuttā, tesaṃ paṭipakkhe dassento dveme bhikkhave kathinassa palibodhātiādimāha. Tattha cattenāti yena cittena so āvāso catto hoti, taṃ cattaṃ nāma, tena cattena. Vantamuttesupi eseva nayo. Sesaṃ sabbattha uttānamevāti.

Thus, having shown the seven withdrawals of the Kaṭhina in the section on 'having taken,' and again in the section on 'having undertaken' and in the sections on 'having taken' and 'having undertaken' for an unfinished robe, those very same withdrawals are shown according to what is possible. After that, within the boundary, without considering the procedure '[deciding] "I will return" or "I will not return,"' but considering only this '[deciding] "I will not return,"' and by the method beginning with 'by an undetermined [robe],' etc., whichever sections are suitable, those are shown. After that, by the method beginning with 'He departs with hope for a robe,' etc., and by the mixed method together with other withdrawals, the withdrawal by cutting off of hope is shown many times. Then, the withdrawals of the Kaṭhina applicable in the cases that have completion as their end are shown by way of one going to another region and by way of one dwelling in comfort. Having thus shown the withdrawal of the Kaṭhina by way of its divisions, now, showing the opposites of those impediments that were said by the Blessed One to be severed by each withdrawal of the Kaṭhina, the Blessed One said the passage beginning with, 'Bhikkhus, these are the two impediments of the Kaṭhina.' Therein, 'by what is abandoned' (cattena) means: the mind by which that residence is abandoned, that is called 'abandoned'; by that abandoning. This same method applies also to 'vomited' and 'released.' The rest is plain everywhere.

Kathinakkhandhakavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Kaṭhina Chapter is finished.

8. Cīvarakkhandhakaṃ

8. The Chapter on Robes

Jīvakavatthukathā

The Story of Jīvaka

326. Cīvarakkhandhake [M 0.0396][V 0.0373] – padakkhiṇāti chekā kusalā. Abhisaṭāti abhigatā. Kehi abhigatāti? Atthikehi atthikehi manussehi; karaṇatthe pana sāmivacanaṃ katvā “atthikānaṃ atthikānaṃ manussāna”nti vuttaṃ. Paññāsāya ca rattiṃ gacchatīti paññāsa kahāpaṇe gahetvā rattiṃ gacchati. Negamoti kuṭumbiyagaṇo.

326. In the Chapter on Robes – `padakkhiṇāti` means skilled, clever. `Abhisaṭāti` means approached. By whom is she approached? By those who desire, by people who desire. However, in the sense of the instrument, having used the genitive case, it was said by the compilers of the canon, 'of those who desire, of people who desire.' And `paññāsāya rattiṃ gacchati` means: taking fifty kahāpaṇas, one goes at night. `Negamo` means a group of householders.
