327. Sālavatiṃ kumāriṃ gaṇikaṃ vuṭṭhāpesīti nāgarā dve satasahassāni, rājā satasahassanti tīṇi satasahassāni, aññañca ārāmuyyānavāhanādiparicchedaṃ datvā vuṭṭhāpesuṃ; gaṇikaṭṭhāne ṭhapesunti attho. Paṭisatena ca rattiṃ gacchatīti rattiṃ paṭisatena gacchati. Gilānaṃ paṭivedeyyanti gilānabhāvaṃ jānāpeyyaṃ. Kattarasuppeti jiṇṇasuppe.

327. `Sālavatiṃ kumāriṃ gaṇikaṃ vuṭṭhāpesi` means: the townspeople, having given two hundred thousand, and the king, one hundred thousand—thus three hundred thousand—and also other requisites such as gardens, parks, and vehicles, established her. The meaning is, they placed her in the position of a courtesan. And `paṭisatena rattiṃ gacchati` means: at night, one goes for one hundred each. `Gilānaṃ paṭivedeyyaṃ` means: I should make known the state of being sick. `Kattarasuppe` means: in a worn-out winnowing basket.

328. Kā me deva mātā, ko pitāti kasmā pucchi? Taṃ kira aññe rājadārakā kīḷantā kalahe uṭṭhite “nimmātiko nippitiko”ti vadanti. Yathā ca aññesaṃ dārakānaṃ chaṇādīsu cuḷamātāmahāmātādayo kiñci paṇṇākāraṃ pesenti, tathā tassa na koci kiñci peseti. Iti so taṃ sabbaṃ cintetvā “nimmātikoyeva nu kho aha”nti jānanatthaṃ “kā me deva mātā, ko pitā”ti pucchi.

328. `Kā me deva mātā, ko pitā`—why did he ask this? It is said that when other princes were playing and a quarrel arose, they would say to him, 'You are motherless, fatherless!' And just as on festive occasions and so forth, stepmothers, grandmothers, and others would send some gifts to other children, so too no one sent anything to him. Therefore, reflecting on all this, in order to know, 'Am I truly one without a mother?' he asked, 'Who is my mother, O lord, and who is my father?'

Yannūnāhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyyanti yaṃnūna ahaṃ vejjasippaṃ sikkheyyanti cintesi. Tassa kira etadahosi – “imāni kho hatthiassasippādīni parūpaghātapaṭisaṃyuttāni, vejjasippaṃ mettāpubbabhāgaṃ sattānaṃ hitapaṭisaṃyutta”nti. Tasmā vejjasippameva sandhāya “yaṃnūnāhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyya”nti cintesi. Apicāyaṃ ito kappasatasahassassa [P 5.1115] upari padumuttarassa bhagavato upaṭṭhākaṃ “buddhupaṭṭhāko aya”nti catuparisantare patthataguṇaṃ vejjaṃ disvā “aho vatāhampi evarūpaṃ ṭhānantaraṃ pāpuṇeyya”nti cintetvā sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dānaṃ datvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā [V 0.0374] “ahampi bhagavā tumhākaṃ [M 0.0397] upaṭṭhāko asukavejjo viya anāgate buddhupaṭṭhāko bhaveyya”nti patthanamakāsi. Tāya purimapatthanāya codiyamānopesa vejjasippameva sandhāya “yaṃnūnāhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyya”nti cintesi.

As for `Yannūnāhaṃ sippaṃ sikkheyyaṃ`, he thought, 'It would be wonderful if I were to learn the physician's craft!' It is said that this thought occurred to him: 'These crafts, such as those of the elephant and the horse, are connected with harming others; the physician's craft has loving-kindness as its prior component and is connected with the welfare of beings.' Therefore, intending only the physician's craft, he thought, 'It would be wonderful if I were to learn a craft.' Furthermore, one hundred thousand eons prior to this one, this Jīvaka had seen a physician of renowned virtue who was the attendant of the Blessed One Padumuttara, praised in the midst of the four assemblies as 'the Buddha's attendant.' Seeing him, he thought, 'Oh, it would be wonderful if I too could attain such a special position!' Having thought thus, for seven days he gave alms to the Sangha with the Buddha at its head, and after paying homage to the Blessed One, he made an aspiration: 'Blessed One, may I too, in the future, become an attendant of a Buddha, like that certain physician.' Being urged on by that former aspiration, he, intending only the physician's craft, thought, 'It would be wonderful if I were to learn a craft.'

329. Disāpāmokkhoti sabbadisāsu vidito pākaṭo padhāno vāti attho. Tasmiñca samaye takkasīlato vāṇijā abhayarājakumāraṃ dassanāya agamaṃsu. Te jīvako “kuto tumhe āgatā”ti pucchi. “Takkasīlato”ti vutte “atthi tattha vejjasippācariyo”ti pucchi. “Āma kumāra, takkasīlāyaṃ disāpāmokkho vejjo paṭivasatī”ti sutvā “tena hi yadā gacchatha, mayhaṃ āroceyyāthā”ti āha. Te tathā akaṃsu. So pitaraṃ anāpucchā tehi saddhiṃ takkasīlaṃ agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “abhayaṃ rājakumāraṃ anāpucchā”tiādi.

329. `Disāpāmokkho` means known and famous in all directions, or foremost. At that time, merchants from Takkasilā came for an audience with Prince Abhaya. Jīvaka asked them, 'From where have you come?' When it was said, 'From Takkasilā,' he asked, 'Is there a teacher of the physician's craft there?' 'Yes, Prince. In Takkasilā resides a physician who is `disāpāmokkho`.' Hearing this, he said, 'In that case, when you go, please inform me.' They did so. He, without asking his father, went to Takkasilā with them. Therefore, it was said by the compilers of the canon, 'Without asking Prince Abhaya,' and so on.

Icchāmahaṃ ācariya sippaṃ sikkhitunti taṃ kira upasaṅkamantaṃ disvā so vejjo “kosi tvaṃ tātā”ti pucchi. So “bimbisāramahārājassa nattā abhayakumārassa puttomhī”ti āha. “Kasmā pana tvamasi tāta idhāgato”ti, tato so “tumhākaṃ santike sippaṃ sikkhitu”nti vatvā icchāmahaṃ ācariya sippaṃ sikkhitunti āha. Bahuñca gaṇhātīti yathā aññe khattiyakumārādayo ācariyassa dhanaṃ datvā kiñci kammaṃ akatvā sikkhantiyeva, na so evaṃ. So pana kiñci dhanaṃ adatvā dhammantevāsikova hutvā ekaṃ kālaṃ upajjhāyassa kammaṃ karoti, ekaṃ kālaṃ sikkhati. Evaṃ santepi abhinīhārasampanno kulaputto attano medhāvitāya bahuñca gaṇhāti, lahuñca gaṇhāti, suṭṭhu ca upadhāreti, gahitañcassa na sammussati.

Regarding "Teacher, I wish to learn the art": It is said that seeing him approaching, that physician asked, "Who are you, my dear?" He said, "I am the grandson of King Bimbisāra, the son of Prince Abhaya." "But why, my dear, have you come here?" Then, having said, "To learn the art in your presence," he said, "Teacher, I wish to learn the art." As for "and he learns much": unlike other princes and the like who, having given wealth to the teacher, learn without doing any work, he was not like that. Rather, giving no wealth, he became a student who pays in service, at one time doing his preceptor's work, and at another time learning the art. Even so, this clansman, being endowed with the aspiration, due to his own intelligence, learned much, learned quickly, investigated it well, and what he had learned was not forgotten.

Satta ca me vassāni adhīyantassa nayimassa sippassa anto paññāyatīti ettha ayaṃ kira jīvako yattakaṃ ācariyo jānāti, yaṃ aññe soḷasahi vassehi uggaṇhanti, taṃ sabbaṃ sattahi vassehi uggahesi[P 5.1116]. Sakkassa pana devarañño etadahosi – “ayaṃ buddhānaṃ upaṭṭhāko aggavissāsako bhavissati, handa naṃ bhesajjayojanaṃ sikkhāpemī”ti ācariyassa sarīre ajjhāvasitvā yathā ṭhapetvā kammavipākaṃ avasesarogaṃ ekeneva bhesajjayogena tikicchituṃ sakkoti, tathā naṃ bhesajjayojanaṃ sikkhāpesi. So pana “ācariyassa santike sikkhāmī”ti maññati, tasmā “samattho idāni jīvako tikicchitu”nti [M 0.0398] sakkena vissaṭṭhamatte evaṃ cintetvā ācariyaṃ pucchi. Ācariyo pana “na iminā mamānubhāvena uggahitaṃ, devatānubhāvena uggahita”nti ñatvāva tena hi bhaṇetiādimāha. Samantā yojanaṃ āhiṇḍantoti [V 0.0375] divase divase ekekena dvārena nikkhamitvā cattāro divase āhiṇḍanto. Parittaṃ pātheyyaṃ pādāsīti appamattakaṃ adāsi. Kasmā? Tassa kira etadahosi – “ayaṃ mahākulassa putto gatamattoyeva pitipitāmahānaṃ santikā mahāsakkāraṃ labhissati, tato mayhaṃ vā sippassa vā guṇaṃ na jānissati, antarāmagge pana khīṇapātheyyo sippaṃ payojetvā avassaṃ mayhañca sippassa ca guṇaṃ jānissatī”ti parittaṃ dāpesi.

Regarding "For seven years I have been studying, yet the end of this art is not apparent," it is said that this Jīvaka learned in seven years all the art that the teacher knew, which other disciples learn in sixteen years. Then this thought occurred to Sakka, the king of the devas: "This one will become the attendant of the Buddhas, the foremost and most trusted one. Come, I shall cause him to learn the method of compounding medicines." Having entered and dwelt in the teacher’s body, he caused him to learn the method of compounding medicines in such a way that, setting aside disease that is the result of kamma, he would be able to treat the remaining diseases with a single application of medicine. But Jīvaka thought, "I am learning in the presence of my teacher." Therefore, as soon as he was released by Sakka—who had considered, "Jīvaka is now capable of treating"—he thought in this way and asked the teacher. But the teacher, knowing, "This was not learned through my power, but through the power of a deva," spoke the words beginning with "Then, speak." "Wandering a yojana all around" means that going out by one gate each day, he wandered for four days. "He gave little provision for the journey" means he gave a small amount. Why? It is said this thought occurred to him: "This is the son of a great family. As soon as he arrives, he will receive great honor from his father and grandfather. Then he will not know the quality of me or of the art. But on the way, when his provisions are exhausted, he will apply the art and will surely know the quality of both me and the art." Thus, he had little provision given.

Seṭṭhibhariyādivatthukathā

The Story Concerning the Treasurer's Wife and Others

330. Pasatenāti ekahatthapuṭena. Picunāti kappāsapaṭalena. Yatrahi nāmāti yā nāma. Kimpimāyanti kimpi me ayaṃ. Upajānāmetassa saṃyamassāti katassa ca rogūpasamassa ca upakāraṃ jānāmāti adhippāyo.

330. "Pasatena" means: with a single cupped hand. "Picunā" means: with a layer of cotton. "Yatra hi nāma" means: she who will indeed cause it to be taken. "Kimpimāyanti" means: "What gift at all will this householder-wife give to me?" "Upajānāmetassa saṃyamassa" means: "We know the benefit of what was done and of the pacification of the disease"—this is the intention of the treasurer's wife.

331. Sabbālaṅkāraṃ tuyhaṃ hotūti rājā kira “sace imaṃ gaṇhissati, pamāṇayutte ṭhāne naṃ ṭhapessāmi. Sace na gaṇhissati, abbhantarikaṃ naṃ vissāsakaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā evamāha. Abhayakumārassāpi nāṭakānampi cittaṃ uppajji “aho vata na gaṇheyyā”ti. Sopi tesaṃ cittaṃ ñatvā viya “idaṃ me deva ayyikānaṃ ābharaṇaṃ, nayidaṃ mayhaṃ gaṇhituṃ patirūpa”nti vatvā alaṃ devātiādimāha. Adhikāraṃ me devo saratūti katassa upakāraṃ me devo saratūti attho. Rājā pasanno sabbākārasampannaṃ gehañca ambavanuyyānañca anusaṃvaccharaṃ satasahassauṭṭhānakaṃ gāmañca mahāsakkārañca datvā tena hi bhaṇetiādimāha.

331. Regarding "May all the ornaments be yours," it is said the king thought, "If he takes this, I will place him in a position of suitable authority. If he does not take it, I will make him a trusted confidant." Having considered thus, he spoke. The thought also arose in Prince Abhaya and the female dancers, "Oh, if only he would not take it!" He also, as if knowing their thoughts, said, "Your Majesty, this is the ornament of my grandmothers; it is not proper for me to take it," and spoke the words beginning with "Enough, Your Majesty." "May the king remember my service" means, "May the king remember the help I have given." The king, being pleased, having bestowed a fully furnished house, a mango grove and park, a village yielding an annual income of one hundred thousand, and great honors, then spoke the words beginning with "Then, speak."

Rājagahaseṭṭhivatthukathā

The Story of the Treasurer of Rājagaha

332. Sakkhissasi [P 5.1117] pana tvaṃ gahapatīti kasmā āha? Iriyāpathasamparivattanena kira matthaluṅgaṃ na saṇṭhāti, assa ca tīhi sattāhehi niccalassa [M 0.0399] nipannassa matthaluṅgaṃ saṇṭhahissatīti ñatvā appeva nāma sattasattamāse paṭijānitvā sattasattadivasepi nipajjeyyāti naṃ evamāha. Teneva parato vuttaṃ “api ca paṭikacceva mayā ñāto”ti. Sīsacchaviṃ uppāṭetvāti sīsacammaṃ apanetvā. Sibbiniṃ vināmetvāti sibbiniṃ vivaritvā. Nāhaṃ ācariya sakkomīti tassa kira sarīre mahāḍāho uppajji, tasmā evamāha. Tīhi sattāhehīti tīhi passehi ekekena sattāhena.

332. Why did he say, "But will you be able, householder?" It is said that because of changing postures, the brain-marrow does not settle well. But for this man, lying motionless for three weeks, the brain-marrow would settle. Knowing this, and thinking, "Having agreed to seven months, he might indeed be able to lie down for even seven days," he spoke to him thus. For that very reason, it was later said by Jīvaka, "Moreover, he was known to me beforehand." "Having torn off the scalp" means having removed the skin of the head. "Having bent the suture" means having opened the suture. "I am not able, teacher." It is said that a great burning arose in his body; therefore, he spoke thus. "By three weeks" means by three sides, with one week for each.

333. Janaṃ [V 0.0376] ussāretvāti janaṃ nīharāpetvā.

333. "Having cleared the people away" means having caused the people to be removed.

Pajjotarājavatthukathā

The Story of King Pajjota

334. Jegucchaṃ me sappīti ayaṃ kira rājā vicchikassa jāto, vicchikavisapaṭighātāya ca sappi bhesajjaṃ hoti vicchikānaṃ paṭikūlaṃ, tasmā evamāha. Uddekaṃ dassatīti uggāraṃ dassati. Paññāsa yojanikā hotīti paññāsa yojanāni gantuṃ samatthā hoti. Na kevalañcassa rañño hatthinīyeva, nāḷāgiri nāma hatthī yojanasataṃ gacchati, celakaṇṇo ca muñcakeso cāti dve assā vīsayojanasataṃ gacchanti, kāko dāso saṭṭhiyojanāni gacchati.

334. "Ghee is repulsive to me." It is said this king was born on account of a scorpion, and for counteracting scorpion venom, ghee is a medicine that is repulsive to scorpions; therefore, he spoke thus. "He will have nausea" means he will belch. "She is one who goes fifty yojanas" means she is able to go fifty yojanas in a single day. It is not only this king's she-elephant; the elephant named Nālāgiri goes one hundred yojanas in a single day, the two horses Celakaṇṇa and Muñcakesa go one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single day, and the slave named Kāka goes sixty yojanas in a single day.

Ekassa kira kulaputtassa anuppanne buddhe ekadivasaṃ bhuñjituṃ nisinnassa paccekabuddho dvāre ṭhatvā agamāsi, tasseko puriso “paccekabuddho āgantvā gato”ti ārocesi. So sutvā “gaccha, vegena pattaṃ āharā”ti āharāpetvā attano sajjitaṃ bhattaṃ sabbaṃ datvā pesesi. Itaro taṃ āharitvā paccekabuddhassa hatthe ṭhapetvā “ahaṃ bhante tumhākaṃ katena iminā kāyaveyyāvatikena yattha yattha nibbattopi vāhanasampanno homī”ti patthanaṃ akāsi. So ayaṃ etarahi pajjoto nāma rājā jāto, tāya patthanāya ayaṃ vāhanasampatti.

It is said that when a certain clansman was seated one day to eat, at a time when a Buddha had not arisen, a Paccekabuddha, having stood at the door, went away. A certain man informed him, 'A Paccekabuddha came and has gone.' He, having heard, said, 'Go! Quickly bring the bowl,' and having had it brought, he gave all the food prepared for himself and had it sent. The other man, having brought it and placed it in the Paccekabuddha's hand, made an aspiration: 'Venerable sir, by this bodily service done for you, wherever I am reborn, may I be endowed with vehicles.' This very person has now been born as the king named Pajjota. Because of that aspiration, this endowment of vehicles has come to be.

Sappiṃ pāyetvāti sappiñca pāyetvā; paricārikānañca āhārācāre vidhiṃ ācikkhitvā. Nakhena bhesajjaṃ olumpetvāti nakhena bhesajjaṃ odahitvā; pakkhipitvāti attho. Nicchāresīti virecesi.

'Having caused ghee to be drunk' means having caused the ghee to be drunk and having explained to the attendants the procedure regarding diet. 'Having taken up the medicine with a fingernail' means having placed the medicine with a fingernail; the meaning is 'having inserted it.' 'He caused to be discharged' means he purged.

Siveyyakadussayugakathā

The Story of the Pair of Siveyyaka Cloths

335. Siveyyakaṃ [M 0.0400] nāma uttarakurūsu sivathikaṃ avamaṅgalavatthaṃ. Tattha kira manussā mataṃ tena vatthena veṭhetvā nikkhipanti, taṃ [P 5.1118] “maṃsapesī”ti sallakkhetvā hatthisoṇḍakasakuṇā ukkhipitvā himavantakūṭe ṭhapetvā vatthaṃ apanetvā khādanti. Atha vanacarakā vatthaṃ disvā rañño āharanti. Evamidaṃ pajjotena laddhaṃ. Siviraṭṭhe kusalā itthiyo tīhi aṃsūhi suttaṃ kantanti, tena suttena vāyitavatthaṃ etantipi vadanti.

335. A cloth called Siveyyaka is an inauspicious charnel-ground cloth in Uttarakuru. There, it is said, people wrap a dead person in that cloth and lay them down. Then, perceiving it as 'a piece of flesh,' birds with trunks like an elephant's trunk lift it up, place it on a peak of the Himalayas, remove the cloth, and eat the corpse. Then, forest-wanderers who see the cloth bring it to the king. Thus, this was obtained by King Pajjota. It is also said that in the Sivi country, skilled women spin thread with three strands, and this is the cloth woven from that thread.

Samattiṃsavirecanakathā

The Story of the Thirty Purgatives

336. Sinehethāti [V 0.0377] kiṃ pana bhagavato kāyo lūkhoti na lūkho? Bhagavato hi āhāre sadā devatā dibbojaṃ pakkhipanti, sinehapānaṃ pana sabbattha dose temeti, sirā mudukā karoti, tenāyaṃ evamāha. Tīṇi uppalahatthānīti ekaṃ oḷārikadosaharaṇatthaṃ, ekaṃ majjhimadosaharaṇatthaṃ, ekaṃ sukhumadosaharaṇatthaṃ. Nacirasseva pakatatto ahosīti evaṃ pakatatte pana kāye nāgarā dānaṃ sampādesuṃ. Jīvako āgantvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “bhagavā ajja nāgarā tumhākaṃ dānaṃ dātukāmā, mā antogāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisathā”ti. Mahāmoggallānatthero cintesi – “kuto nu kho ajja bhagavato paṭhamaṃ piṇḍapāto laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tato cintesi – “soṇo seṭṭhiputto khettaparikammato paṭṭhāya aññehi asādhāraṇānaṃ khīrodakasecanasaṃvaddhānaṃ gandhasālīnaṃ odanaṃ bhuñjati, tato bhagavato piṇḍapātaṃ āharissāmī”ti iddhiyā gantvā tassa pāsādatale attānaṃ dassesi. So therassa pattaṃ gahetvā paṇītaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ adāsi. Therassa ca gamanākāraṃ disvā “bhuñjatha bhante”ti āha. Thero tamatthaṃ ārocesi “bhuñjatha bhante, ahaṃ aññaṃ bhagavato dassāmī”ti theraṃ bhojetvā gandhehi pattaṃ ubbaṭṭetvā piṇḍapātassa pūretvā adāsi, taṃ thero āharitvā bhagavato adāsi.

336. Regarding 'should be moistened': Is the Blessed One's body rough, then? It is not rough. Indeed, deities always put divine nutritive essence into the Blessed One's food. However, a moistening treatment moistens the humors everywhere in the body and makes the veins soft. For that reason, this one spoke thus. Regarding 'three lotus-handfuls': one was for the purpose of removing coarse humors, one for removing medium humors, and one for removing subtle humors. Regarding 'soon he became of normal nature': when his body was thus of its normal nature, the city-dwellers prepared an offering. Jīvaka came and said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, today the city-dwellers wish to give an offering to you. Do not enter the village for alms.' The Elder Mahāmoggallāna thought: 'From where, indeed, today would it be proper for the Blessed One to receive the first alms-food?' Then he thought: 'Soṇa, the merchant's son, from the time of preparing the field, eats rice from fragrant paddy, which is not common to others, grown by sprinkling with milk-water. From there I will bring alms-food for the Blessed One.' Having gone by psychic power, he showed himself at the base of his palace. Soṇa, having taken the elder's bowl, gave excellent alms-food. And having seen the elder's manner of departure, he said, 'Eat, venerable sir.' The elder explained the matter. Soṇa said, 'Eat, venerable sir. I will give another portion for the Blessed One.' Having had the elder eat, and having anointed the bowl with perfumes and filled it with alms-food, he gave it. The elder, having brought it, gave it to the Blessed One.

Rājāpi kho bimbisāro “ajja bhagavā kiṃ bhuñjissatī”ti vihāraṃ āgantvā pavisamānova piṇḍapātagandhaṃ ghāyitvā bhuñjitukāmo ahosi[P 5.1119]. Bhagavato [M 0.0401] dvīsuyeva piṇḍapātesu bhājanagatesu devatā ojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu – yañca sujātā adāsi; yañca parinibbānakāle cundo kammāraputto; aññesu kabaḷe kabaḷe pakkhipiṃsu, tasmā bhagavā rañño icchaṃ jānitvā apakkhittojameva thokaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ rañño dāpesi. So paribhuñjitvā pucchi – “kiṃ bhante, uttarakuruto ābhataṃ bhojana”nti? “Na mahārāja, uttarakuruto; apica kho taveva raṭṭhavāsino gahapatiputtassa bhojanaṃ eta”nti vatvā soṇassa sampattiṃ ācikkhi. Taṃ sutvā rājā soṇaṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā cammakkhandhake vuttanayena asītiyā kulaputtasahassehi saddhiṃ soṇassa āgamanaṃ akāsi. Te bhagavato dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sotāpannā jātā. Soṇo pana pabbajitvā arahatte patiṭṭhito. Bhagavāpi etadatthameva rañño piṇḍapātaṃ dāpesi.

King Bimbisāra also, thinking, 'What will the Blessed One eat today?' came to the monastery and, just upon entering, smelled the fragrance of the alms-food and became desirous of eating. Deities infused nutritive essence into only two of the Blessed One's alms-foods once they were in the bowl: that which Sujātā gave, and that which Cunda, the smith's son, gave at the time of the Parinibbāna. Into other alms-foods, they infused it morsel by morsel. Therefore, the Blessed One, knowing the king's wish, had a small portion of the alms-food, into which the essence had not yet been infused, given to the king. Having eaten, he asked, 'Venerable sir, is this food brought from Uttarakuru?' 'No, great king, not from Uttarakuru. But rather, this is the food of a householder's son, a resident of your own country.' Having said this, he told of Soṇa's splendor. Hearing that, the king became desirous of seeing Soṇa and, by the method spoken in the Cammakkhandhaka, arranged for Soṇa to come with eighty thousand sons of good family. They, having heard the Blessed One's Dhamma discourse, became stream-enterers. Soṇa, however, having gone forth, was established in Arahantship. The Blessed One also had the alms-food given to the king for this very purpose.

Varayācanakathā

The Account of Requesting a Boon

337. Evaṃ [V 0.0378] katabhattakicce bhagavati atha kho jīvako komārabhacco taṃ siveyyakaṃ dussayugaṃ ādāya…pe… etadavoca. Atikkantavarāti ettha vinicchayo mahākhandhake vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Bhagavā bhante paṃsukūliko bhikkhusaṅgho cāti bhagavato hi buddhattaṃ pattato paṭṭhāya yāva idaṃ vatthaṃ, etthantare vīsati vassāni na koci gahapaticīvaraṃ sādiyi, sabbe paṃsukūlikāva ahesuṃ. Tenāyaṃ evamāha. Gahapaticīvaranti gahapatīhi dinnacīvaraṃ. Dhammiyā kathāyāti vatthadānānisaṃsapaṭisaṃyuttāya kathāya. Itarītarenāpīti appagghenapi mahagghenapi; yena kenacīti attho. Pāvāroti salomako kappāsādibhedo. Anujānāmi bhikkhave kojavanti ettha pakatikojavameva vaṭṭati, mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavaṃ na vaṭṭati. Mahāpiṭṭhiyakojavanti uṇṇāmayo pāvārasadiso kojavo.

337. When the Blessed One had thus completed his meal duties, then Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking that pair of Siveyyaka cloths... (and so on)... spoke thus. Regarding 'the boon has been surpassed,' the decision here should be understood in the manner stated in the Mahākhandhaka. Regarding 'Venerable sir, the Blessed One is a rag-robe wearer, and so is the community of monks,' indeed, from the time the Blessed One attained Buddhood until this cloth arose, for twenty years in the interim, no one accepted a householder's robe; all were exclusively rag-robe wearers. For that reason, he spoke thus. 'Householder's robe' means a robe given by householders. 'With a Dhamma talk' means with a talk connected to the benefits of the gift of cloth. 'Even with one or the other' means whether of little value or of great value; by any whatsoever, this is the meaning. 'A shawl' (`pāvāra`) means a cloak with fleece, of various kinds such as cotton. Regarding 'I allow, monks, a `kojava`,' here only an ordinary `kojava` is allowable; a large-backed `kojava` is not allowable. 'A large-backed `kojava`' means a `kojava` made of wool, similar to a shawl (`pāvāra`).

Kambalānujānanādikathā

The Account of the Permission for Woolen Blankets and So Forth

338. Kāsirājāti kāsīnaṃ rājā; pasenadissa ekapitikabhātā esa. Aḍḍhakāsiyanti ettha kāsīti sahassaṃ vuccati taṃ agghanako kāsiyo[M 0.0402]. Ayaṃ pana pañcasatāni agghati, tasmā “aḍḍhakāsiyo”ti vutto. Tenevāha – “upaḍḍhakāsīnaṃ khamamāna”nti.

338. ‘The king of Kāsī’ means the king of the Kāsīs; he is the elder brother of King Pasenadi, having the same father. Here, regarding ‘a half-Kāsī blanket,’ a ‘kāsī’ is said to be a thousand; a blanket worth that is a ‘kāsīya.’ But this one is worth five hundred; therefore, it is called a ‘half-kāsīya.’ For that very reason, the Compiler of the Canon said: ‘suitable for a half-kāsī.’

339. Uccāvacānīti sundarāni ca asundarāni ca. Bhaṅgaṃ [P 5.1120] nāma khomādīhi pañcahi suttehi missetvā kataṃ; vākamayamevātipi vadanti.

339. ‘Of various kinds’ means both fine and not fine. What is called ‘hempen cloth’ (bhaṅga) is made by mixing five kinds of threads, such as linen and so on. Some also say it is made only of bark-fiber.

340. Ekaṃyeva bhagavatā cīvaraṃ anuññātaṃ na dveti te kira itarītarena cīvarenāti etassa “gahapatikena vā paṃsukūlena vā”ti evaṃ atthaṃ sallakkhiṃsu. Nāgamesunti yāva te susānato āgacchanti, tāva te na acchiṃsu; pakkamiṃsuyeva. Nākāmā bhāgaṃ dātunti na anicchāya dātuṃ; yadi pana icchanti, dātabbo. Āgamesunti upacāre acchiṃsu. Tenāha bhagavā āha – “anujānāmi bhikkhave āgamentānaṃ akāmā bhāgaṃ dātu”nti. Yadi pana manussā “idhāgatā eva gaṇhantū”ti denti, saññāṇaṃ vā katvā gacchanti “sampattā gaṇhantū”ti sampattānaṃ sabbesampi pāpuṇanti. Sace chaḍḍetvā gatā, yena gahitaṃ, so eva sāmī. Sadisā susānaṃ okkamiṃsūti sabbe samaṃ okkamiṃsu; ekadisāya vā okkamiṃsūtipi [V 0.0379] attho. Te katikaṃ katvāti laddhaṃ paṃsukūlaṃ sabbe bhājetvā gaṇhissāmāti bahimeva katikaṃ katvā.

340. Regarding ‘Only one robe was allowed by the Blessed One, not two,’ it seems those monks understood the meaning of the text ‘by one or the other robe’ as ‘either by a householder’s robe or by a rag-robe.’ Regarding ‘they did not wait,’ until those monks returned from the charnel ground, the others did not stay; they just left. Regarding ‘unwilling to give a share,’ this means not giving due to unwillingness; but if they wish, a share should be given. Regarding ‘they waited,’ they waited in the vicinity of the charnel ground. For that reason, the Blessed One said: ‘I allow, monks, to give a share to those who are waiting, even if you are unwilling.’ Furthermore, if people give, saying, ‘Let only those who have come here take it,’ or if they leave after making a sign, saying, ‘Let those who have arrived take it,’ then it reaches all who have arrived. If they have departed after abandoning it, whoever has taken it, he alone is the owner. Regarding ‘they entered the charnel ground together,’ all entered equally; or it also means they entered in one direction. Regarding ‘they made an agreement,’ it means having made an agreement already outside the charnel ground, thinking, ‘We will all divide and take the rag-robe that is obtained.’

342. Cīvarapaṭiggāhakanti yo gahapatikehi saṅghassa dīyamānaṃ cīvaraṃ gaṇhāti. Yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyyātiādīsu cīvarapaṭiggāhakesu pacchā āgatānampi attano ñātakādīnaṃ paṭhamataraṃ paṭiggaṇhanto vā ekaccasmiṃ pemaṃ dassetvā gaṇhanto vā lobhapakatikatāya attano pariṇāmento vā chandāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Paṭhamataraṃ āgatassāpi kodhavasena pacchā gaṇhanto vā duggatamanussesu avamaññaṃ katvā gaṇhanto vā “kiṃ vo ghare ṭhapanokāso natthi, tumhākaṃ santakaṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti evaṃ saṅghassa lābhantarāyaṃ karonto vā dosāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo pana muṭṭhassati asampajāno, ayaṃ mohāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Pacchā āgatānampi issarānampi bhayena paṭhamataraṃ paṭiggaṇhanto vā “cīvarapaṭiggāhakaṭṭhānaṃ nāmetaṃ bhāriya”nti santasanto vā bhayāgatiṃ gacchati [P 5.1121] nāma. “Mayā idañcidañca gahitaṃ, idañciṃdañca na gahita”nti evaṃ jānanto gahitāgahitaṃ jānāti nāma. Tasmā yo na chandāgatiādivasena gacchati, ñātakaaññātakaaḍḍhaduggatesu visesaṃ akatvā [M 0.0403] āgatapaapāṭiyā gaṇhāti, sīlācārapaṭipattiyutto hoti, satimā medhāvī bahussuto, sakkoti dāyakānaṃ vissaṭṭhavācāya parimaṇḍalehi padabyañjanehi anumodanaṃ karonto pasādaṃ janetuṃ, evarūpo sammannitabbo.

342. ‘A robe-receiver’ is one who accepts a robe being given to the Sangha by householders. Among robe-receivers, regarding ‘one who would not go the wrong course of desire,’ and so on: one who accepts first for his own relatives and others even if they arrived later, or accepts showing affection for a certain person, or appropriates for oneself due to a greedy nature, is called one who goes the wrong course of desire. One who, due to anger, accepts later from one who arrived first, or accepts while showing contempt for poor people, or causes an obstacle to the Sangha’s gain by saying things like, ‘What, is there no place in your house to keep this? Take your property and go,’ is called one who goes the wrong course of aversion. Furthermore, one who is of lapsed mindfulness and is not clearly comprehending is called one who goes the wrong course of delusion. One who accepts first from powerful people even if they arrived later, due to fear, or who is fearful and trembling, thinking, ‘This position of robe-receiver is burdensome,’ is called one who goes the wrong course of fear. One who knows thus, ‘This and that has been accepted by me, and this and that has not been accepted,’ is called one who knows what has been accepted and not accepted. Therefore, one who does not go by way of the wrong courses of desire and so on; who does not make a distinction among relatives and non-relatives, the wealthy and the poor, but accepts in the order of arrival; who is endowed with virtuous conduct and practice; who is mindful, wise, and learned; and who, while giving the anumodanā, is able to generate confidence in the donors with clear speech and with well-rounded words and phrases—such a person should be appointed.

Evañca pana bhikkhave sammannitabboti ettha pana etāya yathāvuttāya kammavācāyapi apalokanenāpi antovihāre sabbasaṅghamajjhepi khaṇḍasīmāyapi sammannituṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Evaṃ sammatena ca vihārapaccante vā padhānaghare vā na acchitabbaṃ. Yattha pana āgatāgatā manussā sukhaṃ passanti, tādise dhuravihāraṭṭhāne bījaniṃ passe ṭhapetvā sunivatthena supārutena nisīditabbanti.

Here, regarding ‘And thus, monks, should one be appointed,’ it is indeed allowable to appoint someone by this formal procedure as stated, or by announcement, within the monastery, in the midst of the entire Sangha, or in a limited boundary. And one who is thus appointed should not stay at the edge of the monastery or in a meditation hall. But in a primary monastery-dwelling, where people who come and go can see easily, one should sit, having placed a fan at one’s side, being well-dressed with the under-robe and well-covered with the upper-robe.

Tattheva ujjhitvāti “paṭiggahaṇameva amhākaṃ bhāro”ti vatvā gahitaṭṭhāneyeva chaḍḍetvā gacchanti. Cīvaranidahakanti cīvarapaṭisāmakaṃ. Yo na chandāgatiṃ gaccheyyātiādīsu cettha ito parañca sabbattha vuttanayeneva vinicchayo veditabbo. Sammutivinicchayopi kathitānusāreneva jānitabbo.

Regarding ‘having discarded it right there,’ it means that saying, ‘Accepting it is our only burden,’ they discard it right at the place of acceptance and leave. ‘A robe-depositor’ means a monk who looks after the robes. Regarding ‘one who would not go the wrong course of desire,’ and so on, here in the case of the robe-depositor and hereafter in all cases, the decision should be understood only in the manner already stated. The decision regarding the appointment should also be known in accordance with what has been explained.

Bhaṇḍāgārasammutiādikathā

The Discourse on the Designation of the Storehouse and So Forth

343. Vihāraṃ [V 0.0380] vātiādīsu yo ārāmamajjhe ārāmikasāmaṇerādīhi avivitto sabbesaṃ samosaraṇaṭṭhāne vihāro vā aḍḍhayogo vā hoti, so sammannitabbo. Paccantasenāsanaṃ pana na sammannitabbaṃ. Idaṃ pana bhaṇḍāgāraṃ khaṇḍasīmaṃ gantvā khaṇḍasīmāya nisinnehi sammannituṃ na vaṭṭati, vihāramajjheyeva sammannitabbaṃ.

343. In the phrases such as 'a dwelling,' whatever dwelling or half-gabled house is in the middle of the monastery, not secluded from monastery attendants, novices, and so forth, and is a place of assembly for all, that should be designated. However, a lodging at the periphery should not be designated. Furthermore, it is not proper for this storehouse to be designated by those who, having gone to a defective boundary, are seated within that defective boundary; it must be designated only in the middle of the monastery.

Guttāguttañca jāneyyāti ettha yassa tāva chadanādīsu koci doso natthi, taṃ guttaṃ. Yassa pana chadanatiṇaṃ vā chadaniṭṭhakā vā yattha katthaci patitā, yena ovassati vā, mūsikādīnaṃ [P 5.1122] vā paveso hoti, bhittiādīsu vā katthaci chiddaṃ hoti, upacikā vā uṭṭhahanti, taṃ sabbaṃ aguttaṃ nāma. Taṃ sallakkhetvā paṭisaṅkharitabbaṃ. Sītasamaye dvārañca vātapānañca supihitaṃ kātabbaṃ, sītena hi cīvarāni kaṇṇakitāni honti. Uṇhasamaye antarantarā vātappavesanatthaṃ vivaritabbaṃ. Evaṃ karonto hi guttāguttaṃ jānāti nāma.

Herein, regarding 'One should know what is guarded and unguarded': that which has no fault in its roofing and so forth is guarded. But that of which the roofing-thatch or roofing-tiles have fallen in some place, whereby it is soaked by rain, or there is entry for rats and so forth, or there is a hole somewhere in the walls and so forth, or termites arise—all that is called unguarded. Having taken note of it, it should be repaired. In the cold season, the door and the window should be kept well closed, for due to the cold, the robes become moldy. In the hot season, they should be opened from time to time for the entry of air. Indeed, one who does so is called one who knows what is guarded and unguarded.

Imehi [M 0.0404] pana cīvarapaṭiggāhakādīhi tīhipi attano vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Tattha cīvarapaṭiggāhakena tāva yaṃ yaṃ manussā “kālacīvara”nti vā “akālacīvara”nti vā “accekacīvara”nti vā “vassikasāṭika”nti vā “nisīdana”nti vā “paccattharaṇa”nti vā “mukhapuñchanacoḷa”nti vā denti, taṃ sabbaṃ ekarāsiṃ katvā missetvā na gaṇhitabbaṃ, visuṃ visuṃ katvāva gaṇhitvā cīvaranidahakassa tatheva ācikkhitvā dātabbaṃ. Cīvaranidahakenāpi bhaṇḍāgārikassa dadamānena idaṃ kālacīvaraṃ…pe… idaṃ mukhapuñchanacoḷanti ācikkhitvāva dātabbaṃ. Bhaṇḍāgārikenāpi tatheva visuṃ visuṃ viya saññāṇaṃ katvā ṭhapetabbaṃ. Tato saṅghena “kālacīvaraṃ āharā”ti vutte kālacīvarameva dātabbaṃ…pe… mukhapuñchanacoḷakaṃ āharāti vutte tadeva dātabbaṃ.

Furthermore, these three—the robe-receiver and so forth—should know their own duty. Therein, firstly, the robe-receiver should not accept all that people give—whether called 'seasonal robes,' 'unseasonal robes,' 'emergency robes,' 'rain-bathing cloths,' 'sitting cloths,' 'coverings,' or 'face-wiping cloths'—by making it into a single, mixed pile. Having accepted them only after separating them, he should give them to the robe-custodian after explaining exactly as stated. The robe-custodian, too, when giving them to the storekeeper, should give them only after explaining, 'This is a seasonal robe... this is a face-wiping cloth.' The storekeeper, too, should keep them with a mark as if they are separate, just as was explained. Thereafter, when the Saṅgha says, 'Bring the seasonal robe,' only the seasonal robe should be given... when it is said, 'Bring the face-wiping cloth,' only that should be given.

Iti bhagavatā cīvarapaṭiggāhako anuññāto, cīvaranidahako anuññāto, bhaṇḍāgāraṃ anuññātaṃ, bhaṇḍāgāriko anuññāto, na bāhulikatāya na asantuṭṭhiyā; apica kho saṅghassānuggahāya. Sace hi āhaṭāhaṭaṃ gahetvā bhikkhū bhājeyyuṃ, neva āhaṭaṃ na anāhaṭaṃ na dinnaṃ nādinnaṃ na laddhaṃ nāladdhaṃ jāneyyuṃ, āhaṭāhaṭaṃ therāsane vā dadeyyuṃ, khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ vā chinditvā gaṇheyyuṃ; evaṃ sati ayuttaparibhogo ca hoti, na ca sabbesaṃ saṅgaho kato hoti. Bhaṇḍāgāre pana cīvaraṃ ṭhapetvā ussannakāle ekekassa bhikkhuno ticīvaraṃ vā dve dve vā [V 0.0381] ekekaṃ vā cīvaraṃ dassanti, laddhāladdhaṃ jānissanti, aladdhabhāvaṃ ñatvā saṅgahaṃ kātuṃ maññissantīti.

Thus, the Blessed One allowed the robe-receiver, the robe-custodian, the storehouse, and the storekeeper—not for the sake of abundance, not for discontent, but rather for the support of the Saṅgha. Indeed, if the monks were to take the robes as they are brought and distribute them, they would not know what was brought and what was not brought, what was given and what was not given, what was received and what was not received. They might give the robes as they are brought to the seat of the elder, or they might cut them into pieces and take them. This being so, there would be improper use, and support for all would not be accomplished. But by storing the robes in the storehouse and, at a time of abundance, giving to each monk three robes, or two each, or one each, they will know what has been received and what has not. Knowing the state of not having received, they will know to provide support.

Na bhikkhave bhaṇḍāgāriko vuṭṭhāpetabboti ettha aññepi avuṭṭhāpanīyā jānitabbā. Cattāro hi na vuṭṭhāpetabbā – vuḍḍhataro[P 5.1123], bhaṇḍāgāriko, gilāno, saṅghato laddhasenāsanoti. Tattha vuḍḍhataro attano vuḍḍhatāya navakatarena na vuṭṭhāpetabbo, bhaṇḍāgāriko saṅghena sammannitvā bhaṇḍāgārassa dinnatāya, gilāno attano gilānatāya, saṅgho pana bahussutassa uddesaparipucchādīhi bahupakārassa bhāranitthārakassa phāsukaṃ āvāsaṃ anuṭṭhāpanīyaṃ katvā deti, tasmā so upakāratāya ca saṅghato laddhatāya ca na vuṭṭhāpetabboti.

Herein, regarding 'Monks, a storekeeper should not be removed': other persons who are not to be removed should also be known. Indeed, four are not to be removed: a more senior monk, a storekeeper, a sick person, and one who has received a lodging from the Saṅgha. Therein, a more senior monk is not to be removed by a more junior one on account of his seniority. A storekeeper is not to be removed on account of having been appointed by the Saṅgha and given the storehouse. A sick person is not to be removed on account of his illness. But as for one who is very learned, very helpful through recitation, questioning, and so forth, and a bearer of burdens, the Saṅgha grants him a comfortable dwelling, having made it a non-removable lodging. Therefore, on account of his helpfulness and because it was received from the Saṅgha, he is not to be removed.

Ussannaṃ [M 0.0405] hotīti bahu rāsikataṃ hoti, bhaṇḍāgāraṃ na gaṇhāti. Sammukhībhūtenāti antoupacārasīmāyaṃ ṭhitena. Bhājetunti kālaṃ ghosetvā paṭipāṭiyā bhājetuṃ. Kolāhalaṃ akāsīti “amhākaṃ ācariyassa detha, upajjhāyassa dethā”ti evaṃ mahāsaddaṃ akāsi. Cīvarabhājanakaṅgesu sabhāgānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ apāpuṇantampi mahagghaṃ cīvaraṃ dento chandāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Aññesaṃ vuḍḍhatarānaṃ pāpuṇantampi mahagghaṃ cīvaraṃ adatvā appagghaṃ dento dosāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Mohamūḷho cīvaradānavattaṃ ajānanto mohāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Mukharānaṃ navakānampi bhayena apāpuṇantameva mahagghaṃ cīvaraṃ dento bhayāgatiṃ gacchati nāma. Yo evaṃ na gacchati, sabbesaṃ tulābhūto pamāṇabhūto majjhatto hoti, so sammannitabbo. Bhājitābhājitanti “ettakāni vatthāni bhājitāni, ettakāni abhājitānī”ti jānanto “bhājitābhājitañca jāneyyā”ti vuccati.

'It is abundant' means it is plentiful, piled up; the storehouse cannot hold it. 'By the assembled (Saṅgha)' means by the Saṅgha standing within the upacāra-sīmā. 'They should distribute' means they should distribute in order after announcing the time. 'He made a clamor' means he made a great noise, saying, "Give to our teacher! Give to our preceptor!" Among the factors for a robe-distributor, one who gives a valuable robe to monks of his own faction, even when it is not due to them, is said to go the way of partiality. One who, not giving a valuable robe to other, more senior monks to whom it is due, gives a cheap one, is said to go the way of aversion. One who, bewildered by delusion, does not know the proper conduct for giving robes, is said to go the way of delusion. One who, out of fear of outspoken junior monks, gives a valuable robe even when it is not due, is said to go the way of fear. One who does not go in these ways, who is like a balance, a measure, and is impartial to all—he should be appointed. 'Distributed and undistributed': one who knows, "This many cloths have been distributed, this many have not been distributed," is said to be one who 'should know what has been distributed and what has not.'

Uccinitvāti “idaṃ thūlaṃ, idaṃ saṇhaṃ, idaṃ ghanaṃ, idaṃ tanukaṃ, idaṃ paribhuttaṃ, idaṃ aparibhuttaṃ, idaṃ dīghato ettakaṃ puthulato ettaka”nti evaṃ vatthāni vicinitvā. Tulayitvāti “idaṃ ettakaṃ agghati, idaṃ ettaka”nti evaṃ agghaparicchedaṃ katvā. Vaṇṇāvaṇṇaṃ katvāti sace sabbesaṃ ekekameva dasagghanakaṃ pāpuṇāti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ; no ce pāpuṇāti, yaṃ nava vā aṭṭha vā agghati, taṃ aññena ekaagghanakena ca dviagghanakena ca saddhiṃ bandhitvā etena upāyena same paṭivīse ṭhapetvāti attho. Bhikkhū gaṇetvā vaggaṃ bandhitvāti sace ekekassa diyamāne divaso nappahoti, dasa dasa bhikkhū [P 5.1124] gaṇetvā dasa dasa cīvarapaṭivīse ekavaggaṃ bandhitvā ekaṃ bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā evaṃ cīvarapaṭivīsaṃ ṭhapetuṃ anujānāmīti attho. Evaṃ ṭhapitesu [V 0.0382] cīvarapaṭivīsesu kuso pātetabbo. Tehipi bhikkhūhi puna kusapātaṃ katvā bhājetabbaṃ.

Having selected means having chosen the cloths thus: 'This is coarse, this is fine, this is dense, this is thin, this is used, this is unused, this is of such a length and such a width.' Having weighed means having determined the value thus: 'This is worth so much, this is worth so much.' Making the portions equal in value means if for all of them a cloth worth ten each is obtained, this is good; if not, that which is worth nine or eight should be combined with another item worth one or two, and by this method, equal shares are to be established; this is the meaning. Having counted the monks and formed a group means if, when giving to each one, the day is not sufficient, I allow that having counted the monks in groups of ten, and having bound ten shares of robes into one group, making one bundle, the shares of robes be established in this way; this is the meaning. When the shares of robes have been established thus, a lot should be cast. Those monks, too, should distribute it among themselves after casting lots again.

Sāmaṇerānaṃ upaḍḍhapaṭivīsanti ettha ye sāmaṇerā attissarā bhikkhusaṅghassa kattabbakammaṃ na karonti, uddesaparipucchāsu yuttā ācariyupajjhāyānaṃyeva vattapaṭipattiṃ karonti, aññesaṃ na karonti, etesaṃyeva upaḍḍhabhāgo dātabbo. Ye pana purebhattañca pacchābhattañca bhikkhusaṅghasseva kattabbakiccaṃ karonti, tesaṃ samako dātabbo. Idañca piṭṭhisamaye [M 0.0406] uppannena bhaṇḍāgāre ṭhapitena akālacīvareneva kathitaṃ. Kālacīvaraṃ pana samakameva dātabbaṃ. Tatruppādavassāvāsikaṃ sammuñjanībandhanādi saṅghassa phātikammaṃ katvā gahetabbaṃ. Etañhettha sabbesaṃ vattaṃ. Bhaṇḍāgārikacīvarepi sace sāmaṇerā āgantvā “bhante mayaṃ yāguṃ pacāma, bhattaṃ pacāma, khajjakaṃ pacāma, appaharitakaṃ karoma, dantakaṭṭhaṃ āharāma, raṅgachalliṃ kappiyaṃ katvā dema, kiṃ amhehi na kataṃ nāmā”ti ukkuṭṭhiṃ karonti, samabhāgova dātabbo. Etaṃ ye ca virajjhitvā karonti, yesañca karaṇabhāvo na paññāyati, te sandhāya vuttaṃ. Kurundiyaṃ pana “sace sāmaṇerā ‘kasmā mayaṃ bhante saṅghakammaṃ na karoma, karissāmā’ti yācanti, samapaṭivīso dātabbo”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'a half-share for novices': Herein, for those novices who are their own masters, who do not perform the work that should be done for the community of monks, who are diligent in recitation and questioning but perform their duties only for their teachers and preceptors and not for others—for them, only a half-share should be given. But for those who perform the work that should be done for the community of monks both before and after the meal, an equal share should be given. And this was said only with regard to an out-of-season robe that has arisen after the robe season and has been placed in the storeroom. A seasonal robe, however, should be given equally. The rains-residence robe that arises there should be received after doing a service for the Sangha, such as tying bundles of brooms. For this is the duty of all here. Regarding the robe in the storeroom, if novices come and make a clamor, saying, 'Venerable sirs, we cook gruel, we cook the meal, we prepare snacks, we clear the ground of green things, we bring tooth-sticks, we prepare dye-bark, make it allowable, and give it. What is it that has not been done by us?' an equal share should be given. This was said referring to those who do it deficiently and those whose performance is not apparent. But in the Kurundī, it is said: 'If novices request, saying, “Venerable sirs, why should we not do the Sangha's work? We shall do it,” an equal share should be given.'

Uttaritukāmoti nadiṃ vā kantāraṃ vā uttaritukāmo; satthaṃ labhitvā disā pakkamitukāmoti attho. Sakaṃ bhāgaṃ dātunti idaṃ bhaṇḍāgārato cīvarāni nīharitvā puñje kate ghaṇṭiyā pahaṭāya bhikkhusaṅghe sannipatite satthaṃ labhitvā gantukāmo “satthato mā parihāyī”ti etamatthaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Tasmā anīhatesu vā cīvaresu appahaṭāya vā ghaṇṭiyā asannipatite vā [P 5.1125] saṅghe dātuṃ na vaṭṭati. Cīvaresu pana nīhatesu ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā bhikkhusaṅghe sannipatite cīvarabhājakena “imassa bhikkhuno koṭṭhāsena ettakena bhavitabba”nti takketvā nayaggāhena cīvaraṃ dātabbaṃ. Tulāya tulitamiva hi samasamaṃ dātuṃ na sakkā, tasmā ūnaṃ vā hotu adhikaṃ vā, evaṃ takkena nayena dinnaṃ sudinnaṃ. Neva ūnakaṃ puna dātabbaṃ, nātirittaṃ paṭiggaṇhitabbanti.

Wishing to cross over means wishing to cross a river or a wilderness; the meaning is wishing to depart for some region after finding a caravan. 'To give his own share'—this was said with reference to this meaning: when the robes have been brought out from the storeroom, made into a pile, the bell has been struck, and the community of monks has assembled, a monk who has found a caravan and wishes to go thinks, 'May I not be left behind by the caravan.' Therefore, it is not allowable to give a share when the robes have not been brought out, or the bell has not been struck, or the Sangha has not assembled. But when the robes have been brought out, the bell has been struck, and the community of monks has assembled, the robe-distributor should give a robe by way of a guideline, having estimated, 'This monk's portion should be of this amount.' For it is not possible to give it exactly equally, as if weighed on a scale. Therefore, whether it is less or more, what is given by such estimation and method is well-given. A deficit should not be given again, nor should a surplus be taken back.

Atirekabhāgenāti dasa bhikkhū honti, sāṭakāpi daseva, tesu eko dvādasa agghati, sesā dasagghanakā. Sabbesu dasagghanakavasena kuse pātite yassa bhikkhuno dvādasagghanako kuso pātito, so “ettakena mama cīvaraṃ pahotī”ti tena atirekabhāgena gantukāmo hoti. Bhikkhū “atirekaṃ āvuso saṅghassa santaka”nti vadanti, taṃ sutvā bhagavā “saṅghike ca [V 0.0383] gaṇasantake ca appakaṃ nāma natthi, sabbattha saṃyamo kātabbo, gaṇhantenāpi kukkuccāyitabba”nti dassetuṃ “anujānāmi bhikkhave anukkhepe dinne”ti āha. Tattha anukkhepo nāma yaṃkiñci anukkhipitabbaṃ anuppadātabbaṃ kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ; yattakaṃ [M 0.0407] tassa paṭivīse adhikaṃ, tattake agghanake yasmiṃ kismiñci kappiyabhaṇḍe dinneti attho.

By an excess portion: There are ten monks, and there are also ten cloths. Among them, one is worth twelve, and the remaining ones are worth ten. When lots are cast on the basis of all being worth ten, the monk for whom the lot worth twelve falls, thinking, 'This much robe is sufficient for me,' wishes to leave with that excess portion. The monks say, 'Friend, the excess belongs to the Sangha.' Hearing this, to show that 'In what belongs to the Sangha and what belongs to a group, there is nothing called "a small amount"; restraint should be practiced in all cases; even one who takes it should feel remorse,' the Blessed One said, 'I allow, monks, when a supplement has been given.' Therein, a 'supplement' means any allowable item that should be added or given in addition. The meaning is: whatever amount is in excess in his share, an allowable item of that much value has been given.

Vikalake tosetvāti ettha cīvaravikalakaṃ puggalavikalakanti dve vikalakā. Cīvaravikalakaṃ nāma sabbesaṃ pañca pañca vatthāni pattāni, sesānipi atthi, ekekaṃ pana na pāpuṇāti, chinditvā dātabbāni. Chindantehi ca aḍḍhamaṇḍalādīnaṃ vā upāhanatthavikādīnaṃ vā pahonakāni khaṇḍāni katvā dātabbāni, heṭṭhimaparicchedena caturaṅgulavitthārampi anuvātappahonakāyāmaṃ khaṇḍaṃ katvā dātuṃ vaṭṭati, aparibhogaṃ pana na kātabbanti evamettha cīvarassa appahonakabhāvo cīvaravikalakaṃ. Chinditvā dinne pana taṃ tositaṃ hoti, atha kusapāto kātabbo. Sacepi ekassa bhikkhuno koṭṭhāse ekaṃ vā dve vā vatthāni nappahonti, tattha aññaṃ sāmaṇakaṃ parikkhāraṃ ṭhapetvā yo tena tussati, tassa taṃ bhāgaṃ datvā pacchā kusapāto kātabbo. Idampi cīvaravikalakanti andhakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'having satisfied the deficiency': Herein, there are two kinds of deficiencies: robe-deficiency and person-deficiency. 'Robe-deficiency' is when, for all, five cloths each have been received, and there are still others, but not even one each is sufficient. They should be cut and given. And by those who are cutting, having made pieces sufficient for small enclosures and the like or for sandal-bags and the like, they should be given. By the lowest limit, it is allowable to give, having made a piece that is four finger-breadths in width and of a length sufficient for a border. However, it should not be made unusable. Thus, herein, the state of insufficiency of robes is 'robe-deficiency'. When it has been cut and given, that deficiency is satisfied; then the casting of lots should be done. Even if, in the share of one monk, one or two cloths are not sufficient, there, having placed another requisite suitable for a monk, to whichever monk is satisfied by that, having given that share to him, the casting of lots should be done afterwards. This too is 'robe-deficiency', thus it is said in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā.

Puggalavikalakaṃ nāma dasa dasa bhikkhū gaṇetvā vaggaṃ karontānaṃ eko vaggo na pūrati, aṭṭha [P 5.1126] vā nava vā honti, tesaṃ aṭṭha vā nava vā koṭṭhāsā “tumhe ime gahetvā visuṃ bhājethā”ti dātabbā. Evamayaṃ puggalānaṃ appahonakabhāvo puggalavikalakaṃ. Visuṃ dinne pana taṃ tositaṃ hoti, evaṃ tosetvā kusapāto kātabboti. Atha vā vikalake tosetvāti yo cīvaravibhāgo ūnako, taṃ aññena parikkhārena samaṃ katvā kusapāto kātabbo.

'Person-deficiency' is when, having counted ten monks each while forming groups, one group is not complete; there are eight or nine. To them, eight or nine shares should be given, saying, “You, take these and divide them separately.” Thus, this state of insufficiency of persons is 'person-deficiency'. When given separately, that deficiency is satisfied. Thus, having satisfied it, the casting of lots should be done. Alternatively, as for 'having satisfied the deficiency': whichever robe-share is deficient, having made it equal with another requisite, the casting of lots should be done.

Cīvararajanakathā

Discourse on Robe-Dyeing

344. Chakaṇenāti gomayena. Paṇḍumattikāyāti tambamattikāya. Mūlarajanādīsu haliddiṃ ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ mūlarajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Mañjiṭṭhiñca tuṅgahārañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ khandharajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Tuṅgahāro nāma eko sakaṇṭakarukkho, tassa haritālavaṇṇaṃ khandharajanaṃ hoti. Loddañca kaṇḍulañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ tacarajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Allipattaṃ nīlipattañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ pattarajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Gihiparibhuttaṃ pana allipattena ekavāraṃ rajituṃ vaṭṭati. Kiṃsukapupphañca kusumbhapupphañca ṭhapetvā sabbaṃ puppharajanaṃ vaṭṭati. Phalarajane pana na kiñci na vaṭṭati.

344. ‘By means of cow dung’ means with cow dung. ‘By means of reddish clay’ means with red earth. Among root dyes, excepting turmeric, all root dye is allowable. Excepting madder and tuṅgahāra, all stem dye is allowable. Tuṅgahāra is a kind of thorny tree; its stem dye is the color of orpiment. Excepting lodda and kaṇḍula, all bark dye is allowable. Excepting allipatta and nīlipatta, all leaf dye is allowable. However, it is allowable to dye a cloth that has been used by a householder with allipatta one time. Excepting kiṃsuka flowers and kusumbha flowers, all flower dye is allowable. As for fruit dye, however, there is nothing that is not allowable.

Sītudakāti [M 0.0408][V 0.0384] apakkarajanaṃ vuccati. Uttarāḷumpanti vaṭṭādhārakaṃ, rajanakumbhiyā majjhe ṭhapetvā taṃ ādhārakaṃ parikkhipitvā rajanaṃ pakkhipituṃ anujānāmīti attho. Evañhi kate rajanaṃ na uttarati. Udake vā nakhapiṭṭhikāya vāti sace paripakkaṃ hoti, udakapātiyā dinno thevo sahasā na visarati, nakhapiṭṭhiyampi avisaranto tiṭṭhati. Rajanuḷuṅkanti rajanauḷuṅkaṃ. Daṇḍakathālakanti tameva sadaṇḍakaṃ. Rajanakolambanti rajanakuṇḍaṃ. Omaddantīti sammaddanti. Na ca acchinne theve pakkamitunti yāva rajanabindu gaḷitaṃ na chijjati, tāva na aññatra gantabbaṃ. Patthinnanti atirajitattā thaddhaṃ. Udake osāretunti udake pakkhipitvā [P 5.1127] ṭhapetuṃ. Rajane pana nikkhante taṃ udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā cīvaraṃ madditabbaṃ. Dantakāsāvānīti ekaṃ vā dve vā vāre rajitvā dantavaṇṇāni dhārenti.

‘Cool water’ is said of uncooked dye. ‘Uttarāḷumpa’ means a circular support; the meaning is, ‘I allow one to place it in the middle of the dye pot, and having surrounded that support, to put in the dye.’ For when done thus, the dye does not overflow. ‘In water or on the back of a fingernail’ means if it is fully cooked, a drop placed in a water bowl does not quickly disperse, and on the back of a fingernail also, it remains without dispersing. ‘Rajanauḷuṅka’ means a dye ladle. ‘Daṇḍakathālaka’ means that same bowl with a handle. ‘Rajanakolamba’ means a dye basin. ‘They knead’ means they press thoroughly. ‘And one should not depart while the drop is unbroken’ means as long as the dripping drop of dye has not ceased, one should not go elsewhere. ‘Stiff’ means hardened due to being over-dyed. ‘To immerse in water’ means to put it in water and keep it there. Furthermore, when the dye has come out, having discarded that water, the robe should be kneaded. ‘Ivory-colored saffron robes’ means that having dyed them once or twice, they wear ivory-colored robes.

Chinnakacīvarānujānanakathā

The Account of the Permission for Cut Robes

345. Acchibaddhanti caturassakedārakabaddhaṃ. Pāḷibaddhanti āyāmato ca vitthārato ca dīghamariyādabaddhaṃ. Mariyādabaddhanti antarantarā rassamariyādabaddhaṃ. Siṅghāṭakabaddhanti mariyādāya mariyādaṃ vinivijjhitvā gataṭṭhāne siṅghāṭakabaddhaṃ; catukkasaṇṭhānanti attho. Saṃvidahitunti kātuṃ. Ussahasi tvaṃ ānandāti sakkosi tvaṃ ānanda. Ussahāmi bhagavāti tumhehi dinnanayena sakkomīti dasseti. Yatra hi nāmāti yo nāma. Kusimpi nāmātiādīsu kusīti āyāmato ca vitthārato ca anuvātādīnaṃ dīghapattānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aḍḍhakusīti antarantarā rassapattānaṃ nāmaṃ. Maṇḍalanti pañcakhaṇḍikacīvarassa ekekasmiṃ khaṇḍe mahāmaṇḍalaṃ. Aḍḍhamaṇḍalanti khuddakamaṇḍalaṃ. Vivaṭṭanti maṇḍalañca aḍḍhamaṇḍalañca ekato katvā sibbitaṃ majjhimakhaṇḍaṃ.

345. ‘Acchibaddha’ means bound like a four-cornered field. ‘Pāḷibaddha’ means bound with long borders both lengthwise and widthwise. ‘Mariyādabaddha’ means bound with short borders in between. ‘Siṅghāṭakabaddha’ means bound in the shape of a crossroads at the place where one border pierces another; the meaning is a four-way intersection. ‘Saṃvidahituṃ’ means to make. ‘Ussahasi tvaṃ ānanda’ means: Ānanda, are you able? ‘Ussahāmi bhagavā’ shows: ‘I am able to arrange it by the method given by You, Blessed One.’ ‘Yatra hi nāmāti’ means: whoever indeed. In phrases such as ‘kusimpi nāma,’ ‘kusī’ is a designation for long strips of cloth, such as the lengthwise border-strips, both in length and in width. ‘Aḍḍhakusī’ is the name for the short strips in between. ‘Maṇḍala’ means the large panel in each section of a five-section robe. ‘Aḍḍhamaṇḍala’ means the small panel. ‘Vivaṭṭa’ means the middle section, which is sewn by joining the maṇḍala and the aḍḍhamaṇḍala together.

Anuvivaṭṭanti tassa ubhosu passesu dve khaṇḍāni. Gīveyyakanti gīvāveṭhanaṭṭhāne daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ aññaṃ suttasaṃsibbitaṃ āgantukapattaṃ. Jaṅgheyyakanti jaṅghapāpuṇanaṭṭhāne tatheva saṃsibbitaṃ pattaṃ. Gīvaṭṭhāne ca jaṅghaṭṭhāne ca pattānamevetaṃ nāmantipi vadanti. Bāhantanti anuvivaṭṭānaṃ bahi ekekaṃ khaṇḍaṃ. Iti pañcakhaṇḍikacīvarenetaṃ vicāritanti. Atha vā anuvivaṭṭanti vivaṭṭassa [M 0.0409] ekapassato dvinnaṃ ekapassato dvinnanti catunnampi khaṇḍānametaṃ nāmaṃ. Bāhantanti suppamāṇaṃ cīvaraṃ pārupantena saṃharitvā bāhāya upari ṭhapitā ubho antā bahimukhā tiṭṭhanti, tesaṃ etaṃ nāmaṃ. Ayameva hi nayo mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttoti.

‘Anuvivaṭṭa’ means the two sections on both sides of that middle section. ‘Gīveyyaka’ means an additional strip sewn with thread for the purpose of strengthening at the place where the neck is wrapped. ‘Jaṅgheyyaka’ means a strip sewn in the same way at the place the shin reaches. They also say that this is the name for the robe-strips at the place of the neck and at the place of the shin. ‘Bāhanta’ means each single section on the outside of the anuvivaṭṭas. Thus, this arrangement is set out in terms of a five-section robe. Alternatively, ‘anuvivaṭṭa’ is the name for all four sections: two on one side of the vivaṭṭa and two on the other side. ‘Bāhanta’ is the name for both ends which, when one wearing a well-proportioned robe gathers it and places it over the arm, stand facing outwards. Indeed, this very method has been stated in the Great Commentary.

Ticīvarānujānanakathā

The Account of the Permission for the Three Robes

346. Cīvarehi [V 0.0385] ubbhaṇḍiketi cīvarehi ubbhaṇḍe kate; yathā ukkhittabhaṇḍā [P 5.1128] honti evaṃ kate; ukkhittabhaṇḍikabhāvaṃ āpāditeti attho. Cīvarabhisinti ettha bhisīti dve tīṇi ekato katvā bhisisaṅkhepena saṃharitacīvarāni vuttāni. Te kira bhikkhū “dakkhiṇāgirito bhagavā lahuṃ paṭinivattissatī”ti tattha gacchantā jīvakavatthusmiṃ laddhacīvarāni ṭhapetvā agamaṃsu. Idāni pana cirena āgamissatīti maññamānā ādāya pakkamiṃsu. Antaraṭṭhakāsūti māghassa ca phagguṇassa ca antarā aṭṭhasu. Na bhagavantaṃ sītaṃ ahosīti bhagavato sītaṃ nāhosi. Etadahosi yepi kho te kulaputtāti na bhagavā ajjhokāse anisīditvā etamatthaṃ na jānāti, mahājanasaññāpanatthaṃ pana evamakāsi. Sītālukāti sītapakatikā; ye pakatiyāva sītena kilamanti. Diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭinti dupaṭṭaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ. Ekacciyanti ekapaṭṭaṃ. Iti “bhagavā attanā catūhi cīvarehi yāpeti, amhākaṃ pana ticīvaraṃ anujānātī”ti vacanassa okāsaṃ upacchindituṃ diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ anujānāti, ekaccike itare. Evañhi nesaṃ cattāri bhavissantīti.

346. ‘Cīvarehi ubbhaṇḍiketi’ means: the robes having been made into a bundle; made in such a way that they become like goods piled up; the meaning is, having been brought to the state of being piled-up goods. ‘Cīvarabhisi’: Here, ‘bhisī’ refers to robes that are folded by putting two or three together in the manner of a bolster. It is said that those bhikkhus, thinking, “The Blessed One will quickly return from Dakkhiṇāgiri,” left the robes they had received at Jīvaka’s residence and went away. But now, believing he would return after a long time, they took them and departed. ‘Antaraṭṭhakāsu’ refers to the eight days between the month of Māgha and the month of Phagguṇa. ‘Na bhagavantaṃ sītaṃ ahosīti’ means the cold did not affect the Blessed One. Regarding ‘Etadahosi yepi kho te kulaputtāti’: It is not that the Blessed One did not know this matter without sitting in the open air; he certainly knew. However, he acted thus for the purpose of making it understood by the great multitude. ‘Sītālukāti’ means those who have a cold nature; those who by their very nature are afflicted by the cold. ‘Diguṇaṃ saṅghāṭinti’ means a double-layered outer robe. ‘Ekacciyanti’ means a single-layered robe. Thus, to cut off the opportunity for the statement, “The Blessed One himself makes do with four robes, but allows us only three,” he permitted a double-layered outer robe, and the other robes to be single-layered. For in this way, they would have four robes.

Atirekacīvarādikathā

The Account of Extra Robes and So On

348. Aggaḷaṃ acchupeyyanti chiddaṭṭhāne pilotikakhaṇḍaṃ laggāpeyyaṃ. Ahatakappānanti ekavāraṃ dhotānaṃ. Utuddhaṭānanti ututo dīghakālato uddhaṭānaṃ hatavatthakānaṃ, pilotikānanti vuttaṃ hoti. Pāpaṇiketi antarāpaṇato patitapilotikacīvare. Ussāho karaṇīyoti pariyesanā kātabbā. Paricchedo panettha natthi, paṭṭasatampi vaṭṭati. Sabbamidaṃ sādiyantassa bhikkhuno vasena vuttaṃ. Aggaḷaṃ tunnanti ettha uddharitvā allīyāpanakhaṇḍaṃ aggaḷaṃ, suttena saṃsibbitaṃ tunnaṃ; vaṭṭetvā karaṇaṃ ovaṭṭikaṃ [M 0.0410] . Kaṇḍusakaṃ vuccati muddikā. Daḷhīkammanti anuddharitvāva upassayaṃ katvā allīyāpanakaṃ vatthakhaṇḍaṃ.

348. ‘Should apply a patch’ (`aggaḷaṃ acchupeyyaṃ`) means one should attach a piece of rag to the torn spot. ‘Rags washed once’ (`ahatakappānaṃ`) refers to those washed a single time. ‘Rags taken out after a season’ (`utuddhaṭānaṃ`) means old cloths, that is, beaten cloths that have been taken out after a long time. ‘From the market’ (`pāpaṇike`) refers to a rag-robe fallen from between market stalls. ‘Effort should be made’ (`ussāho karaṇīyo`) means a search should be made. There is no limit here; even a hundred layers are allowable. All this was said on account of a bhikkhu who consents to it. Herein, regarding ‘a patch, sewing’ (`aggaḷaṃ tunnaṃ`): a patch (`aggaḷaṃ`) is a piece for adhering, applied after removing the worn part; sewing (`tunnaṃ`) is stitching together with thread; making by rolling is a rolled stitch (`ovaṭṭikaṃ`). A signet-ring stitch (`muddikā`) is called `kaṇḍusakaṃ`. ‘Strengthening’ (`daḷhīkammaṃ`) is a piece of cloth for adhering, having made a supporting layer on top without removing the worn part.

349-351. Visākhāvatthu uttānatthaṃ. Tato paraṃ pubbe vinicchitameva. Sovaggikanti saggappattahetukaṃ. Tenevāha “sovaggika”nti[P 5.1129]. Sokaṃ apanetīti sokanudaṃ. Anāmayāti arogā. Saggamhi kāyamhīti saggopapannā.

349-351. The story of Visākhā (`Visākhāvatthu`) is clear in meaning. What follows has already been decided before. ‘Leading to heaven’ (`sovaggikaṃ`) means being a cause for attainment of heaven. Therefore, the Blessed One said, ‘leading to heaven.’ ‘Dispelling sorrow’ (`sokanudaṃ`) is so called because it dispels sorrow. ‘Without illness’ (`anāmayā`) means without disease. ‘In a heavenly body’ (`saggamhi kāyamhi`) means reborn in heaven.

353. Puthujjanā kāmesu vītarāgāti jhānalābhino.

353. ‘Worldlings free from lust for sensual pleasures’ (`puthujjanā kāmesu vītarāgā`) refers to those who have attained jhāna.

356. Sandiṭṭhoti [V 0.0386] diṭṭhamattakamitto. Sambhattoti ekasambhogo daḷhamitto. Ālapitoti “mama santakaṃ yaṃ iccheyyāsi, taṃ gaṇhāhī”ti evaṃ vutto. Etesu tīsu aññataranāmena saddhiṃ jīvati, gahite attamano hotīti imehi gahitavissāso ruhati.

356. ‘An acquaintance’ (`sandiṭṭho`) is a friend who is merely seen. ‘An intimate’ (`sambhatto`) is a firm friend with whom one shares things in common. ‘One who can be addressed’ (`ālapito`) is one who has been told, “Take whatever of my property you wish.” Trust (`vissāso`) is established (`ruhati`) in one who is endowed with these factors: living together (`jīvati`) with someone of any of these three types, and being pleased when something is taken (`gahite attamano hoti`).

Pacchimavikappanupagacīvarādikathā

The Account of Robes, etc., Not Subject to the Final Determination

359. Paṃsukūlakatoti katapaṃsukūlo. Garuko hotīti jiṇṇajiṇṇaṭṭhāne aggaḷāropanena garuko hoti. Suttalūkhaṃ kātunti sutteneva aggaḷaṃ kātunti attho. Vikaṇṇo hotīti suttaṃ acchetvā acchetvā sibbantānaṃ eko saṅghāṭikoṇo dīgho hoti. Vikaṇṇaṃ uddharitunti dīghakoṇaṃ chindituṃ. Okiriyantīti chinnakoṇato gaḷanti. Anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍanti anuvātañceva paribhaṇḍañca. Pattā lujjantīti mahantesu pattamukhesu dinnāni suttāni gaḷanti, tato pattā lujjanti. Aṭṭhapadakaṃ kātunti aṭṭhapadakacchannena pattamukhaṃ sibbituṃ.

359. ‘A rag-robe wearer’ (`paṃsukūlakato`) means one who has made a rag-robe. ‘It becomes heavy’ (`garuko hoti`) means it becomes heavy from placing patches on very worn spots. ‘To make a simple patch with thread’ (`suttalūkhaṃ kātuṃ`) means to make the patch with thread only. ‘It gets a distorted corner’ (`vikaṇṇo hoti`) means for those who sew while repeatedly pulling the thread, one corner of the `saṅghāṭi` becomes long. ‘To remove the distorted corner’ (`vikaṇṇaṃ uddharituṃ`) means to cut off the long corner. ‘They are scattered’ (`okiriyanti`) means threads fall out from the cut corner. ‘The lengthwise border and the widthwise border’ (`anuvātaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ`). ‘The borders get ruined’ (`pattā lujjanti`) means the threads placed at the ends of the large borders fall out, and because of that, the borders get ruined. ‘To make a checkerboard pattern’ (`aṭṭhapadakaṃ kātuṃ`) means to sew the end of the border with a checkerboard-pattern stitch.

360. Anvādhikampi āropetunti āgantukapattampi dātuṃ. Idaṃ pana appahonake āropetabbaṃ. Sace pahoti, āgantukapattaṃ na vaṭṭati, chinditabbameva.

360. ‘Even an extra piece may be added’ (`anvādhikampi āropetuṃ`) means to add an extra patch. However, this should be added to a robe that is insufficient. If the robe is sufficient, an extra patch is not allowable; it must be cut off.

361. Na ca bhikkhave saddhādeyyanti ettha sesañātīnaṃ dento vinipātetiyeva. Mātāpitaro pana sace rajje ṭhitā patthayanti, dātabbaṃ.

361. Herein, regarding ‘And, monks, a gift of faith should not be wasted’ (`na ca bhikkhave saddhādeyyaṃ`): one who gives to relatives other than one's parents simply squanders it. But as for one's parents, even if they are established in sovereignty, if they desire it, it should be given.

362. Gilānoti [M 0.0411] gilānatāya gahetvā gantuṃ asamattho. Vassikasaṅketanti vassike cattāro māse. Nadīpāranti nadiyā pāre bhattaṃ bhuñjitabbaṃ hoti. Aggaḷaguttivihāroti sabbesveva cetesu gilānavassikasaṅketanadīpāragamanaatthatakathinabhāvesu aggaḷaguttiyeva pamāṇaṃ. Gutte eva hi vihāre etesu kāraṇesu nikkhipitvā bahi gantuṃ vaṭṭati, na agutte. Āraññakassa pana vihāro na sugutto hoti, tena bhaṇḍukkhalikāya pakkhipitvā pāsāṇasusira rukkhasusirādīsu [P 5.1130] suppaṭicchannesu ṭhapetvā gantabbaṃ.

362. ‘A sick person’ (`gilāno`) is one who is unable to take his robe and go on account of sickness. ‘The rainy-season period’ (`vassikasaṅketa`) refers to the four months of the rainy season. ‘The far side of the river’ (`nadīpāraṃ`) means food is to be eaten on the far bank of the river. ‘A monastery secured with a bolt’ (`aggaḷaguttivihāro`) means that in all these cases—the state of being sick, the rainy-season period, the crossing of a river, and the spreading of the Kathina—the security of the monastery by means of a bolt is the standard. Indeed, only in a secure monastery is it allowable on these grounds to leave one's robe and go outside; it is not allowable in an insecure one. However, a forest-dweller's monastery is not well-secured; therefore, he should put his belongings in a large storage pot and place it in a well-concealed spot such as a rock crevice or a tree hollow before departing.

Saṅghikacīvaruppādakathā

Discussion on the Arising of Robes Belonging to the Sangha

363. Tuyheva bhikkhu tāni cīvarānīti aññattha gahetvā haṭānipi tuyheva; na tesaṃ añño koci issaroti. Evañca pana vatvā anāgatepi nikkukkuccā gaṇhissantīti dassetuṃ [V 0.0387] idha panātiādimāha. Tasseva tāni cīvarāni yāva kathinassa ubbhārāti sace gaṇapūrake bhikkhū labhitvā kathinaṃ atthataṃ hoti, pañcamāse; no ce atthataṃ hoti, ekaṃ cīvaramāsameva. Yaṃ “saṅghassa demā”ti vā denti, “saṅghaṃ uddissa demā”ti vā denti, “vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa demā”ti vā denti, “vassāvāsikaṃ demā”ti vā denti, sacepi matakacīvaraṃ avibhajitvā taṃ vihāraṃ pavisanti, taṃ sabbaṃ tasseva bhikkhuno hoti. Yampi so vassāvāsatthāya vaḍḍhiṃ payojetvā ṭhapitaupanikkhepato vā tatruppādato vā vassāvāsikaṃ gaṇhāti, sabbaṃ suggahitameva hoti. Idamettha lakkhaṇaṃ, yena tenākārena saṅghassa uppannaṃ vatthaṃ atthatakathinassa pañcamāse, anatthatakathinassa ekaṃ cīvaramāsaṃ pāpuṇātīti. Yaṃ pana “idaṃ idha vassaṃvutthasaṅghassa demā”ti vā “vassāvāsikaṃ demā”ti vā vatvā dinnaṃ, taṃ anatthatakathinassāpi pañcamāse pāpuṇāti. Tato paraṃ pana uppannaṃ vassāvāsikaṃ pucchitabbaṃ – “kiṃ atītavasse idaṃ vassāvāsikaṃ, udāhu anāgatavasse”ti! Kasmā? Piṭṭhisamaye uppannattā.

363. “O monk, those robes are indeed yours”—meaning, even if they are taken and carried elsewhere, they are still yours; no one else has authority over them. And having said this, to show that in the future too they will take them without hesitation, the Blessed One spoke the passage beginning with `idha pana`. Those robes are his until the dismantling of the Kathina: if, having obtained monks who complete the quorum, the Kathina is spread, then for five months; if it is not spread, then only for one robe-month. Whatever is given with the words, “We give to the Sangha,” or “We give, dedicating it to the Sangha,” or “We give to the Sangha that has completed the rains-residence,” or “We give the rains-residence robe”; and even if they enter that monastery without having divided the robe of a deceased monk, all of it belongs to that very monk. And whatever rains-residence robe he takes for the purpose of the rains-residence—having applied an increase, or from a deposit that was set aside, or from what arises there—all of it is well-taken. This is the characteristic here: by whatever means cloth that has arisen for the Sangha reaches one who has spread the Kathina, it is for five months; for one who has not spread the Kathina, it is for one robe-month. But what is given with the words, “We give this here to the Sangha that has completed the rains-residence,” or “We give the rains-residence robe,” that reaches even one who has not spread the Kathina for five months. But a rains-residence robe that has arisen after that should be asked about: “Is this rains-residence robe for the past rains-residence, or for the future rains-residence?” Why? Because it arose in the period subsequent to the robe-season.

Utukālanti vassānato aññaṃ kālaṃ. Tāni cīvarāni ādāya sāvatthiṃ gantvāti ettha tāni cīvarāni gatagataṭṭhāne saṅghikāneva honti, bhikkhūhi diṭṭhamattamevettha pamāṇaṃ. Tasmā sace keci paṭipathaṃ āgacchantā “kuhiṃ [M 0.0412] āvuso gacchasī”ti pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “kiṃ āvuso mayaṃ saṅgho na homā”ti tattheva bhājetvā gaṇhanti, suggahitāni. Sacepi esa maggā okkamitvā kañci vihāraṃ vā āsanasālaṃ vā piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ gehameva vā pavisati, tatra ca naṃ bhikkhū disvā tamatthaṃ pucchitvā bhājetvā gaṇhanti, suggahitāneva.

The 'season' means a time other than the rainy season. Regarding 'Having taken those robes and gone to Sāvatthī': here, those robes are indeed Sangha property in every place they go, and the mere sight by the monks is the measure. Therefore, if some monks, coming along the path, ask, “Friend, where are you going?” and upon hearing the matter, say, “What, friend, are we not the Sangha?” and divide and take them right there, they are well-taken. Even if this one, having deviated from the path and while wandering for alms, enters some monastery, or a rest hall, or even a single house, and there, other monks, having seen him, having asked about the matter, divide and take them, they are indeed well-taken.

Adhiṭṭhātunti ettha adhiṭṭhahantena vattaṃ jānitabbaṃ[P 5.1131]. Tena hi bhikkhunā ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā kālaṃ ghosetvā thokaṃ āgametvā sace ghaṇṭisaññāya vā kālasaññāya vā bhikkhū āgacchanti, tehi saddhiṃ bhājetabbāni. No ce āgacchanti, “mayhimāni cīvarāni pāpuṇantī”ti adhiṭṭhātabbāni. Evaṃ adhiṭṭhite sabbāni tasseva honti, ṭhitikā pana na tiṭṭhati.

Regarding 'should determine,' the one determining should know the procedure. Therefore, that monk, having struck the bell, having announced the time, and having waited a little, if monks arrive by the bell signal or the time signal, the robes should be divided with them. If they do not arrive, he should determine, 'These robes accrue to me.' When thus determined, all of them become his, but the established procedure does not stand.

Sace ekekaṃ uddharitvā “ayaṃ paṭhamabhāgo mayhaṃ pāpuṇāti, ayaṃ dutiyabhāgo”ti evaṃ gaṇhāti, gahitāni ca suggahitāni honti, ṭhitikā ca tiṭṭhati. Evaṃ pāpetvā gaṇhantenāpi adhiṭṭhitameva hoti. Sace pana ghaṇṭiṃ paharitvā vā appaharitvā vā kālampi ghosetvā vā aghosetvā vā “ahamevettha mayhameva imāni cīvarānī”ti gaṇhāti, duggahitāni [V 0.0388] honti. Atha “añño koci idha natthi, mayhaṃ etāni pāpuṇantī”ti gaṇhāti, suggahitāni.

If, having taken them out one by one, he takes them thinking, 'This first share accrues to me, this second share accrues to me,' and so on, then the robes taken are well-taken, and the established procedure stands. Even when one takes them by causing them to accrue in this way, it is indeed a valid determination. But if, whether having struck the bell or not, or whether having announced the time or not, he takes them thinking, 'I alone am here, these robes are for me alone,' they are badly taken. Or, if he takes them thinking, 'There is no one else here, these accrue to me,' they are well-taken.

Pātite kuseti ekakoṭṭhāse kusadaṇḍake pātitamatte sacepi bhikkhusahassaṃ hoti, gahitameva nāma cīvaraṃ. Nākāmā bhāgo dātabbo. Sace pana attano ruciyā dātukāmā honti, dentu. Anubhāgepi eseva nayo.

Regarding 'when the lot is cast': as soon as the lot-stick is cast for one portion, even if there are a thousand monks, the robe is considered taken. A share should not be given against their will. But if they wish to give according to their own preference, let them give. In a subsequent share, this is the same method.

Sacīvarānīti “kālacīvarampi saṅghassa itova dassāma, visuṃ sajjiyamāne aticiraṃ hotī”ti khippaṃyeva sacīvarāni bhattāni akaṃsu. There āgamma uppannānīti tumhesu pasādena khippaṃ uppannāni.

Regarding 'with robes': Thinking, 'We will give the timely robe to the Sangha from these very robes as well; if prepared separately, it would take too long,' they quickly prepared the meals together with robes. Regarding 'they arose on account of the elders': this means, 'they arose quickly through faith in you.'

Saṅghassa demāti cīvarāni dentīti sakalampi cīvarakālaṃ saṇikaṃ saṇikaṃ dentiyeva. Purimesu pana dvīsu vatthūsu pacchinnadānattā adaṃsūti vuttaṃ. Sambahulā therāti vinayadharapāmokkhatherā. Idaṃ pana vatthuṃ saddhiṃ purimena dvebhātikavatthunā parinibbute bhagavati uppannaṃ, ime ca therā diṭṭhapubbā tathāgataṃ, tasmā purimesu vatthūsu tathāgatena paññattanayeneva kathesuṃ.

Regarding 'They give robes, saying, “We give to the Sangha”': this means they give them slowly, slowly throughout the entire robe-season. But in the three previous stories, it was said by the compilers of the canon that `adaṃsu` ('they gave') was used because the act of giving was a completed one. 'Many elders' means elders who are leaders, expert in the Vinaya. But this story, together with the previous story of the two brothers, arose after the Blessed One had attained Parinibbāna. And these elders had previously seen the Tathāgata; therefore, in the previous stories, they spoke only according to the method laid down by the Tathāgata.

Upanandasakyaputtavatthukathā

The Story of Upananda the Sakyan Son

364. Gāmakāvāsaṃ [M 0.0413] agamāsīti appeva nāma cīvarāni bhājentā mayhampi saṅgahaṃ kareyyunti cīvarabhājanakālaṃ sallakkhetvāva agamāsi. Sādiyissasīti gaṇhissasi. Ettha ca kiñcāpi tassa bhāgo na pāpuṇāti. Atha kho “nagaravāsiko ayaṃ mukharo dhammakathiko”ti te bhikkhū “sādiyissasī”ti āhaṃsu. Yo sādiyeyya āpatti dukkaṭassāti ettha pana kiñcāpi lahukā āpatti, atha kho gahitāni gahitaṭṭhāne [P 5.1132] dātabbāni. Sacepi naṭṭhāni vā jiṇṇāni vā honti, tasseva gīvā. Dehīti vutte adento dhuranikkhepe bhaṇḍagghena kāretabbo.

364. Regarding 'He went to the village residence': he went only after having marked the time of the robe-distribution, thinking, 'While they are distributing robes, they might indeed show me favor as well.' Regarding 'Will you consent?': it means 'Will you take it?' Here, although a share does not rightfully come to him, nevertheless, those monks, thinking, 'This one is a city-dweller, eloquent and a Dhamma-preacher,' said, 'Will you consent?' Regarding 'Whoever should consent, there is an offense of wrong-doing': here, although it is a minor offense, nevertheless, the items taken must be given back in the place where they were taken. Even if they are lost or worn out, it is his own liability. When told, 'Give it back,' if he does not give, he should be made to pay the value of the goods on account of his relinquishment of responsibility.

Ekādhippāyanti ekaṃ adhippāyaṃ; ekaṃ puggalapaṭivīsameva dethāti attho. Idāni yathā so dātabbo, taṃ dassetuṃ tantiṃ ṭhapento idha panātiādimāha. Tattha sace amutra upaḍḍhaṃ amutra upaḍḍhanti ekekasmiṃ ekāhamekāhaṃ vā sattāhaṃ sattāhaṃ vā sace vasati, ekekasmiṃ vihāre yaṃ [V 0.0389] eko puggalo labhati, tato tato upaḍḍhaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ dātabbaṃ. Evaṃ ekādhippāyo dinno hoti. Yattha vā pana bahutaranti sace ekasmiṃ vihāre vasanto itarasmiṃ sattāhavārena aruṇameva uṭṭhāpeti, evaṃ purimasmiṃ bahutaraṃ vasati nāma. Tasmā tato bahutaraṃ vasitavihārato tassa paṭivīso dātabbo. Evampi ekādhippāyo dinno hoti. Idañca nānālābhehi nānūpacārehi ekasīmavihārehi kathitaṃ, nānāsīmavihāre pana senāsanaggāho paṭippassambhati. Tasmā tattha cīvarapaṭivīso na pāpuṇāti. Sesaṃ pana āmisabhesajjādi sabbaṃ sabbattha antosīmagatassa pāpuṇāti.

Regarding 'one intention': this means one purpose; the meaning is, 'Give just the share of one person.' Now, in order to show how that should be given, laying down the textual tradition, the Blessed One said, 'Here, however...' and so on. Therein, regarding 'half there, half there': if he resides for one day each or seven days each in each monastery, then from each monastery, half of what one individual receives should be given. Thus, 'one intention' is given. Or regarding 'wherever more': if, while residing in one monastery, he causes the dawn to arise in the other once a week, he is said to reside more in the former monastery. Therefore, his share should be given from that monastery where he resided more. In this way, too, 'one intention' is given. And this has been said with reference to monasteries with a single boundary, having various gains and various precincts. However, in a monastery with different boundaries, the taking of a lodging is annulled. Therefore, a share of robes is not obtained there. However, all the rest, such as material things, medicine, and so on, is obtained everywhere by one who has gone within the boundary.

Gilānavatthukathā

The Story of the Sick Monk

365. Mañcake nipātesunti evaṃ dhovitvā aññaṃ kāsāvaṃ nivāsetvā mañcake nipajjāpesuṃ; nipajjāpetvā ca panāyasmā ānando muttakarīsakiliṭṭhaṃ kāsāvaṃ dhovitvā bhūmiyaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ akāsi. Yo bhikkhave maṃ upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyyāti yo maṃ ovādānusāsanīkaraṇena upaṭṭhaheyya, so gilānaṃ upaṭṭhaheyya; mama ovādakārakena gilāno upaṭṭhātabboti ayamevettha attho. Bhagavato ca gilānassa ca upaṭṭhānaṃ ekasadisanti evaṃ panettha attho na gahetabbo. Saṅghena upaṭṭhātabboti yassete upajjhādayo tasmiṃ vihāre natthi, āgantuko hoti ekacāriko bhikkhu, so saṅghassa bhāro, tasmā saṅghena [M 0.0414] upaṭṭhātabbo. No ce upaṭṭhaheyya, sakalassa saṅghassa āpatti. Vāraṃ ṭhapetvā jaggantesu pana yo attano vāre na jaggati, tasseva āpatti. Saṅghattheropi vārako na muccati. Sace sakalo saṅgho ekassa bhāraṃ karoti, eko vā vattasampanno bhikkhu [P 5.1133] ahameva jaggissāmīti paṭijaggati, saṅgho āpattito muccati.

365. Regarding 'They laid him on the bed': having washed him thus and having made him wear another ochre robe, they made him lie down on the small bed. And after having made him lie down, the venerable Ānanda, having washed the ochre robe soiled with urine and feces, spread it out neatly on the ground. Regarding 'Bhikkhus, whoever would attend to me, he should attend to the sick': whoever would attend to me by carrying out my advice and instruction, he should attend to the sick; the sick person should be attended to by one who carries out my advice—this alone is the meaning here. The meaning that attending to the Blessed One and attending to the sick are identical should not be taken here.
